Take them first as what they plainly were: portable wealth. Gold needs no explanation, and frankincense and myrrh were resins traded up from southern Arabia at enormous cost — the kind of goods that moved by caravan under guard. This is a fortune arriving in a working family's house.

And it arrives immediately before a flight into a foreign country. Joseph is about to be told to leave in the night, with no notice, no destination arranged and no means of support in Egypt. Then the funds turn up, carried a thousand miles by strangers who had no idea what they were for.

The old reading — gold for a king, incense for a priest, myrrh for one who would die — is genuinely ancient and it may well be right; myrrh in particular reappears at his burial (Jn. 19:39). Matthew does not say so, and a commentary should not pretend he does. But he does not need to, because the plainer providence is remarkable enough: God funded the exile before he announced it.

Which is worth having when a provision arrives that seems disproportionate to anything currently going on. Sometimes it is not for now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — The Flight to Egypt and the Return to Nazareth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The holy family flees to Egypt to escape Herod's massacre of Bethlehem's infant boys, returns after Herod's death, and settles in Nazareth — each movement fulfilling a specific Old Testament text. Matthew sees in these events not merely historical geography but the recapitulation of Israel's story: Jesus relives the Exodus (out of Egypt), the Exile (the weeping of Rachel), and Israel's wilderness sojourn (settling in a despised region). The Son of God is doing in himself what Israel failed to do: he is the true Israel, perfectly faithful where the nation was not. Three items the summary passes over. Verses 19-20 contain a quiet oddity: "those who sought the child's life are dead" is plural, though only Herod had died — because Matthew is quoting Exodus 4:19 almost word for word, God's word to Moses in Midian, with the direction of travel reversed. Herod died at Jericho in the spring of 4 BC, which is why Jesus was born several years before the year we number 1 — an error not in Scripture but in the sixth-century monk who built the calendar. Verses 21-22 are the fifth dream in two chapters (1:20; 2:12, 13, 19, 22), and the verse-by-verse takes up the question readers actually carry: whether God still guides this way, and what to do with a vivid dream. Note that Joseph's fear of Archelaus was reasonable on its own terms and the dream confirmed his ordinary judgement rather than overruling it. Verse 23 is the hardest fulfilment quotation in the Gospel, because no Old Testament verse says the Messiah will be called a Nazarene — and Matthew signals as much by writing "prophets" in the plural, naming nobody and quoting nothing. The strongest reading is Isaiah 11:1, where the shoot from Jesse's stump is a netser; the theme of the despised one (Isa. 53:2-3) very likely stands behind it too. And the name stuck: it is what Pilate wrote over his head, how the angel identified him at the tomb, and what the risen Christ called himself from heaven on the Damascus road (Acts 22:8).
verseByVerse.theology: Matthew's three fulfillment quotations here (Hos. 11:1; Jer. 31:15; and possibly Isa. 11:1 or Judg. 13:5 for "Nazarene") reveal his typological reading of history: Israel's great narrative events were not merely past occurrences but prophetic templates waiting for their ultimate fulfillment in Christ. Jesus does not merely happen to visit Egypt; he is the true Son whom God calls out of Egypt. The slaughter of the innocents does not merely echo Rachel's weeping; it is the event that makes the older weeping fully intelligible. This is not proof-texting but fulfillment theology.
verseByVerse.examples: The massacre of Bethlehem's infants is the event that silences easy answers about suffering. Matthew does not explain it; he quotes Jeremiah's lament and moves on. Rachel weeping for her children who are no more: there are moments when the only honest response to evil is grief, not explanation. The Messiah's birth caused suffering for the innocent. His death would be the answer to that suffering — not by explaining it away, but by entering it and overcoming it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, "Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and remain there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him." And he rose and took the child and his mother by night and departed to Egypt
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph obeys immediately — "by night," without waiting for morning's reassurance or daylight's practicality. The urgency is real: Herod will move quickly. Egypt, the land of Israel's ancient bondage, now becomes the place of the Messiah's refuge — a reversal rich with symbolic freight. The one who will lead the new exodus must first reenact the sojourn in Egypt. Joseph's role in these chapters is entirely reactive to divine commands: he is told, he does. His is the faith that acts without arguing, that obeys without understanding the full plan. It is a form of faith harder than heroism — the faith of silent, sustained obedience to a voice only he has heard.

Say plainly what is happening in this verse, because familiarity has smoothed it over. A family wakes in the dark, takes what it can carry, and crosses a border to escape a ruler who wants their child dead. They arrive in a foreign country with no standing, no relatives named in the text, no language of their own spoken in the street, and no idea how long they will be there. There is a word for people in that position, and the word is refugees. The Son of God spent part of his childhood as one.

This is not decoration on the story; it is the kind of thing God evidently wanted in the record. He could have protected the child in Bethlehem — he had already shown he could redirect a caravan of Persians with a dream. Instead he sent him down the road every displaced family has walked. It means that when Scripture returns again and again to the sojourner and the stranger, and commands Israel to remember that they were strangers in Egypt themselves, the command now has a face. Whatever any of us thinks about borders and policy, and Christians in good conscience differ, no follower of this King is at liberty to speak of people fleeing violence with contempt. He was carried out of one such night in his mother's arms.

And there is comfort in it as well as instruction. If your own life has been marked by upheaval you did not choose — moved on, uprooted, made to start again somewhere that was not home — you are not outside the experience of Christ, and you are not outside the plan of God. Those years in Egypt were not an interruption of his mission. They were part of it, and Matthew will tell you in the next verse that Scripture had them written down in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: and remained there until the death of Herod. This was to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, "Out of Egypt I called my son." Then Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem and in all that region who were two years old or under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the wise men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hosea 11:1 originally referred to the Exodus — God calling Israel, his corporate son, out of Egypt. Matthew sees Jesus as the true Son who fulfills that type: where Israel as God's son repeatedly failed in the wilderness, Jesus the true Son will succeed. The recapitulation is intentional, not coincidental.

This raises a fair question that troubles many an honest reader: Hosea was not even predicting the future — he was looking back at Israel and the Exodus. So is Matthew bending his words to fit Jesus? Here is the sound and simple answer. The word "fulfill" does not always mean "a prediction has come true"; often it means "filled full" — brought at last to the completion God always intended. For God himself wrote a pattern into Israel's history: Israel was his "son" (Ex 4:22), carried down into Egypt and led out again. That pattern was no accident but a shadow cast ahead, waiting for the true Son who would walk the same road and, unlike Israel, never once fail. Matthew is not playing loose with Hosea; he is reading the Old Testament exactly as the risen Christ taught his disciples to read it — as one story, by one Author, about one Savior (Lk 24:27). Two rules keep this honest, and we must hold them both: first, we never erase what a text meant in its own day (Hosea truly did mean the Exodus); second, we read every text in the light of the whole Bible, whose center is Christ. That is no license to make a verse say whatever we please — it is learning to see the Author's single design running from Genesis to the manger.

Then comes the massacre: Herod's fury at being "tricked" reveals that he knew he was pursuing a child, not an army — and killed infants anyway. The slaughter of the innocents is history's first Golgotha-shadow: the powers of this world respond to the presence of Christ with violence against the most vulnerable.

It has to be said that no ancient writer outside Matthew mentions this massacre. Josephus, who chronicles Herod's reign at length and spares him nothing, records no such thing — and that silence is regularly produced as proof that Matthew made the story up. It is worth answering, because the objection sounds stronger than it is.

Begin with the scale, which Christmas art has thoroughly distorted. Bethlehem was a village, not a town — a few hundred people at most. The boys aged two and under in a place that size would have numbered perhaps half a dozen, perhaps twenty. There is no host of martyred innocents in white robes; there is a handful of families in a hamlet, and one terrible morning. Then set that against the reign it belongs to. This is the man who murdered his wife Mariamne, executed three of his own sons, and had his teenage brother-in-law drowned in a swimming pool for being too popular; who on his deathbed ordered the leading men of the nation penned in the stadium at Jericho and killed the moment he died, so that the country would be weeping on the day of his funeral whether it wished to or not. Beside all that, the deaths of a few peasant infants in a village five miles from Jerusalem is, horribly, the sort of thing a historian summarising such a reign might not think worth the ink.

An argument from silence is weak at the best of times, and weakest of all for small events far from the capital. Josephus wrote the better part of a century later, selecting from a reign crowded with atrocities, and had no reason to care about a claimant nobody in Jerusalem had heard of. Matthew, by contrast, was writing within living memory and in the region, for readers who had grandparents alive at the time — the worst possible audience to invent a local atrocity for.

But do not let the answer make the thing small. The reason it did not trouble the chroniclers is precisely the reason it should trouble us: in the ledgers of power, poor children in an unimportant village do not count. God keeps a different ledger. Matthew gives these families four verses and the words of a prophet, and heaven has not forgotten one of those names.

verseByVerse.quote: Then was fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah: "A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted, because they are no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeremiah 31:15 was originally the voice of exile — Rachel, the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, mourning as her descendants were led into Babylonian captivity past her grave at Ramah. Matthew hears that ancient lament finding its ultimate utterance in the weeping of Bethlehem's mothers. Matthew does not soften this or provide an explanation — he simply names the grief. The gospel does not protect the innocent from all suffering; it enters human suffering and redeems it from within. These children died because Christ was born; they are the first witnesses to the fact that his coming brings not comfort but a sword (Matt. 10:34) — before it brings the peace that passes understanding.

The same kind of fulfillment is at work here as in verse 15: not a bare prediction ticking over, but an ancient pattern in the life of God's people brought to its deepest point (see the note there). Yet Jeremiah's words carry a buried comfort that Matthew surely means us to find. That cry of weeping stands in the most hope-filled chapter the prophet ever wrote — the very next breath is, "Keep your voice from weeping... there is hope for your future, declares the LORD, and your children shall come back" (Jer 31:16–17), and a few lines on comes the promise of the new covenant itself (Jer 31:31–34). So even Bethlehem's tears are quoted from a page drenched in promise. Rachel weeps — but not forever, and not without hope.

But the question underneath this passage has to be asked out loud, because every honest reader asks it and no commentary should walk past it. God sent an angel to warn Joseph. He sent no angel to the house next door. Why was one child carried to safety in the night while the others were left to the swords? It is the sharpest form of the oldest question there is, and it is put here at the very beginning of the Gospel, where nobody can pretend the New Testament has not noticed.

The first thing to say is what Scripture itself does with it, which is refuse to explain. Matthew offers no theodicy, no reason, no consoling remark about a better plan. He quotes a mother who refused to be comforted, and he leaves her refusal standing without correcting her. That should be held onto by anyone who has been told that grief is a failure of faith. The Bible puts an inconsolable woman in the Christmas story and does not rebuke her. There are losses that are not to be tidied up, and God is not embarrassed by tears he has recorded on purpose.

The second thing is to admit the limit. We are not told why the warning came to one house. Scripture leaves a great deal in the dark on this, and says so — the secret things belong to the LORD our God (Deut 29:29) — and a commentary that manufactures an answer here is not being faithful but presumptuous. If you have lost a child, no one on this earth can tell you the reason, and anyone who offers you one is guessing.

But there is a third thing, and it is not a guess. The child who was rescued that night was rescued for Golgotha. The reprieve was real and it was temporary; thirty years later the sword that missed him in Bethlehem found him on a hill outside Jerusalem, and this time the Father sent no angel and no dream. Whatever else is true of God, he is not a God who keeps his own family clear of the grief he permits in yours. He entered it, at the deepest point, deliberately. That is not an explanation of your loss. It is the presence of someone in it with you who knows exactly what it cost. And it is why Jeremiah's next sentence — your children shall come back — is not a poetic flourish but a promise with a cross and an empty tomb standing behind it.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Herod died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying, "Rise, take the child and his mother and go to the land of Israel, for those who sought the child's life are dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod dies, and the word comes: return. The phrasing echoes Moses' call to return to Egypt after those who sought his life were dead (Exod. 4:19) — another deliberate typological link. Jesus is the new Moses; his infancy recapitulates the great lawgiver's story. But Jesus is more than Moses: Moses led Israel out of Egypt; Jesus will lead a new humanity out of bondage to sin and death. The connection between the two deliverers is not coincidence but the plan of the one author who inspired both Testaments. Matthew's Gospel is saturated with this sense: the old story was always pointing here.

There is a small oddity in the angel's wording that is easy to read past and is not an accident.

Those who sought the child's life are dead. Plural. But only one man had sought the child's life, and only one man had died — Herod.

The reason is that the sentence is a quotation. In Midian, God said to Moses: Go back to Egypt, for all the men who were seeking your life are dead (Exod. 4:19). Matthew has reproduced it almost word for word, plural and all, and has simply reversed the direction of travel — Moses is told to go back to Egypt, Joseph to come back from it.

So the parallel the entry above notes is not a general resemblance. Matthew has put the Exodus sentence into the angel's mouth and left the grammar showing.

And there is a fact about Herod's death worth having, because it is the hinge on which the family's exile turns. Josephus describes the end in some detail: a disease that produced fever, ulceration, convulsions and worms, borne with increasing rage, at Jericho in the spring of what we call 4 BC. It was during that final illness that he had the leading men of the nation shut in the stadium with orders that they be killed the moment he died, so that the country would be in mourning on the day of his funeral whether it wished to be or not. His sister quietly countermanded it.

Which produces the arithmetic most people find surprising: if Herod died in 4 BC and Jesus was born before that, then Jesus was born several years before the year we number 1. The error is not in Scripture but in a sixth-century monk, Dionysius Exiguus, who was asked to construct a calendar from the incarnation and miscalculated by a few years. The date on the wall is wrong; the events are not.

Then the pastoral thing, which is in the instruction Joseph had been given: remain there until I tell you (v. 13). No duration. He was told to go and told he would be told when to come back, and then he waited in a foreign country with a small child and no idea whether it would be months or a decade. It turned out to be a few years, and he only knew that afterwards.

That is the ordinary shape of waiting on God, and it is worth naming for anyone in the middle of one. Joseph was not given a date. He was given a person who promised to speak again, and the promise was kept.

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and took the child and his mother and went to the land of Israel. But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there, and being warned in a dream he withdrew to the district of Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph's fear of Archelaus is historically well-grounded: Archelaus was as brutal as his father, later deposed by Rome for his cruelties. Divine guidance does not override prudence; here the dream confirms what ordinary wisdom already suspected. The withdrawal to Galilee is divinely directed, not merely circumstantially determined. God's providence operates through human fears, political realities, and family decisions — not only through dramatic angelic interventions. He is equally sovereign in the ordinary as in the spectacular. Joseph acts on both the dream and the danger, and God honors both.

This is the fifth dream in two chapters (1:20; 2:12, 13, 19, 22), which raises a question readers genuinely carry: does God still guide like this, and if I have a vivid dream, should I act on it? A few things bring it into focus.

Notice first how rare this cluster is. Scripture covers thousands of years, and guidance by dream is concentrated at a handful of hinge-points in redemptive history — Joseph in Egypt, Daniel in Babylon, and here at the arrival of the Messiah. It is not the ordinary way God led even his own people; the Israelite in the next village was not waiting on dreams, he had the law, the priest and the counsel of the wise. Notice second that every dream in this chapter tells Joseph something he could not have worked out and needed urgently — a murder plot, a death, a danger over the next hill. None of them tells him what to believe or how to live. For that, God had already spoken.

And notice what sits right beside the dream in this very verse. Joseph is afraid of Archelaus, and his fear was entirely reasonable — the man was so brutal Rome eventually removed him. God does not overrule that fear or scold him for it; the dream confirms what ordinary judgement had already concluded. That is the pattern to take away. God guides most of us most of the time through the means he has actually given: the Scriptures, prayer, wisdom, circumstances, and the counsel of people who know us. He remains entirely free to speak more directly, and in parts of the world today he still does, often to people who have no Bible in their language yet. But the test never changes and it is never subjective: anything that contradicts what he has already said in his Word is not from him, whatever it felt like at four in the morning. If a dream moves you to obey Scripture, obey Scripture. If it moves you against it, or merely flatters you, put it down. We have something steadier than the night: the prophetic word, more fully confirmed (2 Pet 1:19).

verseByVerse.quote: And he went and lived in a city called Nazareth, so that what was spoken by the prophets might be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No single Old Testament verse uses the word "Nazarene" — Matthew writes "prophets" (plural), suggesting a thematic rather than verbatim fulfillment. The most likely background is Isaiah 11:1, where the Messiah is called a neser (branch/shoot) from Jesse's stump, with a possible wordplay on Nazareth. Nazareth was a despised village — "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" (John 1:46). That the Messiah would be identified with such a place fulfills the prophetic pattern of the Servant who had no form or majesty, who was despised and rejected (Isa. 53:2–3). Jesus was rejected before he preached a word. His address was scandal enough.

This verse is the hardest of Matthew's fulfilment quotations, and the difficulty should be stated before it is answered: there is no verse in the Old Testament that says the Messiah will be called a Nazarene. Not one. Search and you will not find it.

And Matthew knows. Look at what he does with his own formula. Everywhere else he writes what was spoken by the prophet, singular, and names him — Isaiah, Jeremiah — and then quotes. Here he writes what was spoken by the prophets, plural, names nobody, and gives no quotation marks around a text. He is signalling that he is pointing at a theme running through the prophets rather than citing a line.

Three explanations have been offered, and the first is much the strongest.

The branch. Isaiah promised that there shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isa. 11:1), and the Hebrew for that shoot is netser — the same consonants that stand behind the name Nazareth. Jeremiah and Zechariah take up the same image with a different word, calling the coming king the Branch (Jer. 23:5; Zech. 3:8; 6:12), which is very likely why Matthew says prophets in the plural. On this reading the village's name is a pun that God arranged: the Branch grew up in Branch-town.

Note also the image itself. A stump is what is left when a tree has been cut down. Isaiah is describing David's royal house reduced to a dead-looking stub — and a green shoot coming out of it. By Joseph's day that was the literal situation: the heir to David's throne was a carpenter in an occupied province.

The Nazirite. Some have suggested nazir, the consecrated one, as with Samson — the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb (Judg. 13:5). It is phonetically close and theologically attractive, and it is probably wrong: Jesus was demonstrably not a Nazirite, since he drank wine and was accused of enjoying it too much (11:19).

The despised one. The third reading takes Nazarene as simply meaning what everyone in that country understood it to mean — a nobody from a nowhere village. Nazareth appears nowhere in the Old Testament, nowhere in Josephus, and nowhere in the Talmud. Archaeology suggests a settlement of a few hundred people at most. Nathanael's reaction is the local verdict in six words: can anything good come out of Nazareth? (Jn. 1:46). On this reading the prophets did foretell it — not in a sentence but in a theme running from Isaiah 53 to Psalm 22: he had no form or majesty that we should look at him… despised and rejected by men.

The three readings are not rivals so much as layers, and Matthew's plural probably permits all of them.

Then the thing that makes this more than a puzzle. The word stuck.

He is Jesus of Nazareth to the crowds, to the demons, to the blind man on the road. It is what Pilate had written over his head in three languages. It is how the angel identifies him at the empty tomb — you seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. It is what Peter preaches at Pentecost. And it is the name the risen and glorified Christ uses of himself, from heaven, to a man on the Damascus road: I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting (Acts 22:8).

He was given a village that was a byword for insignificance, and he took its name and kept it.

He did not drop it at the resurrection. He could have. There were better addresses available — Bethlehem had the prophecy, Jerusalem had the temple, and heaven itself had been his address before the world was made.

What he answers to instead, in glory, with the wounds still on him, is the name of the poor village nobody expected anything from, given to him as a slight by people who thought they knew where he was from.

2.theology:
Typology and the Unity of Scripture. Matthew 2 demonstrates the Reformed doctrine of the unity of the two Testaments through typological fulfilment. When Matthew reads “Out of Egypt I called my son” as fulfilled in Jesus, he is not wresting Hosea from its context. He is reading with the grain of Scripture’s own logic: Israel was God’s son (Exod. 4:22), whose history was a pattern that pointed forward to the Son of God. The Old Testament is not a collection of proof texts waiting to be claimed; it is a single story moving toward a single climax.

Reformed biblical theology, developed through scholars like Geerhardus Vos and continued by Edmund Clowney, has called this “redemptive-historical” interpretation: reading every text in the light of its place in the one story of God’s redemptive purpose. Matthew 2 is a masterclass in this method. Every Old Testament quotation is not forced but organic — the story was always moving here, toward the child in Bethlehem, the flight to Egypt, the return to the land, the settlement in Galilee of the nations (Isa. 9:1–2).
2.examples:
Then: The Magi represent the first fruits of the Gentile mission that will be formally commissioned in Matthew 28. They come from outside the covenant, guided by general revelation (the star), and are brought to special revelation (the Scriptures) and to the King himself. This is the pattern of mission throughout Acts: Cornelius, the Ethiopian eunuch, the Philippian jailer — each guided by a mixture of seeking and sovereign orchestration to the one who is the answer to every longing.

Now: In our world, the contrast of chapter 2 repeats daily: people with no theological background travelling great distances (literally and metaphorically) to find Jesus, while those with full access to Scripture never move toward him. Church membership without worship, theological knowledge without seeking — this is Jerusalem troubled but not travelling. The question Matthew 2 poses is not “how much do you know?” but “are you moving toward the King?” The Magi found him because they went. That remains the condition of finding him today.

3.title: The Voice and the Voice
3.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, <sup>2</sup>“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” <sup>3</sup>For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah when he said, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’” <sup>4</sup>Now John wore a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey. <sup>5</sup>Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him, <sup>6</sup>and they were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins. <sup>7</sup>But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? <sup>8</sup>Bear fruit in keeping with repentance. <sup>9</sup>And do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father,’ for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. <sup>10</sup>Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. <sup>11</sup>I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. <sup>12</sup>His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.” <sup>13</sup>Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. <sup>14</sup>John would have prevented him, saying, “I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” <sup>15</sup>But Jesus answered him, “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he consented. <sup>16</sup>And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him; <sup>17</sup>and behold, a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.”
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is a chapter of two voices. The first voice is John’s: rough, wilderness-forged, prophetic, urgent. He wears the clothes of Elijah (2 Kgs. 1:8) and preaches with Elijah’s directness. Repent. The kingdom is not arriving on your terms. Your ancestry will not protect you. Bear fruit — now, because the axe is already laid to the root. John’s preaching is the sound of the law doing its proper work: exposing the bankruptcy of religious privilege and the urgency of genuine turning.

The second voice is the Father’s: tender, declarative, public. This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased. It comes from heaven, over the Jordan, spoken not to John or the crowd but to Jesus himself — or perhaps through Jesus to the whole watching world. The Father is not waiting to see how the ministry goes before rendering his verdict; he speaks it before the first sermon, before the first miracle, before the temptation is overcome. The approval is unconditional, grounded not in performance but in person and covenant.

Between the two voices stands the baptism — and the question it raises: why does the sinless one need a baptism of repentance? Jesus answers it: to fulfil all righteousness. He is not confessing sin; he is identifying with sinners. The one who needs no baptism submits to it on behalf of those who need it most. This is the logic of substitution, enacted in water before it is enacted in blood. The baptism of Jesus is the first act of the atonement.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — John the Baptist and the Baptism of Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John the Baptist appears in the wilderness preaching repentance, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy of a voice preparing the way. His ministry draws crowds from Jerusalem and all Judea, but he reserves his sharpest words for the Pharisees and Sadducees — those who came for baptism without repentance. Jesus then comes from Galilee to be baptized by John, and at his baptism the heavens open, the Spirit descends as a dove, and the Father speaks: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased." The Trinity is present at the inauguration of the Son's public ministry. Several things the summary passes over, all treated in full below. Verse 4's clothing and diet are not a costume: camel's hair and a leather belt are Elijah's uniform (2 Kgs. 1:8), whose return was promised before the day of the LORD (Mal. 4:5); locusts were the one insect the law permitted (Lev. 11:22) and wild honey is what the wilderness gives away, so John lives on what God provides and takes nothing from anybody — which is precisely why nobody can buy him. The Jordan itself matters: it is where Israel crossed into the land (Josh. 3), where Elijah was taken up (2 Kgs. 2), and where Naaman went down a leper and came up clean (2 Kgs. 5:14). Note the direction of travel — the crowds go out of the towns to the river, leaving the land the way their ancestors entered it and coming back in through the water. John is asking Israel to start again from the beginning. Verse 9 contains a pun English cannot show: in Aramaic, stones are abanim and children are banim — take away a letter and the rubble becomes the family of God — and he says it standing at the river where Joshua set up twelve stones from the riverbed as a memorial to the twelve tribes (Josh. 4:1-7). Verses 13-14: Nazareth to the Jordan is sixty to eighty miles, three or four days on foot; and behind that walk lie eighteen years of which Scripture says nothing at all, since Luke last showed him at twelve and now says he was about thirty. The Son of God spent roughly six-sevenths of his life on earth doing work nobody recorded — and that was not preparation for obedience, it was obedience. John's protest is an imperfect verb, "he kept trying to prevent him", and his theology in it is impeccable while his conclusion is wrong: right premises do not guarantee a right conclusion about what God will do next. Verse 15's "to fulfil all righteousness" is the answer and the hinge of the chapter — not personal repentance but substitution enacted in water before it is enacted in blood.
verseByVerse.theology: John's baptism is a baptism of repentance, anticipating the one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. He is the last of the old-covenant prophets and the first herald of the new. His insistence on fruit worthy of repentance cuts against every form of religious privilege — ancestry, tradition, institutional membership. You cannot inherit faith; you must repent. Jesus's baptism is not a baptism of personal repentance (he has no sin) but an act of identification and consecration: he enters the waters of judgment on behalf of sinners and emerges declared righteous by the Father. The Spirit's descent and the Father's voice confirm him as the inaugurator of the new age.
verseByVerse.examples: John confronted the religious establishment with their false security: "Do not presume to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.'" The same temptation runs through every tradition — to substitute membership for repentance, heritage for faith, attendance for transformation. John's question to each worshiper is still the right one: is there fruit? Not feeling, not knowledge, not ancestry — fruit. The tree is known by what it produces.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John's first word is repent — not "God loves you" or "you are enough" but a call to a complete turning of direction. Repentance (metanoia) is not mere remorse or behavioral adjustment; it is a change of mind so fundamental that it reorients the whole life. The reason given is the nearness of the kingdom: the rule of God in the person of his King is arriving, and the appropriate response to the arrival of the holy King is not celebration but self-examination. John does not soft-pedal the entrance requirement. He announces the kingdom as good news — but good news that demands an honest reckoning with who you are before the King you are about to meet.

But what did that turning actually look like for the people standing on the riverbank? To a Jew, repentance was an old and weighty word — the Hebrew teshuvah, a "returning," coming home to the LORD they had wandered from. The prophets had thundered it for centuries: "Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God" (Hos 14:1); "rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joel 2:12–13). It was concrete, never sentimental: confession of sin, often with fasting and ashes, and a real forsaking of idols. Yet John pressed it to a shocking edge. There was in his day a baptism for Gentiles converting to the God of Israel; John now made Jews — sons of Abraham, temple-going, law-keeping — come down into that same water, as though they too were outsiders who needed to come in. Repentance meant letting go of every proud "but I have Abraham as my father" (v. 9) and turning with the heart. And John demanded proof: "bear fruit in keeping with repentance" (v. 8) — share your coat, deal honestly, stop your extortion (Lk 3:10–14). A turning you could see.

And today? The heart of it has not changed an inch. Repentance is still a Spirit-given change of mind that turns from sin to God and from self-trust to Christ — not a single tearful moment but the daily set of a whole life (it was Luther's very first thesis that the believer's entire life is one of repentance). Our temptation is just the old one in new dress: we lean on our churchgoing, our baptism, our decent name, our Christian family — our own "child of Abraham." John's word still falls like an axe at the root (v. 10): none of that is the turning itself. Yet hear the sweetness in it — this is no demand to earn God's favor. It is the "godly grief" that "produces a repentance that leads to salvation" (2 Cor 7:10), the homeward turn of a heart that grace has already begun to thaw. We repent not to make the King draw near, but because in Christ he already has.

And notice the phrase John uses for what is arriving, because this is its first appearance in the Gospel and Matthew will use it about thirty times more: "the kingdom of heaven." Read Mark and Luke at the same points and you will find "the kingdom of God." Two names, and readers reasonably ask whether they are two things.

They are one thing. Matthew writes for Jewish readers, and reverent Jews of that period avoided pronouncing the divine name, putting a respectful substitute in its place — "Heaven" being the commonest. It is ordinary speech in the Bible: the prodigal comes home saying "I have sinned against heaven" (Luke 15:21), and he does not mean the sky. Daniel had already said it outright: "Heaven rules" (Dan. 4:26). So "the kingdom of heaven" is simply "the kingdom of God" said the way a devout Jew would say it, and Matthew keeps the idiom his readers used.

If that needs proving, Matthew proves it himself. Watching the rich young man walk away, Jesus says it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven — and in the very next sentence, easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God (19:23-24). Two consecutive verses, one subject, both names. Some have taught that the kingdom of heaven is an earthly kingdom for Israel and the kingdom of God a separate spiritual reality; the men who hold this love the Scriptures and read them carefully, but those two verses are very difficult to carry. (What the kingdom actually is, and where the Reformed and dispensational readings part company, is set out more fully at 4:17.)

One more thing, since the word misleads. "Kingdom of heaven" does not mean heaven, and John is not preaching about where you go when you die. A kingdom is a reign before it is a realm — the word is about a King exercising rule. What is at hand is not a place opening up but a throne being occupied, here, on this earth, in a man about to walk down to this river. That is why the only fit response is to turn round.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah when he said, "The voice of one crying in the wilderness: 'Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.'" Now John wore a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah 40:3 announced a voice that would prepare the way of the LORD — the divine name, Yahweh — for his coming. Matthew applies it to John preparing the way for Jesus, a staggering identification: Jesus is Yahweh coming to his people. John's clothing and diet identify him as a prophet in the tradition of Elijah (2 Kings 1:8), whose return before the great day of the LORD was promised in Malachi 4:5. His diet is of a piece with it: locusts were the one insect the law allowed Israel to eat (Lev. 11:22), and wild honey is simply what the wilderness gives away. He lives on what God provides and takes nothing from anybody, which is precisely why no one can buy him. John is not wearing prophet's clothes as a costume; he inhabits the prophetic calling with his whole life, refusing comfort, refusing the establishment, living in the wilderness as a sign that the old order is passing and something wholly new is coming.

And what did "prepare the way... make his paths straight" mean to those who first heard it? It is, indeed, the language of a royal arrival. In the ancient East, before a great king set out, crews went ahead to ready the road — filling in the valleys, cutting down the hills, clearing the rocks, straightening the bends — so the king's procession could sweep through unhindered. Isaiah's very next verse paints it plainly: "Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill be made low... and the rough places a plain" (Isa 40:4). But the King in view is no earthly monarch; it is the LORD himself. Isaiah 40 opens the great book of comfort to a people in exile, and its promise is a new exodus: God coming in person to lead his people home across the desert, like a shepherd-king at the head of the march (Isa 40:10–11). The "highway in the wilderness" was that homeward road (cf. Isa 35:8).

By Jesus' day the verse had become a watchword of hope. The wilderness community at Qumran, beside the Dead Sea, took these very words and withdrew into the desert "to prepare the way of the LORD," certain God was about to act. So when John appears in that same wilderness crying Isaiah 40:3, every devout ear caught the freight of it: the King is coming — ready the road. And the road-work, then as now, is the heart: the proud hills of self-righteousness brought low, the sunken valleys of despair filled with hope, the crooked dealings made straight. Repentance is simply how a sinner levels the ground for a holy King.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him, and they were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowds streaming to John in the wilderness is itself a fulfillment of prophetic pattern: the people going out to meet God's word in the wild places, as Israel had once done at Sinai. Baptism in John's context was not a new rite but a well-known practice: Gentile converts to Judaism underwent ritual washing as a symbol of cleansing from their old life. John applies it to Jews — a radical provocation. He is saying: you need to be cleansed too. You are no cleaner before God by birth than any Gentile. The confession of sins was the necessary accompaniment — there is no point to the washing without the honesty it symbolizes.

What sins would those people have confessed as they went down into the water? We are not left to guess, for John himself named some when the crowds pressed him, "What then shall we do?" To ordinary folk he said: you keep two coats while your neighbor shivers and goes hungry — that tight-fisted selfishness is sin (Lk 3:11). To the tax collectors, who fattened their purses by charging more than Rome required: your greed and extortion (Lk 3:13). To the soldiers: your bullying, your false accusations, your grumbling discontent with your pay (Lk 3:14). And to the Pharisees and Sadducees who came, his word was sharper still — their pride, their hypocrisy, their smug trust in being "children of Abraham" (vv. 7–9). Behind it all lay the sins the prophets had forever exposed: dishonest scales and withheld wages (Mal 3:5), worship that was all lips and no heart (Isa 29:13), the quiet idolatry of loving money and reputation more than God. Run the list down the Ten Commandments and you meet every one of them. And if we are honest, we meet ourselves there too — their sins were not strange and ancient relics; they were ours.

It is worth asking why the Jordan, because the river is not incidental and Israel's memory of it was long.

This is the water Israel crossed to come into the land at all. The priests carrying the ark stepped in, the flow stopped upstream, and a nation walked over on dry ground into the inheritance (Josh. 3). It is where Elijah struck the water with his rolled-up cloak, crossed, and was taken up in the whirlwind (2 Kgs. 2:8-11). It is where Naaman the Syrian general, told to wash seven times, went down a leper and came up clean (2 Kgs. 5:14).

Entry, ascent, and cleansing — all at the same muddy, unimpressive river.

And notice the direction of travel in this chapter. The people are not going to the temple. They are going out — out of Jerusalem, out of the towns, out to the wilderness and down to the river, which is to say they are leaving the land the way their ancestors entered it, and coming back in through the water.

That is a strange thing for a nation to do voluntarily, and it is exactly what John's baptism meant. He was not offering a ceremony to add to their religion. He was asking Israel to start again from the beginning — to go back outside, admit they had no more claim on the land than a Gentile convert, and come in again by grace.

Which is why the establishment could not bear it, and why the crowds came in their thousands.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, "You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bear fruit in keeping with repentance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John's sharpest words are for the most religious. The Pharisees and Sadducees were theological opponents of each other — John addresses them as a single brood. "Vipers" evokes the serpent of Eden: they are children of the deceiver, carrying poison under religious clothing. "Who warned you?" — John is skeptical of their motives. They may be coming for social reasons, political reasons, curiosity — but without genuine repentance. The test is fruit: repentance that produces no change in behavior is not repentance. John refuses to process them through the rite without pressing the reality. A baptism received without repentance is just getting wet.

Single out that command — "bear fruit in keeping with repentance" — for it is the very thing John is after. The picture is an orchard: a tree shows what it truly is by what hangs on its branches, not by its leaves. It is an old image; Israel was God's vineyard, planted and tended and looked to for a harvest of justice (Isa 5:1–7). So John is saying, in effect: do not show me your pedigree or your ceremonies; show me a changed life. Concretely that meant what he would soon tell the crowds — share your coat, deal honestly, stop your extortion (Lk 3:11–14); and Paul would later echo the very phrase, pressing men to "do works worthy of their repentance" (Acts 26:20). But notice the order, for it is everything. Fruit does not make a tree good; a good tree bears good fruit. John is not telling these men to manufacture good works in order to earn their standing — that was the Pharisees' whole mistake; he is telling them that real repentance always shows, that a turning no one can see is no turning at all. And the branch bears fruit only by staying joined to the vine (Jn 15:5): the change John demands is one only the Coming One can work in a heart.

A word on these two parties, for they could hardly have been less alike. The Pharisees were the great lay movement of the common people — their name likely means "the separated ones." Zealous for the Law, they hedged it round with a vast "tradition of the elders," the oral rules meant to guard every commandment, and they were scrupulous about tithing, ritual purity, and the Sabbath. They believed firmly in the resurrection of the dead, in angels and spirits, in a coming judgment and Messiah. Devout and admired by ordinary folk, they were undone by the very thing they prized: their religion curdled into the self-righteous show Jesus would later lay bare (Matt 23). The Sadducees were the opposite number — the wealthy priestly aristocracy who ran the temple, the high-priestly families and their circle. They held only the five books of Moses as binding and flatly denied the resurrection, angels, and any life beyond this one (Acts 23:8); worldly, here-and-now men who kept comfortable terms with Rome to guard their power. When the temple fell in A.D. 70, they vanished with it.

Bitter rivals, then — yet here they walk down to the Jordan together, and one day they will conspire together to kill the Lord. Nothing unites enemies like a shared threat to their religion. John sees through the unlikely alliance in an instant, and will not flatter it: "You brood of vipers."

And what did they hear in "the wrath to come"? Not a new idea at all, but one straight from their own Scriptures. The prophets had long spoken of "the Day of the LORD" — a coming day when God would pour out his anger on sin, judge the wicked, and set the world right: "a day of wrath... of distress and anguish" (Zeph 1:15), the day that "comes, burning like an oven" (Mal 4:1), of which Malachi asked, "who can endure the day of his coming?" (Mal 3:2). Amos had warned that for the complacent it would be darkness and not light (Amos 5:18–20). By John's day this expectation had ripened, sharpened further by the rabbis and the apocalyptic writers into a settled hope of a great Day of Judgment when Messiah would come, the dead would rise, and God's wrath would fall. But here lay the deadly assumption John meant to shatter: the Pharisee and Sadducee took it for granted that this wrath was for Gentiles and sinners — that they, as sons of Abraham, would stand safe among the spectators. John's question lands like a thunderclap: "Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?" The fire is not only for pagan Rome and the obvious sinner; it is for every unrepentant heart, the religious ones first of all. And the only shelter is not ancestry but repentance — and, as the next verses will show, the Coming One who himself will pass through the fire for his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not presume to say to yourselves, "We have Abraham as our father," for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The appeal to Abrahamic descent was the deepest form of Jewish religious security — covenant membership by birth. John demolishes it: God could make Abrahamic children from the pebbles underfoot if he chose. The covenant is not a biological inheritance; it is a gift received through faith and evidenced by fruit. The axe already at the root signals eschatological urgency: this is not a gentle warning but an imminent verdict. The tree that produces no fruit is not warned again — it is cut down. John is announcing judgment as the context in which repentance must occur. Grace is real, but so is the ax.

This is the place to pause, for verse 10 can sound like salvation by works: bear fruit, or be cut down and burned. Hear the Reformed answer plainly. We are saved by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone; our works add nothing to the verdict, for we are justified not by what we do but by what Christ has done, received by faith (Eph 2:8–9). Yet — and this is the hinge — the faith that justifies is never a faith that stays alone. A living faith bears fruit as surely as a living tree does; "faith apart from works is dead" (Jas 2:17). So John is not saying that fruit earns life; he is saying that fruitlessness exposes death. The barren tree is cut down not because it failed to earn its place, but because its barrenness proves it was never truly alive. When Scripture speaks of a judgment "according to works" (Rom 2:6), it means our works are the evidence brought into the court, not the price paid at the bar — they reveal the root, they do not become it. The old summary holds: we are saved by faith alone, but not by a faith that is alone. And even the fruit is grace, for God must first make the tree good; an axe never yet turned a dead tree into a living one. That making-alive is the Coming One's work, not ours.

And there is a flash of wit in it that English cannot show. John is speaking Aramaic, and in Aramaic and Hebrew alike the two words sit almost on top of each other: stones are abanim, children are banim. From these abanim God can raise up banim. Take away a letter and the rubble at your feet becomes the family of God. It is a pun, and it is deadly serious — the distance between a stone and a son of Abraham is nothing whatever to the God who made both out of the dust.

And notice where he is standing when he says it. This is the Jordan. When Israel first came into this land, Joshua had twelve men carry twelve stones up out of this very riverbed and set them as a memorial to the twelve tribes, "that this may be a sign among you" forever (Josh. 4:1-7). John stands at that river, gestures at the stones, and tells the sons of Abraham that God could begin the twelve tribes again from the rocks if he chose. Their descent secures them nothing. God has never once been short of raw material: he made Adam from the ground and Abraham's own heir from a dead womb (Rom. 4:19).

verseByVerse.quote: I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John's self-description is striking in its humility: he is not worthy to carry the sandals of the one coming. Carrying a master's sandals was a task too degrading for a Jewish disciple to perform for his rabbi — and John says he is not even at that level. The contrast between water-baptism and Spirit-and-fire baptism is the contrast between the outer symbol and the inner reality. The Spirit transforms; the fire purifies or judges. The winnowing image makes the point concrete: the coming one will separate the genuine from the counterfeit — not eventually, not symbolically, but finally and completely. There is no third category between wheat and chaff.

Single out the three things John says here. First, his water baptism: "I baptize you with water for repentance." The water was a sign, no more — an outward washing that pictured the inward cleansing the people sought, and sealed their turning from sin as they made ready for the King. It could wet the body and mark the confession, but it could not change the heart; it pointed beyond itself to One who could. (Ezekiel had long before married the two: clean water sprinkled, and a new heart and Spirit given — Ezek 36:25–27.)

Second, the contrast. John is the greatest of the prophets, yet he says he is not fit even to carry the sandals of the Coming One — the task of the lowest slave. He gives the sign; Jesus gives the substance. John can lower you into the river; only Jesus can baptize you in the Spirit. The forerunner washes the outside; the King transforms the inside.

Third, that baptism "with the Holy Spirit and fire." The Spirit-baptism is the great gospel promise: the Coming One pours out God's own Spirit to give new birth, to indwell and transform — poured out in full at Pentecost (Acts 2). But what of the fire? Here readers differ. Some take it as the Spirit's refining warmth on believers, recalling Pentecost's "tongues as of fire." The better reading, though, is fire as judgment, and the context settles it: the same passage has the fruitless tree "thrown into the fire" (v. 10) and the chaff burned "with unquenchable fire" (v. 12) — and one does not refine wheat with unquenchable fire. John speaks to a mixed crowd, and the one Messiah's coming divides it in two: he baptizes the repentant with the Spirit unto life, while the impenitent he meets with the fire of judgment. And here is the wonder for all who are his — the reason the wheat need never dread that fire is that the Coming One would himself pass through it for them at the cross.

Single out that last picture, for John's whole message lies inside it once you see the farm behind it. Picture an ancient threshing floor — a flat, hard patch of ground out on a breezy hilltop. The cut grain is spread there and trodden until the kernels break loose from their dry husks. Then the farmer takes his winnowing fork, a broad wooden shovel, and tosses the whole mass up into the evening wind. The heavy, solid grain drops straight back to the floor; the light, empty chaff is caught by the wind and blown aside. He gathers the good wheat into his barn to keep, and sweeps up the useless chaff to burn.

Now hear what John is telling them. The Coming One is not only the Savior who gives the Spirit — the winnowing fork is already in his hand, so he is also the Judge. Until he comes, wheat and chaff lie mingled on the one floor, and to the eye they look like a single heap: the truly repentant and the merely religious stand side by side in the crowd at the Jordan, much alike. But his coming is the wind that sorts them. What has real weight — a heart truly turned, a faith that bears fruit — falls safely to the floor and is gathered in; what is hollow husk is swept away. There are only two heaps and only two destinations: the barn or the fire, and "unquenchable fire" means the verdict is final. And the fork is in his hand now — not a distant threat but a present summons (the prophets had long used the image; "the wicked are like chaff that the wind drives away," Ps 1:4). So the metaphor puts one plain question to every heart: when the wind blows, will I prove wheat or chaff? And the gospel answer is just as plain — the chaff is not bad wheat but empty husk, and the way to be found wheat is not to be impressive in oneself but to come to the Coming One in repentance and faith, the very One who took the fire in his people's place.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. John would have prevented him, saying, "I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus comes from Galilee — the despised north, far from Jerusalem — to submit to baptism by his own forerunner. John's protest is theologically precise: the baptism is a baptism of repentance, and Jesus has nothing to repent of. The logic runs the wrong direction: the sinless one should not be washed by the sinner; the one who baptizes with the Spirit should not be baptized with water. John understands more about Jesus than most of Israel does. His protest is not false modesty but accurate theological reflection. The question he raises — "why would you come to me?" — is the right question, and Jesus's answer is astonishing.

Three things are packed into these two verses, and the first is a distance.

Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan. Nazareth to the Jordan crossings is somewhere between sixty and eighty miles depending on the route, and the route mattered — most Galileans went the long way round through Perea to avoid Samaria. That is three or four days on foot, in sandals, carrying what he needed.

He walked for the better part of a week to stand in a queue.

The second is what he was walking away from, and it is the largest silence in the New Testament. Luke says he was about thirty years of age when he began (Lk. 3:23). Matthew last showed him as a small child in Egypt; Luke gives us one incident at twelve. Between that and this river there are eighteen years about which Scripture says precisely nothing.

Eighteen years in a workshop in a village of a few hundred people. No sermons, no miracles, no disciples, and no record. The Son of God spent roughly six-sevenths of his life on earth doing work that nobody thought worth writing down — and it is worth stating plainly that this was not wasted time or preparation for the real thing. It was obedience. Those years are part of the righteousness he is about to say he came to fulfil.

The third is John's protest, and the Greek is stronger than the English. John would have prevented him is an imperfect — he kept trying to stop him. This was not one polite demurral but a struggle at the water's edge.

And notice what he says: I need to be baptized by you. This is the man who has just called the religious leadership a brood of vipers and told the crowds he was not fit to carry the Coming One's sandals. Of all the men on that riverbank he had least reason to think himself dirty, and he is the one who says out loud that he needs washing.

Which is worth having as a rule. The people most conscious of their own need are almost never the people you would nominate. John is the greatest man born of women, on his Lord's own testimony (11:11), and his instinctive reaction on meeting Jesus is to ask to change places in the water.

A note on whether John knew him. The two were relatives — Elizabeth and Mary were kinswomen, and their sons were six months apart. Yet John says in the fourth Gospel, twice, I myself did not know him (Jn. 1:31, 33). There is no contradiction: John means he did not know him as the Messiah until the promised sign came, which is precisely the descent of the Spirit he is about to witness. Family acquaintance and messianic certainty are different things, and the hill country of Judea is a long way from Nazareth for two families with no reason to travel.

Then the thing to take away. John's theology here is impeccable and his conclusion is wrong. He has correctly identified who Jesus is, correctly understood what his own baptism means, correctly deduced that the sinless one does not need it — and on the strength of three correct premises he tries to stop the Son of God doing what he came to do.

It is a useful warning for people who reason carefully about God. Right premises do not guarantee a right conclusion about what he should do next, because he is always working with more of the picture than we have. John's mistake is the best kind of mistake, made for the best reasons, and Jesus corrects it in one sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus answered him, "Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness." Then he consented. And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him;
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Fulfill all righteousness" is one of Matthew's key phrases: Jesus came not to bypass the law's requirements but to meet them all on behalf of his people. His baptism is not personal repentance but solidarity — he enters the waters of judgment as the representative of sinners, identifying with the people he came to save. The opening of the heavens signals the end of the silence between God and his people that had lasted since Malachi. The Spirit descending as a dove echoes the Spirit hovering over the waters of creation (Gen. 1:2) — a new creation is beginning. At the inauguration of Jesus's ministry, all three persons of the Trinity are present and active.

Was the Spirit not already with Jesus before this moment? Indeed he was — fully, and from the very first. This child was conceived by the Holy Spirit (1:20); as the eternal Son he was never for one instant without the Spirit, never less than fully God, never touched by sin. So we must not picture the Spirit arriving where he had been absent, nor imagine (as some old errors taught) that Jesus only now became the Son or the Christ. Nothing changes in his person at the Jordan.

What happens, then, is two things at once, and both are true. First, it is his anointing. "Christ" means "Anointed One," and here the Father visibly anoints him with the Spirit to begin his public work as Messiah — Isaiah's long-promised Servant: "Behold my servant... I have put my Spirit upon him" (Isa 42:1; cf. Isa 61:1; Acts 10:38). The Spirit who had always dwelt in him now equips the incarnate Son, in his true humanity, for the ministry that begins this very day. Second, it is a sign for others to see. John himself tells us he did not know for certain who the Messiah was until he watched the Spirit descend and remain on him — that was the appointed sign (Jn 1:32–34). So the dove was no empty show; it was God's own testimony, pointing out his Son to John, and through John to us. And mark the sweetness: the Spirit comes to rest, to abide — not to flutter off again as he had with the prophets of old. The very One on whom the Spirit now settles is the One who will pour that same Spirit out on all who are his (v. 11). He is anointed as Head, that the oil might run down to the whole body.

verseByVerse.quote: and behold, a voice from heaven said, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father's voice at the Jordan combines two Old Testament texts: Psalm 2:7 ("You are my Son") and Isaiah 42:1 ("my servant... in whom my soul delights"). Psalm 2 is the royal psalm of the messianic King; Isaiah 42 is the first Servant Song of the suffering Servant. From the beginning, the Father defines his Son's identity in both categories: he is the triumphant King and the obedient Servant who suffers. The words "with whom I am well pleased" are spoken before Jesus has done anything in his public ministry — before a sermon, before a miracle, before the cross. The Father's delight is not earned; it is given. This is the fountain from which all of Jesus's ministry flows: he acts out of a secure identity, not toward an uncertain approval.

And now the question that decides whether this verse is biography or gospel: is that word ever spoken over anyone else? Because every human being alive is trying to hear it from somebody. We spend our lives auditioning — for a parent whose approval never quite arrived, for an employer, for a congregation, for an audience of strangers on a screen — and the ache underneath all of it is the ache to hear a voice we trust say: you are mine, and I am pleased with you. Matthew has just recorded that sentence being said out loud over a man standing in a river. The question is whether it has anything to do with us.

It has everything to do with us, and the link is not imitation but union. The Father speaks this over his Son; and the believer is in the Son. That is why Paul can say we are "accepted in the Beloved" (Eph 1:6) — not accepted alongside him, or accepted for trying to be like him, but accepted in him, our life now "hidden with Christ in God" (Col 3:3). It is why the Spirit of God's Son is sent into our hearts so that we cry Abba, Father, and why the same Spirit "bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God, and if children, then heirs" (Gal 4:6; Rom 8:16-17).

Watch how the exchange works, because it runs in both directions and it began here in the water. At the Jordan the sinless one stepped into the place of sinners, taking a washing he did not need. At Golgotha he stepped into the place of sinners again, taking a judgment he did not deserve. He took what was ours — the guilt, the verdict, the abandonment, and on the cross the silence where a voice from heaven should have been. And what he gives in exchange is what was always his: the standing, the sonship, and the Father's welcome. "For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Cor 5:21). The word said over him at the Jordan is said over everyone hidden in him.

Two things follow, and they are worth holding tightly. The first is for the reader still frightened by the winnowing fork a few verses back, wondering whether he is wheat or chaff. Notice when the Father speaks: before a single sermon, before one miracle, before the cross. If the Father's delight in his Son was not produced by performance, then the delight he has in those who are in his Son is not produced by ours either — and you will not settle the question by inspecting your feelings, but by looking away from yourself to the one you have come to. The way in is the way John preached all through this chapter: turn, and come. It has never been anything else.

The second is a guard, because this is not the modern notion that God approves of everyone exactly as they are and nothing more need be said. The same chapter has an axe at the root and a fire that is not quenched, and John was not preaching self-acceptance. The word is spoken over those who are in the Beloved, and there is a door to be walked through to get there. But once through it, hear this and let it do its work: the verdict on your life has already been announced, in public, by the only voice that finally matters — and it was not a verdict you earned, and it is not one you can now forfeit by having a bad week. He is well pleased. Not with your performance. With his Son, and with you in him.

3.theology:
The Trinity at the Jordan. Matthew 3:16–17 is one of the clearest Trinitarian texts in the New Testament. The Son stands in the water; the Spirit descends upon the Son; the Father speaks from heaven. Three distinct persons, one divine act. Reformed theology has always insisted that the doctrine of the Trinity is not a late addition to Christian thought but the grammar of the gospel itself — the structure of reality that makes salvation possible.

The baptism of Jesus is a Trinitarian event. The Father approves; the Spirit empowers; the Son obeys. This pattern runs through the whole New Testament: the Father sends, the Son accomplishes, the Spirit applies. The atonement is Trinitarian (the Father gave, the Son died, the Spirit regenerates); the church is Trinitarian (baptised in the name of Father, Son, and Spirit, Matt. 28:19); the Christian life is Trinitarian (praying to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit). The Jordan reveals the shape of everything that follows.
3.examples:
Then: John the Baptist stands in a long line of prophets who prepared the way for God’s action: Moses before Joshua, Elijah before Elisha, Isaiah before the return from exile. Each was a voice, not the Word; each pointed away from himself. John is the culmination of this pattern — the last and greatest of the preparers. His greatness lay precisely in his self-effacement: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). Every faithful preacher, teacher, and leader stands in John’s tradition: making straight the way, getting out of the way.

Now: The Father’s declaration over Jesus at the baptism — This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased — is the word every human being is searching for. We spend our lives seeking approval: from parents, employers, social media, achievement. The gospel announces that in Christ, the deepest possible approval has already been given — not because of what we have done but because of who he is and what he has done. The restless search for significance ends not in achievement but in adoption: we are accepted in the Beloved. That is the word the Father spoke at the Jordan, and it is addressed to everyone who is hidden with Christ in God (Col. 3:3).

4.title: The Tested King
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. <sup>2</sup>And after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry. <sup>3</sup>And the tempter came and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread.” <sup>4</sup>But he answered, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.’” <sup>5</sup>Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple <sup>6</sup>and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you,’ and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’” <sup>7</sup>Jesus said to him, “Again it is written, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’” <sup>8</sup>Again, the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. <sup>9</sup>And he said to him, “All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me.” <sup>10</sup>Then Jesus said to him, “Be gone, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.’” <sup>11</sup>Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and were ministering to him. <sup>12</sup>Now when he heard that John had been arrested, he withdrew to Galilee. <sup>13</sup>And leaving Nazareth he went and lived in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali, <sup>14</sup>so that what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: <sup>15</sup>“The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles — <sup>16</sup>the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light, and for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, on them a light has dawned.” <sup>17</sup>From that time Jesus began to preach, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” <sup>18</sup>While walking by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon (who is called Peter) and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. <sup>19</sup>And he said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.” <sup>20</sup>Immediately they left their nets and followed him. <sup>21</sup>And going on from there he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them. <sup>22</sup>Immediately they left the boat and their father and followed him. <sup>23</sup>And he went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction among the people. <sup>24</sup>So his fame spread throughout all Syria, and they brought him all the sick, those afflicted with various diseases and pains, those oppressed by demons, those having seizures, and paralytics, and he healed them. <sup>25</sup>And great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis, and from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the axis on which the Gospel turns. The Spirit who descended at the baptism immediately drives Jesus into the wilderness — not as abandonment but as commission. The forty days echo Israel’s forty years in the wilderness, where God’s people failed at every test. Jesus succeeds at every one, and he does it using the same weapon available to Israel and to us: the written Word of God. Three times the devil attacks; three times Jesus answers with Deuteronomy. The true Israel passes where the nation failed.

Each temptation targets a specific aspect of Jesus’ identity and mission. Turn stones to bread: use divine power for personal comfort. Throw yourself from the temple: leverage God’s promises for public spectacle. Bow to me: gain the kingdoms without the cross. Every temptation is a shortcut past suffering to glory — and Jesus refuses every one. There is no crown without the cross, no glory without the grave, no kingdom without Calvary. Satan offers the destination without the path; Jesus insists on the path.

Then the ministry begins — in Galilee of the Gentiles (Isa. 9:1), the region of mixed ethnicity and questionable reputation, the last place a respectable rabbi would choose as his base. The people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light. The light does not go to the well-lit; it goes to the dark. And the first disciples he calls are working men with nets and boats — not scribes with scrolls. The kingdom of heaven is staffed from the margins, then and now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Temptation of Jesus in the Wilderness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Immediately after his baptism, the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. The forty days echo Israel's forty years in the wilderness; the three temptations echo Israel's great failures — bread, testing God, idolatry. But where Israel fell, Jesus stands. He defeats each temptation not by miraculous power but by the word of God alone, quoting Deuteronomy three times. The temptations are not trivial: they are the offer of the kingdom by a shortcut — bread without suffering, glory without the cross, dominion without death. And he overcomes not merely as our example but as our champion — the last Adam and true Israel, whose perfect obedience is reckoned to all who are his, so that we now resist temptation not to win God's favor but from within the victory he has already won for us. Two things the summary passes over. Verse 2's hunger is the ground of the first temptation — the devil does not waste his best offer on a man with full hands, and he waits for the sixth week. And verse 11 is not the end of the matter: Luke adds that the devil departed "until an opportune time" (Lk. 4:13), and Matthew shows where those times came. At Caesarea Philippi, when Peter says the suffering shall never happen, Jesus answers with the same words he used here — "Get behind me, Satan" (16:23) — because it is the same offer, the crown without the cross, arriving from a friend. And at Golgotha the passers-by shout "if you are the Son of God, come down from the cross" (27:40), which is the identical formula the devil used twice in this wilderness (vv. 3, 6). The temptation that opens the ministry is the temptation that closes it. Note also the quiet irony of the angels: the devil had proposed a scenario in which angels would catch him spectacularly before a temple crowd, and Jesus refused — so they come instead in an empty desert with nobody watching, and the verb is an imperfect (they kept ministering) of the ordinary word for waiting at table. What he would not seize, he was given.
verseByVerse.theology: The temptation of Jesus is not merely a test of personal willpower but a cosmic conflict at the hinge of redemptive history. The devil who succeeded in Eden now faces the second Adam in a wilderness, and loses. Jesus is revealed as the true Israel — obedient where the nation failed — and the true Adam — resisting the serpent where the first man did not. His weapon is the word of God alone: not angelic power, not divine fiat, but the Scripture he has internalized and believes. This models the Christian's resource in temptation: not mystical experience but the word of God believed and obeyed.
