The parable's whole force is that the two figures are not of the same order, and that the man who cannot see it has probably never looked properly at his own.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Purity of heart — singled out by Kierkegaard as "willing one thing" — is the undivided, unalloyed devotion of the whole inner person to God. The promise is breathtaking: they shall see God. The beatific vision — direct knowledge of the divine presence — is the ultimate human destiny, promised here not to the theologically sophisticated but to the single-hearted. Complexity of mind is no substitute for simplicity of devotion.

Think of a man who worships on Sunday with one eye always on his money, his image, his comfort; his heart is divided, the water cloudy. The pure in heart is the one whose loves have been simplified, who wants God more than the gifts of God — and only such clear water can mirror the face of heaven.

If your heart feels anything but pure, look away from it to him: the only truly pure in heart gives us his own cleanness now (1 Cor 1:30), washes us day by day, and will make us spotless when we see him (1 Jn 3:2). The fight to be pure is itself a fruit of grace, not a bid for it.

This beatitude is an answer to a question, and the question is in the Psalms.

Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? And who shall stand in his holy place? — and David answers his own question: He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who does not lift up his soul to what is false (Ps. 24:3-4).

That is the temple question. Who may come up? Who may go in and not be struck down? And the answer given a thousand years earlier is the phrase Jesus uses here — and to it he attaches something David did not dare to write. Not merely shall stand in his holy place but shall see God.

Which is the largest promise in the eight, and it should be measured against what the Old Testament says about the possibility. Moses asked to see God's glory and was refused: you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live (Exod. 33:20). He was hidden in a cleft of rock and shown the back. Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up and cried out that he was undone. Nobody in the entire Old Testament sees the face of God and walks away comfortable.

And Jesus, sitting on a hillside in Galilee, tells a crowd of fishermen and farmers that some of them will.

Then the word pure, which is katharos — the ordinary term for clean, used of washed dishes and clear water and metal with the dross taken out. Its opposite is not wicked but mixed. So the purity in view is less about achieving a standard than about not being adulterated: one loyalty rather than two, an undivided heart rather than a better one.

Which is a mercy, because a divided heart is the honest description of most Christians most of the time, and this is precisely what the New Testament promises God is working on. The single-heartedness is the destination, and the wanting of it is the evidence.

And it is worth ending where the promise ends, because nothing else in the eight reaches this far. Everything a Christian is offered — forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, the resurrection of the body, a new heaven and a new earth — is a gift from God. This one is God himself.

Moses asked for it and was told no. The prophets circled it. And the whole long arrangement of tabernacle and temple and curtain and priesthood existed to say, in the most emphatic architecture ever built, that this was the one thing not available.

Then a man on a hill said the curtain would come down, and thirty-odd years later it did — torn from the top, which is the end nobody could reach.

They shall see God. Not know about him more accurately. Not sense him more strongly. See him, with the face, as one sees a friend — and it was purchased by the only man who ever had a pure heart, who was made sin so that people who never had one could look at his Father without dying.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peacemakers are not peacekeepers — they do not merely avoid conflict but actively work to reconcile what is broken. The title "sons of God" reflects the character of the Father, who is himself the great Reconciler (2 Cor. 5:18–19). To make peace is to participate in the divine work.

Picture the friend who, when two others fall out, refuses to take a side and instead walks back and forth between them, bearing the awkwardness and even the blame, until clenched fists become clasped hands. That costly go-between work is the family likeness of God, who in Christ stepped between heaven and earth to make peace by his blood (Col 1:20).

We can only make peace because peace was first made with us: Christ "is our peace" (Eph 2:14), reconciling us by his blood (Col 1:20) before ever sending us out to reconcile others.

The word Jesus uses is unusual enough to be worth flagging: eirenopoios occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. It is a compound — peace plus make — and the making is the point. Not peace-lovers, not peace-wishers, not people who find conflict distasteful. People who go and do something about it.

Which is why the distinction between peacemaking and peacekeeping matters so much practically. Keeping the peace usually means arranging for a difficulty not to be mentioned. It is cheap, it is quiet, and it is very often the opposite of what this verse commends, because the thing left unsaid goes on rotting. Making peace means going into the difficulty on purpose, which is expensive and nearly always uncomfortable, and it is the reason the beatitude sits where it does — immediately before persecution. Peacemakers get hit from both sides. That is the job.

Then the promise, and there is a small grammatical detail in it. They shall be called sons of God is a passive with no agent named — the construction Jews used precisely to avoid saying God will call them out loud. It is God who does the calling. Not the two parties who were reconciled, who may well be ungrateful; not the watching community, which may take a different view. The verdict comes from somewhere else.

And sons of God is a statement about family likeness rather than status. In Hebrew idiom a son of something means one who bears its character — sons of thunder, son of encouragement, sons of disobedience. To be called a son of God is to be recognised as having done what God does.

Which is worth stating plainly, because it fixes what peacemaking actually costs. God did not make peace by overlooking anything, or by persuading the offended party to be reasonable, or by arranging for the matter not to come up. He made peace by the blood of his cross (Col. 1:20) — by absorbing the whole cost himself so that the wrong could be genuinely dealt with rather than genuinely ignored.

So a peacemaker in this sense is not somebody with a talent for smoothing things over. It is somebody willing to carry a cost that is not theirs in order that something broken can be properly mended. There is no cheaper version, and the family resemblance is the willingness to pay.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The final beatitude closes the bracket: the kingdom of heaven belongs to the persecuted just as it belongs to the poor in spirit (v. 3). Persecution for righteousness' sake is not random suffering but the suffering that comes specifically from kingdom allegiance. The world does not persecute the harmless; it persecutes those whose righteousness exposes its darkness. The blessing of the persecuted is that they are in good company.

It need not be a prison cell. It may be the colleague quietly sidelined for refusing to fudge the figures, or the teenager frozen out for not joining the cruelty in the group chat. When obedience to Christ costs you something at others' hands, you are not unblessed — you stand exactly where the citizens of the kingdom have always stood.

And the persecuted are blessed because they suffer with the One who was cast out for them; in him the kingdom is already theirs, untouchable by any who revile them.

This is where the bracket closes, and it is worth seeing how tightly.

Verse 3: theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Verse 10: theirs is the kingdom of heaven. The same six words, and the six beatitudes between them all promise something in the future tense — shall be comforted, shall inherit, shall be satisfied, shall receive mercy, shall see God, shall be called.

Only the first and the last are in the present. The set opens and closes with something already owned.

Which is a deliberate arrangement, and its effect is this: the poor beggar at the front door and the hunted disciple at the back are told the identical thing, and it is the only thing in the list they do not have to wait for.

Then the qualifier, which is the whole of the verse's honesty: for righteousness' sake. Jesus is not blessing suffering as such, and he is not blessing every cost a Christian pays. Peter drew the line as sharply as it can be drawn: let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer or as a meddler (1 Pet. 4:15). Being disliked because one is difficult, or tactless, or self-righteous, or wrong about something, is not persecution. It is consequences.

And the guard runs the other way too, because in comfortable countries this verse gets reduced to social awkwardness while a very large part of the church elsewhere is in genuine danger. Both distortions are worth avoiding: manufacturing a persecution one does not have, and quietly deciding the verse belongs to history.

The honest position for most Western Christians is neither. It is to notice that the verse describes a normal condition of kingdom life, to ask why it so rarely touches us, and to be careful what conclusion we draw from the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eighth beatitude shifts from third person ("they shall") to second person ("you") — it becomes personal. Persecution "on my account" identifies Jesus as the issue: it is allegiance to him, not merely being good, that draws the world's opposition. The command to rejoice is not false cheerfulness but eschatological perspective: the reward is in heaven, where no moth destroys and no thief breaks in. The link to the prophets is crucial: persecution does not mark the disciple as having failed; it marks them as standing in the line of those who faithfully proclaimed the word of God to a resistant generation. To be persecuted for Christ is to be in the best possible company.

Such suffering is no sign of God's frown but a mark of union with his Son, who was reviled first and in your place; the great reward is grace upon grace, not wages owed.

Two shifts happen here and both are deliberate.

The first is the pronoun. Eight times Jesus has said blessed are those — third person, a description of a category. Now: blessed are you. He turns from describing to addressing, and he does it in the last one, after the crowd has had eight sentences to work out whether they are in the list.

The second is the ground. Verse 10 said persecution for righteousness' sake. Verse 11 says on my account.

Those are made equivalent, and the substitution is enormous. A man on a Galilean hillside has just replaced the abstract standard of righteousness with himself, in consecutive sentences, without argument or explanation, in front of people who would stone a man for less. Nobody in that crowd could have missed it.

Then the command, and it is the least natural instruction in the sermon: rejoice and be glad. The second verb is agalliao, which is not quiet contentment — it means to leap, to exult, the word for the kind of gladness that gets up and moves.

He is not telling them to pretend the slander does not hurt. He is telling them that when it comes there is something to be glad about, and he gives two reasons rather than one.

The first is forward: your reward is great in heaven. The second is backward, and it is the more immediately useful: for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.

That is a strange comfort until you feel its weight. The natural reading of being attacked for your faith is that something has gone wrong — that you have handled it badly, or that God has withdrawn, or that the whole thing was a mistake. Jesus offers a different diagnostic: this is what happened to Isaiah, and Jeremiah, and Elijah, and every man God ever sent. If it is happening, you are standing where they stood.

The company is the argument. It is not that suffering proves you are right — plenty of people suffer for being wrong. It is that this particular kind of suffering, for this particular reason, has a long and honourable history, and the people in it are the ones God kept sending.

verseByVerse.quote: You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet. You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Both metaphors are declarative — "you are" — not aspirational ("you should become"). The identity precedes the calling. Salt in the ancient world was the primary preservative: before any form of refrigeration, packing fish or meat in granular salt drew out moisture and inhibited bacterial growth, extending the useful life of food by weeks or months. The Galilean fishing industry that employed Peter and Andrew depended entirely on this process — salted fish from the Sea of Galilee were traded through markets across the empire. Salt was so valuable it was sometimes used to pay wages; the Latin salarium (salary) derives from sal, salt. Disciples function as salt in exactly this way: they slow moral and social decay by their presence in the world. A community of truthful, faithful, just people in a neighborhood does not transform it by force or noise but by the quiet, persistent influence of transformed lives — the way salt works through meat: slowly, thoroughly, from the inside. Tasteless salt is useless — the warning is against a Christianity so fully assimilated into its culture that it has nothing left to preserve or season. Light is simpler still: it is inherently visible. A city on a hill cannot choose to be hidden; its very existence makes it seen. The Christian life is unavoidably public — not in the sense of performance but in the sense of testimony. The question is not whether to be visible but what the visible life will say about the one who gave it.

But that warning about salt losing its taste unsettles people, so face it directly. Pure salt cannot stop being salty; that is simply what the compound is. The salt of that region, however, was dug from around the Dead Sea and came mixed with other minerals, and if it lay damp the salt itself could leach away and leave a white residue that looked exactly like salt and did nothing whatever. It had not turned into something else. It had gradually lost the one property that made it worth having, while keeping the appearance entirely.

That is the danger being named, and it is worth being honest about how it happens, because it is never a decision. Nobody wakes up and resolves to become indistinguishable. It happens by a hundred small accommodations — the joke you laugh at because not laughing would be awkward, the figure you round in your favour because everyone does, the opinion you keep to yourself for so long that you stop holding it. Each one is minor. The cumulative effect is a life that is now, on close inspection, exactly like every other life in the office, with a religious residue on top.

So ask the diagnostic question rather than the anxious one. The anxious question is "have I lost my saltiness?", and it tends to produce either despair or a burst of forced intensity that fades by Thursday. The better question is: if someone who knows me well were asked what difference Christ has actually made to how I work, spend, speak and treat people, could they name anything? Not something impressive — something different. If nothing comes to mind, that is not a verdict; it is information, and it is exactly the kind of thing the next chapter and the rest of this Sermon set about changing. And notice the tense Jesus uses throughout: not become salt, but you are the salt of the earth. He is not issuing a target. He is telling his disciples what he has already made them, and then warning them not to waste it.

verseByVerse.quote: Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lamp on a stand gives light to all in the house — not selected people, not just those who deserve it. The purpose of good works is not self-promotion (chapter 6 will condemn that) but the glory of the Father. The distinction is crucial: works done to be seen by others for their praise are hypocrisy; works done before others so that God is praised are witness. The same deed — giving to the poor, visiting the sick, speaking truth — can be either, depending on whose glory it seeks. Jesus calls his disciples to a visible, costly life whose visibility is always directed upward: not "look at me" but "look at my Father." Light points beyond itself to its source.

All of which leaves the practical question this passage is famous for and rarely answers: what does being salt and light actually look like on an ordinary Tuesday, without turning into the person at work everyone quietly avoids?

Start by noticing that the two pictures do different jobs, and most of us fail at one or the other. Salt works by being different — quietly, thoroughly, from the inside, and largely without announcing itself. Light works by being seen. So there are two ways to fail here, and they are opposite. The first is the salt that leached away: you are perfectly pleasant, entirely assimilated, and nobody around you could name a single thing about your life that would need explaining if there were no God. The second is the lamp under the basket: you are visibly different — honest, unusually kind, unwilling to join the pile-on — and nobody has ever been told why. Everyone thinks you are simply a nice person. The first failure has nothing to say; the second has something to say and never says it.

Made concrete, the saltiness is mostly unglamorous. It is the expense claim that is accurate when nobody checks. It is declining to join the character assassination in the group chat, without making a speech about it. It is how you speak to the person who can do nothing for you — the cleaner, the junior, the difficult customer — when there is no audience. It is being the one who tells the truth when the truth is expensive, and being known for it. None of that requires a platform, and none of it makes you insufferable; people notice it precisely because it is rare.

And the light is simply being ready to say why, when the question comes — and it does come, eventually, to people who live like that. Not a prepared speech; a plain answer, briefly given: this is what I believe, and this is the difference it has made. Peter puts it exactly this way — always ready to give a reason for the hope that is in you, and he adds, with gentleness and respect (1 Pet 3:15). The manner is part of the instruction.

Then hold onto the test in the verse itself, because it settles the fear of showing off. The aim is not that people should think well of you; it is that they should give glory to your Father who is in heaven. That is a usable measure. If the effect of your visible life is that people admire you and never once think about God, the lamp is pointing the wrong way, however bright it is. And if you feel you have been poor at this — dim, tasteless, silent for years — remember what a lamp is. It produces no light of its own. It only holds up something that was lit from elsewhere, and it can be lit again this morning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–48 — The Law Fulfilled: A Righteousness That Exceeds
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus addresses the relationship between his teaching and the law of Moses: he has not come to abolish but to fulfill. He then gives six antitheses — "You have heard... but I say to you" — in which he does not contradict the law but penetrates to its interior logic. Murder begins in anger; adultery begins in the look; divorce fractures the covenant; oaths corrupt speech; retaliation perpetuates violence; hatred divides what love should unite. The section climaxes with the demand: "You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect." — a standard no one reaches by effort, which is exactly why it drives us to the Christ who fulfilled the law in our place and to the Spirit who reshapes us from within.
verseByVerse.theology: The antitheses reveal that the law was always concerned with the heart, not merely the external act. Jesus does not introduce a new, stricter morality; he discloses the full depth of what God always intended. The Pharisees' righteousness was wide but shallow — it covered the surface of behavior without reaching the roots of motive and desire. The righteousness Jesus requires exceeds theirs not by adding more external rules but by going deeper into the same terrain. This is why grace must precede the Sermon on the Mount: no one can produce this righteousness by effort; it must be worked in us by the Spirit of the one who fulfilled the law perfectly. To "fulfill" the law (v. 17) is not to abolish it but to bring it to its goal: by his flawless obedience Jesus meets its every demand, in himself he embodies the types and shadows that pointed forward, and at the cross he bears its curse. And the righteousness that "exceeds" the Pharisees comes in two layers — first the perfect righteousness of Christ credited to us through faith, the only righteousness that truly opens the kingdom, and then the real if imperfect righteousness the Spirit grows in a regenerate heart. So the very law that drives the unbeliever to Christ by exposing his sin becomes, for the believer, the shape of a Spirit-empowered life of love. Read this way, the towering standard of verse 48 humbles without crushing: it sends us to Christ for a righteousness we cannot produce, and then to the Spirit who produces it in us.
verseByVerse.examples: The demand for perfection (v. 48) has driven interpreters in two directions: some make it an impossible ideal that drives us to grace; others read it as a call to wholeness or completeness (the Greek teleios can mean "complete" or "mature"). Both are partially right: the standard is God's own character, which we cannot reach by effort, but which the Spirit progressively conforms us to (2 Cor. 3:18). The sermon is both a mirror that shows us our need and a map of the life the Spirit produces in those who have received the kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. For truly, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus flatly denies that he has come to abolish the Law or the Prophets — that is, the whole Old Testament. He has come to fulfill them, and that word means far more than merely to obey. He fulfills the law in every dimension at once. He fulfills its demands, keeping perfectly by his own obedience what Israel and all of us have broken. He fulfills its types and shadows, for the sacrifices, the temple, the priesthood, and the feasts all pointed forward to him, and he is the reality they foreshadowed (Lk 24:44). He fulfills its penalty, bearing on the cross the curse the law pronounces on those who break it (Gal 3:13). And he fulfills its true meaning, pressing its commands to their full inward depth, as the rest of this chapter will show. The law prescribed and demanded a righteousness no sinner could ever produce; Jesus is the one who at last produced it, embodied it, and is himself its goal (Rom 10:4).

That is the key to the next line. Not the smallest letter (the iota, the Hebrew yod) nor the tiniest pen-stroke of the law will pass away — it stands utterly secure — "until all is accomplished." The law is not scrapped; it is carried to its appointed completion, and that completion is reached above all in Christ: in his perfect life, his atoning death, and his resurrection, with the final consummation still to come when heaven and earth themselves pass away. This is why Paul can say the believer has "died to the law" and is no longer under it (Rom 7:4–6). He does not mean the law was a mistake; he means that, now that Christ has accomplished it and borne it for us, we are released from it as a covenant of works — no longer under its demand to "do this and live," and no longer under its condemnation, because Jesus met the demand and absorbed the curse in our place.

What, then, is our relationship to the law now? It still has vital work to do — but different work for different people. For the one not yet in Christ, the law is God's faithful schoolmaster: by exposing sin and silencing every excuse, it strips away the illusion of self-righteousness and drives the sinner to the only Savior who can rescue him (Gal 3:24; Rom 3:20). The law cannot save, but it can, mercifully, make us desperate for the One who can. For the one already in Christ, the law is no longer a ladder to climb for salvation or to earn God's love; that love is already ours, freely, in his Son. Yet the moral heart of the law — which is love, love for God and neighbor (Rom 13:10; Matt 22:37–40) — remains the very shape of the redeemed life. (Its old shadows, the ceremonies and sacrifices, have done their work and found their home in Christ; its abiding moral substance stands.) What was once an external code demanding from without, the Spirit now writes on the heart from within (Jer 31:33), enabling us to walk in it — not as cowering slaves earning a wage, but as beloved children, free at last to love (Rom 8:3–4). This is the glad paradox: freed from the law as a way to be saved, freed for the law as the way of love, and carried along in it now by the power of the Spirit.

It is worth noting, with respect, how this passage looks through dispensational eyes, since many faithful believers (perhaps your own fellowship) read it that way. Dispensational theology stresses a sharp distinction between Israel and the church and between the successive eras, or dispensations, of God's dealings. On this reading the Law of Moses was given to national Israel as a single, unified code, and at the cross that whole code came to an end for the believer; the Christian now lives not under the Law of Moses at all but under "the law of Christ" (Gal 6:2; 1 Cor 9:21), the commands of the New Testament. Many dispensationalists are therefore wary of the Reformed threefold division of the law (moral, ceremonial, civil) and of calling the Mosaic moral law the believer's rule; they prefer to say we follow Christ's commands, led by the Spirit. Classic dispensationalists also tended to read the Sermon on the Mount as primarily kingdom law — ethics belonging to the coming earthly kingdom — with only secondary application to the church now, though many today (the progressive dispensationalists) apply it directly to Christian living.

The difference from the covenantal reading offered above is real, yet narrower than it first appears. Both sides gladly confess that we are saved by grace through faith and not by law-keeping, that the believer is not under the Mosaic law as a covenant of condemnation, that Christ fulfilled the law, and that the law still convicts the sinner and drives him to Christ. The chief divergence lies in the framework: where the Reformed see one covenant of grace running through both Testaments and the moral law abiding as the believer's guide (the third use), the dispensationalist sees a sharper break — the Mosaic code ended, and the believer now guided by the law of Christ. In practice both walk the same road of Spirit-empowered love; they chart it differently. (See the note at 4:17 on the kingdom for the larger picture behind this difference.)

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Feel first the shock of these words. In that world the scribes and Pharisees were the gold standard of holiness; no one was reckoned more devout. So when Jesus says you must out-righteous the most righteous men alive or you "will never enter the kingdom of heaven," it lands like a thunderclap. The ordinary listener thinks: if they fall short, what hope is there for me? The Pharisee bristles: who is this to say my righteousness is not enough? Jesus means to unsettle them both — to close off every road of self-confidence before he opens the only door that works.

"Relaxes" on the surface warns any teacher who loosens God's commands and trains others to do the same. But there is a sharp irony here, and Jesus surely has the Pharisees in view: the men who looked strictest were in truth the great relaxers. They buried the law under a mountain of extra rules, yet hollowed out its real weight — and at points their traditions actually cancelled God's commands. Jesus would later expose exactly this: by their rule of "Corban" they let a man neglect his own aged parents and so "made void the word of God" by their tradition (Mark 7:9–13). To keep the letter while killing the heart, and to prize human tradition over God's clear word, is the worst relaxing of all.

How should we hear it today? You may worry: if not one command may be relaxed, must you still keep the Sabbath, the food laws, the feasts? Read it with verses 17–18 in hand. Jesus upholds the law's full authority — but he fulfills it, and its ceremonial, shadow parts (sacrifices, clean and unclean foods, holy days, the Sabbath as a sign) reach their goal in him. They were "a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ" (Col 2:16–17). So we honor those laws not by repeating the shadows but by trusting the One they always pointed to; to rest in Christ is not to relax the law but to keep it at its deepest. The moral substance abides in full force — and a rhythm of rest and worship remains God's good gift — while the verses just ahead show Jesus pressing that moral law deeper than the Pharisees ever dreamed. Freed from the ceremonial burden, we are bound more sweetly to love.

Notice, too, that the one commended both "does them and teaches them." Teaching is not enough; the kingdom prizes doing. This is the note James will sound: "be doers of the word, and not hearers only" (Jas 1:22); a faith that produces nothing is dead (Jas 2:17). But hear it through the gospel: this is about the trajectory of a life, not the perfection of it. The "great in the kingdom" are not the flawless but the sincere — those whose hearts mean to obey, who keep turning back after every stumble, and whose doing springs from grace received, not merit earned.

What, then, was wrong with the Pharisees' righteousness, and what must exceed it? Their flaw was not too much obedience but hypocrisy: they did their good works for their own honor rather than for God — a costume worn for the applause of men, as chapter 6 will lay bare (alms, prayer, and fasting done "to be seen"). A righteousness that surpasses theirs must therefore be of a wholly different kind, and it comes in two layers. First and foundationally, it is a righteousness that is not our own at all: the perfect righteousness of Christ, credited to us through faith (Phil 3:9). That alone truly exceeds the Pharisees and opens the kingdom, for it is flawless — and it is a gift. Then, flowing out of that gift, comes a real if imperfect righteousness of the heart: the Spirit giving a new heart and moving us to walk in God's ways (Ezek 36:26–27). Theirs was wide, shallow, and for show; this is deep, genuine, and for God.

So let the verse land as Jesus intends. He sets the bar impossibly high — surpass the holiest people you know — not to crush you, but to drive you off your own righteousness and into his. Received by faith, his perfect righteousness becomes yours; and the same grace that clothes you sends the Spirit to make you, slowly and truly, into the kind of person these words describe. The mountain you could never climb turns out to be, in Christ, first a gift and then a joy. You are not weighed, found wanting, and sent away; you are clothed, accepted, and changed from the inside out. Obey, then — not to win a love you lack, but because that love is already, freely, yours.

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said to those of old, "You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment." But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever insults his brother will be liable to the council; and whoever says, "You fool!" will be liable to the hell of fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first antithesis penetrates murder to its root: anger. The law prohibited the act; Jesus prohibits the inner state from which the act grows. He is not adding a new law alongside the old but revealing what the old law always implied about the seriousness of human life and the dignity of persons made in God's image. Every insult is an assault on someone who bears the divine image. The escalating liability — judgment, council, hell — tracks the escalation of contempt: from anger (the emotion) to insult (the word) to "you fool" (the verdict that dismisses a person as worthless). To preach the full force of this image, a congregation needs to know what each level of liability actually was. "Judgment" referred to the local town court — a council of twenty-three elders in each village, the normal venue for property disputes and lesser offences. "The council" was the Sanhedrin, the Great Council in Jerusalem: seventy-one members, the supreme religious and judicial authority of all Israel, convened only for the gravest capital cases. "Hell of fire" is Gehenna — the Greek form of ge-hinnom, the Valley of Hinnom, a ravine running along the south side of Jerusalem. Its history was notorious: it was the site where King Manasseh had sacrificed children to the Ammonite god Molech (2 Kings 23:10), an act so abominable that King Josiah defiled the valley afterwards to prevent any future use. By the time of Jesus, the Valley of Hinnom had become Jerusalem's garbage dump — a place where refuse smoldered continuously, where the bodies of executed criminals were disposed of, and where the fires never quite went out. That perpetually burning ravine outside the city wall had given first-century Jews their primary image for the place of eternal judgment. The escalation is therefore not merely rhetorical but architectural: from the village court to the supreme national tribunal to the judgment seat of God himself — three levels of accountability corresponding to three levels of contemptuous speech. Jesus treats contemptuous speech as a moral catastrophe, not a social failing. The tongue that dismisses a person as worthless attacks someone who bears the image of God.

But is all anger sin? No — there is such a thing as holy anger. God himself is "angry with the wicked every day" (Ps 7:11); Jesus looked around "with anger" at hard hearts (Mark 3:5) and drove the money-changers from his Father's house. So Scripture can say, "Be angry and do not sin" (Eph 4:26). When you hear that a child has been abused or the innocent crushed and something in you burns, that fire can be right — it is love for the good recoiling at evil, a faint echo of God's own heart. Yet holy anger is rarer than we like to think, and it bears clear marks: it is stirred by God's concerns, not our wounded pride; it stays under control rather than flaring into contempt or revenge; it is slow, for "the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:19–20); and it spends itself in doing good and seeking justice, never in writing a person off as worthless. Hold most of our anger up to that test and we find it is really about us — our rights, our comfort, our honor — which is precisely the anger Jesus warns against.

So what should you do the next time anger rises? First, be slow — do not speak or strike in the heat; "a soft answer turns away wrath" (Prov 15:1). Second, look underneath it: ask what was really threatened, and you will usually find a bruised pride or a cherished idol rather than the glory of God — name it honestly to him. Third, take the anger to God before you take it to the person; pour it out to him and leave room for his justice, for "vengeance is mine, says the Lord" (Rom 12:19). Fourth, remember the gospel: you are the servant forgiven an unpayable debt (Matt 18:21–35), and the cross both shows that your own sin deserved wrath and that Christ has borne it — and that memory melts contempt into mercy. Then move toward the person: forgive, bless, and where you can, be reconciled — which is exactly where the next verses lead. And when the anger is the holy kind, let it drive you to your knees and into action for the wronged, never into bitterness. When you fail — and you will — do not despair; confess it, receive fresh forgiveness, and let the Spirit go on retraining your heart. He is not finished with you yet.

verseByVerse.quote: So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The practical implication of the first antithesis is stunning: reconciliation with a brother takes priority even over temple sacrifice. Not "after worship, attend to relationships" but "before worship, attend to relationships." God is not honored by worship offered by an unreconciled heart. The sequence is precise: remember, leave, go, reconcile, return. The gift waits at the altar while you attend to the broken relationship — because the God to whom the gift is offered cares more about the brother than the offering. This principle runs through all of Scripture: "I desire mercy and not sacrifice" (Hos. 6:6; Matt. 9:13). Vertical worship and horizontal relationship cannot be separated.

Notice carefully whose fault is in view: "your brother has something against you." This is not the case where someone has wronged you (that is Matthew 18:15); here you are the one in the wrong, and your brother is rightly aggrieved — and yet the burden to act still falls on you. Put the two passages side by side and the net is complete: if someone sins against you, you must go to him (18:15); if you have sinned against someone, you must go to him (here). Neither the wronged nor the wrongdoer is left an excuse to sit still. Love takes the first step in both directions.

What, then, does "be reconciled" actually look like? Suppose you have wounded your brother — a cutting word, a broken promise, a wrong quietly covered up. You are to go, and to go humbly. You name the specific sin plainly: "I was wrong to speak to you the way I did." You do not dress it up, excuse it, or smuggle in blame — no "I'm sorry if you were offended," no "but you started it." You own it, show real sorrow, and ask the costly little question pride hates: "Will you forgive me?" Where damage can be repaired or repaid, you repair it. And your brother, for his part, is called to forgive as God in Christ forgave him (Eph 4:32) — to say, and to mean, "I forgive you," and then to keep that word: not to rake it up again, not to hold it over your head, not to nurse it in his own heart or rehearse it to others. Forgiveness is a promise to bury the matter, as God buries our sins and remembers them no more (Jer 31:34).

But what if the brother will not be reconciled — what if you go, confess honestly, and are met with a cold shoulder? Are you now trapped, unable to worship with a clear heart? No. Paul gives the freeing limit: "If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all" (Rom 12:18). So far as it depends on you. You are answerable for your own part — honest confession and a genuine reaching out; you are not answerable for the other man's response, which you cannot control. Having truly sought peace, you may come and worship with a clear conscience, leaving your brother in God's hands and standing ready to be reconciled the moment the door opens. Another's unforgiveness can grieve you, but it cannot hold your worship hostage.

verseByVerse.quote: Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are going with him to court, lest your accuser hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the guard, and you be put in prison. Truly, I say to you, you will never get out until you have paid the last penny.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The court parable extends the teaching about reconciliation into practical urgency: settle debts before they reach judgment. The application is both horizontal (literal legal prudence) and eschatological (settle your account with God while there is time). The "last penny" (the smallest Roman coin) conveys the completeness of the debt that must be paid if reconciliation is refused and judgment comes. Jesus consistently frames the urgency of repentance in terms of limited time before a judgment that cannot be appealed. The window for reconciliation — with brothers, with God — is now. It will not always be open. The wise person settles debts while settlement is still possible.

That last line has carried more weight than it can bear. "You will never get out until you have paid the last penny" has long been cited, along with its parallel in Luke 12:59, in support of purgatory — a place of temporary punishment after death from which the soul is released once its debt is discharged. The word until does seem to promise an end to the sentence, and it is fair to ask why we do not read it so.

Three things stand in the way. The first is what kind of speech this is. Jesus is not drawing a map of the afterlife; he is urging two men at law to settle before they reach the courthouse steps, and he does it with the most ordinary scene imaginable — a debtor dragged off to prison. Doctrine cannot be read off the furniture of a parable. By the same method one would conclude from another of his stories that God is a judge who helps people only to stop them pestering him (Luke 18:1-8), which is the precise opposite of what that parable teaches.

The second is the idiom itself. A man in a debtors' prison could not earn; that was the whole horror of the institution. Locked up, he had no means of paying, and his family had to find the money or he stayed. So "until you have paid the last penny" is not a release date but a closed door — the same way we say a thing will happen when the cows come home, meaning it will not. The until measures the hopelessness of the debt, not the length of the stay.

And the third is what Scripture says the debt of sin actually cost. It was never a sum a sinner could work off by degrees, in this life or another. It was paid, in one payment, by someone else — and his own word for it was that it is finished (John 19:30). A purgatory in which the believer pays off a remainder implies that something was still outstanding when he said it. (The other verse pressed into this service, "either in this age or in the age to come," is handled at 12:32.) So take the urgency exactly as Jesus means it: settle now, on this side, while the road to the court still runs. But the settling he wants is not the first instalment of a payment plan. It is the empty-handed surrender of a man who has finally understood he cannot pay, throwing himself on the mercy of the One who already has.

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said, "You shall not commit adultery." But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second antithesis goes to the root of adultery: the intentional look of desire. Jesus does not criminalize involuntary attraction but the cultivated, intentional gaze — the look that uses another person as an object for self-gratification. The heart is the seat of adultery before the body is. This teaching demolishes every defense that stops at "I haven't done anything wrong" — the interior life is the domain of God's law as much as the external act. It also shows what adultery really is: the violation of covenant love, which begins not with the body but with the refusal of the heart to honor the exclusive claim of marriage. Faithfulness in marriage is a matter of the eyes and the heart, not only the bedroom.

Put some real-life color on this, for the line truly matters. It is no sin to notice that someone is beautiful — God made beauty, and the eye that registers it is working as he designed. Nor is the first, involuntary glance a sin, any more than the first arrival of a tempting thought is. Being tempted is not the same as sinning; our Lord himself "was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin" (Heb 4:15). What Jesus condemns is the second look that becomes a lingering, the desire deliberately fed, the imagination invited to stay and feast. Luther put it homely: you cannot stop a bird from flying over your head, but you can stop it building a nest in your hair. The bird is the temptation; the nest is the sin.

So consider your own case: your eyes keep getting drawn where they should not linger, you look away — and then walk off weighed down with guilt. Hear this clearly: the looking away is not your failure, it is your obedience — a small daily victory, and heaven is not frowning at it. Much of the burden you feel is false guilt, the accuser heaping condemnation on someone who actually fought and won, and "there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Rom 8:1). Where you truly did let the gaze linger and feed, the remedy is not to wallow but to confess it at once and receive the cleansing already promised (1 Jn 1:9), then walk on forgiven. And for the fight itself Scripture hands you tools: make Job's covenant with your eyes (Job 31:1); bounce the glance away quickly and flee rather than negotiate (2 Tim 2:22); and do not merely suppress the thought but replace it — turn the heart to Christ, give God thanks, even breathe a prayer for that person as a soul you will meet at the judgment, not an object to be used. Deepest of all, the cure for a wandering eye is a captured heart: as Christ becomes our greater treasure and joy, purity grows less from gritted teeth and more from love. The aim is not to never feel temptation, but to grow ever more satisfied in your Savior — and you can lift your head.

verseByVerse.quote: If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into hell. And if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body go into hell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hyperbole is violent precisely because the stakes are real. Jesus is not teaching self-mutilation — a blind man can still lust, a handless man can still sin. He is teaching the radical, decisive, immediate action required when sin has a foothold. "If your right eye" — the favored, dominant eye — "causes you to sin": even your best faculty, your sharpest tool, must be sacrificed if it is the instrument of your fall. Nothing is too precious to surrender in the war against sin. The repeated reference to hell (Gehenna, the valley of refuse outside Jerusalem associated with judgment) underscores that the war is not about self-improvement but about eternal life. Sin is not inconvenient; it is lethal.

What might such "cutting off" look like in your ordinary week? Start with the picture Jesus is using: a surgeon amputating a gangrenous limb. No one enjoys losing a hand — but better to lose the hand than let the poison take the whole body. That is the logic: deal with sin as ruthlessly as a doctor deals with spreading death. Now make it concrete. First, if the phone in your pocket has become the doorway to lust through late-night scrolling, the "eye" must go — install a filter, hand the phone to your spouse at night, even trade the smartphone for a plain one. The device is good; if it is the bridge to sin, the bridge comes down. Second, if a certain friendship, or an old flame, keeps dragging you into gossip, drink, or compromise, you may have to step back from it — even a dear relationship, if it is the hook that keeps catching you. Third, if the road home runs past the bar, or the bottle sits waiting in the cupboard, change the road and empty the cupboard; stop feeding the very thing you are trying to starve. Notice that in each case what is surrendered is something good or precious (the right eye, the right hand) — Jesus is not asking us to give up obvious evils only, but to part with anything, however valued, that has become the instrument of our fall. Radical? Yes. But no one haggles with gangrene.

Two guards, because this is one of the most misused paragraphs in the sermon and it has done real damage in both directions.

It is not literal, and the church has known that from the start. Origen is reported to have castrated himself over the next chapter's logic and the church regarded it as a tragedy, not an example. The decisive argument is internal: cutting off a hand does not stop a man wanting, and removing an eye does not touch the heart. Jesus has just spent six verses relocating sin from the act to the desire behind it. A remedy that dealt only with the limb would contradict everything he had said in the previous breath.

What the hyperbole does is set a price. He is not telling anyone to maim himself; he is saying that if it came to a choice between a maimed life and a lost soul, the arithmetic is not close — and that most of us have never once made a decision at anything like that exchange rate.

And it is not despair. A reader who takes sin seriously can hear this passage as a demand for a purity he knows he does not have, and conclude that the fire is his. Notice where it sits: eight verses after Jesus said the kingdom belongs to the bankrupt, and in a sermon preached by the one who would shortly be cut off in the place of everyone listening. The severity is real and it is not the last word.

Then the practical question, which is the only reason the paragraph is here. What does it look like to obey it? It looks like removing the thing that is actually feeding the sin, at real cost, before the moment of temptation rather than during it — the account deleted, the route home changed, the friendship ended, the device left downstairs. Every one of those is somebody's right hand: genuinely useful, genuinely missed, and genuinely the thing that keeps the wound open.

verseByVerse.quote: It was also said, "Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce." But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third antithesis addresses divorce. The certificate of Deuteronomy 24:1 was a concession to hardness of heart, not God's design (Matt. 19:8). Jesus restores the original intention: marriage is a covenant, and its dissolution is not a legal technicality but a moral rupture. The exception for sexual immorality acknowledges that the covenant can be broken by the other party; but apart from that, remarriage constitutes adultery — the ongoing violation of a covenant that God intended to be permanent. Jesus is not creating a hierarchy of sins but exposing the gravity of what society had trivialized. Marriage is not a contract to be terminated; it is a covenant image of God's own faithfulness to his people.

Let us walk through this slowly, because Jesus packs a great deal into a few words. In his day divorce had become casual and one-sided: a man could hand his wife a certificate and send her off, sometimes for the flimsiest reason (one famous rabbi allowed it even for a spoiled meal). It left women shamed and destitute, for a divorced woman usually had to remarry simply to survive. When Jesus says such a man "makes her commit adultery," he means this: because the divorce was not on valid grounds, in God's sight she is still bound to her first husband — so when she remarries (as she almost must), that new union counts as adultery, and the guilt traces back to the husband who wrongly cast her out. And "whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery" follows for the same reason: if her divorce was illegitimate, she is still another man's wife in God's eyes, and to marry her is to take what was not free to be taken.

Does this, then, forbid every divorced person from ever remarrying? Not quite — and the hinge is that small phrase, "except on the ground of sexual immorality." By making an exception, Jesus signals that there is a ground on which a marriage is genuinely broken, where divorce is permitted and a later remarriage is not adultery. So the sweeping "no remarriage" one might hear at first is really aimed at remarriage after an unjust, groundless divorce. Where there is true biblical ground, the picture changes.

Here we step onto contested ground, where faithful, Christ-loving brothers land in different places — so hold your convictions firmly but your charity wider. The historic Reformed position (as in the Westminster Confession) recognizes two grounds on which divorce is permitted and the innocent party is free to remarry: first, sexual immorality, the exception Jesus names here and in 19:9; and second, the willful, irreparable desertion Paul addresses — "if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so... the brother or sister is not enslaved" (1 Cor 7:15). Others read the exception more narrowly and conclude that no remarriage is permitted while the former spouse lives. Both camps are seeking to honor the same Lord and the same texts; this is a place for humility, not contempt.

That frame answers your two questions. If a marriage is broken by adultery, the innocent spouse — the one sinned against — is, on the mainstream Reformed reading, free to remarry; the covenant has been shattered by the other's unfaithfulness, and the exception clause exists precisely for such a case (a minority would still counsel against it, and they should be respected). And what of violence and heavy abuse? Scripture does not name it in so many words here, yet two things must be said plainly. First, and without any hedging: an abused spouse must get to safety — God never calls anyone to remain in danger, and the church must protect, never pressure. Second, many faithful pastors rightly judge that brutal, unrepentant abuse is itself a profound breaking of the marriage covenant, a true desertion of every vow to love and cherish, and so falls under the principle of 1 Corinthians 7. On that reading divorce is indeed permitted; some brothers would frame it more cautiously as separation, but none should ever bind a victim to ongoing harm. The God who hates the treachery of unjust divorce (Mal 2:16) does not delight in the slow destruction of one of his children.

Through it all, keep two truths together. Marriage is holy, a living picture of Christ's unbreakable covenant with his church (Eph 5:31–32), and divorce is always a tragedy, never a triviality. Yet for the reader who carries a broken marriage or a remarriage in his past, these words are not a sentence of permanent condemnation. There is full forgiveness at the cross for every sin, this one included, and grace to walk faithfully from today forward. Jesus guards marriage so fiercely because he is himself the Husband who will never divorce his bride — and that faithfulness is at once our standard and, when we have failed it, our refuge.

verseByVerse.quote: Again you have heard that it was said to those of old, "You shall not swear falsely, but shall perform to the Lord what you have sworn." But I say to you, Do not take an oath at all, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God, or by the earth, for it is his footstool, or by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King. And do not take an oath by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. Let what you say be simply "Yes" or "No"; anything more than this comes from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This fourth antithesis addresses oaths. The law permitted them and required that they be kept; the trouble was the whole system of evasion that had grown up around them. People swore by lesser things — heaven, earth, Jerusalem, their own head — treating such oaths as less binding than one sworn by God's name, a tidy loophole for the careful liar. Jesus cuts straight through it: every oath finally invokes God, for everything is his. Heaven is his throne, earth his footstool, Jerusalem his city, and you cannot so much as turn one hair white or black — your very head is his, not yours. There is no oath that does not call on God, and so no oath you can quietly break.

But the real target lies deeper than oath-formulas. The very need for oaths exposes how unreliable ordinary speech has become; an honest person reinforcing his word with a vow is half-admitting that his plain word is not trusted. So Jesus calls for a people whose word simply stands: "Let what you say be simply Yes or No." This is not a ban on every solemn vow in a lawful setting — Paul himself calls God as his witness (2 Cor 1:23), and God swears by his own name — but a call to such everyday truthfulness that reinforcement becomes pointless. Anything piled on top "comes from evil," a symptom of the fall's fracturing of human speech. In the kingdom a Christian's bare word should be as good as another man's sworn oath.

Does this mean you must blurt out everything you know? No. To be truthful is not the same as to be transparent about all things at all times. Scripture nowhere commands us to tell everyone everything; it forbids us to deceive. There is room for holy discretion — for keeping a confidence, for guarding what is not ours to share, for the wise silence Jesus himself kept before his accusers (26:63; 27:14), for simply declining a question that is not rightly asked. The line is clear: you may keep silent, but you may not lie; you need not say all, but what you do say must be true. Love will sometimes hold its tongue, but it will never speak a falsehood.

Two things about the oath-taking, since the passage is short and the practice it addresses has vanished.

The system Jesus is dismantling was an elaborate one. The rabbis had worked out which oaths were binding and which were not, and the distinction ran on whether the divine name was invoked. Swearing by the temple was not binding; swearing by the gold of the temple was. Swearing by the altar was not binding; by the gift on the altar, it was. Jesus takes the whole apparatus apart in chapter 23 with obvious contempt (23:16-22), and here he goes to the root: heaven is God's throne, earth is his footstool, Jerusalem is his city, and you cannot even change the colour of your own hair. There is no neutral object in the universe to swear by. Everything belongs to him, so every oath drags him in.

Which exposes what the graded system was really for. It was a machinery for lying honestly — for producing a form of words that sounded binding to the hearer while leaving a door open for the speaker. Anyone who has read a contract knows the instinct has not died.

And the alternative Jesus gives is startlingly small: let what you say be simply yes or no. Not a better formula — no formula. The reason a man reaches for an oath is that his bare word is not thought sufficient, and the remedy is not a stronger oath but a word that does not need one.

A note on scope, since Christians have divided over it. Some, notably the Quakers and the Anabaptists, have refused all oaths including in court, at considerable cost. The majority position, and the better one, is that Jesus is addressing the casual oath-taking of daily speech rather than the solemn judicial oath: God himself swears by his own name (Heb. 6:13), Paul repeatedly calls God as witness (Rom. 1:9; 2 Cor. 1:23), and Jesus himself answers the high priest when put under oath (26:63-64). But those who take the stricter line deserve respect rather than argument; they are erring, if at all, on the side of taking their Lord at his word.

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said, "An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth." But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also. And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Jesus turns to retaliation. "An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth" (the lex talionis) was never a license for revenge; it was a courtroom rule limiting punishment to fit the crime — a mercy, really, restraining the runaway blood-feuds of a violent world. Jesus now carries his disciples beyond even that restraint, from measured justice to refused vengeance.

The fifth antithesis on non-retaliation has been the most discussed and most misapplied. "Do not resist evil" does not mean passive acquiescence to all injustice; it means refusing the spiral of personal vengeance. The slap on the right cheek in the ancient context was typically a backhanded blow — an insult, not an assault. Turning the other cheek is not offering to be beaten twice; it is refusing to be drawn into the cycle of honor-shame retaliation. Similarly, surrendering the cloak with the tunic (all one had) is not masochism but a willingness to absorb personal loss rather than fuel a legal war. Jesus is teaching a transformed relationship to personal rights: hold them loosely, suffer loss without bitterness, refuse the calculus of revenge.

Bring it home to today. The "slap on the cheek" is rarely a literal blow for you; it is the insult, the affront to your pride — the colleague who belittles you in the meeting, the driver who leans on the horn and gestures, the cutting reply waiting to be typed under someone's post. The flesh wants the last word, the comeback, the even score; to turn the other cheek is to let the insult fall without firing back, refusing to feed the quarrel. The "tunic and cloak" is the personal grievance over money or property — the neighbor whose careless mowing wrecks your hedge, the handyman who overcharges, the relative who never repays the loan — and here it means being willing to swallow a loss rather than wage a bitter war to defend every last right. It reaches even into the home: when a spouse snaps or a teenager throws a barbed word, the kingdom way is to answer with calm instead of returning fire and letting the cycle spin on.

This is not a doormat's passivity, nor does it cancel the protection of the weak or the place of lawful justice; it is the deliberate surrender of personal vengeance. And you can let go of your rights like this only because they are safe in better hands. You follow the One who, "when he was reviled, did not revile in return... but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly" (1 Pet 2:23) — the Christ who absorbed the ultimate wrong, our sin, and answered it with a cross. When you know your honor and your future are secure in such a Savior, you can afford to lose an argument, swallow an insult, and even bless the one who wronged you.

verseByVerse.quote: And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. Give to the one who begs from you, and do not refuse the one who would borrow from you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The compelled second mile refers to the Roman practice of impressment — a soldier could compel a civilian to carry his pack one mile. Going a second mile is the voluntary act that transforms the resentful conscript into the willing servant. It is one of Scripture's most potent images of grace operating in ordinary, coerced situations. The command to give to beggars and not refuse borrowers extends the principle to economic life: the disciple holds his resources with an open hand, shaped by the generosity of the God who gives to all. None of this abolishes prudence or property rights; it reorients the heart's default posture from self-protection to self-giving.

Picture it today. The second mile is the willing extra: the worker who does more than the bare minimum and serves "heartily, as for the Lord" (Col 3:23); the man who, asked for one favor, cheerfully gives a little more; the believer who keeps serving a demanding boss or an awkward neighbor with grace instead of grumbling. This is the good sense in the common phrase "go the extra mile." But mark the limits, for love is not the same as having no boundaries. The extra mile is a free gift of love, not bondage to another's every demand. It does not mean endless overtime that swallows your evenings and starves your family — for caring for your household is itself a command of God (1 Tim 5:8), and a man who neglects his wife and children to chase his employer's approval (or his own ambition) has not gone the extra mile; he has merely changed which duty he is failing. Jesus himself withdrew to rest and pray, and said no when love required it. The point is a generous, willing heart — held by a wisdom that weighs the other things God has also given you to do.

The same heart, and the same wisdom, govern giving. "Give to the one who begs" forbids the tight fist and the grasping spirit that says, "what is mine is mine." The disciple's default is open-handed, ready to part with his money for someone in need. Yet generosity is meant to be wise, not naive, for love seeks a person's real good. Where the state already provides for basic needs, or where organized begging-rings exploit both the giver and the poor souls they put on the street, simply handing over cash may not help and can even feed harm — an addiction, or a criminal handler. There love still gives, but gives shrewdly: a meal rather than money, support to a shelter or mercy ministry that truly lifts people, time and the gospel alongside the gift. Two ditches line this road. One is the hard heart that hides its stinginess behind "they'd only waste it"; the other is a thoughtless giving that funds the very thing destroying a man. Walk between them — and when in doubt, lean to the side of open-handed mercy, for it is better now and then to be taken advantage of than to nurse a miserly heart.

verseByVerse.quote: You have heard that it was said, "You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy." But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same? And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing than others? Do not even the Gentiles do the same? You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This sixth and final antithesis is the most radical of all. "Hate your enemy" was never in the law of Moses; it was a popular gloss that fenced the word "neighbor" so as to shut enemies out. Jesus tears the fence down: love has no exception clause. To love an enemy is not merely to tolerate him or refrain from harming him; it is active goodwill that seeks his welfare even while he seeks your ruin — and its sharpest form is prayer, for to pray for a persecutor is to stand before God on his behalf and to begin to want for him what God wants. This is humanly impossible, which is precisely the point: only the grace of the kingdom can produce it.

Why love like this? Because it is the family likeness of God himself, who "makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust" — his kindness falls even on those who curse him. To love only those who love you back is mere reciprocity; it costs nothing and proves nothing, for even tax collectors and pagans manage that. The kingdom calls for a love that reaches past tribe, family, and affinity to the very people outside the circle. And we have known this love ourselves: "while we were still enemies" God loved us and gave his Son (Rom 5:8). We are simply to pass on the love that first reached us.

That is why Jesus can say, "You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect." The word (teleios) means whole, complete, undivided as much as flawless: the Father's "perfection" here is the wholeness of a love that knows no exceptions. His children are called to that same undivided love — not as a crushing legal bar, but as the shape of the life the Spirit is steadily growing in those who belong to him.

What might this look like for you? It is praying, by name and for their good, for the colleague who undermined you or the relative who has turned cold. It is the neighbor everyone gossips about finding his walk shovelled and no note left. It is choosing words that bless rather than bite about the one who wronged you, and quietly doing him a kindness when the chance comes. It is refusing to gloat when an enemy stumbles. None of it waits for the other person to deserve it — that is exactly the point.

But hear clearly what this does not mean. To love an enemy is not to pretend that evil is good, nor to leave the wicked unopposed. You may love a man and still report his crime, still shield the weak from him, still let just consequences fall — for God himself, all kindness, is also the righteous Judge. Nor does it mean staying in harm's way: loving an abuser does not require remaining his target, and praying for a violent man is fully compatible with getting yourself and others to safety. Enemy-love seeks the offender's true good and refuses personal revenge; it does not abolish justice, wisdom, or self-protection. Love and a clear-eyed stand against evil are not enemies.

5.theology:
The Law and the Gospel: The Threefold Use of the Law. Reformed theology has distinguished three uses of the law: the civil use (restraining evil in society), the pedagogical use (revealing sin and driving us to Christ), and the normative use (guiding the life of the believer). Matthew 5 exercises the second use with particular intensity: Jesus presses the law so deeply inward that no one can claim compliance, and in doing so drives every hearer to the mercy of the one who fulfilled what we cannot.

But Matthew 5 also exercises the third use: the Beatitudes, the salt and light images, and the love of enemies are not legal demands for the unregenerate but the description of the life the Spirit produces in those who are already citizens of the kingdom. The Sermon on the Mount is simultaneously gospel (this is what the kingdom looks like) and law (this is what you cannot achieve without the Spirit). Held together, they produce the only life worth living: dependent, transformed, and directed toward the glory of the Father.
5.examples:
Then: The Beatitudes describe the whole history of faithful Israel: Abel the righteous who was persecuted, Abraham the meek who sojourned in a land not his own, Hannah who mourned and was comforted, David the poor in spirit who wrote “a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 51:17). The Beatitudes are not new values; they are the values of the faithful covenant people, now fully embodied in the King who pronounces them and perfectly exemplified in his own life.

Now: The world’s beatitudes are the inverse of Jesus’: blessed are the confident, the successful, the powerful, the popular, the comfortable. The Sermon on the Mount is a collision with that value system at every point. The Christian who takes these beatitudes seriously will find themselves increasingly out of step with the surrounding culture — and increasingly at home in the kingdom. The persecution promised in verses 10–12 is not a possible outcome but a promised one: the world does not celebrate the values of the kingdom because the world is not the kingdom. But the kingdom is coming — and the persecuted will inherit it.

6.title: The Hidden Life of the Kingdom
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them, for then you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven. <sup>2</sup>Thus, when you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may be praised by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. <sup>3</sup>But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, <sup>4</sup>so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. <sup>5</sup>And when you pray, you must not be like the hypocrites. For they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, that they may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. <sup>6</sup>But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you. <sup>7</sup>And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words. <sup>8</sup>Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him. <sup>9</sup>Pray then like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. <sup>10</sup>Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. <sup>11</sup>Give us this day our daily bread, <sup>12</sup>and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. <sup>13</sup>And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. <sup>19</sup>Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, <sup>20</sup>but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. <sup>21</sup>For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. <sup>24</sup>No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money. <sup>25</sup>Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? <sup>26</sup>Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? <sup>33</sup>But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. <sup>34</sup>Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is a sustained meditation on hiddenness. Give in secret. Pray in secret. Fast without showing it. The recurring phrase is “your Father who sees in secret will reward you” — and it upends the entire economy of religious performance. If God sees in secret, then the audience that matters most cannot be seen. The religious life that performs for human approval has traded the eternal reward for the temporary one, and the exchange is catastrophic.

At the centre of the chapter stands the Lord’s Prayer — six petitions that together describe the whole of what the kingdom life looks like in communion with the Father. First, God’s glory: hallowed be your name. Then God’s reign: your kingdom come. Then dependence: daily bread. Then forgiveness: both received and given. Then protection: from temptation, from evil. The prayer moves from adoration to petition, from God’s agenda to human need, from the cosmic to the daily. It is the complete grammar of prayer in twenty-five words.

The chapter ends with an antidote to anxiety that is also a diagnosis of its cause. Anxiety is the fruit of serving the wrong master (v. 24). When God and money compete for ultimate allegiance, anxiety is the symptom of the conflict. The cure is not financial security but reorientation of treasure: seek first the kingdom, and the Father who clothes the lilies and feeds the birds will add what you need. This is not a prosperity promise; it is a priority promise. When the kingdom is first, everything else finds its proper place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Piety Before the Father: Giving, Prayer, and Fasting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus addresses three practices central to Jewish piety — almsgiving, prayer, and fasting — and in each case distinguishes the performance of these acts for human recognition from the genuine practice of them before God. The hypocrites have their reward: human applause, now and fully paid. Those who give, pray, and fast before the Father alone receive what the Father alone can give. The section includes the Lord's Prayer as the model of kingdom-oriented prayer: God-centered in its priorities, dependent in its petitions, and honest about the human need for forgiveness. Some details the summary passes over, all treated in the verse-by-verse. The prayer's shape: six petitions in two halves of three — the first three each say your (name, kingdom, will), the second three each say us (give us, forgive us, lead us not). Nothing about our needs appears until God has been addressed three times, and the first three are not requests for God to acquire anything — his name is already holy and his will already done in heaven; they ask that these become true here. Every pronoun in the prayer is plural. There is not one singular pronoun in it: a man praying alone at three in the morning still cannot say "me", and is asking for bread for people he has never met. Daily (v. 11) is epiousios, a word that appears nowhere in Greek literature before this — Origen, a native speaker, thought the evangelists had coined it. The two likely readings ("necessary for existence" and "for the coming day") arrive at the same place: one day's supply, asked one day at a time, which is the manna arrangement of Exodus 16 put into every Christian's mouth. Debts (v. 12) is Matthew's word, the commercial term for what is owed; Luke has "sins"; the familiar "trespasses" came in through Tyndale and the Prayer Book. A trespass is a line crossed and is over when it is over; a debt is a sum outstanding, which is the truer picture.
