And the tense of "as we also have forgiven" is past — already done, before the asking — matching 5:23-24, where the gift is left at the altar until the matter downstairs is settled.
verseByVerse.theology: The three acts — giving, prayer, fasting — are not optional extras but the basic disciplines of covenant life: relationship with the neighbor (giving), relationship with God (prayer), and relationship with the self (fasting). Jesus does not question whether his disciples will do these things; he assumes they will ("when you give," "when you pray," "when you fast"). The question is motive and audience. Hypocrisy is not performing religious acts — it is performing them for the wrong audience. The hypocrite plays to the crowd; the disciple plays to the Father. The Father's reward — his presence, his approval, his delight — is infinitely superior to human applause.
verseByVerse.examples: The Lord's Prayer contains the whole theology of the kingdom in miniature. It begins with the Father's character and glory (hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done) before turning to human need (daily bread, forgiveness, protection). The order is the order of Christian living: God first, then us. The disciple who prays this prayer daily is being trained in a way of seeing the world: God's kingdom is the primary reality; my needs are real but secondary; forgiveness received must be forgiveness extended.

verseByVerse.quote: Beware of practicing your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them, for then you will have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse is the banner over everything that follows. Jesus is about to give three examples of devotion — giving, prayer, and fasting — and this single warning governs all three: beware of doing your righteousness to be seen. Notice that it is not the deeds he forbids but the audience you perform them for. Only a chapter earlier he said, "Let your light shine before others, that they may... give glory to your Father" (5:16); here he says, do not parade your righteousness to be glorified yourself. The same act can spring from opposite hearts: the question is whether you are living before the eyes of the crowd or the eyes of your Father.

This struck close to home, for showy piety was the very air the religious elite breathed. Among the most admired teachers of the day, devotion had become a kind of public theater — alms given with fanfare, long prayers offered where the most people would notice, fasting worn on the face for all to see. In a culture built on honor and shame, religion was a recognized road to status, and Jesus' hearers would have known exactly the sort of person he meant.

And what does he mean by "no reward from your Father"? Simply this: if you do your righteousness to win human applause, then human applause is the whole of your pay — and that is all you will ever get. You chose your paymaster. The one who performs for the crowd is settled up by the crowd; nothing further is owed him from heaven — not because the Father is stingy, but because the deed was never really done for him. This "reward" is not the earning of salvation, which is God's free gift; it is the Father's fatherly delight and recompense over what his children do out of love for him. To trade that boundless, eternal reward for a few moments of being noticed is the worst bargain a soul can make.

The tension a careful reader feels here should be named, because it is real. One chapter ago Jesus said let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works (5:16). Now: beware of practising your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them.

Both cannot be softened into vagueness, and the resolution is in the last five words of the second one.

The issue is never visibility. Almsgiving, prayer and fasting were public activities in that culture and could not have been otherwise; a man who gave to the poor was seen doing it. What Jesus forbids is the visibility being the point — the in order to. And the two commands even have the same endings pulling in opposite directions: 5:16 says people should see and give glory to your Father, while the hypocrite here wants people to see and think well of him.

So the test is not whether anybody knows. It is what you would feel if nobody ever did — and, harder, what you feel when somebody else gets the credit for something you did.

The word for reward in verse 2 is worth having, since Jesus repeats it three times in this section. Apecho was the ordinary commercial term stamped on a receipt: paid in full. Papyrus bills of sale from the period use it constantly. So the sentence is not they have had some reward. It is: the account is settled, the receipt is issued, and there is nothing further outstanding.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus, when you give to the needy, sound no trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may be praised by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your giving may be in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hypocrites' trumpet-sounding before their charitable gifts is almost certainly hyperbole — a vivid image of the person whose generosity requires an audience. "They have received their reward" translates a commercial term (apechousin): paid in full, the account settled, nothing more coming. Human praise is real but small, present but passing; the Father's reward is eternal and overflowing — but it goes to those who were not chasing the lesser thing.

But notice what should drive our giving in the first place: not reward at all, but mercy. The very phrase "give to the needy" means literally to do an act of mercy — help reaching down to the poor because their need stirs our compassion. We give because we have seen a brother in want and love will not look away (1 Jn 3:17), and because we are imitating a God who is rich in mercy and gave to us when we could never repay (Eph 2:4). So the secrecy Jesus commands is not coldness; it is love so taken up with the person in need that it forgets itself. Giving to be seen keeps one eye on the mirror; giving for mercy's sake has both eyes on the neighbor and on God.

The instruction that the left hand not know what the right is doing is not a command to be deceptive but to be unselfconscious — to give without the inner register of self-congratulation that counts and remembers and expects recognition. Genuine generosity is not only hidden from others; it is, ideally, hidden from ourselves. We give, and we move on. The Father "who sees in secret" is the most attentive and the most just of all possible audiences: nothing done for him is missed, nothing is undervalued, nothing is forgotten. The reward is not named precisely because its content exceeds specification — it is the gift of God himself, which is everything.

Picture it simply. You hear of a young family at church who have fallen behind on their rent. You could write the check after the service, mention it to a few friends, and feel the warm glow of being known as a generous person — and that glow would be the whole of your pay. Or you can slip the money to the pastor in an unmarked envelope, "for the Hendersons, and please don't say who," then walk away and very nearly forget you did it. No one claps. But the Father saw — the Father who misses nothing, undervalues nothing, forgets nothing — and that quiet envelope, given for love and not for show, is laid up with him forever. Which giver would you rather be?

verseByVerse.quote: And when you pray, you must not be like the hypocrites. For they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, that they may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Standing prayer was normal Jewish practice — the posture of prayer. Jesus is not condemning the posture but the location chosen for maximum visibility: the synagogue and street corner, where the most people would notice. The alternative is not a different posture but a different room — the private room with the door shut, where the only audience is the Father. The room (tameion) was typically an inner storeroom, the most private space in a house. The point is not that only private prayer counts but that the motive of all prayer must be communion with the Father, not the cultivation of a reputation for piety. God responds to the cry of the heart, not the performance for the crowd.

Taken flatly, though, "go into your room and shut the door" would close every prayer meeting in the world, and that plainly is not what he means. The proof is four verses away. The prayer he is about to teach begins our Father, and keeps it up all the way through — give us, forgive us, lead us not. That is not a prayer for a man alone in a storeroom; it is a prayer that assumes company. He himself prayed aloud at the mouth of Lazarus's tomb and said openly that he did it for the sake of the people standing there (John 11:41-42), and his church prayed together from its first days — in an upper room, in a house at midnight, with one voice after Peter and John were released (Acts 1:14; 4:24; 12:12).

What he is regulating is the audience, not the address. The hypocrites had chosen their spot for the sightlines; the sin was in the choosing. So the question to put to yourself is not where you are standing but whether you would still say this if no one could hear it. And that is exactly why the shut door is the cure: it is the one place where the audience has been removed, so the habit formed there comes out honest everywhere else. A man who prays impressively in the meeting and never once alone has the very disease being described here. The closed door is not the enemy of public prayer; it is what makes public prayer truthful.

Two practical notes, since this is one of the few places Jesus gives instructions about the mechanics of prayer.

The room of verse 6 is tameion — not a bedroom but a storeroom or pantry, the inner room of a small house, often the only one with a door that shut and usually without a window. It was the least impressive space available. Jesus is not describing a study or a prayer-corner; he is naming the cupboard.

Which is worth knowing because it removes the last excuse. Nobody needs a suitable place. The instruction was given to people whose houses had one usable door, and it was the door of the larder.

And then the thing that is easy to miss in a passage about secrecy: your Father who sees in secret. The phrase occurs three times in this section, once for each discipline. It is not primarily a warning that God is watching. It is the promise that somebody is — that the giving nobody thanked you for, the praying nobody counted, and the fasting nobody noticed were all, in fact, observed.

The hypocrite's real problem is not that he wants an audience. It is that he has settled for a small one.

verseByVerse.quote: And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words. Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Gentile error is not length but magic — the assumption that words multiply and repetition compels divine attention. Pagan prayer often treated the gods as powers to be manipulated through the right formula repeated often enough. Jesus forbids this not because brevity is always better but because prayer is not a technique for bending God's will but a conversation with a Father who already knows. The staggering statement — "your Father knows what you need before you ask him" — does not make prayer superfluous; it makes prayer a relationship rather than a transaction. We pray not to inform God but to align our desires with his, to open our lives to what he already knows we need.

But this verse has troubled a great many people, so let it be said plainly what it does not forbid. It does not forbid long prayers: Jesus once spent the whole night praying (Luke 6:12). It does not forbid praying the same thing more than once: in Gethsemane he prayed the same words three times over (26:44), and he told a whole parable to teach his disciples to keep on asking and not lose heart (Luke 18:1-8). And it does not forbid a set form of words — which we know beyond argument, because in the very next sentence he gives one. The cure he prescribes for empty phrases is a written prayer of twenty-five words.

The word behind "empty phrases" suggests babbling, and the error he names is precise: they think that they will be heard for their many words. That is prayer treated as a mechanism — the right formula, said often enough, to work the desired result. It is the difference between a child speaking to his father and a man operating a machine. Once you see that, the anxiety about repetition falls away, because vainness is a quality of the heart and not of the vocabulary. The Psalms have been the church's prayer book for three thousand years and the Lord's Prayer has been said daily for two, and neither is vain when it is meant; while a man can babble quite as emptily off the top of his head as off a page, and often does, when he is really only filling silence or performing fluency for whoever is listening.

So pray at length when your heart is full, and briefly when it is not. Bring the same request back tomorrow, and the day after. Use the words others have written when your own will not come — that is what they are for. Only do not imagine that God is worn down by volume or won over by technique. He is a Father who already knows, and the reason to speak to him is not to inform him but to be with him.

verseByVerse.quote: Pray then like this: "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer opens not with our needs but with God himself — his name, his kingdom, his will — before it ever reaches our bread. Jesus teaches us to begin with the relationship and with God's glory; the very ordering retrains the heart, for we are made for God's agenda, not merely his assistance.

And feel first the wonder of the address: "Our Father." The eternal God, who needs nothing, who flung the galaxies into being and dwells in unapproachable light, invites us to call him Father. In the Old Testament hardly anyone dared address God so personally; yet Jesus hands his ragged disciples the family word. We can do this only because the Son has made us sons and daughters and the Spirit cries within us, "Abba! Father!" (Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6). This is no distant force and no stern tyrant, but the Father of the prodigal who runs down the road to meet his returning child. And it is "our" Father — we never pray alone, but as part of a great family. That a sinner like you may look up and say "Father," and be heard, and be loved, is a marvel that should never grow stale.

"Hallowed be your name." The word "hallowed" simply means treated as holy, honored, held precious. A name in the Bible stands for the whole person, so God's name is God himself as he has made himself known. This petition therefore asks: may you, Lord, be revered and loved and taken seriously — in a world that uses your name as a curse or forgets it altogether, in your church, and (here it turns personal) first of all in my own heart, on my own lips, in my own life. It is a prayer that God would stop being treated as common — and it begins with me ceasing to treat him so. Before I ask God for anything, I ask that he be honored as the treasure he is.

"Your kingdom come." Is the kingdom here already, or still to come? Both — and the prayer holds the two together. God's saving reign has truly arrived in Jesus (see the note at 4:17) and presses forward now wherever the gospel takes root and hearts bow to the King; yet its full and visible glory still waits for Christ's return. So to pray "your kingdom come" is to ask two things at once: extend your reign today — in me, in the lost being saved, in your church — and hasten the day you come again to make all things new. We pray it standing in the overlap of the ages, longing for more of what has already begun.

"Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven." In heaven God's will is done perfectly, gladly, without delay or grumbling; the angels delight to obey, and nothing there resists him. This petition asks that earth become like that — that God's good and perfect will be embraced and obeyed here as joyfully and fully as it is above. And, as ever, it starts at home: it is the prayer of a surrendered heart that says with Jesus in the garden, "not my will, but yours, be done" (Lk 22:42). It is at once submission (let your will, not mine, rule me), mission (let your will sweep over this rebellious world), and hope (let the day come when heaven and earth are one and every knee gladly bows).

verseByVerse.quote: Give us this day our daily bread,
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Give us this day our daily bread." After God's name, kingdom, and will, the prayer turns to our needs — and the very first is the humblest: bread, and only for today. "This day," not this year; like the manna that fell one morning at a time (Ex 16), it trains us in daily dependence rather than self-sufficient hoarding.

And do not think this petition is only for the poor. The man with a full bank account needs it just as much — perhaps more — for wealth tempts us to forget that every loaf comes from the Father's open hand. Money in the bank cannot make your heart beat, hold off illness, or secure tomorrow; rich and poor alike live, each day, on mercy. So Scripture prays, "give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me, lest I be full and deny you" (Prov 30:8–9). To ask for daily bread when the cupboard is stocked is to confess, gladly, that it is all gift.

And "bread" stands for more than food. The old teachers were right that under this one word we may bring to God everything we need for body and life: health and work, shelter and provision, strength for the day's tasks — yes, and wisdom for the meeting, patience with the children, courage for the hard conversation. Whatever today actually requires of you, you may ask your Father for it here, one day at a time. He welcomes the small, ordinary, practical requests of his children.

There is a genuine puzzle in this petition and it is worth knowing about, because it is one of the most famous unsolved problems in the Greek New Testament.

The word translated daily is epiousios, and before the Lord's Prayer it does not appear in Greek literature at all. Not in the classical authors, not in the Greek Old Testament, not — with one disputed and now lost papyrus scrap — in the everyday documents that have survived from the ancient world. Origen, writing in the third century and reading Greek as his own language, said flatly that it seemed to have been coined by the evangelists.

So nobody is entirely sure what it means. Three readings compete.

The first takes it from a root meaning necessary for existence: give us the bread we need to live. The second takes it as for the coming day — which in the morning means today's bread and in the evening means tomorrow's, and either way is one day's supply. The third, which Jerome adopted in the Latin, renders it supersubstantial, and a long tradition has read the petition as asking for the bread of the Lord's Supper.

The first two are the likely ones, and they arrive at the same place: enough for one day, asked for one day at a time. The third is almost certainly not what Jesus meant, and it is worth saying why — the whole context is unmistakably ordinary. Debts, temptation, evil. And beyond that, this prayer was given to men who had not yet been to the Supper, which was still three years away.

What the strangeness of the word does confirm is the manna. Israel could not gather manna for two days without it breeding worms, and the whole arrangement was designed to make a nation ask again every morning. This petition puts the same arrangement into the mouth of every Christian who has ever prayed it.

One more thing, and it runs through the entire prayer: every pronoun in it is plural. Give us. Our daily bread. Forgive us our debts. Lead us not. Deliver us.

There is not one singular pronoun in the Lord's Prayer. A man can pray it alone in a room at three in the morning, and he still cannot say me. He is asking for bread for people he has never met — which quietly makes it impossible to pray this prayer and remain unconcerned about whether anybody else has any.

verseByVerse.quote: and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." Here a real fear can rise up: am I earning God's forgiveness by forgiving others? Must I perform mercy in order to purchase pardon? No — and it is vital to see why. The forgiveness God grants is bought entirely by the blood of Christ and received by faith alone, never earned by anything we do (Eph 1:7). This petition is not a price tag on pardon.

What, then, does the "as" mean? It is a correspondence, not a payment. We come asking mercy as people who are themselves showing mercy — for the forgiven heart forgives. Jesus made this unforgettable in the parable of the servant forgiven a debt he could never repay, who then seized a fellow servant by the throat over a trifle (Matt 18:21–35). His refusal to forgive proved he had never really grasped the mercy shown to him. So an unforgiving, grudge-nursing heart is no small fault; it is evidence that God's grace has not truly landed.

It helps, too, to hold two things apart. Our standing before God as forgiven children — our justification — is settled once for all by faith and cannot be lost. But our daily fellowship with the Father, like a child's warmth with a parent, is chilled when we cling to bitterness; so we keep coming, keep confessing, keep being cleansed. That is why the order always runs from grace outward: "forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you" (Eph 4:32). We forgive because we have been forgiven, not in order to be. So if forgiving someone feels impossibly hard, do not grit your teeth and try to earn heaven by it — go back and look again at the mountain of debt God cancelled for you at the cross. A heart melted by mercy received becomes, almost without trying, a heart that gives mercy away.

Two notes on the wording, since congregations say this prayer in at least three different forms and people wonder which is right.

Matthew's word is debts — opheilemata, the ordinary commercial term for what is owed. Luke, recording the prayer on a different occasion, has sins in the first half and then everyone who is indebted to us in the second (Lk. 11:4). Both are recording the same underlying Aramaic, where the word for a debt had long been used for a sin: something owed and not paid.

The familiar English trespasses comes from neither. It entered through Tyndale and reached most of the English-speaking world through the Book of Common Prayer, and it is a fair enough rendering of the idea — though something is lost. A trespass is a line crossed. A debt is a sum outstanding, and it goes on being outstanding whether or not anyone mentions it.

Which is the more uncomfortable picture, and the truer one. Sin is not only a series of boundary violations, each of which is over when it is over. It is an account that accumulates.

The second note is the tense, and it settles the question the entry above has been answering. As we also have forgiven our debtors is a past tense in the Greek — already done, before the asking. Not as we promise to forgive, and not as we are willing to forgive if pressed. The petition assumes a man comes to God having already dealt with what he holds against other people.

Which is exactly what Jesus says elsewhere in this sermon: if you are bringing your gift to the altar and remember that your brother has something against you, leave the gift, go, be reconciled, and then come and offer it (5:23-24). The order is the same. Settle it downstairs before you come up.

verseByVerse.quote: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Lead us not into temptation" does not imply that God tempts his people (James 1:13) but asks that he not allow us to be brought into trials beyond our strength (1 Cor 10:13). The prayer owns our fragility before temptation and casts the whole burden of protection on the Father. "Deliver us from evil" — the Greek can mean "the evil one" (Satan) or "evil" as a force; both are true. So the prayer ends just where it began: in dependence on the Father, not in self-confidence.

And here a reader with an open Bible meets a puzzle. In church we end the prayer, "For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever. Amen" — but the ESV stops at "deliver us from evil" and drops that ending to a footnote. Why? Because the oldest and best manuscripts of Matthew do not have it; it appears first in later copies. Almost certainly the early church, praying this prayer aloud in worship, added a fitting note of praise at the close (its words echo David's "Yours, O LORD, is the kingdom... and the power and the glory," 1 Chron. 29:11), and over time that beautiful response was copied into the text itself. So it is not part of what Matthew wrote — but there is nothing wrong with praying it. It is thoroughly biblical, and it ends the prayer exactly where the prayer means to end: not on our need or the evil one's threat, but on the Father whose the kingdom and the power and the glory are, forever. Pray it freely; just know why your Bible sets it in a footnote.

Two further things, one about the shape of the prayer and one about what the last petition is actually asking for.

The shape. There are six petitions and they fall into two halves of three. The first three are about God and every one of them says your: your name, your kingdom, your will. The second three are about us and every one says us: give us, forgive us, lead us not.

Nothing about our needs is mentioned until God has been addressed three times over. That is not because our needs are unimportant — half the prayer is about bread, guilt and danger, which is a fair summary of what a human life actually contains. It is because the order teaches something. A prayer that begins with me will very often never get past me.

And the first three petitions are not, on inspection, requests for God to acquire anything. His name is already holy; his kingdom is already coming; his will is already done in heaven. What they ask is that these things become true here — that the hallowing, the reign and the obedience arrive on the ground where the person praying is standing. Which means the first half of the prayer is asking God to change the world, and it starts with the one praying it.

The last petition. Lead us not into temptation — and the Greek word is the one that covers both testing and tempting, as at 4:1, where the Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness precisely to be tested. The knot is untied the same way here. God tests and does not tempt; the enemy tempts. The prayer is not asking God to stop doing something he does; it is the honest request of somebody who knows his own weakness and would rather not be brought to the edge at all.

Which is a striking thing for the Lord to teach. He does not tell his disciples to pray for courage under trial, or for strength to prevail. He tells them to ask not to be tried — and then, when it comes anyway, to ask to be got out. There is no bravado anywhere in it.

And deliver is a strong verb: to drag out of, to rescue from. It is the word for pulling somebody clear of something that has hold of them.

verseByVerse.quote: For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verses 14–15 turn the forgiveness-petition into a direct, sobering statement: those who forgive receive forgiveness; those who refuse to forgive find the same barrier raised before them. This is the one petition Jesus singles out to underline, the one that carries its own condition.

Yet the severity here is not a withdrawal of grace but a revelation of what genuine grace-reception looks like. The one who has truly grasped the enormity of his own forgiveness cannot keep withholding it from others — as the parable of the unforgiving servant will dramatize (18:21–35). An unforgiving heart is no small spiritual weakness; it is evidence that the grace of the gospel has not yet sunk in. (See verse 12 for why this is correspondence, not payment: we forgive because we have been forgiven, never in order to be.)

But a command this sharp needs one thing said clearly, because being unclear about it has done real damage to real people: forgiveness and reconciliation are not the same thing, and Jesus is commanding the first. Forgiveness is one-sided and unconditional — you can do it whatever the other person does, and you are told to. Reconciliation takes two, and it depends on the other person's repentance. Jesus himself puts the condition on the second and not the first: if he repents, forgive him (Lk 17:3); and Paul writes, with a realism worth noticing, if possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Rom 12:18). He knew it would not always be possible, and he did not lay the failure at the door of the one who tried.

So be exact about what you are being asked to do. To forgive is to give up your right to collect — to cancel the debt, to stop rehearsing the offence, to refuse to make them pay in the small currencies we actually use for it: the cold silence, the story retold to a friend, the reminder produced at the useful moment. That is a decision rather than a feeling, and it usually has to be made again tomorrow.

And be equally exact about what you are not being asked to do. You are not being asked to say it did not matter — God never says that about sin, and the cross is the measure of how much it mattered. You are not being asked to feel warmly, or to stop the memory hurting; forgiveness is a promise about how you will treat someone, not an emotion you must manufacture. You are not required to hand trust back as though nothing had happened — forgiveness is free, but trust is rebuilt slowly and only where there is real change, and it is not unforgiving to say so. You are not obliged to stay within reach of someone who is still harming you or your children; a person can be forgiven entirely from a safe distance, and where there is danger that is exactly where it should be done. And you are not obliged to shield an offender from lawful consequences — God gave the magistrate the sword (Rom 13:4), and reporting a crime is not revenge.

What if they are not sorry, and never will be? You can still release your own claim, and the Lord did it in front of you from the cross, praying for men who had not repented and were not going to that afternoon. What waits on their repentance is not your forgiveness but the restored relationship — and that may never come. That is a grief, and it is not your sin.

Finally, for anyone reading this carrying something too heavy to lift. The test of forgiveness is not that the wound has stopped aching, nor that you never think of it; it is whether you have stopped wanting their ruin and stopped trying to collect. If you cannot get there yet, do not pretend otherwise to God. Tell him plainly that you are unable, and ask him to make you willing to be made willing — that prayer is honest, and he has never despised it. This command was never a demand to feel differently by Friday. It is the slow work of a heart being melted by a mercy it never deserved, and the melting is his to do.

verseByVerse.quote: And when you fast, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces that their fasting may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, that your fasting may not be seen by others but by your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The turn to fasting follows the same logic as giving and prayer. The hypocrites fast dramatically, inviting sympathy and admiration for their spiritual rigor; they disfigure their faces so the fast will be noticed — and that applause is their whole reward. The gloomy, advertised face is the announcement of piety, which is precisely what real fasting must never be.

The instruction to anoint the head and wash the face is the instruction to appear normal — to conceal the fast from public view. Fasting was typically visible; Jesus reverses the signal: dress as if you are not fasting, so the fast stays between you and God alone. The pattern is now familiar — the secret act, the seeing Father, the certain reward. The three disciplines together shape the whole person: generosity toward others, communion with God, discipline of self — each practiced habitually, privately, and before the Father whose reward outweighs all human recognition.

Should you be fasting, then, if you never have? Start with what Jesus actually says: "when you fast," not "if" — just as with giving and praying, he simply assumes his disciples will do it. He fasted himself (4:2), and when asked why his disciples did not, he answered that the wedding guests do not fast while the bridegroom is with them, "but the days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast" (9:14–15) — that is, in this present age, ours. And the early church did: they fasted and prayed before sending out missionaries (Acts 13:2–3) and appointing elders (Acts 14:23). Yet notice what is missing — nowhere is fasting laid down as a law with required days (that was the Pharisees' way, twice a week and on show). So fasting is a freedom and a privilege, not an obligation: no one should bind your conscience to it or let you feel condemned for neglecting it, and yet neither should you simply shrug off what your Lord plainly assumed his people would do.

Why fast, and for what? Fasting is voluntarily setting aside food (or some other comfort) for a season in order to seek God. It intensifies prayer, especially at weighty moments and decisions (Acts 13:2–3; Ezra 8:21–23); it humbles us in repentance and grief over sin (Joel 2:12); and above all it turns the body's hunger into a cry of the heart — "man shall not live by bread alone" (4:4) — a way of saying, "Lord, I want you more than I want food." It is not a hunger strike to twist God's arm, not a diet for self-improvement, and not a badge of piety to flaunt; it adds nothing to a standing already complete in Christ. We fast not to be loved but because we are loved, hungering for more of him. And there is a tender thread in it: we fast because the Bridegroom is away for now, longing until he comes and the fast gives way to the wedding feast (9:15).

How, in practice? Start small and simple — skip a meal or a day, drink water, and let each pang of hunger send you to prayer; fasting without seeking God is merely dieting. Pair it with Scripture and prayer, for the whole point is to feed on God. Keep it hidden, exactly as these verses urge — between you and your Father, no gloomy face, no announcement. And use wisdom with your health: if illness, pregnancy, or a fragile history makes food-fasting unwise, you may set aside other comforts instead — screens, sweets, leisure — for God looks at the heart, not the empty stomach. Do it as worship, free of legalism and free of guilt: not a box to tick, but a way to say, with your whole body, "you are better to me than bread."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–34 — Treasure, Vision, and Trust: Seeking the Kingdom First
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of chapter 6 addresses anxiety about material provision through three related teachings. Disciples are commanded not to store up earthly treasure (perishable, vulnerable) but heavenly treasure (imperishable, secure). The eye as the lamp of the body: a healthy eye (generous spirit) fills the whole person with light; a diseased eye (stinginess) fills it with darkness. You cannot serve both God and money. Then the great anxiety passage: do not be anxious about food or clothing, because the Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies knows your needs. Seek first the kingdom and his righteousness, and everything else will be added. The verse-by-verse carries three things this summary does not. The three enemies of treasure are not decorative: wealth took three forms and Jesus names the destroyer of each — fine cloth eaten by moth, grain and metal by the second word (which means "eating away" and covers rust, corrosion and vermin), and coin, which neither can touch, taken by the thief, whose verb means "to dig through" (mud-brick walls were tunnelled, not forced). Every exit is closed before the point is made. The eye is a Hebrew idiom, not an optical metaphor: "a good eye" meant a generous person and "an evil eye" a stingy one (Prov. 22:9; 28:22), which is why these verses sit between the treasure and the money rather than interrupting them. And mammon is an Aramaic word Jesus leaves untranslated, whose root appears to be the one behind Hebrew "faith" and our "amen" — most likely meaning that in which one puts one's trust, which makes the sentence almost self-evident. On the anxiety passage, note that the command comes three times (vv. 25, 31, 34), that the birds are not idle (they do not sow, reap or store — that is, they do not hoard against a future they cannot see), that the "lilies" are probably the wild anemones that carpet Galilee for a few weeks and are then swept up as oven fuel, and that "O you of little faith" is a word almost unique to Matthew which he uses four times, every time to disciples and never to unbelievers. The guard on anxiety is the most important thing in the section and is given in full below: this passage has been used to tell people with anxiety disorders that their illness is sin, and that is a cruelty the text does not authorise.
verseByVerse.theology: The teaching on anxiety is not a command to be carefree but to be properly ordered: anxiety is the symptom of inverted priorities — seeking the lesser things first and trusting God to manage them, rather than seeking God first and trusting him to manage everything else. The birds and lilies do not "seek" anything in the human sense; they simply exist in dependence on the Creator who provides. The disciple is not to live without thought for the future but without anxious preoccupation with it — trusting the Father's knowledge and provision while attending to the kingdom. Anxiety is fundamentally a theological problem: it reflects a practical unbelief in the Father's care.
verseByVerse.examples: "Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness" is the organizing principle of the entire Sermon on the Mount. Everything else — the beatitudes, the antitheses, the disciplines of chapter 6 — flows from this reorientation of desire. The person who is genuinely seeking God's kingdom first finds that anxiety about secondary things diminishes, not because circumstances change, but because the center of gravity of the heart has shifted. Worry is the heart occupied with what it fears it won't have; trust is the heart occupied with the One who has everything and gives freely.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light, but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness! No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sets two treasuries side by side, and the contrast is not now-versus-later but secure-versus-doomed. Earthly treasure has three enemies — moth, rust, and thief — and every earthly possession is already drifting toward one of them. Treasure in heaven (mercy shown, obedience offered, lives invested in for God) lies beyond the reach of all three. He is not banning savings or property; he is forbidding the heart that makes accumulation its great project. The question he presses is simply: what are you building, and will it last?

Then he exposes how the heart actually works: "where your treasure is, there your heart will be also." We assume the heart leads and our money follows; Jesus says it runs the other way — put your money somewhere and your heart moves in after it. Do you want to love God's kingdom more? Invest in it, and watch your affections follow. The eye drives the same point home: a "healthy" eye (the word means single, clear, generous) floods the whole person with light, while a "bad" eye (grudging, stingy) leaves everything dark — and the darkness that imagines itself light ("how great is the darkness!") is the worst kind of all, for the miser who calls his grip mere prudence cannot even see his own night.

Finally the knife: "No one can serve two masters... you cannot serve God and money." A slave in that world belonged wholly to one owner; divided loyalty was no loyalty at all. God and money (Mammon — wealth set up as a rival lord) issue opposite commands: one says hold loosely and give, the other says grip tight and keep; one says trust me, and so does the other. You cannot obey both with the same heart. Money is a good servant and a deadly master, and Jesus forces the question of which it has become to you.

So what should you actually do? Hold your money with an open hand. Earn honestly, and save and provide wisely — that is good stewardship, not greed — but give generously and gladly, steadily sending treasure on ahead to heaven through care for the poor, the work of the church, and the spread of the gospel; let your giving lead your heart God-ward. Run the simple diagnostics: Where do my daydreams drift? What would rob my peace if I lost it? What could I not bear to part with? And hold the whole of it loosely, as a steward and not an owner, trusting your Father for tomorrow rather than your bank balance.

And what does this not mean? It is not a call to poverty, nor a sin to own a home, hold a pension, or enjoy God's good gifts with thanksgiving — for God "richly provides us with everything to enjoy" (1 Tim 6:17). Saving for your family is not the same as hoarding; planning is not the same as trusting in riches. The issue is never the figure in your account but the master of your heart: a poor man can worship money as surely as a rich man, and a rich man can hold his wealth open-handed for God. Jesus is not against money in your wallet; he is against money on the throne. Dethrone it, and you are free.

Three details make this sharper, and the last one is the whole sermon in a word.

The three enemies are not decorative. Wealth in that world took three forms, and Jesus names the specific destroyer of each. Fine cloth — a man's wardrobe was capital, and Joseph's brothers came home with changes of clothing as plunder — was eaten by moth. Grain and metalwork were consumed by the second word, which means eating away and covers rust, corrosion and vermin equally. And coin, which neither moth nor rust can touch, is taken by the thief, whose verb literally means to dig through — mud-brick walls were tunnelled rather than forced.

So the list is complete. There is no form of earthly wealth that has no predator, and Jesus has closed every exit before making his point.

The eye is a Hebrew idiom, not an optical metaphor. The word for healthy is haplous, meaning single, simple, undivided. But behind it stands ordinary Jewish speech in which a good eye means a generous person and an evil eye means a stingy one. Proverbs uses it exactly so: whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor (Prov. 22:9), and a stingy man hastens after wealth — literally a man with an evil eye (Prov. 28:22).

Which explains what these three verses are doing between the treasure and the money. They are not a change of subject. Generosity is the light; grasping is the dark.

And "money" is the word that contains the argument. Jesus does not use the Greek for money. He uses an Aramaic word, mamonas, which he leaves untranslated — and its root appears to be the same one that gives Hebrew its word for faith, and behind our amen. The likeliest sense is that in which one puts one's trust.

If that is right, then the name of the rival god is simply the thing you rely on, and the sentence becomes almost self-evident: you cannot rely on God and on the thing you rely on instead of God.

Note also that serve is douleuo, which is not employment. It is the verb for being a slave — belonging to somebody, not working for them. Nobody in that world had two owners.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith? Therefore do not be anxious, saying, "What shall we eat?" or "What shall we drink?" or "What shall we wear?" For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That "therefore" ties this straight to money: anxiety is simply Mammon-service in another dress — the heart gripped by what it dreads losing. So Jesus floods the fear with reasons. From the greater to the lesser: if God gave you life and a body, will he not give the food and clothes to sustain them? From creation: the birds neither sow nor store, yet your Father feeds them; the wildflowers neither toil nor spin, yet they outshine Solomon in his robes — and you are worth far more than sparrows, and longer-lived than grass that is here today and burned tomorrow. From sheer futility: not one anxious hour ever added a single hour to anyone's life. Worry is the illusion of control — it drains today without mending tomorrow.

Jesus names the disease gently: not unbelief but "little faith" — faith that truly knows God yet has not learned to rest in him. The pagans make food, drink, and clothing the great chase of their lives; the believer's difference is not that he has no needs but that he has a Father who knows them — love, wisdom, and limitless power meeting in the One who feeds the birds. So the cure is not to stop needing but to re-aim the heart: "seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added." Make God's reign your organizing priority, and the necessities fall into place behind it. And take it a day at a time: today's troubles are enough for today; do not haul tomorrow's into it.

Picture it. The sparrow on the windowsill never lies awake doing sums, yet it is fed — and you are worth a thousand sparrows. The weed in the ditch is dressed finer than a king for a single day before the mower comes; will your Father forget to clothe his own child? Worry, someone said, is like a rocking chair: plenty of motion, and it gets you nowhere. But hear what this does not mean: it is no ban on work or planning. The birds are busy all day gathering the food God provides; diligence and sensible saving are not the enemy — gnawing dread that crowds out trust is. So work hard, plan wisely, and then hand the result to your Father; when the fear rises, turn it into prayer (Phil 4:6); and each morning seek his kingdom first, and trust the rest to follow.

And what is it, day to day, to "seek first" the kingdom? Not to bolt a religious slot onto a self-centered life, but to re-center the whole of life on Christ as King. It means giving God the first of your time, not the leftovers — meeting him in his Word and in prayer before the rush swallows the day; pursuing his righteousness, actually growing in holiness and obedience; and letting his concerns — the lost, the church, the poor, the spread of the gospel — shape how you spend your money, your hours, your strength. At every fork the question quietly shifts from "which path gives me the most comfort?" to "which most serves my King?" Put him at the center, and he himself promises to carry the rest.

Now the guard, and it is the most important thing on this page.

This passage has been used to tell people with anxiety disorders that their illness is a sin, and the damage done by that is real and is still being done. So it needs saying plainly.

Jesus is addressing a settled orientation of the heart — a way of organising a life around what one is afraid of losing. He is not addressing a medical condition. Clinical anxiety is not disobedience: it is a body doing something it was not designed to do, with a racing heart and a chest that will not loosen and a mind that will not stop, and it arrives uninvited in people who love God very much and would give anything to be free of it.

Three things follow. First, the command do not be anxious is not a lever to be pulled harder. A Christian who could stop by deciding to would have stopped years ago. Second, medical help is not a failure of faith, any more than a splint is; God heals through means and always has. Third — and this is the pastoral heart of it — a person in that condition should read this passage for its reasons rather than its imperative. Jesus does not simply forbid anxiety; he spends nine verses arguing against it, patiently, from creation and from the Father's character. That is how he treats frightened people. He is not standing over them; he is reasoning with them.

And the phrase he chooses for the disciples is the gentlest rebuke in the Gospels: O you of little faith. Oligopistos is almost unique to Matthew, who uses it four times (here; 8:26; 14:31; 16:8) — and every single time it is said to disciples, never to unbelievers. It is not a word for people who have no faith. It is a word for people who have some, and are frightened anyway.

Then the text itself, which is more concrete than the English shows.

The verb is merimnao, and it is very probably related to the verb meaning to divide. Anxiety pulls a mind in two. And it is worth knowing that Paul uses the same word approvingly — he is anxious for the churches (2 Cor. 11:28), and commends Timothy as one who will be genuinely concerned for the Philippians (Phil. 2:20). So Scripture is not against caring. It is against being torn.

Notice also that the command comes three times — verses 25, 31, and 34 — which is how the passage is built. It is stated, argued, restated, argued again, and then closed.

The birds are not idle and Jesus does not say they are. He says they do not sow, reap, or gather into barns — that is, they do not farm and they do not store. Any bird works from first light to dusk and a good deal harder than most of us. What they do not do is hoard against a future they cannot see, and that is the precise point of comparison.

The lilies were probably not lilies. Krinon most likely covers the wild anemones and poppies that turn the Galilean hillsides scarlet for a few weeks each spring and are gone. And the fate Jesus gives them is the ordinary one: in a country with almost no timber, dried grass and wildflowers were the fuel. They were swept up and burned to heat an oven for a single batch of bread.

That is the argument at its full strength. God dressed a weed more finely than Israel's richest king for a life of about three weeks, ending as kindling.

One curiosity in verse 27, since translations differ. The word rendered a single hour to his span of life is pechys, which is a cubit — a measure of length, about eighteen inches. And the noun with it can mean either height or lifespan. So it is either add eighteen inches to your height or, taking life as a road to be walked, add a single step to your span. Most modern versions take the second, and either way the point stands: worry has never once altered a measurement.

Then the last verse, which is nearly humorous: tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Tomorrow is personified as perfectly capable of managing its own worrying without help from today. And the closing line is a proverb — sufficient for the day is its own trouble — with no promise attached that the trouble will be small. Jesus does not say tomorrow will be fine. He says today has enough in it already.

6.theology:
Prayer and the Fatherhood of God. The Lord’s Prayer is the fullest Trinitarian statement about prayer in the New Testament. We pray to the Father, in the name of the Son (the one who taught us to pray this way and who intercedes for us, Rom. 8:34), in the power of the Spirit (who helps us in our weakness and intercedes with groaning too deep for words, Rom. 8:26). Reformed theology has always understood prayer as Trinitarian from beginning to end: the Father hears, the Son mediates, the Spirit enables.

The address “Our Father” is the fruit of adoption — the doctrine that those who trust in Christ are received into the family of God with all the rights and privileges of sons (Gal. 4:5–6). We do not pray as strangers petitioning a distant deity; we pray as children talking to a Father who knows us, loves us, and has already given us his Son. The confidence of Christian prayer rests entirely on the prior act of God in adoption, not on the fervency or frequency of the one praying.
6.examples:
Then: The contrast between secret devotion and public performance runs through the Old Testament. Hannah prayed so quietly that Eli thought she was drunk (1 Sam. 1:13) — and God heard. Daniel opened his window toward Jerusalem and prayed three times a day without announcement, in full view of a hostile empire (Dan. 6:10). The great saints of Israel prayed to an audience of One — and their prayers are the ones that shaped history. The hypocrites who prayed on street corners are forgotten; their reward was fully paid and fully spent.

Now: The anxiety Jesus addresses in verses 25–34 is the defining emotional experience of our age. Financial anxiety, career anxiety, health anxiety, relationship anxiety — the modern world has more to worry about (in terms of information access about possible threats) than any previous generation. Jesus’ answer is not information management but kingdom orientation: seek first the kingdom, and the Father who holds all things will hold yours. This is not naive — it is the most realistic posture available to a creature who is not God. You are not in control of tomorrow; the Father is. Trust the Father.

7.title: The Narrow Gate
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Judge not, that you be not judged. <sup>2</sup>For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you. <sup>3</sup>Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? <sup>4</sup>Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ when there is the log in your own eye? <sup>5</sup>You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye. <sup>6</sup>Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you. <sup>7</sup>Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you. <sup>8</sup>For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. <sup>9</sup>Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? <sup>10</sup>Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? <sup>11</sup>If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him! <sup>12</sup>So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets. <sup>13</sup>Enter by the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction, and those who enter by it are many. <sup>14</sup>For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few. <sup>15</sup>Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. <sup>16</sup>You will recognize them by their fruits. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? <sup>17</sup>So, every healthy tree bears good fruit, but the diseased tree bears bad fruit. <sup>21</sup>Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. <sup>24</sup>Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. <sup>25</sup>And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. <sup>26</sup>And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. <sup>27</sup>And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was the fall of it. <sup>28</sup>And when Jesus finished these sayings, the crowds were astonished at his teaching, <sup>29</sup>for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.
7.overview:
Chapter 7 concludes the Sermon on the Mount with a series of choices, each framed as a binary: the wide gate or the narrow, the false prophet or the true, the one who hears and does or the one who hears and does not. The Sermon that began with Beatitudes ends with warnings. The kingdom is real and its entrance is narrow; the alternatives are easy and lead to destruction. This is not the comfortable conclusion of a TED talk; it is the solemn close of the greatest sermon ever preached.

The famous “Judge not” (v. 1) is the most misquoted verse in the Bible. Jesus is not prohibiting all moral discernment — he commands it in verse 6 (discern who receives what is holy) and verses 15–16 (recognise false prophets by their fruit). He is prohibiting hypocritical judgment: condemning in others what you excuse in yourself. The log-and-speck image is both humorous and devastating — the person with a beam in their eye offering to perform eye surgery. Self-examination must precede fraternal correction.

The parable of the two builders is the Sermon’s climax and its challenge. Both builders hear the words of Jesus; both face the same storm. The difference is foundation: rock or sand. And the foundation is not intellectual agreement with Jesus’ teaching but doing it — the obedience that grows from genuine faith. The crowds are astonished at the end because Jesus teaches with authority, not as the scribes. He does not say “thus says the LORD”; he says “I say to you.” He is the rock on which the house is built.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Judgment, Prayer, and the Two Ways: Concluding the Sermon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Sermon on the Mount concludes with four warnings and a call. The warning against judging hypocritically (vv. 1–6), the invitation to persistent prayer (vv. 7–12), and the double warning about the narrow gate and false prophets (vv. 13–23) all converge on the final parable of the two builders (vv. 24–27). The Sermon does not end gently: it ends with a stark choice between two gates, two trees, two confessions, two foundations — and the crowds are astonished not by the gentleness of what they heard but by the authority of the one who said it. The verse-by-verse fills in what a 29-verse summary cannot. On "judge not": the proof that it cannot mean what the world takes it to mean is inside this same chapter — v. 6 requires the hearer to identify "dogs" and "pigs", vv. 15-20 require him to identify false prophets by their fruit, and vv. 21-23 have Jesus distinguishing those who did the Father's will from those who did not. All within twenty-two verses of the command. Elsewhere he settles it in one sentence: "Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment" (Jn. 7:24); and Paul asks, "Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge?" (1 Cor. 5:12). "With the measure you use" is a rabbinic formula (measure for measure) and is an offer of a choice — a man sets the standard he will be tried by. The speck and the log are a tradesman's joke: karphos is a wood chip, dokos is a roof beam, both from the same building yard, told by a carpenter to people who had watched carpenters work. And v. 6 is a crossover (an X): it is the pigs that trample and the dogs that turn and attack. On prayer (vv. 7-11): "how much more" is the standard rabbinic argument from lesser to greater — and the premise slipped in without pause is that the audience are evil, stated as an agreed fact on the way to proving how kind God is. Bread/stone and fish/serpent are things that look alike (Galilean limestone weathers into loaf-shaped lumps; the lake held a whiskered catfish a Jew could not eat) — so the fear being answered is not malice but substitution. The golden rule (v. 12), absent from the summary above, is treated at length in the verse track. On false prophets: "sheep's clothing" may be the prophetic uniform itself (Zech. 13:4 has false prophets putting on a hairy cloak to deceive), and "ravenous" is harpax, from the verb to snatch — what defines him is that he is taking something. The fruit test cannot be run quickly, and that is not a defect: much damage has been done by men whose fruit would have been obvious in five years and who were given authority in five weeks. "I never knew you" (vv. 21-23) is likewise absent above and is given the fullest treatment in the chapter below. On the two houses: Luke supplies the detail that bites — the wise man dug deep (Lk. 6:48). In that country a dry wadi bed is the most inviting summer site there is, flat and easy to dig; digging down is slow, costly, and invisible when the house is finished. Both houses look identical. And "these words of mine" puts his own sayings where Israel's wisdom tradition put the Torah (Ps. 1:2). Note finally that this closing section is four pairs narrowing — two gates, two trees, two confessions, two foundations — and in every one the wrong option is the comfortable one and the two are hard to tell apart from outside. On the closing formula (v. 28): "when Jesus finished these sayings" occurs five times in Matthew and only five (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1), each sealing a discourse — five books of teaching from a man who came out of Egypt, through the water, and through forty days in the wilderness. Moses gave five books from a mountain. And "astonished" is ekplesso, to be struck out of position, in the imperfect: they went on being knocked sideways.
verseByVerse.theology: The command not to judge (v. 1) is the most misquoted verse in the Sermon and one of the most misunderstood in the Bible. Jesus does not prohibit discernment (he commands it in v. 6 and vv. 15–20); he prohibits the hypocritical judgment that ignores one's own sin while scrutinizing another's. The warning about false prophets extends the theme: discernment is required, but it must begin with self-examination. The Sermon ends where it must — with the question of foundation. Hearing Jesus's words and not doing them is not neutrality; it is the choice of sand. The storm will decide what you built on.
verseByVerse.examples: The final verse — "he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes" — is Matthew's first and defining portrait of Jesus as teacher. The scribes taught by citing authorities: "Rabbi X says..." Jesus taught by assertion: "I say to you." This is either the most arrogant teaching in human history or the teaching of the one to whom all authority belongs. Matthew does not leave the reader in the middle. The crowd was astonished. The question is what they did with the astonishment.

verseByVerse.quote: Judge not, that you be not judged. For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you. Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, "Let me take the speck out of your eye," when there is the log in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye. Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Judge not" has become secular culture's favorite verse — the one command everyone still keeps. But Jesus means something precise. He is not banning moral evaluation or the naming of wrong (he does both all through the Sermon); he is banning the hypocritical tribunal of the self-righteous, who build careful cases against others while suppressing the evidence against themselves. And the warning has teeth: "with the measure you use it will be measured to you." The harsh judge is the one most exposed to harsh judgment — from God, who sees every page of the file.

The picture that follows is deliberately absurd: a man with a plank jutting from his own eye, leaning in to perform delicate surgery on the speck in his brother's. The speck is real — the brother does have a fault — but the log makes the would-be surgeon both blind and dangerous. Notice, though, that Jesus does not say "leave the speck alone." He says, "first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly" to help. Self-examination is not an excuse never to correct; it is the qualification for correcting rightly — humbly, as one patient helping another, not as a spotless judge.

And this is where verse 6 belongs — it may look out of place, but it is no stray fragment. Having warned against being too severe a judge, Jesus now warns against being no judge at all. "Dogs" and "pigs" picture those who have shown settled, aggressive contempt for holy things; to keep pressing pearls upon them is only to watch the treasure trampled and to invite their attack (cf. 10:14). So the two sayings are a matched pair, the two ditches on either side of the road: verses 1–5 say, do not be censorious; verse 6 says, do not be naive. Real discernment walks between them — humble about ourselves, yet wise about where we spend what is holy.

For you, then: deal honestly, and first, with your own sin before you reach for a brother's; when you must correct, do it gently, as a fellow sinner and not a saint sitting in judgment; and stay wise — keep holding out Christ, but do not mistake love for the refusal ever to discern, nor go on forcing holy things upon those who only want to trample and turn. Neither a harsh heart nor a gullible one, but a clear and humble eye.

The proof that "judge not" cannot mean what the world takes it to mean is inside this same chapter, and it is worth laying out, because no verse in the Bible is quoted more often by people who have read nothing around it.

Verse 1 says judge not. Verse 6 requires the hearer to work out which people are dogs and which are pigs — a judgement, and a severe one. Verses 15 to 20 require him to identify false prophets by inspecting their fruit — another judgement, sustained over time. Verses 21 to 23 have Jesus himself distinguishing those who did the Father's will from those who did not.

All of that is in the same sermon, within twenty-two verses of the command. Whatever judge not forbids, it cannot forbid the very things Jesus requires in the next breath.

And he settles it elsewhere in one sentence: Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment (Jn. 7:24). The problem was never judging. It was judging badly — from the outside, on appearances, by a standard the judge exempts himself from.

Paul is equally direct about the church's own business: Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? (1 Cor. 5:12).

So the verse has been made to mean almost exactly the opposite of what it says. It is not a prohibition on moral discernment. It is a warning to the man who exercises it while holding himself outside its reach.

Two things in the wording sharpen it.

The measure. With the measure you use it will be measured to you is a rabbinic formula — measure for measure — the ordinary Jewish way of saying that God's dealings answer to ours. And notice it is not a threat of arbitrary retaliation. It is an offer of a choice: the standard a man applies is the standard he is electing to be tried by, and he sets it himself, every time he opens his mouth about somebody else.

And the eye. The two objects are worth having exactly, because the joke is sharper in Greek and it is a tradesman's joke. The speck is karphos — a wood chip, a splinter, a bit of dry stalk. The log is dokos — a roof beam, the main timber spanning a room.

Both are from the same building yard. A man with a joist projecting from his eye socket is leaning in to extract a splinter from somebody else's, and the image was told by a carpenter to people who had watched carpenters work. It is meant to be laughed at, and the laugh is the argument: nobody would think this reasonable if they could see it from outside.

Which is the whole difficulty. The man with the beam is the one person in the room who cannot see it.

And verse 6 has a shape that most readers miss. Dogs, then pigs; then trampling, then attacking. Read it again and the pairing crosses over: it is the pigs that trample the pearls underfoot, and the dogs that turn and attack. Two lines laid out as an X, which is a common Hebrew and Aramaic arrangement and a good sign that the saying was carefully made rather than tacked on.

The animals are not pets. Dogs in that world were scavengers running loose round a village, and what is holy most likely means consecrated meat from the sacrifices. The picture is a man tossing the offering off the altar to the strays in the street.

verseByVerse.quote: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Ask... seek... knock" are present-tense imperatives: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. Prayer here is the posture of radical dependence — an admission that what we most need lies beyond our power to produce. That fits everything before it: the Sermon has described a life impossible by human effort, and now Jesus shows where the strength for it comes from. The demands drive us to our knees, and the door is one that opens.

Why pray with such confidence? Because of who we are asking. No decent father, handed a request for bread, slips his child a stone; asked for a fish, he does not palm off a snake. And if flawed, sinful parents still know how to give good gifts, "how much more" will the perfect Father give good things to his children. Our boldness rests not on our worthiness, nor on our persistence as a technique, but on his settled goodness.

So what may you bring? Anything that befits a child of this Father and his kingdom: daily provision, wisdom for a hard decision, the salvation of a wayward son, courage to obey the very commands of this Sermon, and — the best gift of all — the Holy Spirit himself (Luke 11:13, where Matthew's "good things" becomes "the Holy Spirit"). And you are to keep coming even when the door seems shut, like a child who knows his father is home.

But hear clearly what this does not mean. It is no blank check, no heavenly vending machine, no promise that whatever we crave will be handed over if only we believe hard enough or ask often enough. The promise is "good things" — and a good Father gives what is good, not always what is wanted. Sometimes the loving answer is "no," or "wait," or "I have something better"; the very picture assumes a child may reach for a serpent thinking it a fish, and a good father will not give it. So a prayer answered differently is not the Father failing but the Father fathering. We ask boldly and persistently — yet always, at heart, "according to his will" (1 Jn 5:14), trusting that he is wiser and kinder than our requests.

One honest puzzle remains: if a believer already receives the Holy Spirit the moment he trusts Christ (Eph 1:13; Rom 8:9), why would Jesus tell us to ask for him? Two things. First, in its own setting the promise looked ahead to Pentecost; the disciples were soon told to wait and pray for the promised Spirit, and they did (Lk 24:49; Acts 1:14; 2:1–4). Second, and for us now: we do not keep asking to receive the Spirit as though we lacked him — we have him already, and for good. We ask, rather, for more of his work — to be filled afresh again and again (Eph 5:18; and Acts 4:31, where already Spirit-filled believers are filled once more for boldness), for his power, his comfort, his help to put sin to death and bear fruit. It is not begging for a Guest we do not have, but asking the Guest who lives within to fill the whole house. And Luke can call him the supreme "good thing" the Father gives, because in giving us the Spirit, God gives us nothing less than himself.

Two details make the argument tighter than the English shows.

The form of the reasoning. How much more is the standard rabbinic move from the lesser case to the greater — if this is true of the small thing, how much more of the large — and it was the commonest tool in a Jewish teacher's hand. Jesus is arguing formally, and the two terms are worth naming: on the small side, a flawed human father; on the large side, God.

And the premise he slips in without pausing is startling. If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts… He is not addressing enemies. This is his own audience, and he calls them evil in a subordinate clause, as an agreed fact requiring no defence, on the way to making a point about generosity.

Which is the sermon in miniature: an assessment of human nature bleak enough to stop most of us in our tracks, deployed as an argument for how kind God is.

The two pairs. Bread and stone, fish and serpent — and they are not random opposites. They are things that look alike.

The limestone of that country weathers into small rounded lumps very much the shape and colour of a flat loaf; the resemblance is close enough that the devil had used it in the wilderness. And the lake produced a long, smooth, whiskered catfish that a Jew could not eat and that any child would take for a snake.

So the picture is not a father handing over something obviously cruel. It is a father palming off a convincing fake — something that looks right in the hand and turns out to be inedible or dangerous.

Which is precisely the fear underneath most unanswered prayer, and it is worth naming. Nobody seriously suspects God of malice. What people quietly suspect is a substitution — that they asked for something and got a stone that resembles bread, near enough to be plausible and no use at all. Jesus says the one thing that is never in the parcel is a counterfeit.

verseByVerse.quote: So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them." This is the famous Golden Rule, and notice its shape: it is positive, not merely negative. The world's wisdom says, "Do not do to others what you would hate done to you" — refrain from harm. Jesus asks more: actively do for others the good you would want for yourself. Picture what you would long for if you stood in their shoes — then go and be that for them. He calls it the summary of "the Law and the Prophets," because love for neighbor, in its most generous and active form, is the very heart of God's law. And it flows straight from what precedes: children who have received good gifts from their Father (vv. 7–11) become, in turn, givers of good gifts to others.

It is often said that Jesus taught nothing new here, and the claim deserves a straight answer rather than a nervous one. Something very like this had indeed been said before. Rabbi Hillel, a generation earlier, was asked to sum up the whole law while standing on one leg and replied: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour — that is the whole Torah. Confucius had said much the same five centuries before that, and so, in their own words, had Greek moralists and the writer of Tobit. The negative form of this rule is one of the commonest things wise men have ever said.

Two things are new all the same. The first is the direction. Every one of those sayings tells you what to refrain from; this one tells you what to do. A man may keep the negative rule perfectly while sitting still and never once troubling himself over anybody — refrain from harm and you have satisfied it. Jesus makes it impossible to obey by inaction: you must look at your neighbour, work out what you would long for if you stood where he stands, and go and be that for him. The one rule is a fence; the other is a road.

The second is the ground it stands on. Notice the so that opens the verse — it reaches back to what has just been said. The reason to treat others this way is not that society runs more smoothly when we do, nor that we may hope for the same treatment in return; it is that we have a Father who gives good gifts to those who ask, and children come to resemble their fathers. Reciprocity is prudence. This is family likeness.

There is a well-known retort that the rule cannot work, because people's tastes differ — do as you would be done by, and you will inflict on your neighbour exactly what you happen to enjoy.
