One detail will stop a reader with an open Bible: Matthew says two demon-possessed men, but Mark and Luke, telling the same story, describe only one — the man called "Legion" (Mark 5:1-20; Luke 8:26-39). This is not a contradiction. "One" does not deny a second; Mark and Luke simply fix their cameras on the more prominent of the pair, the vocal ringleader whose story was unforgettable, while Matthew, ever the careful witness, notes that there were in fact two. Matthew does the same at Jericho, where he counts two blind men and Mark names only Bartimaeus (20:30; Mark 10:46). It is the difference between a photograph that frames one face and a report that records the whole company — and the God who inspired all three Gospels was pleased to give us both angles.

A second difficulty in the same verse concerns the place name, and it is worth setting out because the manuscripts genuinely disagree and a footnote in most Bibles says so.

Matthew's copies divide between Gadarenes, Gerasenes and Gergesenes, and Mark's and Luke's divide the same way. The geography is the reason. Gerasa is a substantial city some thirty miles south-east of the lake, which no herd could rush down into from there. Gadara is about six miles off, close enough that its territory may well have run to the shore. And Gergesa — modern Kursi, on the eastern bank — is the only one of the three actually on the water, and it has a steep slope running straight into the lake.

Origen noticed the problem in the third century, visited the region, and concluded for Gergesa. He may have been right; he may also have been tidying. The likeliest account is simpler: the district was known by the name of its nearest major town, as we might say a thing happened outside Manchester without meaning the city centre, and different writers reached for different landmarks.

What is not in doubt is the terrain the story requires, and it exists: a steep bank on the eastern shore of the lake, in Gentile country, with tombs cut into the hillside above it.

One further thing about the demons' words. They call him Son of God — and it is worth noticing who else says that in this Gospel, and when. The next voice to say it plainly is Peter's at Caesarea Philippi, and the one after that belongs to a Roman officer watching him die (27:54). The confession that costs a man everything to make, the demons make on sight and instantly, and it does them no good whatever.

Their question is the more chilling half: have you come here to torment us before the time? They are not disputing the outcome. They know there is a fixed date and that it goes against them; the only thing in doubt is the calendar. Nothing in the New Testament states the demonic predicament more economically — a settled conviction about the future combined with no intention whatever of changing course.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a herd of many pigs was feeding at some distance from them. And the demons begged him, saying, "If you cast us out, send us away into the herd of pigs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The demons do not dispute Jesus's authority to cast them out — they beg only for the destination. Even their request must be submitted to him; they cannot act without his permission. The pigs are unclean animals in Jewish law — an appropriate destination for unclean spirits. There is dark irony in the request: the demons prefer anything to the abyss, even the bodies of animals. Jesus permits it. The permission is not explained — Matthew does not supply a theological rationale. The sovereign permits what the sovereign permits, and the outcome (the demons's evident capacity for destruction, the pigs' death) is part of the revelation of what these beings do when given freedom. The demonic destroys whatever it inhabits.

The question this passage raises and does not answer must be asked out loud, because a thoughtful reader will ask it and deserves better than silence: what about the man who owned the pigs?

Mark says there were about two thousand of them (Mk. 5:13). That is not a smallholding; it is a substantial business, and somebody's living, and quite possibly the living of the herdsmen who ran away and of their families. In a single afternoon it was destroyed.

Four things can be said honestly, and one thing cannot.

The first is that the destruction is the demons' work, not Jesus'. He does not send them into the pigs; they ask, and he permits. What follows is exactly what verse 31 should have led anyone to expect — the thing that had been driving two men to live among graves and cut themselves does the same to a herd of animals within a minute of getting hold of them. The pigs are not punished. They are a demonstration, and the demonstration is of what the demons do, not of what Jesus does.

The second is that this was Gentile territory, which is why there were pigs at all. It is sometimes suggested that Jewish owners were being judged for keeping unclean animals. That will not stand: the region was the Decapolis, the owners were almost certainly Gentiles, and they were breaking no law of their own.

The third is the valuation Jesus states elsewhere in this very Gospel, and it is not a comfortable sentence but it is his: of how much more value is a man than a sheep! (12:12). Two men who had been living in tombs, uncontrollable, self-harming, beyond anyone's reach, were given their minds back. Set against that, a herd of livestock is a real cost and a small one, and the town that made the opposite calculation is the villain of the story rather than its victim.

The fourth is that Jesus never explains, and the Gospels never apologise. Matthew records the loss, records the town's reaction, and moves on. That silence is itself instructive: the account does not treat the objection as unanswerable, and it does not treat it as trivial either.

What cannot honestly be said is that it did not matter. It mattered a great deal to somebody, and the text lets that stand — which is a good deal more truthful than the sermons that tidy it away.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Go." So they came out and went into the pigs, and behold, the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the waters. The herdsmen fled, and going into the city they told everything, including what had happened to the demon-possessed men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Go" — one word in Greek. The same sovereign economy of speech that stilled the storm casts out the Legion. The rush of two thousand pigs (Mark 5:13) into the sea dramatizes what would have happened to the men if the demons had remained. The herdsmen's report carries the news to the city — and the city's response will be to ask Jesus to leave. The miracle that liberates two men destroys an economic asset. The community calculates its loss, not its gain. Two sons of Adam restored to their right minds are valued less than a herd of pigs. This is not only ancient callousness; it is the universal human tendency to resist the disruptive grace that costs us something.

The word is worth pausing on because it is the third time in this chapter that everything turns on one of them.

Go. A single syllable in Greek. To the leper: be clean. To the centurion: let it be done. To the wind and sea: peace. And now to a legion of demons who have terrorised a district for years and whom no chain could hold: go.

No formula, no ritual, no invocation of a higher name. Every Jewish exorcist of the period worked with elaborate procedures — incantations, roots, rings, the names of angels; Josephus describes one at some length. Jesus uses one word and does not raise his voice.

Then the detail Matthew includes that most storytellers would cut: the herdsmen fled, and going into the city they told everything, including what had happened to the demon-possessed men.

The men who ran are the reason the story exists. They were employees who had just watched their employer's herd go over a cliff, they had every reason to say nothing or to shade the account, and instead they went into town and reported the whole thing — including, Matthew is careful to say, the part about the two men.

So the first evangelists in the Decapolis were a group of frightened pig-keepers delivering a report that was mostly about their own catastrophe. And their testimony was accurate. They did not leave out the healing to make the loss look worse.

What the town did with it is the next verse, and it is the saddest in the chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, all the city came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him, they begged him to leave their region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They begged him to leave their region" — the same word used by the demons in verse 31 (parekaloun). The city begs as the demons begged; their request is essentially the same. They want Jesus gone. Two men set free, a demonic stronghold broken, an entire community freed from the terror of those tombs — and the response is to ask the healer to go away. The economy of the region, represented by the drowned pigs, matters more than the liberation of two neighbors. Jesus grants their request: he will not stay where he is not wanted. This is the most terrible expression of God's sovereignty — that he honors human rejection by departing. The Gadarenes got what they asked for.

Do not rush past how sobering this is. We are fond of a Jesus who relentlessly pursues every sinner and never, ever lets go — and the seeking Shepherd of Luke 15 is gloriously real. But here is the other side of the truth, the side we prefer to forget: when a people settle their hearts against him and say "depart," he can and does take them at their word. This is the judgment Paul names in Romans 1, where three times "God gave them up" — handed them over to the very sins they preferred (Rom 1:24, 26, 28). The most fearful answer God ever gives to a prayer is to grant the request "leave me alone." The Gadarenes asked him to go, and he went.

Scripture sounds this warning more than once. "My Spirit shall not abide in man forever" (Gen 6:3). Of stubborn Israel: "I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels" (Ps 81:12). Of idol-wedded Ephraim: "leave him alone" (Hos 4:17). Over Jerusalem Jesus himself wept, "How often would I have gathered your children... and you would not! See, your house is left to you desolate" (23:37–38) — he grieves to leave, but he leaves. Yet hear the mercy folded inside the warning: today he has not left. The door still stands open, and he still knocks (Rev 3:20). So this story is no counsel of despair but a summons to urgency: "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts" (Heb 3:15); "seek the LORD while he may be found, call upon him while he is near" (Isa 55:6). The terror is real — and so, right now, is the open door.

8.theology: The authority of Christ. Chapter 8 is a sustained meditation on the authority of the Son of God. He has authority over disease (leper, fever), over distance (servant healed at a word), over demons (v. 16), and over creation (storm). Reformed theology insists that this authority is not delegated but inherent: Jesus is not a prophet with God’s power on loan but the eternal Son in whom all the fullness of deity dwells bodily (Col 2:9). His healing word and his saving word are the same — both accomplish what they declare. The centurion’s faith grasps this: faith is resting on the word of One who has absolute authority to perform what he promises.
8.examples:
Then: A Roman officer, trained in chains of command, recognized the absolute authority of Jesus. His faith put to shame those who had grown up with the Scriptures but had domesticated their expectations of the Messiah.

Now: We live in a therapeutic culture that regards faith as a psychological coping mechanism. The centurion’s faith is the opposite: it is epistemically grounded in the nature of the One trusted. We trust Christ not because belief makes us feel better but because he is the Lord of heaven and earth whose word does not return void. When we pray, we address the One who stilled the Sea of Galilee.

9.title: The King’s Authority to Forgive
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And getting into a boat he crossed over and came to his own city. <sup>2</sup>And behold, some people brought to him a paralytic, lying on a bed. And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven.” <sup>3</sup>And behold, some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man is blaspheming.” <sup>4</sup>But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said, “Why do you think evil in your hearts? <sup>5</sup>For which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? <sup>6</sup>But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins” —he then said to the paralytic— “Rise, pick up your bed and go home.” <sup>7</sup>And he rose and went home. <sup>8</sup>When the crowds saw it, they were afraid, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to men. <sup>9</sup>As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him. <sup>10</sup>And as Jesus reclined at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples. <sup>11</sup>And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” <sup>12</sup>But when he heard it, he said, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. <sup>13</sup>Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.’ For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.” <sup>35</sup>And Jesus went throughout all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction. <sup>36</sup>When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. <sup>37</sup>Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; <sup>38</sup>therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.”
9.overview:
Chapter 9 begins with the most audacious claim in Jesus’ ministry: “Your sins are forgiven.” The scribes immediately see the implication — only God can forgive sins — and charge blasphemy. Jesus responds by healing the paralytic as evidence that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. The miracle is the sign; forgiveness is the substance. This is Matthew’s thesis: Jesus has come not primarily to heal bodies but to heal souls, not primarily to liberate from Roman occupation but to liberate from the bondage of sin and guilt.

The call of Matthew himself is a microcosm of the gospel. A tax collector — a collaborator with Rome, a social and religious outcast — is called with a two-word summons. He rises and follows. The banquet that follows is a picture of the kingdom: Jesus eating with the unworthy, the Pharisees scandalized, Jesus quoting Hosea 6:6 (“I desire mercy, not sacrifice”). The chapter closes with Jesus surveying the harassed crowds with compassion and calling for labourers. The mission of the King now extends through his people.

Read straight through, the chapter reveals a second pattern woven beneath the miracles: in story after story faith stands beside unbelief, and the two are sifted apart. The paralytic comes carried by friends whose faith Jesus sees (v. 2) — while the scribes silently cry blasphemy. Matthew rises at a word — while the Pharisees mutter at the table. The ruler kneels and the unclean woman reaches, both in bold faith — while the hired mourners laugh him to scorn. The blind men confess “Yes, Lord” — while the watching Pharisees, at the chapter’s climax, sneer that he casts out demons “by the prince of demons” (v. 34). The same Jesus, the same works — and they divide every heart that meets them: some come empty-handed and receive everything, while others, certain they need nothing, receive nothing and only harden. This is the dividing line the whole Gospel will trace, and it is why the chapter closes not in triumph but in compassion for the harassed and helpless crowds (vv. 36–38) — the harvest is plentiful, and this faith must be carried to them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Forgiveness, Fellowship, and Fasting: Who Has Authority?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus returns to Capernaum and heals a paralyzed man by first forgiving his sins — triggering the first direct conflict with the scribes. He then calls Matthew the tax collector and eats with sinners, outraging the Pharisees. When John's disciples ask why Jesus's disciples don't fast, Jesus answers with three images: the bridegroom, the unshrunk cloth, and the new wine. The old forms cannot contain the new reality that has arrived. What the summary cannot hold. The scribes never spoke — Matthew says they said it "to themselves" (v. 3), and Jesus answers the unspoken charge, which is itself a claim as large as the one being disputed (Jer. 17:10; 1 Kgs. 8:39). And their theology is correct: only the offended party can waive an offence, and no priest in Israel ever forgave anybody — he declared a forgiveness God had granted. So the alternatives really are God or blasphemer, and they could see it. Jesus does not call their conclusion mistaken but evil (poneros) — the indictment is of a heart that settled the question before weighing it. On the title: Son of Man does two contradictory things at once, which is why he chose it. In Hebrew idiom it means simply "a human being" (God calls Ezekiel that ninety times), and in Daniel 7:13-14 it is the highest title in the Old Testament — dominion, glory, an everlasting kingdom. Innocuous enough to say in public, loaded enough that anyone who had read Daniel knew. And the two decisive words in v. 6 are on earth: everyone believed sins were forgiven in heaven; the disputed point is that the transaction can be completed here, by a voice, without temple, priest or sacrifice. Note also that the crowd's "authority to men" is plural (v. 8) — Matthew alone has it, and this is the Gospel that will record the keys given to Peter (16:19) and binding and loosing given to the church (18:18). On Matthew's booth: it was a customs post on the Via Maris at the frontier between Antipas's and Philip's territory, and the point most often missed is that Peter could go back to fishing and Matthew could not — a tax franchise was a purchased concession with men queuing for it. He burned the bridge in the act of crossing it. And Hosea 6:6 is Matthew's own verse: he quotes it twice (9:13; 12:7) and no other New Testament writer quotes it at all, both times against men who are technically correct and pastorally monstrous.
verseByVerse.theology: The paralytic episode is the theological pivot: Jesus claims authority to forgive sins, which belongs to God alone. The scribes are theologically right that only God forgives sins; they are catastrophically wrong in their conclusion that Jesus is therefore blaspheming. The miracle of healing is offered as proof of the greater miracle of forgiveness — the visible confirms the invisible. Matthew's call and the meal with sinners then demonstrate what forgiveness looks like in practice: the Physician comes for the sick, not the healthy.
verseByVerse.examples: The three images of newness — bridegroom, cloth, wineskins — announce that Jesus is not a reform of Judaism but its fulfillment and transformation. The joy of the bridegroom's presence cannot be contained in old mourning forms. The new covenant is not a patch on the old but its completion. The Pharisees' question about fasting reveals that they are still thinking in terms of the old forms; Jesus is announcing that the age of the bridegroom has begun.

verseByVerse.quote: And getting into a boat he crossed over and came to his own city. And behold, some people brought to him a paralytic, lying on a bed. And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, "Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Their faith" — not only the paralytic's but his friends', whose effort carried him to Jesus. Faith is not always individual; the community of faith can carry those whose own faith is weak or absent. Jesus sees the faith of the group and responds to the paralytic. "Take heart, my son" — words of tender paternal address before any act of healing. Then the unexpected: before addressing the paralysis, Jesus addresses the deeper problem. "Your sins are forgiven" would have stunned the room. The man came for his legs; Jesus goes straight to his soul. The physical need is real and will be addressed; the spiritual need is deeper, and Jesus addresses it first. And weigh the grammar of what he says, because the whole gospel is folded into it. He does not say "God will forgive you if you do this" or "seek God and perhaps you will find pardon." He says "your sins are forgiven" — a verdict handed down, an accomplished thing, spoken over a man who has done nothing yet but be carried through a door. This is what the Reformers meant by justification: not a process by which a sinner is slowly made good enough, but a declaration in which the Judge himself pronounces the guilty righteous. It is a courtroom word before it is a hospital word. The man leaves with his legs mended, which everyone could see; he leaves with his record cleared, which no one could see and which mattered infinitely more. And the declaration is not cheap. The Judge who pronounces the pardon here will pay for it himself, outside a city wall, so that the verdict is not merely merciful but just.

Go back, though, to the two words the entry began with, because a great deal of comfort is packed into them and one sentence does not exhaust it. Their faith. Not his. Matthew is careful: the man is carried, which means he could not come, and what Jesus responds to is the faith of the people who brought him. Mark adds that when the crowd blocked the door they went up and dug through the roof — this was not a polite gesture but a determined, undignified, expensive piece of persistence.

Two sorts of reader should stop here. The first is the one doing the carrying. You have a husband who will not come, a son who has walked away, a friend sunk in a depression too heavy to pray out of. You cannot believe on their behalf — notice that Jesus still speaks to the man himself, pardons him personally, and commands him personally to rise; nobody is saved by proxy. But you can carry them to where Jesus is, and that is a real work with a real promise attached. It looks like praying for them by name for years without visible result, keeping the relationship intact so that there is still a stretcher available when they finally need one, refusing to make your love conditional on their agreement, and being willing to look foolish and go through the roof. Keep carrying. This is the one story in the Gospels where the faith that moved Jesus belonged to the friends.

The second is the reader who suspects he is the paralytic. Your faith feels too thin to count; you are not sure it would qualify as faith at all. Then look hard at what this man contributes to the scene, because it is nothing whatever. He does not argue his case, express his confidence, or say a word. He is carried in horizontal and helpless, and the first thing he hears is take heart, my son, your sins are forgiven. That is what the church is for on the days you cannot hold yourself up — it is why we sing together when you cannot sing, and why others pray when your own praying has dried up. You are not required to arrive under your own power. God has never been fussy about how a person gets to the door.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, some of the scribes said to themselves, "This man is blaspheming." But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said, "Why do you think evil in your hearts?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scribes' reasoning is correct as far as it goes: only God can forgive sins (Isa. 43:25; Mark 2:7). Therefore a man who claims to forgive sins is either God or a blasphemer. They choose blasphemer — not because the evidence compels it, but because their hearts are already closed to the alternative. Jesus knows their thoughts — another claim to divine knowledge. He does not deny that forgiveness belongs to God; he implicitly claims to be the God who forgives. The question "why do you think evil in your hearts?" presses at the motivation behind their theological conclusion: is this a genuine inquiry after truth, or is the conclusion already settled?

Three things sharpen this, and the first is easily missed because Matthew states it flatly.

They said it to themselves. The scribes did not speak. Matthew says some of the scribes said to themselves — the charge was formed silently, in the room, and never left anybody's mouth.

And Jesus answers it out loud.

So before the paralytic moves a muscle, a claim has already been made that is as large as the one being disputed. The scribes object that only God can forgive sins; the man they are objecting to has just read their minds. Jeremiah says of God, I the LORD search the heart and test the mind (Jer. 17:10), and Solomon prayed to the one who alone knows the hearts of all the children of mankind (1 Kgs. 8:39). The evidence for the disputed claim is supplied by the manner of the reply.

Their theology is right. This has to be said clearly, because these men are usually treated as fools. They are not being stupid. Isaiah has God saying I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake (Isa. 43:25) — the doubled pronoun is emphatic and the point is exclusivity. A sin is an offence against God, and only the party offended can waive it. No priest in Israel ever forgave anybody; the priest declared a forgiveness God had granted through the prescribed sacrifice.

Which is why the scribes' logic is not merely defensible but correct. If this man is not God, he is committing blasphemy. There is no third option available, and the scribes could see it.

An honest note on the grammar. Your sins are forgiven is a passive, and a passive of this kind was a common Jewish way of avoiding the divine name — so in principle Jesus might be announcing that God has forgiven rather than claiming to do it himself. The scribes plainly did not hear it that way, and Mark records their reasoning in full: Who can forgive sins but God alone? (Mk. 2:7). Jesus does not correct them. He proceeds to prove the claim they think he has made.

And his question is sharper than it looks. Not why do you think this? but why do you think evil in your hearts? — poneros, the word used of wicked men and of the evil one. He calls their reasoning wicked, which would be outrageous if the reasoning were merely mistaken. It is not the conclusion he indicts but the closed heart underneath it: they had settled the question before they weighed it, and settled it against a man who had done them no harm.

verseByVerse.quote: "For which is easier, to say, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Rise and walk'? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" — he then said to the paralytic — "Rise, pick up your bed and go home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The argument is elegant: saying "your sins are forgiven" is unverifiable — no one can check it. Saying "rise and walk" is immediately testable. Jesus will provide the verifiable miracle as evidence for the unverifiable claim. If he can do the greater (command a paralyzed body to move), he can do the lesser (forgive sins) — because both require the same divine authority. "The Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" is the first time Matthew uses "Son of Man" as a self-designation in connection with authority. The title from Daniel 7:13-14 — the one given dominion over all — is here claiming that dominion extends to the forgiveness of sins. The healing is not a distraction from the theology; it is the proof of it.

Two things about the title, since this is where Matthew first attaches it to authority.

Son of Man is Jesus' own preferred way of speaking about himself. It occurs about thirty times in Matthew and almost every one is on his own lips; hardly anybody else in the New Testament uses it of him. He was not obliged to adopt it, and the reason he did is that it does two contradictory things at once.

On its face it is the most modest title available. In Hebrew idiom son of man simply means a human being — God addresses Ezekiel that way ninety-odd times, and it means roughly mortal. A man could use it of himself without claiming anything at all.

And in Daniel 7 it is the highest title in the Old Testament. Behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man… and to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away (Dan. 7:13-14).

That is the paradox he wanted. A phrase innocuous enough to be said in public without triggering an immediate riot, and loaded enough that anyone who had read Daniel would know exactly what was being claimed. It let him tell the truth about himself at a pace the hearers could bear — and when he finally used it plainly, under oath before the high priest, they tore their robes and convicted him on the spot (26:64-65).

The second thing is two small words in verse 6: on earth.

Everyone in that room believed sins were forgiven in heaven. The disputed point is the location. This man is saying the transaction can be completed here, in a crowded house in Capernaum, by a voice — without a temple, without a priest, without a sacrifice, and without waiting.

And the argument he builds is worth following exactly, because it is more careful than it first appears. He asks which is easier to say — and the answer is obvious: the forgiveness, because nobody can check it. Any charlatan can pronounce absolution and walk away. So he takes the harder, testable claim and stakes the untestable one on it, in public, with a paralysed man as the instrument. If the mat does not move, everything he has just said about sins is exposed within the minute.

It is an argument only one kind of person can afford to make.

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and went home. When the crowds saw it, they were afraid, and they glorified God, who had given such authority to men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The paralytic rises, takes his mat, and goes home — the three actions commanded, performed in order, completed without explanation. The crowd's response combines fear and glorification: they are frightened by what they have witnessed (the appropriate response to a theophany) and they give glory to God. "Who had given such authority to men" — they perceive correctly that the authority comes from God but frame it as God having granted authority to a human representative. This is partially correct: Jesus is the Son of Man through whom God acts. The full truth — that the one acting is himself God the Son — will take the whole Gospel to disclose. But the crowd's instinct to glorify God is the right beginning.

There is one word in the crowd's response that Matthew alone records, and it is worth stopping on because it is strange.

They glorified God, who had given such authority to men.

Plural. Not to this man, which is what Mark's crowd effectively says (we never saw anything like this) and what the situation would lead anyone to expect. Matthew writes anthropois — to human beings.

Two readings are available and they are not exclusive.

The first is that the crowd is speaking loosely, as crowds do — awed at the idea that God has entrusted such authority to somebody in human form, without working out the theology of who this particular somebody is. On that reading their words are imprecise and their instinct is sound.

The second is that Matthew has kept the plural because he can see where it goes. This is the Gospel that will record Jesus giving the keys of the kingdom to Peter (16:19), and telling the church that whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven (18:18). It is the Gospel written by a man who knew that the risen Christ would breathe on his disciples and say if you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven (Jn. 20:23).

The authority to forgive sins is Christ's alone. But the announcing of it was going to be handed to men — ordinary ones, of the sort standing in that room — and Matthew lets a crowd say more than it knew.

Note also what the two verbs do together: they were afraid, and they glorified God. Fear first. That is the consistent biblical response to God acting close at hand, and it is a healthier reaction than the one usually produced today, which is enthusiasm. Something had happened in that house that made people frightened, and the fear turned into worship rather than away from it.

verseByVerse.quote: As Jesus passed on from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, "Follow me." And he rose and followed him. And as Jesus reclined at table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were reclining with Jesus and his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew the tax collector is called with the same two-word command as the fishermen: "Follow me." Tax collectors were despised as collaborators with Rome and known for dishonest exaction — they were excluded from synagogue life and considered beyond the pale of respectable Jewish society. Matthew does not hesitate. He rises from his tax booth — abandoning a lucrative position — and follows. The immediate consequence is a meal: Matthew hosts Jesus, and the guest list is the crowd that Jesus has come to save. Reclining at table in the ancient world was an act of fellowship and equality — to eat with someone was to accept them. Jesus accepts sinners at table. This is the shape of the kingdom.

A reader comparing the Gospels meets a small puzzle here: Mark and Luke tell this same call, but they name the man Levi — "Levi the son of Alphaeus" (Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27). Are Levi and Matthew the same person? Almost certainly yes: he bore two names, as many Jews of the day did, and "Matthew" — which means "gift of God" — may well be the name he took, or was given, when the gift of God laid hold of him at that booth. And notice a quiet grace in it. When Matthew comes to write his own Gospel, he does not polish the record. Others, listing the twelve apostles, simply name him; he alone writes "Matthew the tax collector" (10:3), pinning the old, shameful label to his name forever. A man truly forgiven does not hide what he was saved from; he makes it the monument of grace.

Two more things, and the second is the sharpest point in the passage.

What the booth actually was. Not a poll-tax office. Capernaum sat on the Via Maris, the great trade road, and it stood at the frontier between the territory of Herod Antipas and that of his brother Philip. The booth was a customs post, and Matthew's job was to assess duty on goods crossing the border — fish, oil, produce, everything moving along the road.

These men bought the right to collect and made their living on the margin, which is why the whole class was hated: the system paid them to overcharge. And a customs officer in a border town, on the busiest road in the region, was very well placed indeed.

And here is the thing worth pausing on. Four fishermen had been called from that same shoreline a few chapters earlier, and they left their nets — but the nets were still there. The boats stayed where they were. When it was all over and they did not know what else to do, Peter said I am going fishing, and six of them went with him, and the trade was waiting (Jn. 21:3).

Matthew's booth was not waiting. A tax franchise was a purchased concession and there were men queuing for it. The moment he stood up and walked away from that table, somebody else had it — probably before the end of the day.

Peter could go back. Matthew could not. Of all the men called in the Gospels, he is the one who burned the bridge in the act of crossing it, and Luke records the detail Matthew is too modest to mention: he left everything, and then threw a large party (Lk. 5:28-29).

Which is the last quiet grace in the passage. Matthew does not tell us it was his house or his feast. He simply writes as Jesus reclined at table in the house, and lets the guest list speak — because the point of the story, in his telling, is not what it cost him but who was invited.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, "Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?" But when he heard it, he said, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick." Go and learn what this means: "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice." For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees' question is addressed to the disciples, not to Jesus — a social strategy for undermining a teacher through his followers. Jesus answers anyway, with the physician analogy. The logic is irrefutable: a doctor goes to the sick, not the healthy. If Jesus is the physician of souls, the appropriate address for his ministry is the population that knows it is sick — tax collectors, sinners, the morally compromised. The Pharisees' implicit self-identification as "healthy" is the most dangerous misdiagnosis in the chapter. The sick person who knows they are sick can receive the physician; the "healthy" person who has never acknowledged their need cannot. Self-righteousness is the one condition that excludes the cure.

"Go and learn" — a rabbinic formula, addressed here to the rabbis as if they were students who had missed the lesson. The Hosea 6:6 quotation ("I desire mercy, and not sacrifice") does not abolish sacrifice; it establishes the priority. Ritual observance without the heart of mercy is not religion but its counterfeit. "I came not to call the righteous, but sinners" — the irony is biting: there are no righteous ones, only those who know they are sinners and those who don't.

The quotation deserves more, because it is one of Matthew's signatures and nobody else in the New Testament uses it.

I desire mercy, and not sacrifice is Hosea 6:6, and Matthew quotes it twice — here, and again at 12:7 when the disciples are criticised for picking grain on the Sabbath. Mark and Luke and John never quote it. Paul never quotes it. It is Matthew's verse, and both times it is deployed against religious men who are technically correct and pastorally monstrous.

The setting in Hosea gives it its edge. Israel is producing an impressive volume of religion and Hosea says their love is like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes early away (Hos. 6:4). It evaporates by breakfast. And then God says what he actually wants — and the word rendered mercy is hesed, the great covenant word for steadfast, loyal, committed love.

Note that the sentence is not an abolition. Hosea was not telling Israel to stop sacrificing; God had commanded the sacrifices. It is a Hebrew idiom of priority — this rather than that meaning this before that, and this without which that is worthless. The same construction turns up when God says he desires obedience rather than burnt offerings.

So the charge is not that the Pharisees are too religious. It is that their religion has come loose from the thing it was for.

And go and learn is a deliberate insult, delivered with a straight face. It was a standard rabbinic formula used by a teacher to a pupil who had not done the reading. Jesus uses it on the professional interpreters of the text he is quoting — and the text he sends them off to study is one they could recite.

One further note on vocabulary. Sinners in these controversies is close to a technical term. It did not mean simply bad people; it meant those who did not keep the purity code — people whose trade or poverty or ignorance put them permanently outside the observant class. Some were immoral. Many were just poor.

Which is why the physician image lands where it does. The Pharisees have divided the population into the clean and the unclean, and Jesus accepts the division and reverses the conclusion: yes, there are two groups, and I have come for the other one.

verseByVerse.quote: And then the disciples of John came to him, saying, "Why do we and the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?" And Jesus said to them, "Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast. No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, for the patch tears away from the garment, and a worse tear is made." Neither is new wine put into old wineskins. If it is, the skins burst and the wine is spilled and the skins are destroyed. But new wine is put into fresh wineskins, and so both are preserved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John's disciples ask sincerely, not with hostility: they and the Pharisees fasted often, yet Jesus' disciples did not. Why? A word on their practice helps. The law of Moses commanded only one fast a year — the Day of Atonement, when Israel was to "afflict" itself (Lev 16:29–31). Every other fast was added by tradition: after the exile, four annual fasts mourned the fall of Jerusalem (Zech 8:19), and by Jesus' day the devout fasted twice a week, on Mondays and Thursdays (cf. Lk 18:12). So the "frequent fasting" they mention was custom, not command. Behind it lay real longing: fasting expressed grief over sin, repentance, and yearning for God to send his deliverance and his Messiah. At its best it was the posture of a people still waiting.

And that is just why Jesus' disciples were not fasting: the waiting was over. "Can the wedding guests mourn while the bridegroom is with them?" Jesus is the long-promised Bridegroom (cf. Isa 62:5; Jn 3:29), and his presence turns the hour into a wedding feast. Fasting belongs to absence and mourning; feasting belongs to the joy of his being here. But mark the shadow that falls across the sentence: "the days will come when the bridegroom is taken away" — the first veiled hint in Matthew of the cross. After he is gone, his people will fast again, as the early church did (Acts 13:2–3), now longing for his return.

The two little parables drive the same point home: do not stitch the new onto the old. A patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment tears away and makes the rip worse; new, still-fermenting wine bursts old, brittle skins, and both are lost. Jesus is the new wine, the kingdom arrived; the "old" is the whole framework of mourning, waiting, and ritual that belonged to the age before the King appeared — the fasting-as-mourning included. You cannot cram the joy of the wedding into the forms of the funeral. This is no attack on the Old Testament, which is old wine now come to full maturity in him; it is a warning against forcing kingdom-life into a religious system too rigid to hold it. The new covenant calls for new wineskins — a life and worship freshly shaped by Christ, not merely patched onto what came before.

So should Christians fast? Jesus plainly assumes we will ("then they will fast"; and "when you fast," 6:16), and the early church did, at prayer and at weighty decisions (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). Yet — tellingly — the epistles lay down no command, no required days, no rule. Fasting is therefore a freedom and a privilege, not an obligation: a way to humble ourselves, sharpen prayer, and hunger for God, never a badge to earn his favor. (The how and why are unfolded more fully at 6:16–18.)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–38 — The Harvest Is Plentiful: Four More Healings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew compresses four more miracles into a rapid sequence: a ruler's dead daughter raised, a hemorrhaging woman healed on the way, two blind men given sight, a mute demoniac freed. The chapter ends with a summary of Jesus's teaching and healing throughout all the cities and villages, and the saying about the plentiful harvest and the few laborers. The pace is breathless — Matthew is showing the sheer scope of Jesus's ministry, the range of human need he addresses, and the consistency of his compassion. Three things the summary leaves out. This is the tenth miracle of a set Matthew has gathered into two chapters, arranged by design rather than chronology — leper, centurion's servant, Peter's mother-in-law, storm, demoniacs, paralytic, ruler's daughter, the woman with the flow of blood, two blind men, mute man. In a Gospel that has already drawn Jesus as the new Moses (a slaughter of infants, called out of Egypt, water, forty days, a mountain, a law), ten mighty works after a mountain of teaching is the shape of the Exodus — with the difference that Moses' ten were plagues that destroyed, and these ten fall on disease, death, storm and the demonic. Verse 34 is the first Beelzebul charge, and it is worth seeing why they had to reach for it: nobody in the New Testament ever denies the miracles, so having ruled out God there was one explanation left. Its position is what chills — the same day and the same evidence produce "never was anything like this seen in Israel" from one group and "he casts out demons by the prince of demons" from the other. (A few early manuscripts omit the verse; the evidence for keeping it is good.) and the closing summary has three words stronger than any English can afford: "harassed and helpless" is eskylmenoi (flayed, mangled — the verb for skinning) and errimmenoi (thrown down, left lying where it fell); "compassion" is splagchnizomai, the churning of the inward organs, the strongest word for pity the language had; and "send out labourers" is ekballo, the very verb Matthew has used all chapter for casting out demons — beg the owner of the field to thrust workers into it. Note too that harvest in the prophets is nearly always judgement (Joel 3:13); Jesus takes the sickle out of it.
verseByVerse.theology: The two miracles of verses 18-26 are intertwined: the ruler's daughter dies while Jesus is on the way to heal her, and the hemorrhaging woman receives healing by touching his garment. Both cases involve women (a girl and a woman), both involve twelve years (the woman's illness, the girl's age in Mark's account), and both require faith that presses past social convention. Jesus stops for the bleeding woman even while the child lies dying — he does not hurry past need in order to reach crisis. Both receive exactly what they need.
verseByVerse.examples: The harvest saying (vv. 37-38) is the theological conclusion of the two miracle chapters: the need is vast, the laborers few, and the solution is prayer — not human strategy, not program development, but asking the Lord of the harvest to send workers. The church has often responded to the harvest by increasing activity; Jesus commands increasing prayer. The two are not incompatible, but prayer is the first and foundational response.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was saying these things to them, behold, a ruler came in and knelt before him, saying, "My daughter has just died, but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live." And Jesus rose and followed him, with his disciples. And behold, a woman who had suffered from a discharge of blood for twelve years came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, for she said to herself, "If I only touch his garment, I will be made well." Jesus turned, and seeing her he said, "Take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well." And instantly the woman was made well. And when Jesus came to the ruler's house and saw the flute players and the crowd making a commotion, he said, "Go away, for the girl is not dead but sleeping." And they laughed at him. But when the crowd had been put outside, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose. And the report of this went through all that district.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A synagogue ruler — a man of religious rank and standing — comes and kneels before Jesus. His faith outruns anything he has yet seen: not merely "heal my sick child" but "my daughter has just died... come and lay your hand on her, and she will live." Jesus rises at once and follows, without a question or a condition. This is how he answers a sincere cry: immediately, going where he is needed.

On the way the story is interrupted — as Matthew means it to be. A woman who had bled for twelve years comes up behind him. Under the law (Lev 15:25–27) such a discharge made her perpetually unclean: barred from synagogue and temple, unable to embrace a friend or receive a greeting without defiling them, cut off for twelve years from the ordinary touch of human belonging. To press through the crowd is to defile everyone she brushes — an act of sheer desperation. She does not announce herself; she reaches: "If I only touch his garment, I will be made well." And what she touches is the tasseled fringe (Num 15:38–40) that symbolized the very law which had shut her out — reaching past the law that condemned her to the One who fulfills it.

Jesus turns: "Take heart, daughter" — the same tender word he gave the paralytic (9:2). He sees the person, not just the affliction. "Your faith has made you well" — not that faith itself healed her, but that it joined her to the One who did. Twelve years end in an instant.

Then he reaches the ruler's house, already loud with flute-players and wailing mourners — the machinery of death. "The girl is not dead but sleeping," he says (the word he will use of Lazarus, Jn 11:11); to the Lord of life, death is a sleep he can break. They laugh — the laugh of those who know a corpse when they see one. He puts them out, takes the girl by the hand (as he had touched the leper), and she rises — egeiro, the word for resurrection itself.

And do not miss why Matthew folds these two stories into one; they are bound by far more than timing. The woman had suffered twelve years; the girl was twelve years old (Mark 5:42) — the child's whole lifetime was the length of the woman's misery. Both are stories of uncleanness and death: the woman ceremonially unclean, the girl a corpse, which was uncleanness at its very height (Num 19:11). By every rule of the law the unclean woman's touch and the dead girl's hand should have defiled him — yet the current runs the other way: his holiness is not stained, it cleanses; his life is not cancelled, it raises (as with the leper at 8:3). And see how the interruption itself preaches: while Jesus stops for the woman, the girl dies — stretching the father's faith from "heal her" to "raise her," and showing that he is Lord not only over long disease but over death itself. A ruler of the synagogue and a nameless, penniless, unclean woman — he has time, touch, and tenderness for them both; he calls her "daughter," and he gives the man back his.

One more thing, for the reader who has Mark or Luke open alongside. There the ruler is named — Jairus — and he comes saying his daughter is at the point of death; only later, while Jesus is delayed with the woman, do messengers arrive with the news that she has died (Mark 5:22-23, 35). Matthew has him say at the outset, "my daughter has just died." It looks like a discrepancy and is in fact a habit. Matthew is the briefest of the three here — he tells in nine verses what Mark takes twenty-three to tell — and he does it by giving the father's request in its final form rather than walking us through the stages. It is what any of us does in summarising: we say a man came asking Jesus to raise his dead daughter, because that is what the errand turned out to be, without retracing every step by which it got there. Matthew is not reporting different words; he is reporting the same event at less length.

Notice that he leaves out the name as well, and the messengers, and the wailing crowd's laughter is kept while their identities go. This is Matthew's way throughout — he compresses the miracle stories and expands the teaching, because his Gospel is built around five great blocks of Jesus's words. A writer's silence is not a denial, and his brevity here is not carelessness. Read the three together and you have the fuller picture; read Matthew alone and you have the point.

The report of it runs through the whole district — as well it might.

One thing more, and it is for readers who have prayed a prayer like Jairus's. Stand where the father is standing. His daughter is dying, he has found Jesus, Jesus has agreed to come — and then Jesus stops. For somebody else. For a woman who had lived with her illness for twelve years and could, on any reasonable calculation, have waited another hour. And in that delay the child dies. Matthew puts the interruption in the middle of the rescue on purpose, and any reader who has watched a clock while heaven said nothing knows exactly what that pause feels like from the inside.

Two things must be said about it, and the second keeps the first from turning cruel. The first is that the delay was not neglect, and it was not the woman winning a competition for his attention. It changed what the father was going to receive. He set out asking for a recovery and went home with a resurrection — and he could not have had the second without the loss that the delay made possible. God's delays are very often the distance between the thing we asked for and the thing he intended to give.

The second is that not everyone gets the child back. Jairus did. Many people have prayed this precise prayer with the same desperation and buried their child anyway, and this passage must never be preached as though the outcome were the promise. It is not. What is promised is what Jesus actually said in the room: that to him the girl was sleeping, and that he can break that sleep whenever he chooses. This raising was a sign, not the destination — the girl grew up and died again in due course — a window opened for a moment onto what he intends to do for every one of his own on the last day. I am the resurrection and the life (Jn 11:25) is the promise; Jairus's daughter is the preview.

And notice who else is in the story, because she is there for a different reader. Twelve years of illness, every resource spent, no cure, and the whole procession of a dying child's rescue stops for her. She is the person in the passage who waited longest and was helped last, and she is the only woman in the Gospels Jesus is recorded calling daughter. If your affliction has outlasted your patience and everyone else's interest, that is the detail to take with you. He was not too busy with the emergency to stop for the long, unglamorous, chronic thing — and when he stopped, he did not merely heal her. He gave her a name in his family.

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus passed on from there, two blind men followed him, crying aloud, "Have mercy on us, Son of David." When he entered the house, the blind men came to him, and Jesus said to them, "Do you believe that I am able to do this?" They said to him, "Yes, Lord." Then he touched their eyes, saying, "According to your faith be it done to you." And their eyes were opened. And Jesus sternly warned them, "See that no one knows about it." But they went away and spread his news through all that district.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus passes on, two blind men follow him, crying the messianic title: "Son of David." They cannot see him, yet they see him more clearly than the Pharisees do. "Son of David" carried the full weight of messianic hope — the promised heir who would restore Israel. Their cry "have mercy on us" echoes Psalm 123, eyes lifted toward the only one who can help; the church inherited this very prayer — Kyrie eleison, "Lord, have mercy" — the oldest Christian liturgical cry, borrowed from these blind men.

Jesus does not heal immediately on the road — he waits until they come inside, until he can ask them directly: "Do you believe that I am able to do this?" The question is not rhetorical but searching: faith must be articulated, not merely assumed. "Yes, Lord" — simple, complete, unhesitating. Jesus then touches their eyes — the second eye-touching in a chapter that is also about the eyes of faith — and pronounces the healing according to their faith. "According to your faith" does not mean that great faith produces great healings; it means that faith is the channel through which the healing of Christ reaches the person who has asked. The measure of their trust determined the measure of their openness to receive what he gives freely.

The stern warning against publicity — repeated throughout Matthew's earlier chapters — is disobeyed immediately and enthusiastically. The two men cannot keep silent about what has happened to them. Matthew records the disobedience without apparent condemnation: the impossibility of keeping silent about an encounter with Jesus is not only understandable but almost inevitable. The healed cannot but speak. At the same time, Jesus's consistent instruction about silence reflects a pastoral wisdom: premature publicity could distort the nature of his mission, attracting crowds for the wrong reasons before the cross had accomplished what his kingdom was actually about. The popular messianic expectation needed correcting before it was inflamed.

There is, in truth, more to this repeated command of silence than first appears — scholars have called it the "messianic secret," and several threads run through it. First, timing: Jesus moved on his Father's schedule toward the cross ("my hour has not yet come"), and a wildfire of publicity could force a premature collision with the authorities before the appointed time. Second, the danger of a sign-only faith: the crowds chased miracles, not the Messiah — "you seek me... because you ate your fill of the loaves" (Jn 6:26) — and Jesus would not build faith on spectacle. Third, and deepest, the title itself could not be rightly understood until the cross defined it. To proclaim "Son of David" or "Christ" without Calvary was to broadcast a false messiah — the political deliverer the crowds would have crowned by force (Jn 6:15). This is why, even after Peter's great confession, Jesus charges the disciples to tell no one (16:20) and at once begins to speak of his death (16:21).

Two things keep this from being a flat rule. Matthew sees in Jesus' reticence the very portrait of Isaiah's gentle Servant: "he will not quarrel or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets" (12:18–21, citing Isa 42) — the opposite of a self-advertising king. And the silence was never absolute: in Gentile country, where no messianic frenzy threatened, Jesus told the freed demoniac to "go and tell" how much the Lord had done for him (Mark 5:19). The secret, then, was provisional — fitted to a work not yet finished. Once the cross and the empty tomb had defined who the Messiah is, the command is gloriously reversed: "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations" (28:19). What had to be hushed before Calvary becomes the news shouted from the rooftops after it.

verseByVerse.quote: As they were going away, behold, a demon-oppressed man who was mute was brought to him. And when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke. And the crowds marveled, saying, "Never was anything like this seen in Israel." But the Pharisees said, "He casts out demons by the prince of demons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mute demoniac is the seventh miracle in Matthew's collection — brought, not self-presenting. He cannot ask for himself. The healing is narrated in two words: cast out, spoke. Matthew does not linger; the accumulation of miracles is the point. The crowd's response — "never was anything like this seen in Israel" — is the accumulative verdict of the two miracle chapters: the ministry of Jesus is unprecedented, exceeding anything the prophets or kings of Israel had done. The Pharisees' response in verse 34 is the dark counterpart: they attribute the unprecedented to the diabolical. The same evidence produces astonishment and attribution to God in the crowd, and attribution to Satan in the religious establishment. The difference is not in the data but in the heart.

The Pharisees' accusation is the beginning of the Beelzebul controversy that will reach its climax in chapter 12. It is the strategy of those who cannot dispute the evidence: attribute the supernatural to the demonic. They do not deny the miracles; they reattribute their source. Jesus does not respond to the charge here — Matthew reserves the full answer for chapter 12 — and simply continues.

Two things are worth adding, and the first sets the whole of chapters 8 and 9 in place.

This is the tenth. Count them: the leper, the centurion's servant, Peter's mother-in-law, the storm, the demoniacs of the Gadarenes, the paralytic, the ruler's daughter, the woman with the flow of blood, the two blind men, and this mute man. Ten miracles, gathered into two chapters, arranged by Matthew rather than by chronology — Mark and Luke scatter several of these elsewhere.

The number is probably not accidental in a Gospel this carefully built. Matthew has already presented Jesus as the new Moses — a child escaping a slaughter of infants, called out of Egypt, passing through water, forty days in the wilderness, a mountain, a law. Ten mighty works following a mountain of teaching is the shape of the Exodus, with one enormous difference: Moses' ten were plagues that fell on Egypt, and these ten fall on disease, on death, on the storm and on the demonic. The signs of the first deliverance destroyed; the signs of this one heal.

And this is where the accusation first appears. Verse 34 is the opening of a charge that will run through the Gospel and reach its crisis in chapter 12, and it is worth seeing why they had to reach for it.

They could not deny the miracles. Nobody in the New Testament ever does — not the Pharisees, not the Sanhedrin, not Herod, not Pilate. The mute man was standing there talking. So there were only two available explanations for a power that was plainly real and plainly not theirs, and having ruled out God they had one left.

Note also the honest textual point: a few early manuscripts omit verse 34 altogether, and some scholars think it was brought in from 12:24. The evidence for keeping it is good and most editions do, but a reader who finds a footnote in his Bible has met a real question rather than an invented one.

What makes the verse chilling is its position. Immediately before it, the crowd says never was anything like this seen in Israel. Same day, same man, same evidence — and one group concludes that God has visited his people while the other concludes that the devil is loose in Galilee.

The difference was never the data.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went throughout all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction. When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. Then he said to his disciples, "The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few;" therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ministry summary of verse 35 mirrors 4:23 exactly, forming a bracket around the Sermon on the Mount and the two miracle chapters: teaching, proclaiming, healing — the three inseparable expressions of the kingdom's arrival. Nothing the Pharisees say stops what God is doing.

Compassion (splagchnizomai) — a word for the churning of the bowels in ancient Greek, the deepest physical sensation of moved pity. Jesus sees the crowds not as an audience or a problem to be managed but as sheep without a shepherd — leaderless, exhausted, and in danger. The image is from Numbers 27:17, where Moses asks God to appoint a successor so that Israel not be "like sheep that have no shepherd." Jesus sees his generation in exactly those terms. The harvest metaphor then shifts the image from need to opportunity: the fields are ready, the workers are scarce. Both images are true simultaneously — the people are lost sheep (need-language) and ripened grain (opportunity-language).

The solution to the labor shortage is prayer, not recruitment. "Pray earnestly" (deethete — beg, implore) to "the Lord of the harvest" — God himself, who owns the field and controls the workers. Jesus does not say: form a committee, develop a strategy, train more preachers (though all of these are legitimate). He says: pray. The implication is that laborers are God's provision, not human production. We do not generate missionaries and church planters by better programs; we receive them from God in response to prayer. The disciples who hear this command are themselves about to be sent (ch. 10) — they will be the answer to the prayer they are instructed to pray. Pray for laborers, and be prepared to be one.

Three words in this passage are stronger than any English version can afford to be, and each one changes the picture.

Harassed and helpless. The first is eskylmenoi, from a verb meaning to flay or mangle — to skin an animal. It is used of something that has been torn about and worried at. The second is errimmenoi, thrown down, flung aside, left lying where it fell.

So the sentence is not they looked tired. It is: mauled, and dumped. That is what Jesus saw when he looked at a religious crowd in first-century Galilee — people who had been savaged by something and abandoned where they dropped.

And the shepherd image names what savaged them. Sheep without a shepherd comes from Moses asking God to appoint a successor (Num. 27:17), and from Micaiah's vision of a leaderless Israel (1 Kgs. 22:17). But the passage standing closest is Ezekiel 34, and it is not gentle: Ah, shepherds of Israel who have been feeding yourselves! Should not shepherds feed the sheep?… The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the injured you have not bound up… and they were scattered, because there was no shepherd (Ezek. 34:2-5).

The flock is not shepherdless because nobody applied for the post. It has shepherds. That is the problem — and Jesus has spent two chapters in conflict with them.

Compassion. Splagchnizomai comes from the noun for the inward organs, and it is the strongest word for pity the language had. It is not a decision to be sympathetic; it is what the body does when something goes through you. And it is almost exclusively a Gospel word, used of Jesus and of three figures in his parables — the father seeing his son on the road, the Samaritan seeing the man in the ditch, the king with the unpayable debt.

Send out. And this is the one that startles. Pray the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers — the verb is ekballo, to throw out, drive out, expel. It is the same verb Matthew has been using all chapter for casting out demons.

Jesus does not say ask God to recruit. He says: beg the owner of the field to thrust workers out into it. Which is a strange way to describe answered prayer until you have watched how people actually get into hard work for God — rarely by strolling toward it, and very often by being moved along by something they did not choose.

One more thing about the harvest. In the prophets, harvest is nearly always an image of judgement: put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe (Joel 3:13). Jesus takes the sickle out of it. The same fields, the same ripeness, the same urgency — and what is being gathered in is people, and the workers are being sent to save them rather than to cut them down.

He looked at a crowd that had been flayed and thrown aside by the men who should have fed them, and what he felt turned him inside out. Then he told his friends to pray, and the next thing he did was answer the prayer himself by sending the men who had prayed it.

9.theology: Justification and the forgiveness of sins. The healing of the paralytic is Matthew’s clearest window into the doctrine of justification. Jesus pronounces forgiveness as a judicial declaration — he does not say “God will forgive you if…” but “your sins are forgiven,” accomplished fact. This is the forensic heart of the gospel: the guilty are declared righteous by the word of the Judge himself, on the basis of the Son’s merit, through faith. The Reformers called this the article by which the church stands or falls. Matthew 9 shows it enacted in history by the King who has authority on earth to forgive sins — the same authority he will exercise from the cross, bearing the penalty that makes the declaration just.
9.examples:
Then: Matthew the tax collector was the last person anyone expected in the kingdom. His conversion was a public scandal and a public testimony. The banquet he threw was evangelism by hospitality: bring the ones who need the physician to the physician.

Now: Every church that welcomes the broken, the addicted, the socially marginal, and the morally compromised is continuing Matthew’s banquet. The temptation of respectable Christianity is the Pharisees’ error: to protect the purity of the community by excluding the sick. Jesus reverses the logic. The church is not a museum of saints but a hospital for sinners — a place where the Great Physician practices.

10.title: Sent as Sheep Among Wolves
10.text: <sup>1</sup>And he called to him his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every affliction. <sup>5</sup>These twelve Jesus sent out, instructing them, “Go nowhere among the Gentiles and enter no town of the Samaritans, <sup>6</sup>but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. <sup>7</sup>And proclaim as you go, saying, ‘The kingdom of heaven is at hand.’ <sup>8</sup>Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received without paying; give without pay. <sup>16</sup>Behold, I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves, so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. <sup>17</sup>Beware of men, for they will deliver you over to courts and flog you in their synagogues, <sup>18</sup>and you will be dragged before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them and the Gentiles. <sup>19</sup>When they deliver you over, do not be anxious how you are to speak or what you are to say, for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour. <sup>20</sup>For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you. <sup>26</sup>So have no fear of them, for nothing is covered that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. <sup>28</sup>And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. <sup>29</sup>Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. <sup>30</sup>But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. <sup>31</sup>Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows. <sup>37</sup>Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. <sup>38</sup>And whoever does not take his cross and follow me is not worthy of me. <sup>39</sup>Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it.”
10.overview:
Chapter 10 is the mission discourse — the second of Matthew’s five great discourses. Jesus commissions the Twelve, gives them his authority, and sends them first to Israel. But the instructions quickly expand beyond a local mission trip to describe the entire missionary existence of the church until the end of the age. Persecution is not an accident but the normal condition of mission: “I am sending you out as sheep in the midst of wolves.” The sheep do not become wolves; they remain sheep — dependent, vulnerable, and under the care of the Shepherd.

The antidote to the fear of persecution is the fear of God. Three times Jesus says “fear not” (vv. 26, 28, 31), anchoring each command in the sovereign knowledge and care of the Father. Not a sparrow falls without him; the hairs of the head are numbered. If the Father governs such small things, he governs the sufferings of his missionaries. The cross appears explicitly in verse 38: discipleship is cruciform. The disciple takes up the cross before the resurrection — only those who lose their lives for Christ’s sake will find them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Twelve Sent Out: Authority, Message, and Provision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus calls the Twelve, names them, and sends them out with authority over unclean spirits and disease. Their mission is confined to Israel: go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, not to the Gentiles or Samaritans. They are to preach the kingdom, heal the sick, raise the dead, and cast out demons — exactly what Jesus himself has been doing. Their provision is radical dependence: no gold, no bag, no extra tunic. Worthy households will host them; unworthy towns will receive judgment. What the summary cannot hold. This is the only time Matthew uses the word "apostles" — once in twenty-eight chapters, at the exact moment they stop learning and start being sent. The Twelve is a claim, not a headcount: ten tribes had been gone for seven hundred years, and Jesus says himself that these men will judge the twelve tribes (19:28), so appointing exactly twelve is the reconstituting of Israel. Note the limits of the delegation — authority over unclean spirits and disease, but not to forgive sins, which is nowhere handed over. The list is in pairs because he sent them out two by two (Mk. 6:7): Peter and Andrew, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew, Thomas and Matthew, James and Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot and Judas. Which sharpens the incompatibility until it draws blood: the Zealot movement existed to expel Rome by violence, and the Jews they killed first were collaborators — men like Matthew, four verses away in the same list. Nothing suggests Jesus arranged a reconciliation or that either changed his politics. On the charge: "raise the dead" is in it, and Matthew alone records that. "You received without paying, give without pay" is dorean twice — and the guard is supplied two verses later, since "the labourer deserves his food" (v. 10) is quoted by Paul to argue that preachers should be supported (1 Cor. 9:14; 1 Tim. 5:18). A worker may be supported; a gift may not be sold. "worthy" (axios) occurs four times in vv. 10-13 and the definition is purely practical — a worthy house is one that opens its door. And staying in one house forecloses the patron-shopping that itinerant teachers were notorious for; a Christian handbook of the next century, the Didache, has to legislate against exactly that. The dust-shaking was the gesture a Jew made leaving pagan soil — performed now on a Jewish town, it is a verdict delivered in mime.
verseByVerse.theology: The mission of the Twelve is an extension of Jesus's own mission: he gives them his authority (10:1) and his message (10:7). Disciples are not innovators but ambassadors — they carry the word and power of the one who sent them, not their own. The restriction to Israel (v. 5-6) is not permanent exclusion of Gentiles but the priority of the gospel going first to the lost sheep of Israel, as Paul will later articulate (Rom. 1:16). The Great Commission (28:18-20) will remove the restriction after the resurrection.
verseByVerse.examples: Radical dependence — no gold, no bag, no sandals beyond what they are wearing — is not poverty for its own sake but trust in the Lord of the harvest to provide through the households that receive them. The kingdom worker is not self-sufficient; they are wholly dependent on God's provision through his people. This dependence is not weakness but testimony: the worker who needs nothing from you has nothing to demonstrate about the kingdom's power to provide.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called to him his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every affliction. The names of the twelve apostles are these: first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother;
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He gave them authority" — the authority is delegated, not inherent. The disciples possess no power of their own; they act under the authority of the one who has "all authority in heaven and on earth" (28:18). The transition from "disciples" (learners) to "apostles" (sent ones) marks the formal commissioning. Matthew lists Peter first — always first in any list of the Twelve — not for theological primacy in the Roman Catholic sense but as the acknowledged leader of the group, the one who most often speaks for them. Andrew, Peter's brother, brought Peter to Jesus (John 1:41) and is listed immediately after him: the first missionary brought the future leader of the apostles.

Three things, and the first is a small statistic worth knowing.

This is the only time Matthew uses the word apostles. Once, in twenty-eight chapters. Everywhere else it is the twelve, or the disciples, or the twelve disciples. And he uses it here, at the precise moment they stop learning and start being sent, which is exactly what the word means — apostolos, one dispatched with a commission.

Mark uses it once too, at the same point. It is not a title these men wore casually.

The number is not a headcount. Twelve is the number of the tribes, and Jesus says so himself later in this Gospel: you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (19:28). Israel had long since ceased to exist as twelve tribes — ten of them had been carried off by Assyria seven hundred years earlier and never came back.

So the appointing of exactly twelve men is a claim before it is an arrangement. He is not recruiting staff. He is reconstituting the people of God, and he starts by naming a twelve.

And notice what he hands over. He gave them authority — exousia, the same word that has been the flashpoint of the last two chapters. The scribes disputed his authority to forgive; the crowd marvelled that God had given such authority to men; he will say at the end of the book that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him.

Here he gives it away, one chapter after having to defend it.

Though notice the limits, because they are exact. Authority over unclean spirits, and to heal disease. Not to forgive sins — that is nowhere delegated in this passage, and the apostles never claim it. They are given the works. The word that only God can speak stays where it belongs.

verseByVerse.quote: James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list includes Matthew identified as "the tax collector" — a humbling self-designation in the Gospel he wrote. It also includes Simon the Zealot (a political radical who wanted to expel Rome by force) and Judas Iscariot, identified from the beginning as the betrayer. Jesus chose a revolutionary and a collaborator, the impetuous and the doubting, the bold and the calculating. The community of the Twelve is not a homogeneous club but a collection of incompatible personalities held together by allegiance to Jesus. That this community became the foundation of the church is testimony to the power of the one who called them — not to the natural compatibility of those called.

The list is arranged in pairs, and the reason is in Mark: he began to send them out two by two (Mk. 6:7).
