The interpretation is direct: the seed is "the word of the kingdom" — the proclamation of the kingdom's arrival in Jesus. The path-hearer does not understand it — not because it is unintelligible but because the heart is closed — and the evil one takes it immediately. The rocky-ground hearer is more alarming: they hear with joy. Immediate, enthusiastic joy. This looks like conversion; it feels like conversion. But the joy is rootless — it has not gone deep enough to survive adversity. Many revivals and many individual conversions have produced this profile: genuine initial response, no lasting change, eventual fall away when the cost becomes real. The joy is not the problem; the shallowness beneath it is.

One word holds this whole chapter together, and it turns up here for the third time.

Does not understand it — syniemi. Matthew uses it at verse 13 (nor do they understand), verse 14 (never understand), verse 15 (understand with their heart), here at verse 19, at verse 23 of the good soil, and at verse 51, where Jesus asks the disciples outright: Have you understood all these things?

Six times in one chapter. It is not a word about intelligence — the root sense is putting things together, bringing them into one place. And it is the thing that distinguishes the first soil from the fourth.

So the path-hearer's problem is not that the word was too difficult. It is that nothing was joined to anything; the seed sat on top of a life it never connected with, and was gone.

Then the second soil, and the detail that ought to unsettle a certain kind of Christian gathering.

He hears the word and immediately receives it with joy.

Joy. Not grudging assent, not intellectual agreement — the visible, immediate, delighted response that everybody in Christian work is glad to see and inclined to count.

And it is the mark of the soil that fails.

That has to be said carefully, because joy is a fruit of the Spirit and this passage is not against it. The good soil is not described as joyless. What the passage does is remove joy from the list of reliable indicators — because the one soil explicitly credited with immediate joy is the one that will not be there in a year.

Which is a hard word for any ministry that measures by response. The path shows nothing and the rocky ground shows everything, and the only soil that can be identified with certainty is the one that is still standing at harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately he falls away. As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it proves unfruitful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"No root in himself" — the shallowness is an internal condition, not primarily caused by external persecution. The persecution reveals what was already lacking. The thorny-ground hearer is the hardest case to identify from outside: they heard the word and received it; they have not yet been tested by persecution and have not yet fallen away. But the thorns are growing. "The cares of the world" (anxiety about daily life) and "the deceitfulness of riches" (the false promise that wealth satisfies) crowd out the word gradually. The plant does not die dramatically; it is choked slowly. The slow spiritual death of the busy, comfortable middle-class Christian is the thorny-ground profile. The word is not rejected; it is gradually crowded into irrelevance.

Two words in these verses are doing more than they appear to.

The first is falls away. The Greek is skandalizetai — the trap word, from the name for the stick that springs a snare. It is the same verb Jesus used in the message to John in prison: blessed is the one who is not offended by me (11:6).

So the rocky-ground hearer does not resign. He is tripped. The picture is not of a man weighing the evidence and withdrawing, but of somebody walking along and going down suddenly over something he did not see coming — which is what persecution actually feels like to a person who was not expecting the Christian life to cost anything.

The second is the deceitfulness of riches. Apate means a deliberate deception, a con. Money is not described here as evil, or as a rival god, but as a liar — something that makes a specific promise and does not keep it.

What does it promise? Security, mostly. That when there is enough, the anxiety will stop.

And it is worth noticing that the same soil contains its opposite. The thorns are the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches — the worry of not having enough and the illusion of having it. Those look like different problems and this parable files them together, because they choke the same plant and they are the same preoccupation viewed from either end.

And the manner of death is the thing to notice. Nothing in this soil is dramatic. The seed germinates, roots properly, and grows. There is no snatching, no scorching, no falling away in a crisis.

It simply produces nothing, over a long period, while remaining green — and the verse is careful to say what is missing rather than what went wrong: it proves unfruitful.

Here is the test, and it is quieter than the others. Not have you fallen away, which a person would notice, but: what is there to show? Take the last five years. Something should have come off this plant by now.

verseByVerse.quote: As for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it. He indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Hears the word and understands it" — the good soil is characterized by understanding: not merely hearing the sound but grasping the meaning and receiving it into the heart as truth. Understanding in Matthew is not intellectual comprehension alone; it is the comprehension that changes the one who comprehends. The fruit that follows is the evidence of the transformation. The variation in yield — hundredfold, sixty, thirty — is important: good soil is not uniform, and the kingdom does not require identical productivity. It requires genuine fruitfulness. The hundredfold yield is extraordinary; the thirtyfold is abundant. Both are acceptable; neither is the unfruitful thorny ground or the barren rocky ground. God is not demanding equal output; he is asking for genuine fruit from genuinely transformed hearts.

Now use the parable for the purpose it was given, because it is not a taxonomy for classifying other people. Jesus told it to a mixed crowd and ended it with he who has ears, let him hear. The only honest question is which soil I am, and it is worth asking with some specific tests rather than in a vague fog.

The path: is there any real hearing at all, or does it slide off the surface? A usable test is not how much you know but when Scripture last changed a decision you had already made. The rocky ground: is the faith attached mainly to feeling, and does it fold when following costs something? Test it against the last time obedience was genuinely expensive — what happened? And the thorny ground, which is the one most readers of a commentary should worry about, because it is not rejection but crowding. Nothing is refused; the word is simply squeezed into a smaller and smaller corner by things that are not even sinful. Test it by looking at where your mind goes when it is unoccupied, and at your calendar and your bank statement, which between them are a fairly ruthless account of what you actually care about.

Then the question that decides whether this parable crushes you or helps you: is the soil fixed? Because if it is, the honest reader who finds himself among the thorns has just been handed a life sentence. It is not fixed, and the Bible is emphatic about it. Real soil cannot change itself; people are not real soil. Hosea says to a hard-hearted nation, break up your fallow ground, for it is time to seek the LORD (Hos 10:12), and Jeremiah says, break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns (Jer 4:3) — which is God commanding the very change the metaphor might seem to rule out. And underneath the command is the promise that makes it possible: I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezek 36:26). That is the one thing no field can do for itself, and it is precisely what he undertakes to do.

So if you have recognised yourself somewhere in the first three, that recognition is not a verdict; it is the beginning of the remedy, and it is more than the crowd on the beach ever got. If the ground is hard, ask him to break it, and put yourself where the word is faithfully preached until it does. If the trouble is shallowness, the answer is roots — and roots grow in the dark, from knowing the Scriptures well enough to stand when the feelings have gone, and from being known by people who will not let you drift. If it is thorns, they have to be named and cut one at a time, because nobody has ever drifted out of thorns; the choking is what happens when nothing is done.

And notice what the parable does not say, which is a comfort to anyone who sows and sees little. Three soils out of four came to nothing, and the harvest was still thirty, sixty, a hundredfold. The sower is not told to stop scattering, or to sow more carefully, or to blame himself for the path and the rocks. He is told what the ground does. Keep sowing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–58 — Six More Parables: The Kingdom's Hidden Growth and Coming Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six parables follow the sower: the wheat and weeds (growing together until harvest), the mustard seed (tiny beginning, great growth), the leaven (invisible transformation of the whole), the hidden treasure and pearl of great price (discovering and selling everything for the kingdom), and the dragnet (mixed catch sorted at the end). Jesus then returns to Nazareth, where his neighbors take offense at him. What the summary leaves out. The weed has a name: zizania is bearded darnel, and three facts make the parable bite. It is indistinguishable from wheat until the ear forms — Jewish tradition treated it as degenerate wheat. It is poisonous, regularly fungus-infected, and the Latin temulentum means drunken because that is how a person looks who has eaten the bread. And sowing it in an enemy's field was a crime under Roman law, which means it happened often enough to legislate for. The master's refusal to weed is agriculturally exact — darnel roots interlace with wheat roots. This was the text at the centre of the donatist controversy, and Augustine answered the rigorists from it; but note the guard runs both ways, since "let both grow together" is not a ban on church discipline (18:15-17). Discipline addresses conduct and is reversible; what is forbidden is sorting by identity, which requires seeing the ear before it has formed. On the mustard seed objection — orchid seed is smaller — three answers: it was a proverb for the very small, the comparison is among seeds a farmer actually sowed ("in his field"), and this is ordinary descriptive speech, as when we say the sun rises. And the image of a great tree with birds nesting is imperial — Nebuchadnezzar's dream tree (Dan. 4:12), Ezekiel's Assyria and his cedar (Ezek. 17:23; 31:6). Jesus attaches empire-language to a garden herb. The chapter is bracketed by a door: he goes out of the house to the crowds (v. 1) and back into the house for the explanations (v. 36). "the field is the world" — not the church, and Jesus defines it explicitly. The two kinds are described by parentage, not performance, which is why sorting by inspection cannot work. The reapers are angels, and the harvest is the end of the age — the sorting is removed from human hands and from the growing season in one sentence. Note also that the weeds are gathered out of his kingdom (v. 41), so the kingdom in its present form contains what will have to be removed; and "causes of sin" is skandala, the trap-word running through 11:6, 13:21 and 13:57. The dragnet is a sagene, not a cast-net — it sweeps everything, and Levitical law (Lev. 11:9-12) meant a Jewish crew sorted catch into permitted and forbidden every working day. And v. 52's scribe trained for the kingdom is very probably Matthew's self-portrait: the evangelist who quotes the Old Testament some sixty times, structures his book in five discourses, and alone records this saying.
verseByVerse.theology: The parables of growth — mustard seed and leaven — correct the disciples' expectation that the kingdom would arrive with obvious power and immediate separation of righteous from wicked. The kingdom begins invisibly, grows slowly, works from within, and will only be sorted at the harvest. The "already-not-yet" structure of the kingdom is the key: it is genuinely present now (the treasure is in the field; the leaven is in the dough) but not yet fully revealed (the harvest is coming). Patience and trust in the hidden growth are the kingdom virtues these parables require.
verseByVerse.examples: The two treasure parables (hidden treasure, pearl) express the supreme value of the kingdom: it is worth selling everything to obtain. The joy of the man who finds the treasure is the joy of someone who has found what makes every other thing trivially small by comparison. This is the experience of genuine conversion — not reluctant sacrifice but joyful exchange, because the thing found is worth infinitely more than everything surrendered. The kingdom is not burdensome; it is the treasure that makes all other burdens light.

verseByVerse.quote: He put another parable before them, saying, "The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field, but while his men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parable of the wheat and weeds addresses the question every serious believer asks about the mixed community of the church: why are there false believers among the true? Why doesn't God sort them immediately? The answer given is complex: the enemy has planted the weeds; the sorting is coming; but it is not yet. The "weeds" (zizania — darnel, Lolium temulentum) represent false disciples who cannot yet be distinguished from the genuine. The choice of darnel is not incidental: every farmer in Jesus's audience knew exactly what it was and why it was so troubling. Darnel is a grass that grows in grain fields and is virtually indistinguishable from wheat through every stage of early growth — the seedlings look identical, the leaves are the same, the stalks grow to the same height — remaining unidentifiable until the grain heads form and reveal that the darnel plant produces no edible grain. By then, the roots are so intertwined that pulling the darnel would uproot the wheat with it. But darnel is not merely a fruitless weed: it is almost invariably infected with a toxic fungus (Neotyphodium temulentum) that causes serious harm — dizziness, convulsions, and in sufficient quantity death — to anyone who eats bread baked from grain mixed with darnel seeds. Palestinian farmers did not regard darnel as a minor nuisance; they regarded it as a genuine danger to the harvest and to those who would eat it. The parable trades on both properties simultaneously: false disciples are indistinguishable from the genuine in the early stages (you cannot see the difference until fruit appears), and they are not merely neutral presences but genuinely harmful. This double reality — outward similarity, inward danger — makes the master's restraint both wise and necessary. The night-planting by the enemy (v. 39 — the devil) explains the mixture: it is not the failure of God's sowing but the deliberate, malicious work of the adversary who exploits the period of growth.

Two details in the setup deserve a moment.

While men were sleeping. That is not an accusation — it is simply night, and men sleep at night. The parable does not fault the household for failing to mount a watch over a field, and no reading should make it a lesson about vigilance.

What the phrase does is locate the sabotage where sabotage always happens: unobserved, at a time when nobody could reasonably have been looking, in a way that left no trace until months later.

And the timing is the cruellest part of it. The enemy chooses the one window in the agricultural year when the crime is both possible and undetectable — after sowing, before germination. Any earlier and the ploughing would bury it wrong; any later and fresh seed on worked ground would be visible.

He knows the calendar. That is what makes him an enemy rather than a vandal.

Then the word for what he does: he sowed weeds in the midst of the wheat.

Not around the edges, not in a corner that could be written off. Through the middle of it, mixed in, so that the two crops would come up interleaved and no line could ever be drawn between them.

Which is precisely the situation the master will describe at verse 29, and the reason his answer has to be what it is. The enemy did not merely add something bad to the field. He arranged it so that removing the bad would cost the good.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the plants came up and bore grain, then the weeds appeared also. And the servants of the master of the house came and said to him, "Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? How then does it have weeds?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The weeds become visible only at the grain stage — when the plants begin to mature and produce fruit, the weeds that bore no grain are distinguishable. Early in the growth, darnel and wheat look identical. This is the pastoral reality of the church: false profession looks like genuine faith in the early stages; the difference appears only as growth and fruit become visible over time. The servants' question is the perennial question of the troubled pastor and the puzzled believer: didn't God sow only good seed? How then the tares? The answer — an enemy did this — does not fully resolve the mystery but locates responsibility: God's field has been invaded, not corrupted from within his sowing.

The weed has a name, and once it is known the whole parable sharpens.

The Greek is zizania, and it is identified with near-unanimity as bearded darnel — Lolium temulentum, a grass that grows throughout the Middle East and infests wheat fields.

Three facts about it matter.

It is indistinguishable from wheat. Not similar — indistinguishable, by eye, until the heads form. The blade, the height, the colour and the habit are the same. Jewish tradition even regarded it as a degenerate form of wheat rather than a separate plant, which tells you how close the resemblance is. Only when the ear comes does the difference appear: wheat bears heavy golden grain and bows over; darnel bears small black seed and stands up straight.

It is poisonous. The seed is regularly infected with a fungus, and eating it produces dizziness, nausea and vomiting — the Latin name temulentum means drunken, because that is what a person looks like who has eaten bread made from contaminated flour. In quantity it can kill.

And sowing it in somebody's field was a known crime. Roman law carried a specific provision against it, which means it happened often enough to need legislating for. This is not an invented scenario. It is agricultural sabotage, and everybody listening would have known of a case.

Which changes the servants' question from puzzlement to alarm.

They are not asking an abstract question about the origin of evil. They have walked out at the wrong moment in the season and discovered that a field they believed was clean is full of something that looks like food and is not, in quantities they cannot now estimate, and it is too late to do anything about it before harvest.

And the master's answer — an enemy has done this — is a diagnosis rather than an explanation. It says who, and it does not say why, and the parable never comes back to that.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "An enemy has done this." So the servants said to him, "Then do you want us to go and gather them?" But he said, "No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The master's refusal to pull the weeds immediately is the parables' most counterintuitive point. The servants offer to solve the problem now; the master sees the risk: immature wheat roots and darnel roots are intertwined. Pulling the weeds prematurely would destroy the wheat. This is the argument against premature ecclesiastical judgment — the attempt to create a pure church by rigorous exclusion can damage genuine believers in the process, and the human ability to distinguish wheat from tares is not sufficient for the task. The separation belongs to the harvest, not to the growing season. The church is to be disciplined (cf. Matt. 18:15-20) but not to attempt the final judgment that belongs only to the Son of Man at the end of the age.

The master's reasoning is agriculturally exact, which is worth saying because it is often treated as a piece of theological convenience.

Darnel roots do not grow beside wheat roots; they interlace with them. In a field where the two have come up together and stood for weeks, pulling one out lifts the other. Any farmer in that audience knew it, which is why the master's answer needs no argument — the servants do not push back.

So the refusal is not sentimentality about the weeds. It is a judgement about what would be destroyed in the process of removing them.

And that has a long and painful history in the church, which is worth knowing.

This parable was the text at the centre of the Donatist controversy in North Africa. After the persecutions, a rigorist party held that the church must be visibly pure — that clergy who had lapsed under pressure were no longer clergy, and that a mixed church was no church at all. Augustine answered them from this passage: the field contains both, the servants are not the reapers, and the demand for a pure church before the harvest is a demand God has explicitly refused.

That argument has had to be made repeatedly since, because the Donatist instinct is perennial and it is always sincere. It arises from a genuine love of holiness, and it always produces the same result: the sharper the sieve, the more wheat goes out with the darnel.

The guard has to run the other way too, and this parable is regularly misused for it.

Let both grow together is not a prohibition on church discipline. Five chapters later Jesus lays out a procedure for confronting sin in the congregation that ends in exclusion (18:15-17), and Paul applies it without hesitation.

The distinction is between two different operations. Discipline addresses conduct, is corrective, is aimed at restoration, and is reversible. What the master forbids is an attempt to sort people by identity — to determine who is finally wheat and who is finally darnel — and that is forbidden because it requires seeing the ear before the ear has formed.

verseByVerse.quote: Let both grow together until the harvest, and at harvest time I will tell the reapers, "Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn." He put another parable before them, saying, "The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The harvest verdict is certain and final: the weeds are gathered first and burned; the wheat is safely gathered into the barn. The judgment is not avoidable; it is only delayed. The patience of the growing season is not laxity toward evil but wisdom about timing. The mustard seed parable follows without pause: the smallest seed in common cultivation, proverbially tiny, yet growing into a tree large enough for birds to nest in. The contrast between beginning and end is the point: the kingdom's origin is astonishingly small (a band of Galilean disciples around an itinerant teacher) and its destiny is vast enough to shelter the nations. The smallness at the start is not evidence of the kingdom's weakness but of its hidden power.

An objection is regularly raised against verse 32 and it deserves a straight answer: the mustard seed is not the smallest seed in the world. Orchid seed is finer, and so are several others.

Three things settle it.

First, smallest of all seeds was a proverb. The rabbis used mustard seed as their standard unit of the very small — measurements of ritual impurity and legal quantity were expressed in terms of it, much as English says a grain of sand without conducting a survey.

Second, the comparison is inside a category the sentence itself supplies: a man took and sowed in his field. Among the seeds a Galilean farmer actually handled, mustard was the smallest by a wide margin, and orchids were not among them.

Third, this is ordinary descriptive speech, and Scripture uses it constantly. We say the sun rises without asserting geocentrism. A speaker who said the smallest seed known to botany would have been answering a question nobody in that field had asked.

Now the plant, and there is a joke in it.

Black mustard grows fast and can reach eight or ten feet in a season — big enough for birds to perch and shelter in, which is what the verse says. It is not a tree, and Jesus does not call it one. He says it becomes greater than the garden plants and becomes a tree in the loose sense of the word.

And the image of a great tree with birds nesting in its branches is not neutral. It is imperial. Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a tree at the centre of the earth, immense, with the birds of the heavens dwelling in its branches (Dan. 4:12). Ezekiel uses the same picture for Assyria, and again for the cedar God will plant on the mountain height of Israel, under which every kind of bird will dwell (Ezek. 17:23; 31:6).

That is the language of empires. And Jesus attaches it to a garden herb.

Which is exactly the correction his hearers needed. They were expecting the cedar — the kingdom arriving with obvious magnificence. He gives them mustard: something small enough to be overlooked, fast enough to be underestimated, growing in a vegetable patch — and ending up with the nations sheltering in it.

verseByVerse.quote: "It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches." He told them another parable. "The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mustard tree's nesting birds may echo Ezekiel's vision of the great tree that shelters all nations (Ezek. 17:23; 31:6) — a vision of universal empire. The kingdom that begins as a mustard seed will grow into the shelter of the nations. The leaven parable adds the dimension of invisible transformation: leaven works from within, invisibly, until the whole batch is leavened. The kingdom does not transform society by external imposition (the constant temptation of political religion) but by the invisible work of the Spirit in individual hearts that gradually permeates the whole. Three measures is a large batch — Abraham's wife Sarah used three measures for the angels' meal (Gen. 18:6). The kingdom is destined to leaven the whole.

A reader who knows his Bible may balk at that, and the objection is a good one. Everywhere else in Scripture leaven stands for corruption. Israel was to sweep it out of the house before Passover (Ex. 12:15); Paul tells the Corinthians that a little leaven leavens the whole lump, and he is talking about tolerated sin (1 Cor. 5:6-8); and Jesus himself, three chapters on, will warn the disciples to beware the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees (16:6) — meaning their teaching, and meaning it as poison. So why is the kingdom leaven here?

Some have concluded that it is not — that this parable is a warning about corruption spreading through the church rather than a picture of the kingdom's growth. It is an honest reading and some careful Christians hold it. But it does not sit well with the sentence itself. Jesus says the kingdom of heaven is like leaven, exactly as he has just said it is like a mustard seed, and he has been describing growth from something small to something total in both. A warning would be a strange thing to introduce with those words and then leave entirely unexplained, in a run of parables he does explain.

The better answer is that leaven is a picture of how a thing spreads, not a verdict on what is spreading. A small hidden agent works quietly through a large mass until nothing is unaffected — that is the image, and it is morally neutral in itself. Sin does that, which is why Paul and Jesus both use it of sin. The kingdom does that too. The same yeast that ruins the batch when it is the wrong yeast transforms the batch when it is the right one, and Jesus is free to take a familiar picture and put it to the use he wants. That is what a parable is: a borrowed everyday thing, pressed into service for one point.

verseByVerse.quote: All these things Jesus said to the crowds in parables; indeed, he said nothing to them without a parable. This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet: "I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew's editorial comment identifies the parabolic teaching method itself as fulfillment of Scripture — Psalm 78:2, spoken of the Asaphite singer who taught Israel through narrative and song. The "hidden things since the foundation of the world" are the mysteries of the kingdom: what God planned before creation, what the prophets glimpsed but could not see fully, now being disclosed through the parables of Jesus. The parables are not concealment but revelation — they reveal to those with ears while remaining opaque to those without. Matthew is insisting that the parabolic method is not Jesus's innovation but God's ancient pattern for disclosing his purposes.

Two things about the quotation, and the first is worth looking up.

Psalm 78 is one of the longest psalms in the Bible — seventy-two verses of Asaph retelling Israel's history from the Exodus to David, with the failures left in. Its opening lines are the ones Matthew quotes: I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings from of old, things that we have heard and known, that our fathers have told us.

And then the psalm's stated purpose: that the next generation might know them… so that they should set their hope in God and not forget the works of God (Ps. 78:6-7).

So the text Matthew reaches for to explain parabolic teaching is itself a piece of parabolic teaching — a long story told to children so that they would not repeat what their fathers had done. The method is older than the Gospel, and it was always aimed at the next generation rather than the current experts.

The second thing is the strength of Matthew's claim. He said nothing to them without a parable. Nothing. That is a sweeping statement about the public ministry, and Mark says the same (Mk. 4:34) while adding the other half: privately to his own disciples he explained everything.

Which is the structure this chapter is built on, and Matthew has drawn it as a diagram. He opens at verse 1 by going out of the house to the crowd; at verse 36 he leaves the crowds and goes into the house with the disciples for the explanation.

Out of the house to the parables, back into the house for the meaning. The chapter is bracketed by a door.

And hidden since the foundation of the world is the phrase to hold. What is being disclosed on that beach is not new information about God's plans. It is old — older than Israel, older than Abraham, in place before there was anything to plan for — and it had been kept.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he left the crowds and went into the house. And his disciples came to him, saying, "Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field." He answered, "The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The withdrawal into the house with the disciples for private explanation is the pattern of rabbinic teaching: the public parable, then the private elucidation for the inner circle. The disciples ask for interpretation — again the mark of good soil, of genuine desire to understand. The Son of Man as the sower identifies Jesus as the one who plants genuine disciples in the world. This is significant: the "man" of the parable (v. 24) is not a generic figure but the Son of Man — the eschatological judge of Daniel 7, who will also be the one who supervises the harvest of verse 41. The same one who sows is the one who reaps. The kingdom from beginning to end belongs to him.

The movement in this verse is the hinge of the chapter, and it is worth seeing as a shape.

Verse 1: Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea, and the crowds gathered.

Verse 36: he left the crowds and went into the house, and the disciples came.

Out to the parables, back for the explanations. Everything the crowd hears is a story; everything the disciples get is the meaning — and the door between them is the same door, opened twice in thirty-five verses.

Which is precisely what he told them at verse 11: to you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given. Matthew is not merely reporting that principle; he has built the chapter to enact it.

And the request itself is the mark of the good soil.

Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field. They did not understand it either. That is worth registering, because it is easy to imagine the twelve as insiders who followed everything — and the plain evidence of this chapter is that they were as lost as anyone and simply asked.

The difference between the fourth soil and the others is not comprehension. It is what a man does when he has not understood.

Then the identification, and it is the largest claim in the parable. The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man.

That title comes from Daniel 7, where one like a son of man is brought before the Ancient of Days and given dominion and a kingdom that shall not pass away. It is the title Jesus uses of himself more than any other, and here it is attached to the sower.

So the man scattering seed in verse 3 — the ordinary figure with a bag, walking a Galilean field — turns out to be the figure of Daniel's vision. And he will appear again at verse 41 sending the angels to reap.

The same person plants and harvests. Nothing in the field belongs to anybody else.

verseByVerse.quote: the field is the world, and the good seed is the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one, and the enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The field is the world — not the church — which means the mixed growth of wheat and weeds describes the whole human community, not just the church's membership. The sons of the kingdom are genuine disciples scattered through the world; the sons of the evil one are those who belong to the devil's community. The harvest is the end of the age — the final judgment. The reapers are angels, not human agents. The parable confirms what the sermon in chapter 7 warned: the final sorting is God's work, not ours. The human church is called to discipleship and discipline, not to final judgment. That belongs to the one who sees what we cannot see and knows what we cannot know.

Three words in verse 38 have done more work in church history than almost any other phrase in the parables, and the entry above has them exactly right: the field is the world.

Not the church. Jesus says it outright, and it is the one element of the parable he defines most explicitly.

That matters enormously for how the parable may be used. Read as a picture of the church, it becomes an argument for tolerating anything inside the congregation — which is what it has often been made to say, and which collides head-on with chapter 18 and with Paul, who tells a church to remove a man.

Read as Jesus defines it, the picture is of the whole human community with two kinds of people growing side by side in it, indistinguishable to the eye, until the end of the age.

And the two kinds are described by parentage, not by performance.

The good seed is the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one. That is Semitic idiom — a son of something belongs to it, bears its character, comes from it. The distinction is not that one group behaves well and the other badly; it is that they have different origins.

Which is a sobering thing to say and a clarifying one. It explains why the sorting cannot be done by inspection: parentage is invisible, and the wheat and the darnel look identical precisely because appearance is not what is being sorted.

Then the two facts about the harvest that remove it from human hands entirely.

The harvest is the end of the age — so not now, not in any reformation or purge or council, and no amount of zeal can bring the date forward.

The reapers are angels — so not us. Not the servants who volunteered in verse 28, and not their successors.

The parable takes the sorting out of the growing season and out of human hands in one sentence, and it leaves the church with a quite different job in the meantime.

verseByVerse.quote: Just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the end of the age. The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin and all law-breakers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eschatological judgment is graphically real: "gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin and all law-breakers." Two categories — causes of stumbling (those who led others astray) and doers of lawlessness (those who lived apart from God's will). Both are gathered out. The kingdom in its present form contains both genuine and counterfeit; the harvest removes all that corrupts, leaving only what is genuine. The Son of Man's kingdom is not permanently mixed; it is presently mixed and finally purified. This is the basis of the believer's patience with the current state of the church and the world: the harvest is coming, the angels are ready, and the Son of Man will act with complete justice.

One phrase in verse 41 should stop a reader, because it says something unexpected.

They will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin and all law-breakers.

Out of his kingdom. Not out of the world — out of the kingdom.

Which means that in its present form the kingdom itself contains things that will have to be removed. That is a considerable admission, and it sits oddly with the way the word is often used, as though the kingdom were by definition the pure part.

It is not, yet. The field is the world and the kingdom is being planted across it, and both good and bad are growing inside the area under cultivation — and the harvest is described as a clearing operation within the King's own territory rather than a conquest of somebody else's.

And the first of the two categories is a word this chapter has already used twice.

Causes of sin is skandala — the trap-triggers, the things people go down over. It was the word in the message to John in prison (blessed is the one who is not offended by me, 11:6) and the word for what happens to the rocky-ground hearer (immediately he falls away, 13:21).

So the things gathered out at the end are, in the first instance, the things that trip people up. Not merely wicked persons considered in themselves, but whatever it was in the field that brought others down.

Which is worth sitting with, because it makes the judgement less abstract. Somebody in that furnace is there partly because of what he did to somebody else's faith.

And notice who does the sending. The Son of Man will send his angels.

Angels belong to God throughout the Old Testament; they are his host, his messengers. Here they are the Son of Man's, dispatched at his order, executing his judgement in his kingdom. The possessive is not decorative, and no first-century Jew would have missed it.

verseByVerse.quote: and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who has ears, let him hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fiery furnace is Matthew's most explicit image of final judgment: weeping and gnashing of teeth, repeated from the chapter 8 warning (8:12). Jesus does not soften the end. The contrast is absolute: those gathered out into the fiery furnace and those who "shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father." The shining righteous echoes Daniel 12:3 — "those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above; and those who turn many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever." The kingdom's final state is glory — not mere absence of suffering, but positive radiance. "He who has ears, let him hear" closes the interpretation as it closed the parable: the call to active, responsible reception of these hard truths.

The promise at the end is a quotation, and it is worth having the original in full.

Daniel is told at the very end of his book, after everything else has been sealed up: And those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above; and those who turn many to righteousness, like the stars for ever and ever (Dan. 12:3).

That sentence comes immediately after the only unambiguous statement of resurrection in the Old Testament — many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt (Dan. 12:2).

So Jesus is not reaching for a poetic flourish. He is quoting the passage that stands closest to what he is describing, in the book from which he takes his favourite title for himself, and he is placing the wheat exactly where Daniel placed the wise.

And he sharpens it. Daniel says they will shine like the brightness of the sky, and like the stars. Jesus says the righteous will shine like the sun.

Stars are numerous and distant and easily lost in a city. The sun is the thing you cannot look at directly.

Which is not a small upgrade, and it is the same word used of his own face on the mountain of transfiguration, where his face shone like the sun (17:2). Whatever happened to him there is what is being promised to them here.

Two further things. In the kingdom of their Father — the possessive again, and this time it is theirs. The kingdom has been the Son of Man's throughout the interpretation; at the last clause it becomes the Father's, and the ones shining in it are his children.

And he who has ears, let him hear closes the explanation exactly as it closed the parable at verse 9. The same formula at both ends, once for the crowd on the beach and once for the twelve in the house — which is a quiet way of saying that being on the inside of the door does not exempt anybody from the condition of the fourth soil.

verseByVerse.quote: The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hidden treasure is found by accident; the pearl merchant seeks by profession — two different paths to the same discovery. Both result in the same action: selling everything. The joy of the man who finds the treasure is the motivating emotion: he does not reluctantly surrender his possessions; he joyfully exchanges them for something worth incomparably more. This is the subjective experience of conversion at its truest: not the grim duty of giving up good things for God, but the delighted exchange of lesser goods for the supreme good. The kingdom found makes everything else look small by comparison — not worthless, but small. Genuine faith always involves this revaluation.

People do stumble over the man's conduct, and it is worth answering rather than pretending nobody notices. He finds treasure in a field that is not his, covers it up again, says nothing to the owner, and buys the field. Put in modern terms it sounds like a man who spots oil under a farm and buys the farm cheap from a seller who does not know. Is Jesus commending sharp practice?

Two things. First and simplest: a parable makes one point, and its details are scenery rather than moral instruction. We have already met this principle at 5:26 — doctrine cannot be read off the furniture of a parable, and neither can ethics. Jesus tells stories about a dishonest manager, an unjust judge, and a thief in the night, and commends none of the three; he takes one feature of each and uses it. Here the feature is joy. Everything in the sentence turns on four words — in his joy he goes — and the selling of everything is what joy looks like when it has found something worth more than everything.

Second, the man's actual conduct was probably less questionable than it sounds to us. In that world buried valuables were common (there were no banks, and invasion was frequent), and the law of the time generally attached what was buried in a field to the field itself. Which means the honest route to the treasure ran precisely through buying the field. He could have pocketed it and walked away; instead he paid for the ground it lay in. What looks to a modern eye like cunning may in fact be the scrupulous option — and either way, it is not what the story is about. What the story is about is a man who found something so valuable that parting with everything he owned felt like getting a bargain.

verseByVerse.quote: who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea and gathered fish of every kind,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The merchant who has handled fine pearls all his life recognizes the pearl of great price instantly — his expertise serves the discovery. He does not need to be told what it is worth; he knows. He sells everything without apparent regret, because the exchange is obviously worth it to one who understands value. The net parable shifts from the individual experience of finding the kingdom to the corporate reality of the gathered community: a net thrown into the sea gathers everything without discrimination — good fish and bad, every kind. The sorting will happen at the shore. The kingdom's proclamation gathers broadly; the final judgment will sort what was gathered. The church should not be surprised that it contains both.

The two treasure parables are a matched pair with one deliberate difference, and the difference is the point.

The man in the field was not looking. He is a labourer working somebody else's land, and he puts a spade into something and stops. Nothing in the story suggests he had any interest in treasure that morning.

The merchant was looking. He is a professional dealer, in search of fine pearls, and finding good ones is what he does for a living. He has spent years training his eye for exactly this.

And both end in the same place, selling everything.

So the pair covers the two ways people arrive. Some are ambushed — they were not seeking anything, and the kingdom turned up in the middle of an ordinary working day. Some searched for years, knew roughly what they were after, and found it at last. The parables refuse to make either route normative.

And there is a note on both worth having, because it is often missed: the joy is not in the sacrifice.

Verse 44 says the man sold everything in his joy. Neither parable presents the selling as a hard thing bravely done. A man who exchanges everything he owns for something worth vastly more has not sacrificed; he has traded up, and he knows it, and he is delighted.

Which is a useful test of how a person actually regards Christ. Whether following him feels like a cost being paid or a bargain being struck says more about the valuation than any statement of belief.

Then the net, and it is a different implement from the one usually pictured.

The word is sagene — a dragnet or seine. Not the cast-net a man throws from the shore, but a long weighted net worked between two boats or drawn to land from the beach, sweeping everything in its path.

Which is why the parable says every kind. A cast-net is aimed. A dragnet is not — it takes what is in the water, and the sorting is a separate operation done later on the sand.

verseByVerse.quote: When it was full, men drew it ashore and sat down and sorted the good into containers but threw away the bad. So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will come out and separate the evil from the righteous
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sorting of the catch echoes the harvest of the wheat and weeds: the work is done at the end, by agents (angels) appointed for the task. The fishermen who drew the net are not the ones who do the final sorting — they bring the catch; the sorting is its own work. The "good" (kala — fine, valuable) fish and the "bad" (sapra — rotten, worthless) are separated with finality. This is the second dragnet-type parable (after wheat and weeds) in the chapter — Matthew doubles the warning about final judgment. Two different images, the same reality: the present mixed state of the kingdom is temporary; the coming separation is final and complete.

The Sea of Galilee makes this parable exact, and the detail matters.

The lake holds a great many species, and Jewish law made an unavoidable distinction among them: only fish with fins and scales could be eaten (Lev. 11:9-12). Everything else — catfish and eels among them — was unclean, and a Jewish fisherman hauling a dragnet up that beach was sorting his catch not merely into saleable and unsaleable but into permitted and forbidden.

So the scene Jesus describes was the ordinary end of every working day for men in his audience: the net up on the sand, the crew sitting down beside it, and the long business of going through the pile by hand.

And the two adjectives are worth having. The good fish are kala — fine, sound, the same word used of the good soil and of the beautiful works of the disciples. The bad are sapra, which is not small or inferior but rotten: putrid, decayed, the word used of a bad tree that cannot bear good fruit (7:17-18).

The category is not disappointing fish. It is fish that have gone off.

Notice also that this is the second time the chapter has ended a parable this way, and the repetition is deliberate.

The wheat and the weeds ended with the reapers separating and burning. The dragnet ends with the angels separating and burning. Two entirely different pictures — a field and a lake, farming and fishing — arriving at exactly the same conclusion in the same chapter.

Matthew is not padding. He has given the warning twice, in the two industries his readers worked in, so that nobody could file it as agricultural imagery and move on.

And in both, the sorting is done by angels, at the end, and not by the workers who brought the catch in.

verseByVerse.quote: and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Have you understood all these things?" They said to him, "Yes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fiery furnace language closes the interpretation as it closed the wheat-and-weeds parable — consistent eschatological warning. Then Jesus turns and asks: "Have you understood all these things?" The disciples answer "Yes" — and they are immediately tested by a further saying about the scribe of the kingdom. Their "yes" is the yes of those who have understood the outline, not the depths; the understanding that comes from hearing with good-soil hearts will continue to deepen as they continue with Jesus. Jesus asks the question not to quiz them but to call them to account for their hearing. The parables are not complete until they are understood and the understanding has borne fruit.

The question and the answer are both worth weighing, and the answer is shorter in Greek than in English.

Have you understood all these things? — and the verb is syniemi, the word that has run through this whole chapter: they do not understand (v. 13), never understand (v. 14), understand with their heart (v. 15), does not understand it (v. 19), hears and understands (v. 23), and now this.

It is the sixth and last occurrence, and it is put to them as a direct question. The chapter has been about the difference between hearing and understanding, and it ends by asking the twelve which side of that line they are on.

They say yes. One word: nai.

And it is worth being honest about what that answer was worth.

Within a few chapters Peter will be told get behind me, Satan for objecting to the cross. They will argue about which of them is greatest. They will fail to cast out a demon and be told it was because of their little faith. At the supper they will still be asking where he is going, and by the end of that night every one of them will be somewhere else.

So their yes was not false, and it was not adequate either. They had grasped the outline of what he said and almost nothing of what it would cost.

Which is a mercy for anybody who has ever said yes to God and discovered later how little he knew he was agreeing to. Jesus does not correct them. He accepts the answer, and then adds one more parable — about a householder bringing out treasure both old and new — as though to say: good, and there is a great deal more in the store.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old." And when Jesus had finished these parables, he went away from there,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scribe trained for the kingdom is the disciple who has learned to read the whole of Scripture — old and new — in the light of the kingdom. The treasure of old things (the Law and the Prophets) and new things (the teaching of Jesus) are both brought out from the same house. This is the hermeneutical principle of the Christian reader: the Old Testament is not superseded by the New but fulfilled by it, and the New Testament is not understood apart from the Old. The Matthean scribe brings both, and the combination produces insight that neither alone could provide. This is also Matthew's self-portrait: he is the scribe trained for the kingdom, bringing old prophecy and new fulfillment onto the same page.

That last suggestion deserves more than a closing clause, because it is one of the most attractive readings in the Gospel and it is very probably right.

Consider who is writing this book. A man who quotes the Old Testament more than any other evangelist — around sixty times, with a further hundred allusions. Who structures his Gospel in five discourses to echo the five books of Moses. Who repeatedly stops the narrative to say this was to fulfil what was spoken by the prophet. Who alone among the four records this saying about the scribe.

And whose own name appears in his own list of apostles with a description nobody else adds: Matthew the tax collector (10:3).

A man who kept records for a living, who knew the Scriptures well enough to weave them into every chapter, and who had been sitting in a customs booth when he was called. If anybody in the New Testament is a scribe trained for the kingdom bringing out things old and new, it is the author of this sentence.

And the word for what he brings out is a storeroom rather than a chest. Thesauros can mean treasure, and here it means the place where treasure is kept — the householder goes to the store and fetches things out.

The order matters too: what is new and what is old. New first. A scribe of the old school brought out the old; this one has something recent to put beside it, and he leads with it.

But he does not discard the old, and that is the whole force of the sentence. He is not a man who has replaced his library. He has had something added to it that makes the rest legible.

Which is the working principle of every page of this commentary, and it is worth stating plainly. The Old Testament is not a preface that can be skipped now that the New has arrived, and the New is not intelligible without it. Darnel and dragnets and mustard seed mean what they mean because Daniel and Ezekiel and the psalms of Asaph are behind them.

Bring out both. That is the instruction.

verseByVerse.quote: and coming to his hometown he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished, and said, "Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? Is not this the carpenter's son? Is not his mother called Mary? And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus returns to Nazareth — the village that knows him as "the carpenter's son," the man whose mother, brothers, and sisters are their neighbors. Their astonishment is genuine: they cannot explain the wisdom and miracles in terms of his background. But instead of reaching upward to account for the extraordinary — "he must be from God" — they reach backward into the ordinary: "we know this family." The familiarity that should have been the greatest privilege (they knew him!) becomes the stumbling block. They reduce him to what they already know instead of letting what they see revise what they know. This is the danger of proximity without faith: knowing about Jesus does not produce knowledge of him.

A reader will pause over the family list: "his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas," and "all his sisters." Are these Jesus's actual siblings? The question matters, because the Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches, holding that Mary remained a virgin all her life, have taken them to be either cousins (so Jerome) or children of Joseph by an earlier marriage (so the Orthodox). The words themselves, however, most naturally mean what they say: these are the later sons and daughters of Joseph and Mary, the younger half-brothers and half-sisters of Jesus — born, unlike him, in the ordinary way. Matthew has already hinted as much, saying Joseph "knew her not until she had given birth to a son" (1:25), and calling Jesus her "firstborn," a word that quietly expects others to follow. There is no need to protect Mary's honour by keeping her a perpetual virgin; her honour is that she bore and raised the Son of God, and then was a mother to his brothers. And there is gospel gold here. These brothers did not believe in him during his ministry — "not even his brothers believed in him" (Jn 7:5) — yet after the resurrection we find them in the upper room praying (Acts 1:14), and two of them, James and Jude, wrote letters that stand in our New Testament, James becoming a pillar of the Jerusalem church. What turns a skeptical younger brother into a man who calls his own brother "the Lord"? Only an empty tomb. The conversion of the brothers of Jesus is one of the quiet, powerful evidences that he rose.

verseByVerse.quote: And are not all his sisters with us? Where then did this man get all these things?" And they took offense at him. But Jesus said to them, "A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They took offense at him" — the same word skandalon used in 11:6 for those offended by the form of Jesus's coming. The townspeople stumble over his ordinariness: they cannot reconcile the wisdom with the workshop, the miracles with the carpenter's hands. The proverb about the prophet without honor in his hometown reflects the consistent biblical pattern: God's spokesmen are received everywhere except home. Familiarity breeds contempt; proximity without faith produces offense rather than worship. The tragedy of Nazareth is the personal tragedy of Jesus: the people who watched him grow up, who saw him daily, refused to worship him. He was rejected not by strangers but by neighbors.

The questions the neighbours ask are worth reading as a group, because they are not stupid and they are not hostile at the start.

Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? That is the right question. Is not this the carpenter's son? Is not his mother called Mary? And his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? And are not all his sisters with us?

Every one of those is accurate. They have the family right, the trade right, the names right. Nobody in Nazareth is mistaken about a single fact.

And then: where then did this man get all these things? — which is the same question they opened with, asked the second time as an objection rather than an enquiry.

That is the whole tragedy of the passage in one paragraph. They began by asking where it came from, assembled a complete and correct account of everything they knew about him, found that it did not explain what they were looking at — and concluded that the problem was with him.

The evidence had raised a question their information could not answer. The right response was to widen the information. They narrowed the evidence instead.

And the word for their reaction is the chapter's own. They took offence at him — eskandalizonto, the trap-word. It has run all through this material: the message to John (11:6), the rocky-ground hearer who falls away (13:21), the causes of sin gathered out at the harvest (13:41), and now his own village.

They did not argue him down. They tripped over him — over the very thing that should have made him easiest to believe, which was that they had known him all his life.

One detail worth having: his sisters are with us. Present tense, still living in the village, presumably married locally. His brothers are named; his sisters are not, but they were there, and their neighbours could point to their houses.

Nothing about this family was mysterious, and that was the difficulty.

verseByVerse.quote: And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The connection between unbelief and the absence of miracles is striking and sobering. Jesus is not powerless; he is choosing not to perform miracles where they would be rejected as further evidence of ordinary presumption. The miracles are acts of grace responding to faith; where faith is absent, the miracles would only deepen the condemnation of those who saw and refused. Mark adds that "he could do no mighty work there" (Mark 6:5) — the "could not" is not inability but the consistent pattern of Jesus: he does not force grace on those who have already made their decision. Unbelief does not limit God's power; it limits the channel through which his mercy flows. The closed heart receives nothing — not because God withholds, but because it cannot receive.

That sentence must be handled carefully, though, because it is one verse away from a cruelty that has done a great deal of damage. Read carelessly it says: miracles run on faith, so if God has not acted in your situation, the fault is the thinness of your believing. Some have been told exactly that over a hospital bed. It is not what the verse means.

Look at what it actually reports. He did not do many mighty works there — and Mark, telling the same visit, says he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them (Mk 6:5). Even in that atmosphere, some were healed. So this is plainly not a mechanism in which a quantity of faith buys a quantity of power. And set it beside the rest of the Gospel: he heals a paralysed man on the strength of his friends' faith and not his own (9:2), he raises the dead, who by definition contribute nothing, and he restores people who do not yet know who he is. Faith is the open hand, never the currency.

What Nazareth's unbelief actually prevented was simpler and sadder. They did not bring their sick to him, because they had already settled who he was — the carpenter's boy, whose family lived down the road. You cannot receive what you have decided not to come for. The verse describes a town that had made up its mind, not a formula governing answered prayer. If you have prayed and not received, this passage is not an accusation against you; the note at 8:16-17 sets out what may and may not be expected, and Paul, whose faith was equal to anything, asked three times and kept his thorn.

But do take the warning that is genuinely here, because it is aimed at exactly the sort of person who reads commentaries. The people who got least from Jesus in his whole ministry were the ones who had been nearest to him longest. They were not hostile; they were familiar. They had him filed. A lifetime of church can do the same thing to a soul — the sermons heard before, the passage you already know, the quiet assumption that there is nothing here you have not met. Nazareth is what happens when knowing about him has replaced knowing him, and this chapter has already told you what that ground is called.

13.theology: The hiddenness and growth of the kingdom. The parables of Matthew 13 develop a theology of the kingdom that runs against both triumphalism and despair. Against triumphalism: the kingdom grows secretly, like leaven, not by worldly power or coercion. Against despair: the smallest seed becomes the largest tree; the handful of leavened dough leavens the whole batch. The kingdom’s smallness is not its failure but its method. Reformed theology has always insisted that the church advances through the ordinary means of grace — word, sacrament, prayer — not through political power or cultural dominance. The harvest will be glorious; the sowing is patient.
13.examples:
Then: The disciples were living through the mustard-seed phase of the kingdom. From their vantage point, a small band of Galileans following a rabbi who was being plotted against by the religious establishment, the kingdom’s glory was not obvious. Jesus tells them: do not judge the end by the beginning.

Now: Every era of church history has felt like the mustard-seed phase. Persecution, secularisation, nominalism — all seem to contradict the kingdom’s advance. The parables of Matthew 13 are the antidote to both despair and triumphalism. The Sower keeps sowing. The leaven keeps working. The net keeps gathering. The harvest belongs to the Lord.

14.title: Bread in the Wilderness
14.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Herod the tetrarch heard about the fame of Jesus, <sup>2</sup>and he said to his servants, “This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead; that is why these miraculous powers are at work in him.” <sup>3</sup>For Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, <sup>10</sup>He sent and had John beheaded in the prison, <sup>11</sup>and his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. <sup>12</sup>And his disciples came and took the body and buried it, and they went and told Jesus. <sup>13</sup>Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by himself. But when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the towns. <sup>14</sup>When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them and healed their sick. <sup>15</sup>Now when it was evening, the disciples came to him and said, “This is a desolate place, and the day is now over; send the crowds away to go into the villages and buy food for themselves.” <sup>16</sup>But Jesus said, “They need not go away; you give them something to eat.” <sup>17</sup>They said to him, “We have only five loaves here and two fish.” <sup>18</sup>And he said, “Bring them here to me.” <sup>19</sup>Then he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass, and taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. <sup>20</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over. <sup>21</sup>And those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children. <sup>28</sup>And Peter answered him, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.” <sup>29</sup>He said, “Come.” So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus. <sup>30</sup>But when he saw the wind, he was afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, “Lord, save me.” <sup>31</sup>Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him, saying to him, “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?”
14.overview:
Chapter 14 moves from Herod’s banquet of death (John’s head on a platter) to Jesus’ banquet of life (five thousand fed in the wilderness). The contrast is deliberate. Herod’s table is supplied by cruelty, vanity, and the murder of a prophet. Jesus’ table is supplied by compassion, prayer, and the creative power of the Creator multiplying what is surrendered to him. John’s death is the herald’s fate; Jesus will face his own; but the meals he gives point beyond death to the resurrection feast.

The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels (besides the resurrection). Matthew frames it with Exodus typology: a desolate place (wilderness), manna-like provision, the Shepherd feeding his people. Jesus looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives — the same fourfold action he will perform at the Last Supper. Every Lord’s Supper echoes this meal. The chapter closes with Peter walking on water — and sinking. The disciples worship: “Truly you are the Son of God.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Death of John and the Feeding of the Five Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Herod Antipas hears of Jesus and fears John has risen from the dead. Matthew then narrates the death of John the Baptist — arrested for condemning Herod's marriage to his brother's wife, beheaded to fulfill a rash oath at a banquet. Jesus withdraws on hearing the news, but the crowds follow him. He heals them and then feeds five thousand men from five loaves and two fish. The feeding is the great Eucharistic sign, anticipating the Last Supper and the heavenly banquet. What the summary cannot hold. Herod is a tetrarch, not a king — Herod the Great's realm was quartered at his death and this son got Galilee and Perea. He wanted the higher title, went to Rome to ask for it, and was exiled for his trouble. He was in power before the nativity and still in power at the crucifixion, and Luke has Pilate send Jesus to him during the trial (Lk. 23:12). His explanation is theologically bizarre: nobody in Judaism expected an individual to be raised in the middle of history, so "this is John, he has been raised" is not a belief he is reaching for — he has invented it on the spot, and said it to his servants, the people who had watched the platter come in. On the geography, Josephus names the prison: Machaerus, a fortress-palace east of the Dead Sea with luxurious apartments above and cells below — so the banquet and the dungeon were in the same building. He also names the girl: Salome. And Matthew calls her a korasion, the diminutive, the same word used of Jairus's twelve-year-old (9:24-25) — a child, put up to it, who goes out to ask her mother what to say. The oath is a quotation: Mark gives it in full, "up to half my kingdom" (6:23), which is what Ahasuerus says to Esther, twice, at a banquet (Est. 5:3; 7:2). A drunken king, a rash promise, a woman with a prepared request, a man's life in the balance — and every element inverts. Esther's request saved a people from a murderer; this one murders a prophet. Note too that Herod and the chief priests are restrained by the same calculation, in almost identical words: both fear the crowd "because they held him to be a prophet" (14:5; 21:46). And verse 12 is the quietest sentence in the chapter — John's disciples walked into a royal fortress to ask for the body, buried what there was, and then went to the one man who had told them who John was. Matthew records no reply. The next thing Jesus does is withdraw; the next thing after that is feed fifteen thousand people. On the day he heard.
verseByVerse.theology: John's death is the dark center of the chapter: the fate of the forerunner anticipates the fate of the one he announced. Herod's fear that Jesus is John raised from the dead is simultaneously wrong (Jesus is not John) and prophetically ironic (the resurrection John could not achieve, Jesus will). The feeding of the five thousand is the messianic act par excellence: the shepherd-king who provides bread for his people in the wilderness, echoing the manna of the Exodus. Jesus takes, blesses, breaks, and gives — the fourfold action of the Last Supper.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' protest — "we have only five loaves here and two fish" — is the protest of faith that has not yet learned what it is living with. They are calculating from what they have; Jesus acts from who he is. "Bring them here to me" is the word for every situation where human resources fall desperately short of human need. The miracle occurs not in the disciples' hands but in his: he takes, blesses, breaks, gives — and twelve baskets remain. Twelve: one for each tribe of Israel, one for each disciple. The abundance of the kingdom always exceeds the need.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Herod the tetrarch heard about the fame of Jesus, and he said to his servants, "This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead; that is why these miraculous powers are at work in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod Antipas — ruler of Galilee, puppet of Rome, murderer of John — hears the reports of Jesus and his guilt-ridden conscience supplies the explanation: this must be John, resurrected. The resurrection of John the Baptist was not a Jewish expectation; Herod has constructed it from his own terror. He knows what he did to John, and the report of miraculous powers working through a Galilean teacher brings it all back. Guilt is theologically productive: it confirms that John was innocent and that Herod's deed was murder. The man who silenced the prophet cannot silence the memory of the prophet's voice. Herod's fear of a resurrected John is the beginning of what should have been repentance but remains only dread.

Two things about the man, because Matthew assumes a reader who knows the family and most of us do not.

He is called the tetrarch, and the title is precise. Herod the Great's kingdom was carved up at his death, and this son got a quarter of it — Galilee and Perea — with the rank of tetrarch rather than king. He wanted the higher title badly, and eventually went to Rome to ask for it, and was exiled to Gaul for his trouble. Mark calls him king once, informally, the way people did.

So the man is a client ruler with a grievance about his own status, ruling the district where Jesus grew up, for the whole of Jesus' life. Antipas was in power before the nativity and still in power at the crucifixion — Luke records Pilate sending Jesus to him during the trial, and the two of them becoming friends that day (Lk. 23:12).

And his explanation is worth weighing, because it is theologically bizarre.

Nobody in Judaism expected a single individual to be raised in the middle of history. Resurrection was a doctrine about the last day and the whole people. What Herod says — this is John, he has been raised — is not an available belief he is reaching for. He has invented it on the spot.

Which is what a guilty conscience does. He is not reasoning from the evidence; he is being visited. And the detail Matthew records is that he said it to his servants — the people who had been in the palace, who had seen the platter come in, and who now had to stand there while their master worked out loud through what he had done.

Luke adds the sequel: Herod kept seeking to see him (Lk. 9:9). He got his wish at the very end, and when he finally had Jesus in front of him he asked for a conjuring trick and got silence.

verseByVerse.quote: For Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because John had been saying to him, "It is not lawful for you to have her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John in prison because he told the truth to power: "It is not lawful for you to have her." Herodias was Herod's niece whom he had married after she divorced his half-brother Philip — a union the Mosaic law prohibited (Lev. 18:16; 20:21). John did not qualify his condemnation for the sake of safety or soften it for political convenience. He said to the king's face what was true, and he paid with his freedom and eventually his life. This is the prophetic calling: to speak the word of God without regard for the consequences, to the powerful as to the powerless. John's imprisonment is not a tragedy of mismanagement; it is the faithful prophet's expected fate in a world that prefers comfortable lies.

The name in this verse has drawn fire, and a reader who has met the objection deserves the answer. Matthew calls Herodias the wife of Herod's brother Philip. Josephus, writing his history of the period, names her first husband as Herod — another son of Herod the Great — and says that Philip the tetrarch married Salome, who was Herodias's daughter. Critics have made a good deal of this: the Gospels, it is said, have muddled the family.

They have not, and the tangle is of Herod's own making. Herod the Great had at least ten wives and a swarm of sons, and he named a remarkable number of them after himself; there are several men called Herod in this family and more than one called Philip. Josephus himself gives some of them two names. In such a household a son known formally as Herod and familiarly as Philip is not a puzzle but an inevitability — and Matthew's readers, living close enough to the events to know the family gossip, would have needed the second name precisely to tell one brother from another. We have already met the same convention in this Gospel with the man who wrote it, who was called both Matthew and Levi (9:9).

It is worth saying plainly why this matters and why it does not. It does not touch the point of the passage in the slightest: whichever brother she left, the marriage was unlawful and John said so and died for saying it. But it is worth knowing that where the Gospels can be checked against an independent historian they hold up under checking — and that an apparent collision, patiently examined, usually turns out to be a detail we were missing rather than an error the writer made.

verseByVerse.quote: And though he wanted to put him to death, he feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet. But when Herod's birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced before the company and pleased Herod,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod wants John dead but fears the crowd's opinion — the tyrant who rules by calculation of popular response, not by conviction. This is the portrait of power without principle: he can imprison the prophet but cannot execute him without calculating the political cost. The birthday banquet opens the window of opportunity that Herodias has been waiting for: her daughter dances, pleases Herod, and the rash oath follows. The dance in context was almost certainly provocative — designed by Herodias to extract the promise she wanted. The powerful man who yielded to popular fear now yields to sexual gratification: two forms of weakness that will seal John's fate.

A note on the geography, because it makes the banquet scene concrete.
