verseByVerse.commentary:
The keys of the kingdom — the authority to open and close the door of the kingdom — are given to Peter and, by 18:18, to the whole community of disciples. The binding and loosing is rabbinic language for rendering authoritative decisions about what is permitted and forbidden. In the context, it refers primarily to the authority to proclaim the gospel (opening the kingdom door to those who believe) and to enforce discipline (18:18). The charge to silence ("tell no one that he was the Christ") reflects the consistent concern: the confession is true, but its public proclamation must wait until the cross has defined what kind of Christ he is. A Messiah without the cross is a category error.

Every phrase here has a history behind it, and without the history the keys are only a metaphor. Isaiah 22 is the passage in view, and it is a small domestic drama. Shebna is steward over King Hezekiah's household — a self-important official caught cutting himself a splendid tomb in the rock — and God announces that he will be pulled out of his post and another man installed. The words of installation are these: I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open (Isa 22:22). The key was a large wooden thing carried on the shoulder, worn where everyone could see it, the badge of the office. And note what the office is. The steward is not the king. He is the man who runs the king's house and decides who is brought in to the king's presence. Any Jew who knew his Isaiah heard all of that the moment Jesus said the word keys. And there is a postscript worth having: the risen Christ takes that very sentence for himself — the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut (Rev 3:7). The key is his. He hands a servant the use of it. He does not hand over the house.

This is where the Roman argument is at its most impressive, and it should be felt rather than brushed aside. Isaiah 22 is not a passage about a man; it is a passage about a post. Shebna is removed and Eliakim is installed, and the whole point of the oracle is that the stewardship continues while the king's house continues. So if our Lord deliberately reached for the one Old Testament text about a royal steward's key, and if he is the Son of David whose house stands forever, then a stewardship is what he has instituted — and a stewardship, unlike a personal compliment, is filled again when its holder dies. Add that the you in this verse is singular, spoken to one man in a room of twelve, and given in the same breath as the new name, and the Roman conclusion is not perverse at all. It may be the reading a first-century Jew would have reached most naturally.

Three things answer it, and the first comes out of Isaiah himself.

The oracle does not end where the argument stops quoting it. Three verses later the whole picture is reversed: the peg that was fastened in a secure place will give way, and it will be cut down and fall, and the load that was on it will be cut off (Isa 22:25). Eliakim, on whom his father's house had been hung, comes down and takes the household with him. That is a strange charter for an office that cannot fail. What Isaiah actually gives is a stewardship with the steward's collapse written into the same paragraph — which is exactly what happens here, four verses later, when the man holding the keys is called Satan.

Then watch Peter use the keys, because Luke shows him using them and then shows him setting them down. A key opens a door, and Peter opens three. At Pentecost he preaches and three thousand Jews come in (Acts 2). At Samaria he is sent for, and the half-caste neighbours whom no respectable Jew would eat with are let in (Acts 8:14-17). On a rooftop in Joppa he is argued out of a lifetime's revulsion, walks into a Gentile house, and the door to the nations stands open from that day to this (Acts 10). Three doors, each opened once and never needing to be opened again. By the council of Acts 15 it is James who sums up and gives the ruling, and after that chapter Peter simply disappears from Luke's account. That is not the career of a man administering a permanent office. It is the career of a doorkeeper who has finished with the doors.

And the authority does not stay in one pair of hands for as much as two chapters. The identical words about binding and loosing are spoken to a whole congregation dealing with an unrepentant brother (18:18), and after the resurrection the authority to forgive and to retain is breathed on the gathered disciples together (John 20:23). Whatever the keys are, Jesus distributes them almost at once.

One honest note on the grammar, since it is often produced as a knock-down blow and is not quite that. The Greek here and at 18:18 is unusual: not simply shall be bound but a future joined to a perfect participle, roughly shall have been bound in heaven. Some press it hard, and argue that heaven does not rubber-stamp the church's decisions; the church announces heaven's. Others reply that the construction is an idiom and will not bear that much weight. The fair verdict is that the grammar alone cannot settle it — but the rest of the New Testament settles the direction anyway, because the apostles never once invent terms of admission. Peter at Pentecost does not decide who may be saved; he tells a crowd what God has done and what they must do about it. The key does not make the door. It opens the one the King built.

All of which sounds remote until you see where it lands, which is on an ordinary Sunday in an ordinary congregation. When a church hears a man confess Christ, baptises him and receives him to the Lord's Table, it is not offering an opinion about his prospects; it is doing on earth a thing Christ authorised, and heaven is not indifferent to it. When a church, after long patience, must finally tell an unrepentant member that his life and his profession no longer agree (18:15-17), that is not a committee being unkind — it is the same key turned the other way. This is why belonging to a real congregation is not an optional extra for people who happen to like institutions: the keys were given to a church, not to individuals with Bibles and strong opinions. And it is why the keys are terrible in the wrong hands, which is the whole substance of what the Reformers said when forgiveness was being sold at a church door. The abuse of the keys does not abolish them. It makes their right use urgent.

Then the last line of the section, which looks like an anticlimax and is nothing of the kind. He has just called Peter blessed for saying it — and now forbids them to say it to anybody. Why put a true confession under guard? Because the word was true and the definition in the hearers' heads was false. Christ, in Galilean mouths, meant a son of David with an army who would clear the Romans out of the country. Say that word in a village and you do not gather disciples, you start a rising. A man who is misunderstood in silence can still be explained later; a man acclaimed on the wrong terms cannot, because every cheer makes the correction more expensive.

So the title is sealed until the cross can say what kind of Christ he is — and look at the very next verse, where the seal and the explanation arrive in the same breath: silence imposed in verse 20, and in verse 21 he begins for the first time to tell them plainly that he must go to Jerusalem and be killed. The order is deliberate. Nor does the seal stay on. At the trial the high priest puts him on oath and asks whether he is the Christ, the Son of God, and this time he answers openly (26:63-64) — because by then the cross is close enough that the word cannot be misheard. And after the resurrection the charge is reversed outright: go and make disciples of all nations (28:19). What was forbidden in a Galilean village is commanded to the ends of the earth.

There is a warning in that sequence for anyone impatient for results. It is perfectly possible to get a man to say the right sentence about Jesus by leaving out what it costs, and to count the sentence as a conversion. Our Lord had that option in front of him, with a crowd ready to take it, and chose silence instead.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–28 — The First Passion Prediction and the Call to Cross-Bearing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From the moment of Peter's confession, Jesus begins to teach that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed, and rise on the third day. Peter rebukes him; Jesus rebukes Peter with the sharpest words in the Gospel: "Get behind me, Satan!" He then calls the crowd and disciples to cross-bearing: whoever loses his life for his sake will find it. The section ends with a warning about the coming of the Son of Man in his Father's glory. Between the two he asks what a man could possibly hand over in exchange for his soul (v. 26), and he closes by promising that some standing there will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (v. 28) — a promise kept six days later on the mountain, as one of the men who heard it says himself (2 Pet 1:16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The first passion prediction marks the watershed of Matthew's Gospel: the confession at Caesarea Philippi is the turning point from which Jesus now sets his face toward Jerusalem. The cross is not an unexpected tragedy but the appointed path. Peter's rebuttal — "Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you" — is the most natural human response and the most spiritually dangerous: it substitutes human preferences for divine purpose. "You are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men" is the diagnosis of every theology that wants a cross-free Christianity. The section then puts a price on the choice. Verse 26 is a market question — what sum would buy back a soul? — and it is left unanswered until 20:28, where the Son of Man gives his own life as the ransom no man could pay. Verse 27 supplies the frame: he will repay each person according to what he has done. That is not a scoreboard, for Matthew twice rules one out — the impressive workers of 7:21-23 are turned away because they were never known, and the sheep of 25:31-46 cannot remember their own good deeds. Works are the evidence of a righteousness received, never the ground of it.
verseByVerse.examples: The cross-bearing saying moves from Jesus's cross to the disciple's: "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me." The disciple's cross is not their personal hardships and inconveniences; it is the public cost of standing with a man under sentence, and the losing of a life organised around self-interest in order to find one organised around Christ. The paradox of verse 25 — finding life through losing it — is the gospel in miniature: the life surrendered to Jesus is the life truly found. Verse 26 makes the same point as a transaction. Ask a man what he would take for his car and he names a figure; ask what he would take for his son and he refuses the category outright. There is one thing in his possession that no market will quote, and it is himself. And verse 28 shows how this Master treats frightened followers: the cross-bearing call is issued on a Monday, so to speak, and by the following week three of them have been taken up a mountain and shown what the road ends in. The order of those two events is the mercy in them, and it is set out at vv. 23-24.

verseByVerse.quote: From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, "Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"From that time" — the same phrase used at the beginning of Jesus's public ministry (4:17), now marking the beginning of his passion-focused teaching. "He must go" — dei, the divine necessity, the "must" of prophetic fulfillment and divine plan. The three stages are specific: suffer, be killed, rise. The resurrection is not an afterthought but part of the original declaration. Peter's rebuke is theologically catastrophic: he takes Jesus aside (literally "pulled him to himself") and rebukes him with the word used for demonic opposition (8:26). The man who just confessed "Son of the living God" is now trying to redirect the living God from his stated purpose. The confession was revelation; this is the flesh asserting itself over the Spirit.

Hold the two halves of this conversation together, because the distance between them is about ninety seconds. In verse 16 Peter says the most exalted sentence any human being has said so far in this Gospel, and Jesus tells him no man taught him it — the Father did. In verse 23 the same man, in the same conversation, is called Satan. Same afternoon, same mouth, and no interval at all in which he might have gradually declined.

That ought to reorganise how a Christian reads his own life. Revelation received does not immunise you against the next hour. The highest moment and the worst are not separated by decades in most people; they turn up in the same week, and sometimes the same conversation. If your walk with God consists of genuine heights followed by collapses that embarrass you, you have not discovered that you are a special case. You have discovered that you are Peter, and Peter is the normal one.

And look at where the collapse came from, because it is not where we expect. Peter is not being wicked here. He is being protective. Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you is affection talking — it is what you say to someone you love who has just told you he is going to die. That is precisely what makes it dangerous. The worst advice most of us ever receive comes from people who love us and cannot bear to see us suffer, and the worst advice we give ourselves is nearly always dressed as care. Satan did not need to find an enemy for this errand. A devoted friend did it for him, sincerely, out of love, within a minute of a God-given confession.

Then watch what Jesus does with him, because this is the part that carries a reader through the rest of his life. He rebukes Peter about as hard as anyone is rebuked in the Gospels — and he does not dismiss him. Six days later Peter is one of the three taken up the mountain. He will go on to deny his Lord outright, with oaths, in a courtyard, and will be restored and commissioned by a charcoal fire. Full severity and unbroken commitment, held together at the same moment. We find that combination almost impossible to imagine, which is why we keep expecting our failures to end the relationship. They did not end his. Do not read your worst moment as your verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: But he turned and said to Peter, "Get behind me, Satan! You are a hindrance to me. For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men." Then Jesus said to his disciples, "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Get behind me, Satan" — the sharpest rebuke in the Gospel, directed at the man just called blessed. Peter is not possessed by Satan; he is voicing Satan's agenda — the agenda of the cross-free kingdom, the Messiah who wins without suffering. "Hindrance" (skandalon — stumbling block): the man who is to be the rock on which the church is built is momentarily the stone that trips up the Savior. The two sayings about following are sequential: deny yourself (refuse the self as the center of your universe), take up your cross (embrace public identification with the condemned Christ), follow (not ahead, not alongside, but behind — in the path he walks). The disciple's life is shaped by the Master's death.

Both of those commands are so familiar that they have gone soft, and each has been misheard in a particular direction. They are worth recovering, because between them they describe what following Jesus actually costs.

Take deny himself first. It does not mean self-hatred, and it does not mean asceticism — going without things for the sake of going without them. Matthew tells you exactly what the word means, because he uses it again in this same Gospel for the most famous denial in history: it is the word for what Peter does in the courtyard when he says I do not know the man (26:70-74). To deny is to disown, to refuse to be identified with, to decline to take someone's side. So to deny yourself is to do to your own claims what Peter did to Jesus — to hear the demand of your own comfort, your own reputation, your own being-in-the-right, and answer, I do not know him. Not to despise yourself. To stop automatically taking your own side.

Then take up his cross, which has suffered worse. The phrase has been flattened until it means a chronic complaint, a difficult relative, a job you dislike — anything one has to put up with. Hear it as the men on that road heard it. A man carrying a crossbeam through a town was not carrying a burden; he was walking to his own execution, in public, and everyone who saw him knew he was not coming back. A cross is not a weight you carry. It is a death you have agreed to.

Which sharpens the question considerably. Your illness is not your cross. Your difficult marriage is not your cross. Your bad back, your awkward colleague, your aging parents — these are afflictions, and Scripture has a great deal to say about them, and God is deeply present in them. But your cross is the specific cost of following Jesus: the thing you would not be bearing if you were not his. The promotion refused because the figures would have to be wrong. The relationship ended. The truth told when a silence would have been cheaper. The money given that you had other plans for. The reputation you have quietly lost among people whose good opinion you wanted.

And the reason for insisting on the distinction is not pedantry. Calling an ordinary hardship a cross is a way of feeling that discipleship is costing us something when it may be costing us nothing at all — which is the very self-deception this Gospel keeps prodding (cf. 4:25). Luke adds one word to this saying that settles its shape: daily. It is not one dramatic renunciation, remembered for years. It is a small repeated decision, most of which nobody sees.

Finally, note the order, and note who gives the command. Deny, take up, follow — and the following is behind him, on a road he walks first. He is not asking for anything he declined to do himself; within a week he will be telling these men plainly what Jerusalem holds for him, and within a year he will carry the beam. And notice the mercy of the arrangement in this very chapter: he says all this, and six days later he takes three of them up a mountain and lets them see the far side of it. He does not ask anyone to carry a cross on bare instruction. He shows them the glory first.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? Or what shall a man give in return for his soul?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The paradox of verse 25 is the gospel's most concentrated summary: self-preservation destroys; self-surrender saves. The life "saved" by refusing the cross — the life of safety, comfort, and social acceptance at the cost of allegiance to Jesus — is the life lost at the end. The life "lost" by following Christ through cross-bearing is the life found in its fullest form. The soul-forfeiting question that follows is the ultimate cost-benefit analysis: even if you gain the entire world (every pleasure, every power, every possession), what is the exchange rate for a soul? There is no currency in which a human soul can be purchased back once forfeited. The question answers itself: the soul is priceless, and therefore no earthly gain justifies its loss.

Read it once more in Greek and the two verses close up into a single argument. Life in verse 25 and soul in verse 26 are the same word, psyche, and it occurs four times in three sentences. Our English versions change the word halfway through, and the change hides the logic. He is not moving from a point about earthly life to a separate point about eternal souls. He is running one word through one argument: the self you clutch, you lose; the self you hand over, you get back; the self cannot be bought at any figure; and there is not a second one available for another attempt. You have one self, and every day you are spending it on something.

Before that is applied, one guard, because the sentence is regularly used to bully decent people. Nothing here forbids ambition. A man is not more spiritual for wanting less; Scripture tells him to work well, provide for his household and be good at what he does. And note the three words that keep this from being a general commendation of sacrifice: for my sake. Jesus does not praise losing your life. Men lose their lives for a country, a company, a cause, a reputation, and lose them altogether. The clause that turns a loss into a finding is not the size of the sacrifice but the name of the person it is made for. Self-denial is not the point of Christianity. He is.

Now the second question, which is sharper than the first and is a market question put to men who understood markets. The word behind in return is antallagma — the sum handed over in an exchange, the price. So he is not being rhetorical. He is inviting a bid: name the figure. And the terrible thing about the question is not that the price is high; it is that there is no price at all. Everything else a man owns converts into something else. A house converts into money, money converts into time, time converts into comfort; there is an exchange rate for all of it. There is exactly one item in his possession that no market will quote, and it is himself.

The test is easy to run and it takes about four seconds. Ask a man what he would take for his car, and he names a figure. His house, and he names a figure, perhaps after a pause. Ask him what he would take for his son, and the question stops being a question — he does not calculate slowly and arrive at a large number; he refuses the whole category, and is offended that it was raised. Jesus is saying that this is what a soul is, and that most people who would be outraged by the second question have been quietly answering the first one about themselves for years, at rates they would be ashamed to write down.

Left there, it is a lecture on prudence. Matthew does not leave it there. The question of verse 26 is asked and not answered, and four chapters later the same Gospel supplies the only answer ever given: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (20:28). The word for the life he gives is psyche, the same word as here, and the word for ransom is the price paid to buy a person out. So the question stands unanswered for four chapters and then the questioner answers it himself, and not with a sum.

It is worth stopping over what that says about him. He knew the arithmetic when he asked. He knew that no man in that circle, and no man since, had anything in his hands worth a single soul — and that every one of them had already sold his own cheaply and could not buy it back. And knowing it, he walked from this conversation to Jerusalem, carried the price to the counter himself, and paid it in the only currency the exchange would accept, which was his own life. The One who warned men not to sell themselves for the world is the One who bought them when they already had. There is no other transaction like it in the universe, and the church has never got over it.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Son of Man is going to come with his angels in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay each person according to what he has done. Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eschatological frame for the cross-bearing call: the Son of Man who goes to the cross is the same Son of Man who will come in glory to judge. The judgment is by deeds — not as the basis of justification (which is by grace through faith) but as the evidence of what a life was truly ordered around. "Some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom" — most naturally refers to the Transfiguration (ch. 17), which is a proleptic vision of the Son of Man's glory. The three who will witness it — Peter, James, and John — are standing here. Six days later they will see it. The cross and the glory are not alternatives; the glory comes through and because of the cross.

That answer needs defending, because this is one of the verses most often produced as proof that Jesus was mistaken. Read flatly it sounds like a dated prediction that failed: he promised to return in glory before his hearers died, and they died, and he did not come. Matthew makes us face the same charge twice more — at 10:23 and at 24:34 — and it is answered in both places; the heart of it is that "the Son of Man coming in his kingdom" is drawn from Daniel 7:13-14, where the Son of Man comes not down to earth but up to the Ancient of Days to be crowned. It is coronation language. It need not mean the last day at all, and here it plainly does not.

But the objection usually pressed against the reading given above is a fair one and deserves an answer of its own. If Jesus meant an event six days away, why speak so solemnly of some standing here not tasting death — as though the interval were long enough for others to die in? Three things. First, the emphasis of the sentence falls on some, not on the waiting: he has just said in verse 27 that the Son of Man will come with his angels to judge, and now he distinguishes — that day is not what you are about to see, but a few of you are about to see something of it. Second, all three Gospels place the saying immediately before the Transfiguration and then date the Transfiguration to the very next week, which is as loud a piece of arrangement as the Evangelists ever make. Third, and best, one of the men standing there tells us himself what he thought he had seen. Writing near the end of his life, Peter defends the promise of Christ's coming by appealing to that mountain: we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty — we ourselves heard the voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain (2 Pet 1:16-18). The man who heard the promise cites its fulfilment.

And see what kind of word this is, coming where it comes. These men have just been told that their Master is going to Jerusalem to be killed and that they must take up a cross behind him. It is the bleakest hour of their training. Into it he drops a promise: before you die, some of you are going to see who I really am. He does not ask them to carry a cross on bare instruction. He gives three of them a look at the far side of it first.

One clause in verse 27 needs more than the line it was given above, because an honest Protestant reader stops dead at it: he will repay each person according to what he has done. Judgment by works, on the lips of Jesus, in the same paragraph as the cross. Say the awkward thing first: the New Testament teaches this everywhere and never apologises for it, and Matthew is the most insistent of all — the men who are turned away in 7:21-23, the account rendered for every careless word in 12:36-37, the sheep and the goats separated in 25:31-46 by what was and was not done.

The resolution is not a softening of the words but a question about what a court is for. Two different questions are asked at any trial: on what ground is this man received, and what was this man actually like? Righteousness is received and never earned; that is settled at the cross and not at the assize. But a righteousness that has been received always shows, and faith is invisible. God does not hold an invisible judgment. The deeds are simply the visible form of the thing, produced in evidence, the way a man's handwriting is produced to show whose hand it was.

And Matthew rules out a scoreboard twice over, in two scenes that should be read together. In 7:21-23 the men rejected are not rejected for a low total; their works are impressive, prophecies and exorcisms and mighty deeds, and the verdict against them is not that they did too little but that they were never known — I never knew you. Works could not supply the relationship. Then in 25:31-46 the sheep are astonished by their own record and cannot remember any of it: when did we see you hungry? On a scoreboard, nobody is ever surprised by his own score. Those two scenes together tell you what kind of judgment this is. It is not an audit. It is a recognition.

Which is why the verse must not be turned into a lash for a tender conscience. Look at whom he is saying it to. These are eleven men who could not follow a warning about bread that morning, one of whom has just been called Satan and will in due course deny him with oaths in a courtyard. He tells them about the judgment not to frighten them but to steady them, as the reason they can afford to lose their lives: the Son of Man is coming in his Father's glory, and nothing spent on him will be mislaid. A man who examines his own deeds and finds them thin has not thereby discovered that he is lost. The question at that day is not how much was done. It is whose he was — and the deeds are only how that shows.

16.theology: The church and the confession. Matthew is the only Gospel that records Jesus using the word “church” (ekklesia — the called-out assembly), and it appears on his lips in only two passages: here, and again in the discipline of 18:17. His promise is breathtaking in its confidence: he will build it, not we; and it will endure against all opposition. The church’s indestructibility rests not on its institutional strength or cultural influence but on the identity of its Lord and the truth of its confession. When the church loses the confession — that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God — it loses the rock on which it stands. The Reformation was at its heart a recovery of this confession: Christ alone, known through Scripture alone, received through faith alone, to the glory of God alone.
16.examples:
Then: Caesarea Philippi was the last place you would expect the church to be founded — a pagan city, politically dangerous territory, far from Jerusalem’s religious centre. Jesus chose it deliberately. The church is born at the margins, in hostile territory, by a divine confession that overturns every human calculation.

Now: The question “Who do you say that I am?” is not a theological quiz but an existential confrontation. Every person who hears the gospel must answer it. Correct doctrine about Jesus (acknowledging him as a great teacher, a moral exemplar, a historical figure) falls short of Peter’s confession. Jesus demands a verdict — not about what others say, but about what you say. The church is built on those who answer as Peter answered, by the same Spirit who revealed it to him.

17.title: The Transfiguration
17.text: <sup>1</sup>And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. <sup>2</sup>And he was transfigured before them, and his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as light. <sup>3</sup>And behold, there appeared to them Moses and Elijah, talking with him. <sup>4</sup>And Peter said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good that we are here. If you wish, I will make three tents here, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah.” <sup>5</sup>He was still speaking when, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice from the cloud said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” <sup>6</sup>When the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were terrified. <sup>7</sup>But Jesus came and touched them, saying, “Rise, and have no fear.” <sup>8</sup>And when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one but Jesus only. <sup>9</sup>And as they were coming down the mountain, Jesus commanded them, “Tell no one the vision, until the Son of Man is raised from the dead.” <sup>14</sup>And when they came to the crowd, a man came up to him and, kneeling before him, said, <sup>15</sup>“Lord, have mercy on my son, for he has seizures and he suffers terribly. <sup>20</sup>He said to them, “Because of your little faith. For truly, I say to you, if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you.”
17.overview:
The Transfiguration is a window into eternity opened for three disciples on a mountain. For a moment the veil of Jesus’ humanity is drawn back and the uncreated glory of the Son shines through: his face blazes like the sun, his garments become white as light. Moses and Elijah appear — the Law and the Prophets — converging on the one they pointed to, discussing the “exodus” he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). The Father speaks from the cloud — the shekinah glory — as he did at the baptism: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.”

The Transfiguration is the answer to Peter’s confusion in chapter 16. Peter could not accept a suffering Messiah. The mountain shows him why the cross is not a defeat: the one who will be crucified is the radiant Son of God, whose glory is momentarily unveiled. The cross does not contradict his glory; it is the appointed path through which his glory reaches the world. The disciples descend the mountain and immediately confront a demon-possessed boy they could not heal — from glory to weakness, from the height to the valley of need, which is always where the church must work.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six days after Peter's confession, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. He is transfigured before them — his face shining like the sun, his clothes white as light. Moses and Elijah appear and speak with him. A cloud overshadows them and the Father's voice speaks: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him." The disciples fall on their faces; Jesus touches them and they see no one but Jesus alone. Coming down, he forbids them to speak of the vision until he is raised from the dead, and answers their question about Elijah: Elijah has already come, in John the Baptist, and was not recognised but treated however his enemies pleased — and so also, he says, the Son of Man will suffer at their hands.
verseByVerse.theology: The Transfiguration is the mountain-top confirmation of Peter's confession: the Son of God whose glory was hidden in flesh is momentarily unveiled. Moses (the law) and Elijah (the prophets) appear alongside Jesus — the whole of the Old Testament represented — and then disappear. Jesus alone remains. The command "listen to him" supersedes Sinai and Carmel: not the law through Moses, not the prophetic word through Elijah, but the Son himself who is their fulfillment. The disciples' prostration and their rising at Jesus's touch enact the pattern of every encounter with the holy: undone by the presence, restored by the touch of grace. There is a quiet fitness in which two men were chosen to stand there. Moses and Elijah are the only two men in the Old Testament who met God on Horeb and asked to see his glory, and each was given something less than he asked: Moses was hidden in a cleft of the rock and shown only the back of the glory as it passed (Exod 33:18-23), and Elijah wrapped his face in his cloak at the mouth of the cave and would not look (1 Kings 19:9-13). Now the two of them stand on a mountain with the glory in front of them, unveiled and in the open, holding a conversation with it. What neither prophet was permitted to see, both of them at last see in the face of a Galilean carpenter. And the descent (vv. 9-13) attaches the vision to the cross: the silence is to hold until the resurrection, and the Elijah question is answered by pointing at a man already dead. John came in Elijah's spirit and power and was killed on a whim; the pattern of the forerunner is the pattern of the King.
verseByVerse.examples: The descent from the mountain with the charge to silence (until the resurrection) and the discussion about Elijah frames the Transfiguration within the larger passion narrative. The glory on the mountain will be followed immediately by the failure to heal the epileptic boy in the valley — the constant movement between mountain-top and valley-floor, between the unveiled glory and the demanding need. The disciples are not left on the mountain; they descend with Jesus to where the need is. Two practical edges run through the descent itself. The first is the order to say nothing (v. 9): three men walk down to nine colleagues who were not invited and are about to have the worst day of their ministry, and they are to keep the greatest experience of their lives to themselves. Not everything God gives is given for circulation; some of it is given to be carried. The second is the plain warning of vv. 12-13. God's own forerunner, the greatest man born of women, was beheaded because a king did not want to look foolish in front of his dinner guests, and God did not prevent it. Faithfulness does not purchase a comfortable outcome. What it secures is a place in a pattern that runs through the Son himself and out the far side on the third day.

verseByVerse.quote: And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. And he was transfigured before them, and his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"After six days" — the specific time marker connects this to the confession and passion-prediction of chapter 16. Six days is also the time Moses waited on Sinai before the glory of God appeared to him (Exod. 24:16). The three disciples (the inner circle of the inner circle) are led up by Jesus himself — he determines who comes and when. The transfiguration is not something that happens to Jesus from outside; it is his own eternal glory momentarily breaking through the veil of his humanity. "His face shone like the sun" — the glory of the incarnate Son, which has been present all along, becomes visible. The light that was in him from the beginning (John 1:4) shines through.

Two small questions first, because a reader with an open Bible will meet both. Which mountain? Matthew says only a high mountain, and the honest answer is that we do not know. Ancient tradition settled on Tabor, and there are churches on it; but Tabor is under two thousand feet and had a fortified settlement on its summit in that century, and six days earlier this party was at Caesarea Philippi, standing at the foot of Hermon, which climbs past nine thousand feet and carries snow most of the year. Hermon is the likelier candidate. Matthew did not think the location worth recording, which is itself a hint about where he wants the eye to go. And the other: Luke says about eight days after these sayings (Luke 9:28) where Matthew and Mark say after six. Luke has written about, and the ordinary Jewish way of counting includes the day you start from and the day you finish on, which turns the same interval into eight. It is one span counted in the two normal ways.

Now the thing itself. The verb is metamorphothe, a passive: he was changed in form. But what changed was not his nature, and this is the hinge of the whole scene. Nothing was added to Jesus on that mountain. Something was stopped being hidden. Set him beside the man standing next to him and the difference is exact. Moses came down from Sinai with his own face shining so that Israel was afraid to come near him — and that light was borrowed, reflected off a glory that was not his, and it faded, and he put a veil over it so that they would not sit and watch it die away (Exod 34:29-35). Here nothing is reflected and nothing is veiled. The light is not falling on Jesus from somewhere else. It is coming out of him.

And Matthew chooses his comparison with care, because he has used it once before in this Gospel. Four chapters back, explaining the weeds and the harvest, Jesus had said that at the end the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (13:43). Now Matthew writes that his face shone like the sun. The same phrase, the same Gospel, the same speaker. What he had promised was waiting for them at the end of the world is standing in front of them on a hillside in the middle of it, out of sequence, so that three frightened men would have something to remember.

But sit for a moment with what the veil implies, because it is harder to take in than the blaze. If this was in him all along, then it was in him at Nazareth. For something like thirty years that face had been an ordinary face in an ordinary village. The neighbours watched him grow up. His mother washed his clothes. Men came to the workshop about a yoke or a door frame and haggled over the price, and went away with no idea at all; later they would say, in a tone of dismissal, Is not this the carpenter's son? (13:55). All that time, this was what was under the surface, held back, day after day, by a decision he kept making. The wonder of the Transfiguration is not that he shone for an hour. It is the thirty years he did not.

And note when it is given. He had told them six days earlier that some standing there would see the Son of Man in his kingdom before they died (16:28), and here is the promise being kept with the ink barely dry. These are men who have just been told to carry a cross behind a Master going to Jerusalem to be killed. He takes the three of them up a hill and shows them who it is they are following. He does not explain the glory to them. He lets them look at it.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with him. And Peter said to Jesus, "Lord, it is good that we are here. If you wish, I will make three tents here, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses (the law) and Elijah (the prophets) appear — Luke tells us they spoke about his departure (exodus) to be accomplished in Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). The whole Old Testament is pointing to and discussing the cross. Peter's offer of three tents is the impulse to prolong the moment, to build a permanent dwelling for the glory. The tabernacle impulse — to house the divine presence — is understandable but misguided: this glory is not for camping; it is for going to Jerusalem and dying. Peter's "if you wish" at least acknowledges the precedence of Jesus's will over his own preference. Matthew's parenthetical (Mark 9:6 — "he did not know what to say, for they were terrified") explains the offer as the speech of overwhelm.

Peter's instinct, though, is one every Christian will recognise, and it deserves more than a smile at his expense. Something overwhelming has happened, and his immediate reaction is to make it permanent — build something, stay here, do not let this end. That is not a foolish impulse. It is worship reaching for permanence, and it is the same impulse behind every attempt to bottle a moment with God.

It is wrong all the same, and the passage shows why twice over. Luke tells us what Moses and Elijah were actually discussing on that mountain: his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Lk 9:31). The glory was not an alternative to the cross; it was a conversation about the cross. A shelter built to keep them all up there would have been a shelter built against the very thing they were talking about. And when Peter has finished speaking, God answers the offer of a tent by sending his own — the cloud overshadows them, and it is not made of anything Peter could have assembled. You cannot house this. It houses you.

Which speaks to something most believers meet and few are taught how to handle. There are seasons when God feels near — a conference, a retreat, a Sunday when the singing landed somewhere it usually does not, a stretch of months when prayer came easily. Almost everyone is given some. Nobody keeps them. And when the sense of it goes, people conclude either that they have sinned it away or that it was never real in the first place.

Look at what actually happened to these three. They came off that mountain within a day into a shouting argument at the bottom, a desperate father, a boy convulsing in the fire, and nine colleagues who had just failed publicly. The glory did not follow them down in any visible form whatever. What they brought down was a memory and a sentence: this is my beloved Son; listen to him. That was the point of the mountain — not the feeling, but a clearer sight of who he is, to be carried into a valley where nothing would look glorious at all.

Peter tells us himself, decades later, what he did with it. He appeals to that day as proof that the church's hope is not a cleverly devised myth — and then, having played his eyewitness card, he says something surprising: and we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place (2 Pet 1:16-19). The man who saw the face shine like the sun points his readers not to the pursuit of another mountain but to their Bibles. That is where the glory is now kept for the rest of us. So do not try to rebuild the tent. Take what you were given, and go down; and notice how the descent begins — he came and touched them and said, rise, and have no fear.

verseByVerse.quote: He was still speaking when, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice from the cloud said, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him." When the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were terrified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cloud — the shekinah cloud of divine presence that led Israel in the wilderness and filled the tabernacle and temple — overshadows them, and the Father speaks. The words are virtually identical to the baptism declaration (3:17) with one addition: "listen to him." At the baptism, the Father declared the Son's identity; at the Transfiguration, he adds the command that responds to the presence of Moses and Elijah: not the law through Moses, not the prophets through Elijah — listen to the Son. He fulfills and supersedes both. The disciples' prostration is the only appropriate response to theophany: face-down, unable to stand before the weight of the divine presence. Terror is the beginning of worship.

The Father's sentence is not one statement but three Old Testament strings sounded together, and a Jew on that mountain would have heard every one of them. This is my beloved Son is the enthronement psalm, where God says to his king, you are my Son, today I have begotten you (Ps 2:7). With whom I am well pleased opens the first of the Servant songs — behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights (Isa 42:1), the servant who will not break a bruised reed. And listen to him comes from Deuteronomy, where God promises to raise up a prophet like Moses from among the brothers, and adds, it is to him you shall listen (Deut 18:15). King, Servant, Prophet, in a single breath, from the throne.

And notice whose words the third one is. Deuteronomy 18 is Moses speaking — and Moses is standing right there. The Father, with Moses at his Son's shoulder, quotes Moses' own promise and points it at Jesus. That is not a slight on Moses; it is Moses getting what he was promised. Nor should the next verse of Deuteronomy be left out, because it tells you what kind of sentence this is: whoever will not listen to my words that he shall speak in my name, I myself will require it of him (Deut 18:19). Listen to him is not a recommendation.

Now weigh how rare this is. God the Father speaks audibly three times in the whole of the four Gospels: at the baptism (3:17), here, and once more in Jerusalem in the last week (John 12:28). Twice he identifies his Son. Once, and only once, he commands anything at all. The entire recorded imperative of God the Father in the New Testament is three words long, and the three words are: listen to him. Everything the church has ever needed to be told about its relation to Christ is in that sentence, and there is nothing else on the list.

The timing has an edge to it as well. Matthew says the cloud came while he was still speaking — while Peter was still speaking. On the one occasion in the New Testament when the Father issues an order, he interrupts a man in the middle of a sentence to say: stop talking and listen to my Son. It is not a cruelty; Peter was frightened and meant well. But it is a shape worth noticing, because the impulse to organise the moment is very nearly always louder than the impulse to hear.

And look at what actually put them on the ground. They had watched a face turn to light and stayed on their feet. They had seen two men dead for centuries appear on a hillside, and Peter had kept talking through it. It was the voice that dropped them. A man can look at glory and find something to say about it. He cannot be addressed by it and remain standing.

A guard is needed here, because a reader who has never felt anything remotely like this in church may quietly conclude that his religion is a poor imitation. It is not. This was given once, on one afternoon, to three men in the whole history of the world, and even they were never asked to reproduce it or to go looking for it again — the one who saw it points his readers to their Bibles rather than to another mountain (see on vv. 3-4). What God asks is not the terror. The terror was there to secure the obedience, and it is the obedience he wants.

Which makes the command unusually easy to measure. Listening, in Scripture, is never the taking in of information; the word means heed, and a man who has heard and not done has not listened. So try it directly. Name the last thing Jesus said that changed a decision you were going to make anyway. Not a verse that comforted you — a sentence of his that cost you something and got obeyed. If the question is hard to answer, it is worth sitting with, because the Father did not say admire him, and did not say discuss him, and did not say build him a tent.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus came and touched them, saying, "Rise, and have no fear." And when they lifted their eyes, they saw no one but Jesus only.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Jesus came and touched them" — the same touch that healed lepers, raised the dead, gave sight to the blind now raises his prostrate disciples. "Rise, and have no fear" — the word of grace that follows every encounter with divine holiness: rise up, because the one who has undone you is also the one who lifts you. "They saw no one but Jesus only" — Moses and Elijah have disappeared. The law and the prophets have taken their appropriate place: not alongside Jesus as equal authorities, but pointing to him and receding before him. The Transfiguration is the visual argument for the canon: Moses speaks, Elijah speaks, then the Father speaks, and the command is to listen to the Son. Jesus alone remains.

Look at the word he uses to lift them, because Matthew has just been using it about something else. Rise is egerthete — the resurrection verb. It is the word in the sentence spoken six days before this, that the Son of Man would be killed and on the third day be raised (16:21); it is the word he will use again on the way down this same mountain (17:9), and again in Galilee a few verses later (17:23). Three men are lying face down in the grass like corpses, and the word he speaks over them is the word for a body coming out of a tomb. It is the first time in this Gospel that the resurrection word is spoken over anybody but himself, and it lands on frightened friends.

And notice that he came to them. They were face down; they could not have found him if they had wanted to. Matthew writes that he came and touched them — he crossed the distance. The hand that reached down was the hand that had been shining a moment earlier, and it is the same hand Matthew has been describing all along: laid on a leper whom nobody else in Israel would go near (8:3), on a woman burning with fever (8:15), on the eyes of two blind men (9:29). Unveiled glory did not alter his habits. He still touches people.

Nor is have no fear a rebuke. He does not tell them they were wrong to be afraid — the terror was the only sane response to what had just happened, and he never says otherwise. He simply takes it away. There is a difference between a Lord who criticises your fear and a Lord who removes it, and every frightened Christian needs to know which one he has.

Then the strangest sentence in the scene: they saw no one but Jesus only. Consider how the mountain ends. Not with more, but with less. The two greatest figures of the old covenant are gone. The cloud is gone. The voice has stopped. What the three men are left holding, as they stand up and brush themselves down, is one man they walked up the hill with and one sentence they will never forget. That is the whole inheritance of the Transfiguration, and it turned out to be sufficient for the rest of their lives.

There is a test in that, and it is uncomfortable to run. Christian life has a way of getting crowded — a cause, a movement, a system that explains everything, a teacher whose books are on the shelf, a method that worked once, three conferences a year. None of it is necessarily wrong. But strip a man's religion down to Jesus alone, take away the scaffolding and the reinforcements, and ask honestly what he would miss. If the answer is that a great deal would be missing, the mountain has something to say to him, because it ended by clearing the field until only one figure was standing in it — and heaven had just called that figure enough.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were coming down the mountain, Jesus commanded them, "Tell no one the vision, until the Son of Man is raised from the dead." And the disciples asked him, "Then why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charge to silence until the resurrection frames the Transfiguration as a proleptic event — a preview of what will be publicly revealed only after the cross and empty tomb. The disciples' question about Elijah shows they are trying to fit what they have seen into their theological categories: they just saw Elijah; the scribes say Elijah must precede the Messiah. The question is genuine and important. Jesus will answer it by reinterpreting Elijah's coming in terms of John the Baptist — the prophetic type fulfilled in a different key than expected. The disciples' confusion is the confusion of those who have witnessed the reality but not yet fully understood the framework that interprets it.

He calls it the vision — horama, a word Matthew uses nowhere else in his Gospel. Not because it was unreal; Peter spent the rest of his life insisting it was not. The word means something shown, and what was shown here belonged properly to a later time. They had been allowed to see out of sequence.

And look at the shape of the silence he imposes, because it is a remarkable thing to say out loud. This is the second gag order in two chapters (16:20), but this one comes with an expiry date attached: tell no one until the Son of Man is raised from the dead. He is so certain of the resurrection that he schedules the release of the news around it, in advance, to men who are about to be told again that he is going to be killed and who will take in only the first half of the sentence. He is making arrangements on the far side of his own grave.

Now the question, which is not idle curiosity and is usually read as though it were. Three men are walking down a hillside doing arithmetic, and it is not going well. The scribes taught from Malachi that Elijah must come first and put everything in order before the great and awesome Day of the LORD. But if Elijah has only just turned up, in front of three witnesses, for a matter of minutes, and has now gone again with nothing whatever restored — then either the scribes were wrong, or that was not really Elijah, or, worst of all, the man beside them who keeps saying he is going to Jerusalem to be killed cannot be the one they confessed him to be. Their question has a question mark on the end and an objection underneath it. They are not asking about a prophecy. They are asking whether the passion prediction can possibly be right.

There is a practical matter in the command too, and it is harder than it looks. These three have just had the experience of their lives, and they are walking down to nine colleagues who were not invited, who have been waiting at the bottom, and who — as the next paragraph will show — have just had the worst day of their ministry. And the three are to say nothing. Not a word, not a hint, not the sort of remark that invites a question. That order has an obvious application, and it cuts against the grain of an age that publishes everything. Not everything God gives is given for circulation. Some of it is given to be carried.

Guard it, though, or it becomes a false modesty or a pious secretiveness, and it is neither: there was a release date on this one, and the man who kept quiet about it for years eventually wrote it down for the whole church. But a Christian who cannot hold a good thing quietly will generally find it turns to currency in his hands — something to be spent on the impression it makes — and what was given to steady him for a valley gets used up before he reaches the bottom of the hill.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "Elijah does come, and he will restore all things. But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they pleased. So also the Son of Man will suffer at their hands."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elijah does come — Jesus affirms the scribal interpretation. But Elijah has already come: John the Baptist, in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17), fulfilled the Malachi 4:5 prophecy. "They did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they pleased" — Herod and Herodias imprisoned and executed John without recognizing his prophetic status. The same pattern awaits the Son of Man: not recognized, subjected to the will of his enemies, suffering at their hands. The forerunner's fate foreshadows the King's. This is not pessimism but the consistent logic of rejection that runs from the prophets to John to Jesus: the world does not receive the one God sends; it does to him whatever it pleases.

A reader with a parallel Bible open will stop here, because John denied precisely what Jesus is affirming. A delegation of priests and Levites went out to the Jordan and asked him flatly, Are you Elijah?, and he answered, I am not (John 1:21). Jesus says he is. The two are not in conflict, because the two questions are not the same question. The priests were asking whether he was Elijah in person — the man who went up in the whirlwind come back down in the flesh, which is what popular expectation had made of Malachi. To that, John's answer is simply accurate: no. What Jesus says is something else, that John came in Elijah's spirit and power (Luke 1:17) and did Elijah's work: the wilderness, the rough clothing and the leather belt that were the old prophet's uniform (see on 3:4), and a public collision with a king and his queen over a marriage. John was not Elijah returned. He was Elijah repeated.

And Jesus had said this once before, with a qualification that is the key to the whole matter: if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come (11:14). That clause does not weaken the claim; it tells you what sort of claim it is. This kind of fulfilment is recognised rather than measured, and it asks something of the person doing the looking. A man determined to have Elijah in person, arriving in the manner he has already decided upon, will stand in front of a camel-hair prophet at the Jordan and see nothing at all. That is not a failure of evidence. It is a failure of willingness, and it is the same failure that will shortly hand this Gospel its crucifixion.

One honest note on the tenses. Jesus says Elijah does come, and he will restore all things, and then says Elijah has already come. Some readers, particularly in the dispensational tradition, take the future tense seriously and expect a further Elijah before the last day, pointing to the two witnesses of Revelation 11 who shut up the sky as Elijah did. That reading deserves to be named rather than waved away; the future tense is really there. The more natural reading of the pair is that Jesus first states the scribal doctrine correctly — yes, that is what Malachi says — and then tells them it has already happened under their noses and they missed it, which is exactly the charge he has been making since chapter 11.

It is worth asking what Malachi said Elijah would restore, because the answer is smaller and better than expected. Not a kingdom, not a temple, not an army: he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the land with a decree of utter destruction (Mal 4:6). The great prophesied national renewal begins in kitchens. It begins with a father and a son under the same roof who have not spoken properly in years, and it is set against the alternative of a country under a curse. Whatever else revival is, Malachi says you would be able to see it at somebody's table.

Now refuse the euphemism in the middle of verse 12. They did to him whatever they pleased sounds like a general statement about opposition. Matthew has already told us exactly what it covers, three chapters back. A king held a birthday party. His wife's daughter danced and pleased the guests. The king, warm with wine and wanting to look magnificent in front of his friends, swore an open-ended oath; the girl was coached by her mother; and the greatest man born of women was beheaded in a cell and his head carried into the dining room on a serving dish (14:6-11). No trial, no charge that would have stood anywhere, no reason on earth except that a man did not want to look foolish at his own table.

That has to be faced, because a great deal of popular Christianity quietly assumes that faithfulness buys a decent outcome. It bought John a cell and an executioner, and God did not intervene. And Jesus, who could have softened it, does the opposite: so also the Son of Man will suffer at their hands. He tells them the pattern holds and that he is the next one in it. Nothing here promises that God will prevent such things. What it promises is that he is not surprised by them, that they were written down in a prophet centuries before, and that the pattern runs straight through his own Son — and out the far side, on the third day.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the disciples understood that he was speaking to them of John the Baptist.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples' understanding — that Elijah-come-already was John — is the beginning of a larger comprehension: if John's suffering was the forerunner's pattern, then Jesus's announced suffering is the fulfillment of the same pattern, not an accident or a failure. The transfigured glory and the announced passion are two sides of the same identity: the suffering Servant who is also the glorious Son. The disciples are being prepared — slowly, through repeated teaching — to face the cross not as the end of their hope but as its appointed center. Understanding comes in stages; Jesus is patient with each stage while never stopping at any of them.

This is the second time in two chapters that Matthew has written then they understood (16:12), and it is worth noticing that he keeps score. He is tracking a curve, not reporting a state, and the curve is slow.

But look carefully at what they had understood, because it was not a fact about John the Baptist. It was a sum. If Elijah has already come, and Elijah was killed by a whim at a dinner party, and Jesus has just said so also the Son of Man, then the conclusion is no longer a matter of prophetic interpretation. It is arithmetic, and it is about the man walking a few feet in front of them. They did not gain a piece of information on that hillside. They lost a hope.

Which marks a real difference that most Christians never notice in themselves: the difference between holding a doctrine and having done the arithmetic on it. A man can agree that Christ was crucified, recite it in a creed weekly, and hold it for thirty years as a proposition he has no quarrel with. Then one day he works out what it implies — about the kind of world he is living in, about what God is prepared to permit, about what it will cost to follow a man on that road — and the same doctrine goes off in his hands. Verse 13 is that moment, and Matthew records it without a word of comfort attached.

Guard it, though, before it becomes a standard nobody meets. Understanding is not the same as readiness. These are the men who understood this on a hillside in Galilee and ran out of a garden in Jerusalem, and one of them swore in a courtyard that he had never met him. So a reader who has genuinely grasped something and then failed to live up to it has not been exposed as a fraud. He is standing exactly where these men stood, and they are the ones the church was built on.

And the thing to carry away is not their slowness but his patience with it. He told them at 16:21 and Peter argued with him. He tells them here and they understand. He will tell them again a few verses on and they will simply grieve (17:23), and again on the road to Jerusalem with the details filled in (20:18-19). Four times over, to men who could not hold it in their heads for a week. He never once made their comprehension the condition of his going. He explained it to them as often as they needed, and then went and did it whether they had understood or not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–27 — The Epileptic Boy, the Second Passion Prediction, and the Temple Tax
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Descending from the mountain, Jesus finds the other disciples unable to heal an epileptic boy. He heals the boy with a rebuke. When the disciples ask why they could not, Jesus answers: this kind goes out only by prayer (and fasting). Jesus then gives the second passion prediction — betrayal, death, resurrection — and the disciples are greatly distressed. The chapter ends with the temple tax episode: Jesus affirms the sons' freedom while paying the tax to avoid giving offense.
verseByVerse.theology: The failure of the nine disciples at the foot of the mountain contrasts dramatically with the glory on the mountain. The disciples had been given authority over unclean spirits and sent out with the commission to use it (10:1, 8), and the other Gospels record that it had worked. Their failure here is attributed to "little faith" (v. 20). The familiar answer about prayer and fasting is verse 21, which the oldest manuscripts of Matthew do not contain; a copyist almost certainly carried it over from Mark 9:29. The words are not Matthew's, but the truth in them is the Lord's own and fits this scene exactly. The mountain of glory does not insulate from the valley of need; it sends back into it with greater resources. The disciples who could not cast out the spirit had stopped depending on the one who gave them authority. The section then turns twice more. The mustard seed of verse 20 is not a demand for a larger faith but for faith in a larger object — the bar is set at the smallest thing in the garden, and the promise that nothing will be impossible is bounded by the Lord's own prayer in the garden, where perfect faith asked for a cup to pass and added, nevertheless, not as I will (26:39). And the second passion prediction (vv. 22-23) shows the disciples changed: after the first they argued, after this one they simply grieve. Three times now the sentence has ended in resurrection, and three times they have heard only the killing.
verseByVerse.examples: The temple tax episode is one of the most revealing about Jesus's identity. The sons of the king do not pay tax to their own father; Jesus, as the Son of the God whose temple it is, owes no temple tax. Yet he pays it — not out of obligation but to avoid causing offense to those who do not yet know who he is. This is the pattern of his whole incarnation: the one who was rich became poor, the one who was free submitted to the constraints of the servant. He was free from the tax; he paid it in service to others. The tax itself makes the point sharper than any comment could. The two-drachma levy was the half-shekel of Exodus 30, collected from every man in Israel as a ransom for his life, to make atonement (Exod 30:12-16). So two collectors stand at a door in Capernaum asking the Son of God whether he means to pay his ransom — and he was on his way to Jerusalem to give his life as a ransom for many (20:28). And for the reader in the valley rather than at the door, vv. 19-23 supply two things to do on an ordinary Monday: after a failure at something God gave you, do what the disciples did and take the exact question to him rather than defending it or burying it; and when grief has heard the hard half of a promise, go back and read the end of the sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to the crowd, a man came up to him and, kneeling before him, said, "Lord, have mercy on my son, for he has seizures and he suffers terribly. For often he falls into the fire, and often into the water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The descent from the Transfiguration leads immediately to crisis: a father whose son is having seizures and falling into fire and water. The contrast between the mountain and the valley — between the unveiled glory and the desperate need — is Matthew's deliberate literary structure. The father kneels and cries "Lord, have mercy" — kyrie eleison, the liturgical cry that has echoed through Christian worship ever since. The description of the boy's suffering is specific and painful: into fire, into water, suffering terribly. The father does not describe a theological problem; he describes a child in danger of his life. Jesus comes from glory to meet exactly this kind of need.

But a reader will stop at the word Matthew uses, and should. The ESV says the boy "has seizures"; older versions call him a lunatic; and Jesus, four verses on, casts a demon out of him. Matthew's verb is seleniazetai — literally "to be moonstruck," from selene, the moon, because such attacks were thought to come and go with its phases. It is a word for what the thing looked like, not a verdict on what caused it, much as we still say a man had a fit. So which was it — was the boy ill, or was he possessed? And behind that sits the larger question pressed hard in our own day: were these simply pre-scientific people calling a disease of the brain a devil?

Matthew has already answered it, and the sentence has been sitting in his Gospel since chapter 4. In his first summary of the ministry they bring to Jesus "those oppressed by demons, those having seizures, and paralytics" (4:24) — three groups, named apart, in a single breath. Matthew knows the difference between a man with a demon and a man with the falling sickness, and distinguishes them as readily as we distinguish a fever from a broken leg. What he tells us here is that in this boy the symptoms of the one had the other behind them. The father reports what he can see. Jesus deals with what is actually there.

Two errors do damage, and the text refuses both. The first makes every seizure, every darkness of the mind, a work of the devil — a cruelty Matthew rules out by the simple fact that he listed the two separately. A believer with epilepsy is not in the enemy's grip; he needs a doctor and the love of his church, not an interrogation. The second error is the fashionable one, that the demonic is merely the old word for a disorder we can now name properly. But the thing in this boy was spoken to, and it answered, and it left; and the one who spoke was not a villager guessing at the moon. (On these powers and why they crowd the Gospels and then recede, see on 8:16-17.) What the father came for, he went home with: a son.

verseByVerse.quote: And I brought him to your disciples, and they could not heal him." And Jesus answered, "O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him here to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples' failure — they who had been given authority over unclean spirits — is the occasion for Jesus's expression of grief and frustration: "O faithless and twisted generation." The lament extends beyond the disciples to the whole generation of unbelief. "How long am I to be with you?" — the question of someone who has invested enormously in those who have not yet received it. The patience of Jesus with his disciples' slowness is extraordinary, but it is not unlimited emotional flatness; he feels the cost of the investment. "Bring him here to me" — the word that solves every problem of human insufficiency: come to Jesus with the need that you could not address. He will not fail where his disciples did.

Whom is he rebuking? Readers assume the nine, and wince on their behalf. But the word he uses is not disciples; it is generation, which is a whole-people word — and it is a quotation. In the Song of Moses, Israel in the wilderness are called a crooked and twisted generation (Deut 32:5), and the Greek word Matthew writes here, diestrammene, is the very word the Greek Old Testament uses there. So Jesus, walking down from a mountain where Moses had been standing at his shoulder an hour before, reaches for Moses' own song about a people who would not trust God, and lays it over the scene in front of him. He is not losing patience with nine men. He is naming where they all are in a very long story.

The feeling in it should not be smoothed away either. How long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? is the nearest thing in Matthew to weariness on the lips of Jesus, and it has an unmistakable Old Testament pedigree: How long shall this wicked congregation grumble against me? (Num 14:27); For forty years I loathed that generation (Ps 95:10). This is not petulance and not a man losing his grip. It is the grief of God at unbelief, a thing the Old Testament reports on nearly every page and which we would rather not hear from Christ, because it makes him harder to manage than the mild figure we prefer.

But now read the two clauses in the order he actually said them, because a great many people need to. O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to bear with you? Bring him here to me. The rebuke and the remedy are in one breath. He does not send the father away to work on his faith and come back when it is stronger. He does not make the healing wait until the complaint has been properly absorbed. He says what is true about the generation, and in the same sentence calls for the child — and the boy is well before the paragraph ends. Anyone who has lain awake convinced that God has finally grown tired of him should read those two clauses in sequence and notice how little time passes between them.

And those four words are the whole cure for a specific and very ordinary disappointment. The father had done a sensible thing. He had brought his son to the right movement and the wrong address: to the men who had healed people before, who had authority to do it, who by every reasonable expectation should have managed it. It did not work. Ministers fail, prayer chains fail, the church that helped somebody else does not help you, and the temptation at that point is to conclude that the whole thing is empty. The instruction is four words long. Bring him here to me.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of him, and the boy was healed instantly. Then the disciples came to Jesus privately and said, "Why could we not cast it out?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The healing is instant — a rebuke, and the demon is gone, and the boy is well. The disciples had attempted the same; why did it fail? Their private question reveals self-awareness: they know they should have been able to do this. They are not rationalizing their failure; they are pressing into understanding it. This is the posture that produces growth: not defending the failure but investigating it. The question "why could we not?" is the question of disciples who are genuinely trying to learn. Jesus will give them the honest answer, which will require their honest acknowledgment of what was lacking in their approach.

The verb is worth a moment. Rebuked is epitimao, and Matthew has used it twice already in memorable places: Jesus rebukes the wind and the sea and there is a great calm (8:26), and Peter takes his Lord aside and rebukes him for talking about a cross (16:22). It is the word for speaking with authority to something that has no business behaving as it is. He uses it on a storm and on a demon; and once, astonishingly, it was used on him by a friend who thought he knew better. Here it takes one sentence, and Matthew adds that the boy was healed from that very hour. What nine men could not do in an afternoon took him a sentence.

Notice too that the disciples came to him privately. They waited until the crowd had thinned and the father had gone home with his son. That is thoroughly human, and it should not be held against them: nobody wants to fail in front of a crowd and then be debriefed in front of the same crowd. The remarkable thing is not that they waited. It is that they asked.

Because look at what they did not do, and measure yourself against the list. They did not quit. They did not defend themselves — not a word about how difficult the case was, how severe the boy's condition, how weak the father's faith, how the crowd had interfered. They did not decide the gift had been quietly withdrawn and go back to fishing. And they did not do the thing most of us do after a public failure, which is to say nothing at all and hope the subject never comes up again. They went to Jesus and asked the exact question: why could we not? And he gave them a straight answer that neither flattered them nor crushed them. That is the entire procedure for a failed attempt at anything he has given you to do — a sermon that died, a conversation with your own child that went wrong, an attempt to help someone out of a habit that has beaten you both. Do not defend it. Do not bury it. Take it to him and ask what was missing.

There is a particular sting in this failure, and it is worth naming, because it is a different wound from never having succeeded. These men had done this before. They had been given authority over unclean spirits and sent out with it (10:1, 8), and the other Gospels record that it worked. So this is the failure of a man at something he used to be able to do, which is a specific kind of misery and is rarely spoken about — the preacher who could once hold a room, the father whose advice used to be wanted, the Christian for whom prayer was once nothing like this hard.
