What is plain is that nothing about the next four days is happening to Jesus. He is setting it up.

verseByVerse.quote: "If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, 'The Lord needs them,' and he will send them at once." This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet, saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord needs them. Six words to say to a stranger whose animal you are untying, and they are extraordinary in both halves.

Take the first half. The Lord — ho kyrios, with the article, absolute, no explanation attached. Jesus is not often reported using that of himself to people outside the circle, and here he sends it ahead of him as the whole of his credentials. No name, no message about who is asking, no promise to return the animal. If the owner asks, tell him the Lord needs them, and that will be sufficient. It was.

Now the second half, which is stranger. Needs. This is the only occasion in the Gospels on which Jesus says he has need of anything, and what he needs is the loan of a young donkey. The one through whom all things were made, walking toward the city where he will be crowned and killed, sends two friends to borrow transport. It is the same condescension that runs through the whole story and is easy to miss because it is so quiet: he had no house, he will borrow an upper room for the supper, he will be laid in a tomb somebody else had cut for himself, and the only thing he ever owned outright at the end was the clothes soldiers gambled over. He owns everything. He arrives owning nothing and asking for a colt.

Then Matthew steps out of the narrative to say what is going on: this took place to fulfil what was spoken by the prophet. He has used that formula a dozen times since chapter 1, and by now the reader should know what he means by it — not that a prediction has ticked over, but that a pattern long written has arrived at the thing it was always shaped for (see on 2:15). The words were on a scroll for five hundred years. Now they are hoofbeats on a road.

One thing not to over-claim, since the text does not. Matthew does not tell us whether the owner had been spoken to in advance or whether he simply released the animals because something in the request made refusal unthinkable. Both are entirely possible and the narrative is indifferent to the question. What it does report is the result: he will send them at once, and he did. Somewhere in that village is a man who lost the use of his donkey for an afternoon and never appears again in the story, and the whole entry into Jerusalem waited on his willingness.

verseByVerse.quote: "Say to the daughter of Zion, 'Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.'" The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zechariah's word for the king is praus, and Matthew's readers had met it twice already. It is the word in the Beatitudes for the meek who inherit the earth (5:5), and it is the word Jesus used of himself when he offered rest to people carrying too much: I am gentle and lowly in heart (11:29). It does not mean weak. It is the word used of a horse that has been broken — all the strength still there, and every ounce of it under control. That is the king riding down the hill.

Then read the next verse of Zechariah, because the prophet explains the donkey himself and almost nobody quotes it: I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the war horse from Jerusalem, and the battle bow shall be cut off, and he shall speak peace to the nations (Zech 9:10). The animal is not a note about the king's humility. It is his policy. He is riding the thing you ride when the war horses have been abolished, and the sentence ends with the nations — the same nations whose only court in the temple he is about to clear by force within the hour.

Set it beside what a triumphal entry actually looked like in that world and the contrast goes further than a change of animal. A Roman triumph had a fixed shape: the general in a four-horse chariot with his face painted red, the spoils of the campaign carried before him, the captured enemy leaders walking in chains behind, and at the end of the route the prisoners executed and bulls sacrificed. Go down the list. This king has no chariot. He has no spoils, having accumulated nothing. He drags no prisoners, having spent three years setting them free. And at the end of his route there is indeed a sacrifice — and it is him.

Which is the thing to hold on to when this scene is preached, as it often is, as the moment Jesus finally accepted the crown. He accepted it in the one form nobody wanted. The crowd on that road was shouting for a king who would deal with Rome, and the king they were shouting at had come to deal with something they had not asked him to touch. He let them cheer. He did not correct the volume, only the meaning, and he did it by choosing his transport.

The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them. Matthew keeps saying this about them, and it is worth noticing how ordinary the obedience is. They were not asked to understand the Zechariah citation or to grasp what was about to happen in the city. They were asked to walk into a village and fetch a donkey, and they did it. A great deal of obedience is that size.

verseByVerse.quote: They brought the donkey and the colt and put on them their cloaks, and he sat on them. Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The spreading of cloaks on the road was the ancient gesture of homage to a king: the same was done for Jehu when he was anointed king of Israel (2 Kings 9:13). The palm branches from the trees add another layer of royal symbolism — palms were associated with the Maccabean victories and with the Feast of Tabernacles. The crowd is welcoming a king with the gestures appropriate to a king, even if they do not understand the full nature of his kingship. Matthew's crowd is large — "most of the crowd" — and the welcome is public and unmistakable. This is the royal entry that the whole ministry of chapters 1-20 has been moving toward.

One detail here has been mocked more than almost any other in Matthew, and it deserves a straight answer. Matthew mentions two animals — the donkey and her colt — where Mark, Luke, and John mention only the colt Jesus rode; and he writes that they put their cloaks "on them, and he sat on them." Did Jesus, the scoffers ask, ride two animals at once, straddling both? And did Matthew, misreading the Hebrew poetry of Zechariah 9:9 (which names "a donkey" and "a colt" in a single parallel line, the Hebrew way of saying one animal twice), clumsily invent a second beast? Neither charge holds. There really were two animals, and Matthew, an eyewitness, simply notices what the others pass over: the colt had never been ridden (Mark 11:2), and an unbroken colt is far steadier with its mother walking beside it — exactly the arrangement a careful observer would recall. As for "he sat on them," the nearest plural is the cloaks: they threw their garments over both animals, and he sat on the garments. Matthew rode nothing into confusion. And far from misunderstanding the parallelism, Matthew — a Jew steeped in the Scriptures — saw the real scene match even the doubled wording of the prophet, and rejoiced to record it. The eye that notices the mother donkey is not the eye of a careless writer but of a man who was there.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting, "Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!" And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred up, saying, "Who is this?" And the crowds said, "This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hosanna is not a cheer, though it has become one. It is hoshia-na, and it means save now — an imperative addressed to God, a cry for help. The crowd on that road was not applauding. It was praying, at the top of its voice, in the words of the psalm every pilgrim sang coming up to the feast: Save us, we pray, O LORD… Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD (Ps 118:25-26).

And they were praying the right prayer with the wrong emergency in mind. Ask that crowd what they wanted saving from and they would have said Rome — the garrison in the Antonia, the taxes, the eagles on the standards, the whole humiliation of being occupied in the land God gave them. It was a real grievance and he did nothing about it. He had come to deal with something they had not thought to mention, and the rescue they asked for was smaller than the one he was carrying up that hill. They were more right than they knew and less right than they thought, which is the usual condition of anybody praying.

Now watch which psalm it is, because Matthew is building something. The crowd shouts Psalm 118:26 on the way into the city. Before the chapter is over Jesus will stand in the temple and quote Psalm 118:22 at the men who run it: the stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (v. 42). Two verses of one psalm, four verses apart on the page — and between them, in the events, lies the rejection, the trial and the cross. The pilgrims sang the welcome. The Lord supplied the verse about what would be done with him.

The whole city was stirred up — and the verb is eseisthe, from the root that gives us seismic. The city quaked. Matthew has used that root before and will use it twice more, and the sequence is worth having: Jerusalem shakes when he enters it; the earth shakes when he dies and the curtain tears (27:51); the ground shakes again at dawn on the third day when the stone is rolled back (28:2). Three tremors, and the city's is the only one caused by people.

The question it shakes out is the right one — Who is this? — and the answer the crowd gives is true and much too small: the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee. It is exactly the answer the villages had been giving all along (16:14), and it is the honour of a great category that is still the wrong one. Note too what they have handed his enemies without meaning to: Nazareth, Galilee. The provincial address will be used against him.

One correction, because it is preached almost every year and it is not accurate. It is commonly said that the same crowd which shouted Hosanna on Sunday shouted Crucify on Friday, and the sermon usually turns on how fickle people are. The text will not support it. These are pilgrims coming up the Jericho road with him, largely Galileans who had followed him for months. The crowd at the trial is a different gathering altogether — assembled early in the morning inside the city, at the praetorium, and Matthew tells us plainly that the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas (27:20). The truth is less tidy than the sermon and worse: it was not that everyone turned. It was that when it mattered, the people who had cheered him were nowhere to be found, and a smaller crowd that had been worked on all night was.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who sold and bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. He said to them, "It is written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer,' but you make it a den of robbers." And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The temple cleansing follows immediately — the entry and the cleansing are the same act of messianic authority extended into the holy place. The money-changers converted Roman coins (bearing the emperor's image, prohibited in temple precincts) to acceptable currency; the dove-sellers provided the offering of the poor. Both services were legitimate; their location in the court of the Gentiles was the problem. Jesus drives out the commerce to restore the space to prayer.

Isaiah 56:7 promises that the temple will be "a house of prayer for all peoples" — including the Gentiles, for whom the outer court was the only available space. Jeremiah 7:11 condemns those who use the temple as a refuge for injustice — a "den of robbers" who retreat to religious performance while exploiting the vulnerable. Jesus applies both texts simultaneously: the court has been turned from prayer-space into market-space, and the market has displaced the Gentiles and the poor who needed it for prayer. Then immediately the blind and lame come to Jesus in the temple and are healed — the space is restored to its purpose: prayer and healing. What the temple was meant to be, Jesus makes it be, in his own person. And that last phrase is worth slowing down over, because it is where this scene is finally pointing. Ask what the temple was actually for, and three answers come back: it was the place where God dwelt among his people, the place where sacrifice was offered for sin, and the place through which prayer went up. Now look at the man standing in the middle of the wreckage of the money tables. He is Immanuel, God with us, so the dwelling is no longer a building (1:23). He is days away from offering the sacrifice that will end the need for every other one. And he is the mediator through whom prayer now reaches the Father (John 14:13-14). John records him saying it outright after a cleansing like this one: destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up — and John adds, "he was speaking about the temple of his body" (John 2:19-21).

So this is not merely a reformer tidying up an institution he intends to keep. It is the reality walking into the shadow and standing there. Within a lifetime the building would be rubble, in AD 70, and the loss — devastating as it was — took nothing away from the people of God that they had not already been given in Christ. The type had handed everything over to the antitype. The house of prayer for all nations turned out to be a Person, and the Gentiles those traders had crowded out would find room in him.

A word is owed on something just slipped past above. John records a temple cleansing too — the tables overturned, the cord of whips, the same words about his body as the temple — but he places it at the very beginning of Jesus's ministry, three years before this one (John 2:13-22), while Matthew, Mark and Luke all place it in the last week. So which is it: did one of them move it? There are two honest answers, and Christians who take Scripture with equal seriousness hold both. Some say there was one cleansing, and John has arranged his Gospel by theme rather than by calendar, putting it early because he wants the temple question raised at the outset. That is not a charge against him; John openly organises his material around signs and feasts rather than a diary. But the simpler answer is that it happened twice, and the details rather suggest it. In John it is oxen and sheep and a whip of cords; here it is the dove-sellers and the money-changers. In John the leaders ask for a sign and get the saying about the temple of his body; here they ask by what authority he acts and get the parable of the tenants. Even the charge at his trial preserves a memory of the earlier saying (26:61) — which is easiest to explain if the words were spoken years before and remembered against him.

And there is nothing strange in the repetition. The trade grew back, as trades do; what a man clears out at the start of three years of ministry will be standing again by the end. Nor is it surprising that Jesus, who came to this temple as its Lord, should have confronted it both when he began and when he finished — an opening statement and a closing verdict, with everything in between as the argument. Either way, and this is the point to carry off, nothing hangs on the answer that touches the meaning of what he did here. The court of the Gentiles had been turned into a market, and the Lord of the house came in and said so.

One further word is owed here, because no passage in the Gospels is quoted more often to justify behaviour. Jesus flipped the tables has become the standing defence of the furious tweet, the walk-out, the scorching email, the man who is rude to his elders and calls it prophetic. So it is worth asking what this scene actually licenses.

Notice first who is acting and in whose house. The whole force of the passage is that the owner has arrived — the Lord of the temple, exercising an authority that belongs to him and to nobody else, over abuses in his own courts. This is not a worshipper losing his temper about the state of the church. It is the proprietor closing a market that had set itself up in his front room. Whatever else may be drawn from it, the one thing it is not is a general permission for angry men to act like the owner.

Notice next what the anger is about. Not a slight to himself. He had been mocked, doubted and plotted against for three chapters without overturning anything. What moves him here is that the poor were being fleeced and the Gentiles — the only people with nowhere else to pray — had been crowded out of the one court that was theirs. His anger runs entirely on behalf of other people, and specifically the ones with least power in the building. That is a searching test. Anger that flares when I am disrespected and stays seated when the weak are exploited is not this anger, whatever it calls itself.

And notice what he does immediately afterwards, because Matthew joins the two without a pause: the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them. The tables go over and the sick come in. If a man's zeal clears a space and nothing tender happens in it, he has done half the scene and the wrong half. (What to do when your own anger rises, and how to tell the holy kind from the other, is set out at 5:21-22.)

verseByVerse.quote: But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children crying out in the temple, "Hosanna to the Son of David!" they were indignant and said to him, "Do you hear what these are saying?" And Jesus said to them, "Yes; have you never read, 'Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Picture where this is happening. Not on the road outside, where a crowd can be dismissed as pilgrims who have got over-excited, but inside the temple courts — the one place on earth where the chief priests were unquestionably in charge — and the noise is coming from children. They have picked up what they heard on the road that morning and are running about the courts of the sanctuary shouting a messianic title at a man who has just overturned the furniture.

Notice precisely what the leaders object to. Not the noise. They do not say, keep them quiet; they say, do you hear what these are saying? The content is the offence. Children are calling him Son of David in the temple and he is not correcting them, and their indignation is at his silence as much as at the words.

What had produced the shouting was, Matthew says, the wonderful things that he did — thaumasia, a word that appears nowhere else in the New Testament and which the Greek Old Testament keeps for the works of God. And here is the whole tragedy of the scene in one sentence: the priests saw the same wonderful things. They watched the blind receive sight in their own courts. The identical evidence produced worship in the children and indignation in the men trained to interpret it.

His answer is a quotation, and it is sharper than it looks. Psalm 8:2, in the Greek version, reads out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise — the Hebrew has a word closer to strength or a bulwark, and the Greek translators rendered the sense of it as praise; either way the point stands, that God establishes something formidable out of the smallest voices there are. But go and read the rest of the line, which he does not need to say aloud to men who knew the psalter by heart. It runs: you have prepared praise, because of your foes, to still the enemy and the avenger. He has just told the chief priests, by quotation, which part of the psalm they are standing in.

Matthew has been building this contrast for ten chapters. It is the same Lord who prayed, I thank you, Father, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children (11:25), and who set a child in the middle of a circle of men arguing about greatness (18:2). Guard it from becoming a sneer at learning: the problem with these men was never that they had studied. It was that their study had become the property of their position, so that a conclusion which would cost them the position had become, quite literally, unthinkable. A child had nothing to lose by saying Son of David out loud.

And have you never read — the question he keeps putting to the professional readers of Scripture (12:3, 12:5, 19:4, here, 21:42, 22:31). It never means they are ignorant of the text. It means they can recite it and have arranged not to be governed by it, which is a condition available to anyone who has owned a Bible for a long time.

verseByVerse.quote: And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany and lodged there. In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And leaving them, he went out of the city. It is the evening of the day he entered Jerusalem as her king, to a shouting crowd, and the question worth asking is where the King of Israel slept that night. Not in the palace. Not in a room in the temple precincts, though he had spent the afternoon acting as the owner of the place. He walked two miles back over the shoulder of the Mount of Olives, in the dark, to a village, and lodged there — at Bethany, which is where Martha and Mary and the brother he had raised from the dead lived. The city that had quaked at his arrival in the morning did not offer him a bed at night.

He does this every night of that week, and it is both prudent and deliberate. Jerusalem at Passover was crammed and watched, the leadership was already looking for a way to take him quietly, and a man who sleeps outside the walls is harder to arrest in the dark. But it is more than tactics. He is not living in the city he came to save. He comes in each morning to teach and goes out each evening, and the last night he spends anywhere near it he will spend in a garden on that same hillside, awake.

Then a small clause that most readers step over: he became hungry. It is early morning, he has walked two miles uphill on an empty stomach, and Matthew tells us so.

Do not hurry past it. This is the man who had multiplied loaves for five thousand people and again for four thousand, and who could have turned any stone on that road into bread and had already declined to do so once, in a desert, when he was a great deal hungrier (4:2-4). The power was never absent; it simply was not for him. Hunger of that kind is not a detail the Gospels are embarrassed by — it is the incarnation showing through the narrative at an ordinary hour on an ordinary road. He got tired. He slept in the stern of a boat. He wept at a graveside. He was hungry on the way to work.

And it matters for what comes next, because it is the hunger that takes him over to the fig tree. The sign about Israel's fruitlessness does not begin as a lesson looking for an illustration. It begins with a hungry man walking toward a tree that looked, from the road, as though it had something on it.

verseByVerse.quote: And seeing a fig tree by the wayside, he went to it and found nothing on it but leaves only. And he said to it, "May no fruit ever come from you again!" And the fig tree withered at once. When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, "How did the fig tree wither at once?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fig trees in Palestine produce small preliminary fruit before or alongside the leaves — a tree in full leaf that has no fruit at all is abnormal. The fig tree's leaves promised what it could not deliver. Jesus' curse of the tree is a prophetic sign-act: Israel, like the fig tree, has had all the outward signs of the kingdom (leaves — temple, priesthood, Torah, prayer) while bearing no fruit of genuine repentance and faith. The immediate withering is the visible judgment on a profession without reality. The disciples' astonishment is at the speed and completeness of the withering — "at once." The cursing of the fig tree is one of the most uncomfortable miracles in the Gospel, but its discomfort is its point: fruitlessness has consequences.

That phrase "at once" needs a note for anyone reading Mark alongside. Matthew has the tree wither immediately and the disciples marvel on the spot; Mark has Jesus curse it on the way in, spend the day in the temple, and the disciples notice it withered "in the morning" the next day (Mark 11:12-14, 20-21). It is the compression we have met before (cf. 9:18): Matthew tells the fig tree as one complete episode rather than splitting it across two days, because his interest is the sign and not the schedule. And the two statements do not actually collide — Matthew says when the tree died, Mark says when the disciples saw it. A tree struck at the root in the morning is dead from that moment, whatever hour the men walking past happen to look up and notice the leaves have gone. Matthew gives you the event; Mark gives you the discovery.

But the question a reader actually brings to this passage has not been asked yet, and it should be, because it is the obvious one. Why curse a tree? It is the only destructive miracle in the Gospels, and on the face of it the scene is unattractive: a hungry man does not find breakfast and kills the tree. Anyone who has felt uneasy here is reading attentively.

The answer is that this is not a miracle of temper but a prophet's sign-act, and Israel had seen the genre for centuries. Jeremiah bought a clay jar, took the elders to the valley and smashed it in front of them (Jer 19). Ezekiel lay on his side for months beside a brick with the city scratched on it (Ezek 4). Ahijah tore a new cloak into twelve pieces and handed ten of them to Jeroboam (1 Kgs 11:30-31). The prophets acted their message when words had stopped landing, and the acting was the sermon. So Jesus, on the morning after clearing the temple and the morning before being asked by what authority he did it, does to a tree exactly what he is about to say concerning the house on the hill.

And notice where the mercy is in the choice, because it is worth saying plainly: in a life in which he raised the dead, fed thousands, healed everyone who came and refused every opportunity to harm a living soul, the one thing he ever destroyed was a plant. He could have made the same point on the temple itself. He made it on a tree by the roadside where nobody was hurt.

The fig had been the picture for Israel since the prophets — when I would gather them, declares the LORD, there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree (Jer 8:13); like the first fruit on the fig tree in its first season, I saw your fathers (Hos 9:10). Everyone standing on that road had the association ready.

And the specific charge is in the leaves, which is where the sharpness lies. A fig in that country puts out small green knobs of early fruit with or before the leaves; a tree in full leaf is making a claim about itself that can be checked from the road. This one was in full leaf out of season and had nothing at all. It was not a barren tree quietly failing. It was a tree advertising. That is why it stands over the temple courts he had walked out of the evening before, where the noise and the traffic and the sacrifices were at full volume and the poor were being fleeced in the one court the Gentiles had.

Which needs a guard for the reader it will frighten, and it will frighten the wrong reader first — the Christian who reads no fruit, and it withered and immediately audits himself and finds very little. Read what was actually condemned. Not smallness; not slowness; not a poor year. The tree was judged for displaying what it did not have. That is a charge against pretence, not against weakness, and the same Gospel has already told you how this Lord handles the genuinely feeble: a bruised reed he will not break, and a smouldering wick he will not quench (12:20). He is ferocious with advertising and unfailingly gentle with frailty, and it is worth knowing which of the two you are before applying this verse.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, "Truly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what has been done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, 'Be taken up and thrown into the sea,' it will happen. And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples ask a question about mechanics — how did the fig tree wither at once? — and get an answer about their own future. That is worth noticing before anything else. They wanted to know how it was done. He tells them what they will be doing.

This mountain. Where is he standing? On the road from Bethany, which crosses the Mount of Olives, with the temple mount in view across the Kidron valley. Both candidates for this mountain are within sight of his outstretched arm, and both carry freight. The Mount of Olives is the hill Zechariah says will be split in two on the day of the LORD (Zech 14:4). The temple mount is the thing the withered tree has just been a parable about. We are not told which he meant, and the ambiguity may be the point: the immovable object in view is a religious system that will shortly be rubble, and he is telling twelve fishermen and tax-collectors that obstacles of that size can be told to move.

The guard on nothing will be impossible was set out where it first appears, at 17:20, and it is not repeated here: faith is not a force that bends God toward us, the size he names is a mustard seed rather than a mountain, and the Lord of perfect faith prayed in a garden for a cup to pass and it did not pass. What this passage adds is the object. Notice what these men are promised authority over. Not fig trees — none of them ever withers anything. Not weather, not illness on demand, not their own circumstances arranged to preference. Look at what they actually moved: within a generation, twelve provincial nobodies with no money, no standing, no army and no education to speak of had put this message into every major city between Jerusalem and Rome, against the settled opposition of both the Sanhedrin and the Empire, and most of them were executed for it and it did not slow down. That is the mountain. It went into the sea.

And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith. Read that clause where Matthew put it — attached to mountain-moving kingdom work, in the temple week, spoken to men about to be sent out. It is not a promise that trust is a mechanism for obtaining things. It is the assurance that the work he is about to hand them will never fail for want of supply, and that they may ask accordingly and enormously.

Which turns the passage on the reader with an uncomfortable question, and it is not the question we usually bring to it. We come asking whether we have enough faith for what we want. The passage asks what we are asking for. Almost nothing in most Christians' praying would require God to move a mountain; a modest tidying of circumstances would cover it. These men were told to expect the impossible because they had been given something impossible to do.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–46 — Authority Questioned: Three Parables of Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chief priests and elders challenge Jesus's authority: by what authority do you do these things? Jesus answers with a counter-question about John's baptism that they refuse to answer, then tells three parables of judgment: the two sons (the one who refused then obeyed vs. the one who agreed but didn't), the wicked tenants who killed the vineyard owner's son, and the implied parable of the rejected cornerstone from Psalm 118. The parables systematically indict the religious leadership of Israel for rejecting God's messengers and the Son himself. The counter-question is not a diversion: John had already answered the authority question in public, so to ask whether John was from heaven is to hand it back in the one form they cannot answer safely. And the verdict between the parables is the sharpest sentence in the chapter — the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom ahead of them (vv. 31-32).
verseByVerse.theology: The authority question and Jesus's counter-question about John expose the leaders' bad faith: they do not want to know the source of Jesus's authority; they want to discredit him publicly. Their refusal to answer John's question (whether from heaven or from men) reveals that they are governed by crowd opinion rather than truth-seeking. Jesus therefore refuses to answer them directly — but he answers indirectly and devastatingly through the three parables. The wicked tenants is the most explicit: they will kill the son, and the vineyard will be given to others who will produce its fruits. Two details carry the tenants parable. Jesus quotes Isaiah's Song of the Vineyard almost item for item (Isa 5:1-2) and then changes it: in Isaiah the vine is at fault, here the vine is fine and the tenants are the problem — the indictment is narrowed off the nation and onto its leaders. And the tenants do not kill the son by mistake. This is the heir — recognition is the motive, which is why unbelief in this chapter is never a shortage of information. Note also 2 Chr 36:15-16, which is this parable written four centuries early: God sent persistently by his messengers, and they kept mocking them, until there was no remedy.
verseByVerse.examples: The rejected cornerstone from Psalm 118:22 — the same psalm shouted at the triumphal entry — completes the argument. The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; what the religious establishment rejects, God establishes as the foundation of his kingdom. The chief priests and Pharisees understood that he was speaking about them — and they wanted to arrest him but feared the crowds. The rejection is comprehensive; the judgment is announced; the crowds are the only restraint preventing its immediate human execution. Two applications. Verse 43's taken away from you is about tenancy, not race — the vineyard is re-let, and the people it was first let to were Jews to a man (see the verse-by-verse on vv. 43-44). And verse 45 is the most sobering sentence here for anyone who reads the Bible well: they perceived that he was speaking about them. The parables landed perfectly, were understood completely, and produced not repentance but an arrest plan. Understanding the text is not the goal, and it is possible to be an excellent reader of Scripture and be destroyed by what you have correctly understood.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching, and said, "By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?" Jesus answered them, "I also will ask you one question, and if you tell me the answer, then I also will tell you by what authority I do these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is not heckling. The chief priests and the elders of the people is the language of an official delegation from the Sanhedrin, and the question they put is the question that body existed to ask. Israel's law required someone to test a man who spoke and acted as a prophet — by what authority, and who gave it (Deut 13:1-5; 18:20-22). They are, on the face of it, doing their job, in the right place, with the right words.

And note what these things covers. In the last twenty-four hours he has ridden into the city arranged like a coronation, cleared the commercial concessions out of the temple court by force, healed in the sanctuary, and stood by while children shouted a messianic title at him and did not tell them to stop. Every one of those is an act of ownership. He has spent a day behaving like the proprietor of the building they administer, and now the administrators have come to ask on what basis.

His reply is a counter-question, and it should not be read as a dodge. Answering a question with a question was ordinary rabbinic procedure, not evasion, and he attaches a promise to it: answer mine and I will answer yours. He is offering them a genuine transaction.

But the counter-question is doing something better than buying time, and this is the part usually missed. He asks about John's baptism — and John is the one man in Israel who had already answered their question publicly. John had pointed at him in front of crowds and said, behold the Lamb of God; John had baptised him and heard the voice from heaven over him (3:16-17); John had said he was not worthy to carry his sandals. So the question was John from heaven or from men? is not a diversion from the authority question. It is the authority question, handed back to them in the one form they cannot answer without convicting themselves. If John was from heaven, they have their answer already and have been refusing it for two years.

There is a principle in that worth carrying out of the temple. Christ does not always answer the question we put; he very often answers the question underneath it, or points at the evidence we have already declined to look at. A man who says he would believe if God would only make it clear is usually a man with something specific already in view that he has decided not to act on. The Lord's habit is to send him back there first.

verseByVerse.quote: The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?" And they discussed it among themselves, saying, "If we say, 'From heaven,' he will say to us, 'Why then did you not believe him?' But if we say, 'From man,' we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold John to be a prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What happens next is remarkable simply as a piece of reporting: Matthew takes us inside the huddle. They discussed it among themselves — and we are given the minutes of a private conversation among the most senior religious men in Israel, standing in the temple, deciding what to say about a prophet of God.

Read the minutes and notice what is missing. If we say from heaven, he will say, why then did you not believe him? But if we say from man, we are afraid of the crowd. That is the whole deliberation. Two options, each assessed purely for what it will cost. Not one syllable about whether John was in fact from heaven. The question of truth is not raised, not dismissed, not even avoided — it never occurs to anyone in the room to bring it up.

That is the difference between a man who is wrong and a man who is corrupt. Being mistaken about John would have been forgivable and correctable. These men are not weighing evidence badly; they have stopped weighing evidence. They are running a different calculation altogether, and running it competently.

And see what they were afraid of. We are afraid of the crowd. These are men who could summon the temple guard, who would shortly arrest a man at night and hold an irregular trial before dawn, who had the standing to get a Roman governor out of bed. They feared the opinion of ordinary people in the street, and the fear governed them. Twenty-one verses later Matthew tells us the same thing again, in almost the same words: they wanted to arrest him and did not, because they feared the crowds (v. 46). The men in charge of Israel's conscience were taking their instructions from Israel's mood.

There is a test in this that most of us fail more quietly than they did. It is not whether you have ever told a lie. It is whether you can recognise the moment when the question in your mind has silently changed from what is true here to what will this cost me to say. It happens in a lunchroom when somebody says something about Christians and you decide, in about a second and a half, that this is not the moment. It happens when a group is settling on a view of a person you know to be unfair. It happens in families over things that were done years ago. The calculation is usually so fast that it does not feel like a decision at all, and that is exactly what these men would have said.

One guard, because the passage is not a call to blurt. Prudence is not cowardice, and Jesus himself told his followers to be as wise as serpents while being harmless as doves (10:16); there are things not to say yet, and moments badly chosen. The difference is what sits in the driving seat. Wisdom asks how and when to say the true thing. What is happening in this huddle is not wisdom deciding the timing. It is safety deciding the content.

verseByVerse.quote: So they answered Jesus, "We do not know." And he said to them, "Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. What do you think? A man had two sons. And he went to the first and said, 'Son, go and work in the vineyard today.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
We do not know. Three words, and they are false, and everyone present knows they are false.

Weigh who is saying them. These are the men whose entire office is to know — to rule on what is clean and unclean, true and false, prophetic and fraudulent; men who had spent their lives in the study of exactly this question and held their positions because they were presumed competent to answer it. And the subject is not obscure. John the Baptist had emptied the towns; Matthew says Jerusalem and all Judea went out to him (3:5). Half the country had an opinion about John. The official custodians of Israel's faith, standing in the temple, publicly declare that they have not been able to form one.

It is a lie, and it is also a confession. What they are actually saying is: we have an answer and we cannot afford it. And that is a more dangerous condition than ignorance, because ignorance can be cured by information and this cannot be cured by anything except repentance.

So Jesus keeps his word exactly. Neither will I tell you. He does not scold them and he does not argue; he simply declines, and the declining is itself the judgment. There is such a thing as forfeiting an answer. To a man who will not act on what he already has, more light is not a kindness — it is only more to be answerable for, which is why Jesus elsewhere says that to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away (13:12).

That has a quiet application to a very common modern position. People often say, in complete sincerity, that they would believe if the evidence were clearer — that they are waiting for something more before they commit. It is worth putting to such a person, gently, the question this passage puts: what would you do if it were clear? Because if the honest answer is that very little would change, then the difficulty was probably never the evidence. These men had watched a prophet, and then watched the wonderful things in their own courts, and their problem was not a shortage of data.

And then, without a pause, he begins to tell them a story. What do you think? A man had two sons. They have refused to answer his question; he will not answer theirs. But he has not finished with them, and what follows is not a rebuke. It is three parables in succession, each one aimed at them, each one still giving them a way to see themselves and turn. He is being more patient than they deserve, and considerably more patient than they will be with him.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he answered, 'I will not,' but afterward he changed his mind and went. And he went to the other son and said the same. And he answered, 'I go, sir,' but did not go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two sons represent two responses to the Father's call. The first refuses outright — insolent, disrespectful — then repents and goes. The second says the right words — "I go, sir" (kyrie — Lord!) — with apparent respect, and does not go. The contrast is between profession and performance, between religious compliance and genuine obedience. The second son's "I go, sir" is the language of the Pharisees who say "Lord, Lord" (7:21) — the right words without the transformed will that produces action. The first son's repentance and going — however rough the initial response — is genuine obedience. God values the repentance that actually changes direction over the profession that leaves everything unchanged.

Jesus asks the question himself — which of the two did the will of his father? — so it is plainly meant to be answered by the reader and not only by the men in front of him. Which son am I?

Most people who read a commentary are in danger of being the second one, and it is worth being exact about why. The second son does not refuse. He is not rude, not rebellious, not absent from the conversation. He says the right thing, in the right tone, using the right title — I go, sir — and everyone within earshot would have thought well of him. His failure is entirely invisible until you go and look at the vineyard. That is the shape of a great deal of respectable Christianity: the answer given years ago at a conversion, a confirmation, a moment of dedication; the language still fluent; the vineyard unvisited.

Notice too that the first son is not held up as a model of manner. He was insolent, and Jesus does not pretend otherwise. What commends him is not his honesty about his reluctance — plenty of people are candidly disobedient and stay that way — but that he changed his mind and went. The parable has no interest in which son felt better about himself. It asks only who ended up in the field.

So take it as a question with a date on it. Not did I once say yes, but: since the last time I said yes to God about something specific, have I actually gone? There is usually one thing in view — a conversation to have, a debt to repay, a habit to end, a person to forgive, money to give, a reconciliation to attempt. You will know it when you read this, because it is the thing that came to mind before the sentence finished.

And take the gospel that is folded into it. The first son's story is the better news of the two, because it means a bad start is not a settled verdict. Nothing prevents a man who said no this morning from being in the vineyard by the afternoon — and the father, in this parable, does not require an apology first. He requires a son in the field. If you have been the second son for twenty years, the door out of that is not despair or a better speech; it is a change of direction today, in one thing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Which of the two did the will of his father?" They said, "The first." Jesus said to them, "Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you. For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. And even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds and believe him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They answer his question correctly — the first — and in doing so pass sentence on themselves, which is the second time in this chapter he has arranged for that (see v. 41). The parable was too plain to get wrong and too small to feel dangerous. Then he tells them what they have just agreed to.

The tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you. Hear it as the men in front of him heard it. Tax collectors were not merely disliked; they were collaborators who bought the right to extract Rome's money from their own neighbours and kept the surplus, they were reckoned ritually unclean, and their testimony was worthless in a Jewish court. Prostitutes were beyond the edge of respectable society altogether, and a good many of them were there because a man had discarded them or hunger had. Those are the two categories Jesus names, in the temple, to the highest religious authorities in the nation, and he puts them in front.

Now guard the sentence, because it says something more merciful than it is usually made to say. The verb is proagousin — they go before you — and it is present tense. He does not say the tax collectors go in and you stay out. He says they are going in ahead of you, which is a statement about the order of a queue, and a queue is a thing you can still be standing in. Even here, at the sharpest moment of the confrontation, the door is not shut in their faces. It is being held open while they are told, with some force, who is walking through it first.

Then the charge, and it is precise: John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him. Not, you did not like him. Not, you disagreed with his methods. You did not believe him — which is why the two sons parable was the right one, because the issue is never eloquence or manner but whether a man goes to the vineyard.

And there is a verb here that ties the parable to its targets with a knot they could not have missed. The first son, in verse 29, changed his mind and went — metamelētheis. In verse 32 Jesus says of them: even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds — ou metemelēthēte. The same word, four verses apart, first describing the son who was commended and then, in the negative, describing the men standing in front of him. He has told a story, made them praise its hero, and then handed them the hero's verb with a not in front of it.

Take the last clause slowly, because it names the hardest condition in the chapter: even when you saw it. They watched it happen. They saw the collaborators pay money back and the ruined women stand in the Jordan and come up new, and it moved them not at all. There is a settled state in which fresh evidence has stopped functioning as evidence — where the very thing that ought to break a man simply confirms him. It is not reached by one bad decision. It is reached by a long series of moments in which the honest answer was known and not acted on, which is precisely what the previous six verses have shown us these men doing in a huddle.

But hold the whole sentence together and it is astonishing rather than merely severe. He is telling the worst news any religious man could hear, and the news is that the door is open to the very people he would have crossed the street to avoid. A tax collector who repented at John's preaching last spring is further into the kingdom of God than the high priest, and there is nothing in the sentence to stop the high priest joining him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear another parable. There was a master of a house who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower and leased it to tenants and went into a far country. When the season for fruit came, he sent his servants to the tenants to get his fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He begins with a quotation, and every man listening recognised it inside five words. A vineyard… a fence around it… a winepress in it… a tower — that is Isaiah's Song of the Vineyard, almost item for item (Isa 5:1-2), and Isaiah had told them who the vineyard was: the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel (Isa 5:7). So the chief priests knew the ending before the story had properly begun. Isaiah's song finishes with the hedge taken away and the vineyard trampled. They stood there and let him tell it.

But he changes it, and the change is the whole point of the parable. In Isaiah the fault is in the vine: the owner looked for grapes and it yielded wild ones. Here the vine is not blamed at all. The vineyard is fine; the crop is coming; what has gone wrong is the tenants. Jesus has taken the best-known indictment of the nation in the prophets and narrowed it — off the people and onto the men who were given charge of them. That is a far more dangerous parable to tell in the temple than Isaiah's, and it is also, if you are an ordinary Israelite in that crowd, considerably more merciful.

The details are not decoration. A fence to keep out animals, a winepress cut into the rock so the harvest could be processed on site, a tower for the watchman to sleep in through the vintage — this is a fully equipped estate, and the labour is all done before the tenants arrive. They inherit a going concern they did not build. Every advantage they enjoy came in the hands of the man they are about to rob.

The arrangement itself was ordinary and resented. Absentee landlords holding Galilean estates and leasing them to tenant farmers for a share of the crop were a live social grievance, and Jesus is using it deliberately: the crowd's instinctive sympathy is with the tenants, right up to the moment the tenants start killing people. It is the same trick as the two sons — get the audience to take a side, then show them which side they took.

And notice what the owner sends for. Not rent in coin. His fruit — the thing the vineyard exists to produce. He is not extracting a fee from an arrangement; he is asking a vineyard to be a vineyard. That is the standing question this chapter keeps putting, to the fig tree in full leaf, to the temple full of noise, and to the men in charge of both: not whether the operation is busy, but whether anything is growing on it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the tenants took his servants and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. Again he sent other servants, more than the first. And they did the same to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three verbs and no explanation: they beat one, killed another, stoned another. The escalation is quick and the parable does not slow down for it, because the people listening did not need it explained. They knew what happened to men sent by God to speak to Israel.

The record is specific enough to name. Jeremiah was beaten and put in the stocks by the chief officer of the temple, and later dropped into a cistern to sink in the mud (Jer 20:2; 38:6). Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest was stoned to death in the court of the house of the LORD by order of the king, and died saying may the LORD see and avenge (2 Chr 24:20-21) — a killing Jesus will name explicitly two chapters later (23:35). Uriah the son of Shemaiah prophesied, fled to Egypt, was extradited and cut down with a sword (Jer 26:20-23). This is not a parable reaching for hyperbole. It is a summary.

And the whole of it had already been written down in one sentence in Israel's own history, at the end of Chronicles, describing the years before the exile: The LORD, the God of their fathers, sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place. But they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words and scoffing at his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD rose against his people, until there was no remedy (2 Chr 36:15-16). That verse is this parable, written four hundred years before it was told.

Which puts the emphasis where the parable puts it, and it is not on the violence. It is on the sending. Again he sent other servants, more than the first. Read that as a landlord and it is absurd — a man whose employees are being beaten and killed does not respond by dispatching a larger party unarmed. Read it as history and it is the patience of God across five centuries: after Elijah, Amos; after Amos, Hosea; after Hosea, Isaiah, Micah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and on, each one sent into a country with a record of what it did to the last one.

Hold the two halves of that together honestly, because both are in the text and each without the other is a distortion. The patience is real and it is nearly unbelievable; God keeps sending long past the point where any reasonable owner would send lawyers instead. And the Chronicler's last clause is also real: until there was no remedy. Patience is not indifference and it is not permanent, and a man who reads the long delay as evidence that nothing is ever going to be said has misread the one thing the parable is about to do next — because after all the servants, there is one more figure standing at the estate gate.

verseByVerse.quote: "Finally he sent his son to them, saying, 'They will respect my son.' But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally he sent his son. The word sits there like a door closing. There is nothing after this; the owner has one more person to send and then the sending is over, and everyone listening in that court could feel the story running out of servants.

They will respect my son is a sentence that puzzles careful readers, and it should be handled honestly rather than hurried past. Does God not know what they will do? He does — this is the same afternoon on which Jesus has already told his disciples in detail that he will be handed over, mocked and crucified. But this is a parable, and it is speaking the way a father speaks. It is not a report on the limits of divine foreknowledge; it is a device to make you feel the size of what is about to be done. The owner sends his boy to men who have killed his staff, and the sentence lets you hear him hoping.

Then the tenants' reasoning, and it is the most frightening line in the parable: This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.

Read it twice. They do not kill him because they mistake him for someone else. They kill him because they know exactly who he is. Recognition is the motive. If he had been another servant they would have beaten him and sent him back; it is precisely his identity as the son that makes the murder worth committing, because with the heir gone the estate is theirs to keep. Jesus is telling the men who will be sitting on his trial that they will not condemn him out of ignorance.

That is worth stating plainly because it corrects a comfortable idea about sin. We prefer to think of unbelief as a failure of information — if people only understood, if the case were made better, if the evidence were clearer. Sometimes it is. But this parable, and this chapter, and the huddle in verses 25 to 27, all say that the deepest form of the thing is not confusion at all. It is a clear-eyed calculation that this man's rightful claim is incompatible with keeping what I have, and a decision to keep it. The tenants' problem was never that they did not know whose vineyard it was. It was that they did.

And the calculation is exactly the one Matthew will show us being made for real. Within days the chief priests and the elders gather in the palace of the high priest and take counsel together in order to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him (26:3-4). The parable was not a warning about something that might happen. They walked out of the temple and did it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Note the order, because it is odd and deliberate: they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. Any ordinary account of a murder would have it the other way round — kill the man, then dispose of the body. Here he is put outside first and killed outside. Matthew's readers, telling this story after the event, knew why the sequence mattered. He was condemned inside the city and executed outside its wall, on a rubbish hill by a road, deliberately beyond the boundary of the holy place. The writer to the Hebrews makes exactly that point about exactly that detail: Jesus also suffered outside the gate (Heb 13:12), the way the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp. The tenants threw the son over the wall to be rid of him, and in doing so put him precisely where the sacrifice belonged.

Then Jesus stops the story and asks them to finish it: when therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?

This is the second time in about fifteen minutes that he has invited these men to pass judgment on a case that is their own. He did it with the two sons — which of the two did the will of his father? — and they answered, correctly, and were told what they had answered. Now he does it again with a heavier case and lets them dictate the sentence. It is an old method and Israel's own scriptures record its most famous use, when a prophet told a king a story about a poor man's lamb and the king, in a fury, pronounced sentence on himself.

But do not mistake what the method is for. It is not a trap in the sense of a snare set to destroy a man; it is a trap in the sense of a mirror set where he cannot avoid it. Everything in this chapter has been an attempt to get these men to see themselves while there is still time — a counter-question about John, a parable about two sons, and now a story in which they are asked to say out loud what such tenants deserve. He is not manoeuvring them toward the sentence. He is manoeuvring them toward recognition, which is the only thing that could have saved them.

And there is a question in it for anyone who reads Scripture regularly, because the danger it exposes is not confined to first-century Jerusalem. It is entirely possible to read a passage with real attention, form a confident judgment about the people in it, and never once notice that the judgment applies to the reader. These men were not bad at listening. They understood the parable perfectly — Matthew says so in verse 45. They simply assumed, until the last possible second, that it was about somebody else.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "He will put those wretches to a miserable death and let out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons." Jesus said to them, "Have you never read in the Scriptures: 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They answer without hesitating, and the vehemence gives them away: he will put those wretches to a miserable death. In Greek it is a hard little piece of wordplay — kakous kakos, bad men badly — the sort of phrase a man produces when he is enjoying the indignation. They have no difficulty at all seeing that such tenants deserve destruction and that the vineyard should go to others who will hand over the fruit. It is, word for word, the verdict Jesus is about to pronounce on them.

Have you never read in the Scriptures? — the question again, to the men who read them for a living (see on v. 16). And what he quotes is Psalm 118, which is where this whole chapter began. The pilgrims coming down the hill four days earlier had been shouting verse 26 of that psalm: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD. Now, standing in the temple with the men who run it, he quotes verse 22: The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. Two verses of one psalm, a few lines apart on the scroll — and between them, in the events of that week, lies everything: the welcome, the refusal, the trial, the cross and the empty tomb. The crowd sang the arrival. He supplied the verse about what would be done with him when he got there.

The image is chosen with some precision. The builders — that is these men. They were the professionals; assessing stone was the whole of their competence; their standing in Israel rested on being the ones who could tell what belonged in the building and what should be thrown off the site. And the one block they inspected and discarded turned out to be the stone the entire structure would rest on. It is not an accusation of wickedness in that line so much as of catastrophic professional failure: they were experts, they examined him, and they got it exactly wrong.

Then the clause that turns the whole thing from tragedy into something else: this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes. Not, this happened despite the Lord's plan. Not, God salvaged something from a disaster. The rejection itself is the Lord's doing. The builders threw the stone off the site and were, in the very act, laying the foundation of a building they had no idea was being put up. Nothing about that excuses them; the parable has just spent six verses establishing that they knew what they were doing and did it anyway. Both are true at once, and Peter will say both in one breath at Pentecost — delivered up by the definite plan of God, and crucified by lawless hands (Acts 2:23).

Sit with that for a moment, because it is the deepest comfort available to anyone whose life contains a rejection that cannot be undone. The stone did not become the cornerstone in spite of being thrown away. It became the cornerstone by being thrown away. That is not a principle that can be turned into a technique or promised over every sorrow, and it should not be offered cheaply to a person still bleeding. But it happened once, publicly, in the most important week in history, and it means that the worst thing men ever did was the thing God was doing. The word Jesus uses for it is marvellous — thaumaste, the same root as the wonderful things the children had been shouting about in verse 15. The children had it right. It is a wonder.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits. And the one who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits" — the most explicit announcement of Israel's leadership's judgment in Matthew. The "people" (ethnos) is the new community of the church, constituted not by ethnic Israel but by those who produce kingdom fruit — Jew and Gentile who receive the Son. The stone becomes a weapon: those who stumble over it are broken (a reference to Isa. 8:14-15, the stumbling stone); those on whom it falls are crushed (Dan. 2:34-35, 44-45, the stone that becomes a mountain). The stone of judgment is the same stone of salvation — the same Christ who is the cornerstone for believers is the crushing stone for those who reject him.

But "taken away from you" has been made to carry a weight it will not bear, and the reader should be told plainly what it does and does not say. It has been used, across some very dark centuries, to teach that God finished with the Jewish people that week and transferred their inheritance to the Gentiles — and worse has been done in the name of that idea than can be written here. Look first at who is being addressed. Not a nation in the abstract: the men standing in front of him, and Matthew tells us two verses later exactly who understood themselves to be meant — "the chief priests and the Pharisees… perceived that he was speaking about them" (v. 45). These are the tenants of the parable, the leadership entrusted with the vineyard, and it is the tenancy that is being revoked. The vineyard itself is not destroyed; it is re-let.

Then look at who received it. The people (ethnos) producing its fruit turned out, in the event, to be a community whose first thousands were Jews to a man — the apostles, the three thousand at Pentecost, Paul, and the whole first generation of the church. Whatever this verse announces, it plainly did not mean the exclusion of Jewish people, since Jewish people are the ones it was first handed to. And Paul, who knew this saying, asks the question in so many words and answers it: "Has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite" (Rom 11:1), before going on to the hope this commentary meets again at 23:39 — the day when Israel says "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord" and means it (Rom 11:25-26).

So the verse is not a transfer of favour from one race to another. It is a warning about tenancy, and the sharp end of it points at the reader before it points at anyone else. The vineyard is let to those who give the owner his fruit; and Paul, having said so, turned and warned the Gentile church in the same breath not to grow smug about it: "do not become proud, but fear" (Rom 11:20). A church that keeps the leaves and yields no fruit has been told, in this very chapter, what happens to trees like that.

verseByVerse.quote: When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he was speaking about them. And although they were seeking to arrest him, they feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They perceived that he was speaking about them. The parables worked. There was no failure of communication anywhere in this chapter: the counter-question landed, the two sons landed, the tenants landed, and these men understood every word of it. Jesus got through completely.

And that is the most sobering sentence in the chapter, because of what happened next. Perfect comprehension produced no repentance whatever. They saw themselves in the story, recognised the verdict, knew who the son was — and went out to arrange the murder. It is worth saying plainly to anyone who reads the Bible seriously: understanding the text is not the goal, and it is not even a reliable step toward the goal. It is possible to be an excellent reader of Scripture and to be destroyed by what you have correctly understood. These men would have passed any examination on the parable of the tenants.

They feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet. There it is a third time — the same fear that decided their answer about John (v. 26), the same fear that will keep them from arresting him in daylight during the feast (26:5). Everything these men do in Matthew's Gospel is governed by the mood of people they despise. They are not free men. They have the offices, the titles, the temple and the guard, and their diary is set by a crowd.

And notice the reason for the fear, because it is bitter: the crowds held him to be a prophet. That is the same estimate the city gave at the entry, when the whole place was shaken and asked who this was and the answer came back, the prophet from Nazareth (v. 11). It is true, and inadequate, and it is the only thing standing between Jesus and immediate arrest. A public opinion that had not yet got him right was, for the moment, the wall around him.

Which is precisely how thin the protection was, and both sides knew it. A crowd that thinks you are a prophet can be persuaded otherwise in four days by men who work at it, and Matthew tells us exactly when and how it was done: on the morning of the trial the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas (27:20). The restraint in verse 46 is not a reprieve. It is a delay, and the men who noted it were already working on it.

So the chapter closes where it opened, on the question of who this is — with a crowd that half knows, a leadership that fully knows and will not have it, and a King who has spent the whole day telling them the truth in stories while the arrest is being planned in the next room. He does not run and he does not soften it. He has three days of teaching left, and he will spend them in the same courts, with the same men listening.

21.theology: Christ as the true Temple. The temple cleansing in Matthew 21 points to one of the great themes of biblical theology: Jesus as the replacement and fulfilment of the temple. The temple was the place where God dwelt with his people, where sacrifice was made, where prayer ascended. Jesus embodies all three functions: he is Emmanuel — God dwelling with his people; he is the Lamb whose self-offering ends the sacrificial system; he is the mediator through whom prayer reaches the Father (John 14:13–14). John’s Gospel makes this explicit (“the temple he had spoken of was his body”, John 2:21). The destruction of the Jerusalem temple in AD 70 was the confirmation that the type had given way to the antitype.
21.examples:
Then: The crowds welcomed Jesus with genuine excitement and completely wrong expectations. They wanted a Maccabean king who would drive out Rome; they got a crucified Servant who would drive out death. The Palm Sunday crowd’s theology is a warning: it is possible to praise Jesus enthusiastically while fundamentally misunderstanding who he is and what he has come to do.

Now: The fig tree is the perennial warning against fruitless religion — maintaining the form of Christian practice without the substance of faith, repentance, love, and transformed life. The church with its worship services, theological conferences, and evangelical brands may be full of leaves. The question Jesus asks of every institution and every individual is the same: where is the fruit?

22.title: The Great Banquet and the Hard Questions
22.text: <sup>2</sup>The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son, <sup>3</sup>and sent his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. <sup>9</sup>Go therefore to the main roads and invite to the wedding feast as many as you find. <sup>10</sup>And those servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, both bad and good. So the wedding hall was filled with guests. <sup>14</sup>For many are called, but few are chosen. <sup>21</sup>They said, “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them, “Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” <sup>29</sup>But Jesus answered them, “You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. <sup>30</sup>For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven. <sup>31</sup>And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God: <sup>32</sup>‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not God of the dead, but of the living.” <sup>37</sup>And he said to him, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. <sup>38</sup>This is the great and first commandment. <sup>39</sup>And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. <sup>40</sup>On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets.” <sup>42</sup>“What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” They said to him, “The son of David.” <sup>44</sup>He said to them, “Then how is it that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord?’
22.overview:
Chapter 22 is a day of public controversy in Jerusalem. The religious establishment sends wave after wave of opponents — Pharisees, Herodians, Sadducees — each with a question designed to trap Jesus. He answers all of them and turns the final question back on his attackers, leaving them silenced. Matthew arranges the chapter as a trial in which the judge is the one in the dock: every party that challenges Jesus is exposed by his answers, and the final question — “Whose son is the Christ?” — reveals that the Messiah is not merely David’s descendant but David’s Lord.

The chapter opens with the parable of the wedding banquet, which recapitulates the entire history of Israel’s rejection of God’s invitations and the extension of grace to the Gentile roads and byways. “Many are called, but few are chosen” is not a statement about the inefficacy of the gospel but about the mystery of election: the call goes out wide; the choice of God secures who will respond. The banquet hall will be full — but with those God has chosen, not those who presumed on their invitation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Parable of the Wedding Banquet and the Question about Taxes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus tells the parable of the wedding banquet: a king invites guests to his son's wedding, they refuse and some kill his servants, the city is destroyed, and the hall is filled instead with whoever is found at the road junctions, both bad and good. One guest is discovered without a wedding garment and is cast out. Then the Pharisees and Herodians, in an alliance of convenience, try to trap him on the Roman poll tax; he asks for a coin, and answers that what bears Caesar's image goes to Caesar and what bears God's image goes to God. They marvel, and leave him.
verseByVerse.theology: The invitation is free, finished and urgent. Everything is ready is perfect tense throughout — the oxen are already slaughtered, nothing is pending, and the only thing outstanding is attendance. And the guests who refuse had already accepted, since invitations in that world went out twice; they are the second son of 21:30 again, whose word and whose feet have parted company. Grace then reaches the road junctions and gathers both bad and good with no screening at the door, which is the Gentile mission in parabolic form. But grace is not universalism: the king walks the room, and the man without the garment is speechless because nothing had been withheld from him — he had declined what was offered, not failed to manufacture what was required. On the tax, Jesus neither divinises Caesar nor anarchises the gospel. The coin bears Caesar's image and may be returned to him; the image on the man is God's, and that Caesar may never have.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice what the first guests were doing instead: one went to his farm, another to his business. Not vice, not blasphemy — a field that needed walking and a shop that needed running. The most effective rival to God in most lives has never been wickedness but respectable occupation, and it works because nobody has to defend it. Indifference and violence end in the same place in this parable, which should sober anyone who has assumed that not being hostile is the same as being safe; nobody here is condemned for opposing the king, only for not turning up. The tax scene has its own sting: asked for a coin, they produced one — in the temple, from men professing scruples about Caesar's tribute, a denarius inscribed Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus and Pontifex Maximus. It is easy to hold a principled objection while living comfortably inside the thing, and be unaware of the gap. The test is not what you would say if asked, but what turns up when somebody says: show me. And verse 22 names the most respectable way of rejecting Christ — they marvelled, and they left him.

verseByVerse.quote: And again Jesus spoke to them in parables, saying, "The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Notice first whose wedding it is. A king who gave a wedding feast for his son — and that single fact governs everything that follows. The guest list is not really about the guests. A royal wedding was the one occasion on which a king put his whole house on display: the herds slaughtered, the cellars opened, the celebration running for days at his expense, and the entire point of it the honouring of his son. To decline an invitation of that kind was not a social lapse. It was a public verdict on the son.

Behind the image stands Isaiah, and his readers knew it: on this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, of rich food full of marrow, of aged wine well refined (Isa 25:6). It is worth registering how unlike most people's picture of the last day that is. The prophet's word for the end is not a courtroom or a cloud or a silence. It is food, and a great deal of it, and company, and wine that has been kept a long time for a particular occasion.
