And the next lines of Isaiah say what is served alongside it: the covering that lies over all peoples swallowed up, death swallowed up forever, and the Lord God wiping the tears off every face (25:7-8).

Then the custom, which most readers do not know and without which the parable's sharpness is lost. Invitations in that world went out twice. A first notice went round well in advance so that people could reserve the day and reply; then, when the animals had been killed and the food was actually on the tables, servants went out a second time to say come now, it is ready. So the people who refuse in the next verse are not strangers turning down a stranger. They had already accepted. They had said yes months ago, and the servants at the door are simply calling in a promise.

Which is the sound of a familiar door closing, because Matthew has just told us this same story in a shorter form. The second son said I go, sir, in the right tone, using the right title, and did not go (21:30). These guests said yes and did not come. It is the chapter's second portrait of the same man, and he is not a rebel. He is a person of good standing whose word and whose feet have quietly parted company.

And Jesus is telling it to the men who had asked by what authority he acted, in the temple, two days before they killed him. He is speaking in parables now, which is both mercy and judgment at once: a story gets past the defences that an argument would only harden, and the same story leaves a man who will not have it holding nothing but an anecdote about catering.

verseByVerse.quote: and sent his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. Again he sent other servants, saying, "Tell those who are invited, See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They would not come. The Greek is ouk ethelon — they were not willing. Not they could not, not they were prevented, not the day was difficult. The obstacle in this parable is never circumstance; it is the will, and Matthew says so in three words before any excuse has been offered.

So the king sends again. That is the second thing to register, and it is not what a slighted monarch does. He has been publicly snubbed by people who had already accepted, and his response is another delegation with a warmer message. The pattern is the one the previous chapter set out at length — servants sent, and then more servants, and then more (21:34-36) — and it is the pattern of every prophet God ever sent into a country with a record of what it did to the last one.

Listen to what the second message actually says, because it is all in the tense. I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Perfect tense throughout: done, finished, standing complete. Nothing is pending. The animals are already killed — and in a world without refrigeration that detail carries weight the modern reader misses. Meat cannot be put back. Once the oxen are slaughtered the king is committed, the cost is already sunk, and every hour of delay is waste. He has made himself vulnerable to their refusal before they refuse.

That is the shape of the gospel invitation and it is worth being exact about it. The church is not sent out to persuade God to be gracious, or to ask people to help him prepare something. It is sent to say that it is finished — panta hetoima, everything is ready — and that the only thing outstanding is attendance. What was still to be done, when Jesus told this parable, would be done within the week, and his last word from the cross would be the one word this message is built on: it is accomplished.

Which puts a plain question to anyone who has been meaning to sort this out for some years. Most people who are not at the feast imagine that they are waiting for something — to understand more, to feel differently, to get a particular part of their life straightened out first, to be the sort of person who belongs at a table like that. Read the message again. There is nothing on the list. The oxen are dead, the tables are laid, and the only sentence left in the invitation is come.

verseByVerse.quote: But they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business, while the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two kinds of refusal, and the parable puts the ordinary one first: they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business. The verb is amelesantes — they could not be bothered, they made light of it. Nobody argues. Nobody sends a message explaining. They simply have something on.

And look hard at what they had on, because this is where the parable stops being about first-century Jerusalem. A farm and a shop. Not vice, not blasphemy, not a rival religion — a field that needed walking and a business that needed running. Both entirely legitimate, both things a responsible man ought to attend to, and both the reason he was not at the wedding. The most effective rival to God in most lives has never been wickedness. It is respectable occupation, and it works precisely because nobody has to defend it. A man who misses the feast for a mistress knows he has done something. A man who misses it for the farm has merely been busy.

That is why indifference is more dangerous than hostility, and it is worth saying so plainly. Hostility at least concedes that the matter is serious. The men who went off to the farm had come to a settled view about a royal wedding invitation without ever once thinking about it, and if you had asked them at the gate they would have said, quite sincerely, that they had nothing against the king. Their diaries had decided it for them years earlier.

Then the second kind: the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them. Jesus has already told these men, twenty verses ago, what Israel did to the prophets, and he is not exaggerating now any more than he was then. Nor is it only history. Within a few years Stephen would be stoned in that city, James the brother of John cut down by Herod's sword, and the men listening to this parable would be the ones authorising it.

Hold the two groups together and notice the strange verdict the parable reaches. The violent men and the busy men are dealt with in the same sentence and end in the same position — outside, with the feast going on without them. That should be sobering to anybody who has quietly assumed that not being hostile is the same as being safe. Nobody in this story is condemned for opposing the king. They are condemned for not turning up.

verseByVerse.quote: The king was angry, and he sent his troops and destroyed those murderers and burned their city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the hardest verse in the parable and it should not be softened. The king was angry, and he sent his troops and destroyed those murderers and burned their city.

Begin with the offence, because read carelessly the verse looks like a monarch burning a town over a declined invitation, and that is not what has happened. The men in verse 6 seized the king's envoys, humiliated them and killed them. In the ancient world the murder of a royal embassy was not a crime of manners; it was an act of war, and it was understood as such by everyone. The king does not respond to a snub. He responds to the killing of his servants by people who hold their land from him.

And the sentence had a date. Jesus is speaking in Jerusalem in about AD 30. Within forty years the city rose against Rome, and in AD 70 Titus took it after a siege that Josephus, who watched it, describes in terms nobody should read quickly: the famine inside the walls, the temple burned, the city levelled so thoroughly that visitors could not tell it had been inhabited. Jesus does not leave this to inference — he says it plainly two chapters later, standing on the Mount of Olives looking at the buildings: not one stone will be left upon another (24:2). It is sometimes suggested that this verse was written into the parable after the event by someone who knew how it turned out. It need not be. A man who predicted the destruction openly and in detail on the Wednesday of that week can be allowed to have alluded to it on the Tuesday.

Now the guard, and it matters more than the history. This verse has been quoted with satisfaction by Christians about Jewish people for the better part of two thousand years, and the satisfaction is a blasphemy. Look at who is being addressed: the tenants, the leadership, the men who had the vineyard on lease (21:45), not a race. Look at who wept over this city and said he had longed to gather her children as a hen gathers her brood, and would not be allowed (23:37) — the same speaker, one chapter later, in tears. And look at what happened to the servants of this very parable in AD 70: the church in Jerusalem was made up of Jewish believers, and they suffered the siege with everyone else. There is no version of this verse in which a Gentile Christian gets to feel comfortable.

What it does say, and says without apology, is that patience has an end. That is not a popular sentence and it is not a cruel one. A God who could be refused forever with no consequence would not be a God who cared what happened; the anger in this verse exists because the invitation was real, the son was real, and the murders were real. Grace that cannot finally be resisted to your own loss was never grace. It was indifference with good manners.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to his servants, "The wedding feast is ready, but those invited were not worthy. Go therefore to the main roads and invite to the wedding feast as many as you find."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those invited were not worthy. Take the word carefully, because it is about to be turned inside out. Worthiness here has nothing whatever to do with merit or quality. The first guests were not disqualified by failing a standard; they were disqualified by not coming. And the people who fill the hall in their place are not more deserving in any respect at all — they are simply willing to walk through a door. In this parable the only unworthiness that matters is refusal, and the only worthiness on offer is an empty stomach.

Go therefore to the main roads. The phrase means the places where the streets run out of the town and meet the open highway — the junctions, the edges, where you find people who are passing through and belong to nobody. These are not the second tier of the guest list. There was no second tier. The king's staff are being sent to gather whoever happens to be standing at a road junction on the afternoon of a royal wedding.

Set the two groups side by side and the reversal is complete. The first had covenant standing, ancestral promise, generations of expectation and a reserved place. The second had no pedigree, no claim, no warning and no reason on earth to think a palace had anything to do with them. And the invitation the second group receives is not a lesser one. They are not let in at the back to watch. They are guests at the wedding of the king's son, with the same food, at the same tables, on the same evening.

Which is the Gentile mission in one sentence, and it also happens to be the story of nearly everyone reading this. If you are not Jewish, you are the person at the road junction. You had no ancestral claim on the God of Israel, no place reserved, nothing to bring, and no grounds for complaint if the servants had walked past you. Paul spends three chapters of Romans on this and never quite gets over it, and neither should we.

There is a test in it for a congregation, and it is uncomfortable and easy to apply. The king's instruction is not invite the people most likely to accept, nor invite the ones who will fit in. It is: go to the junctions and bring in whoever is there. A church whose membership looks like a careful selection from one part of one town has not been to the main roads. It has been to the people it already knew.

verseByVerse.quote: And those servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, both bad and good. So the wedding hall was filled with guests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Both bad and good. Notice the order. Matthew could have written it the other way round and it would have read more comfortably, but he puts the bad first, and the phrase is not a piece of realism apologising for the standard of guest. It is the point. The servants were told to gather everyone they found, and they did, and nobody at the door was assessed.

That is worth pressing, because we do not really believe it. There is no screening in this verse. No pause to establish whether a man at the junction has the sort of history that suits a royal occasion, no discreet enquiry, no probation. The instruction was comprehensive, the servants obeyed it comprehensively, and the hall filled with a crowd that would not have been admitted to any other event in the kingdom.

And then: the wedding hall was filled. The verb is passive and the parable does not say who filled it. What it does say is that the room the original guests left empty did not stay empty. The son's wedding was not going to be attended by a thin scattering of people who happened to be free. The king had determined that there would be a full house, and there was.

Guard it against the reading it always attracts, which is come as you are and stay as you are. The very next verse is about a man who came as he was and was not clothed, and the parable that welcomes the bad without a question at the door also has a king who walks the room. Both halves are in the story and neither is negotiable: nothing whatever is required to get in, and something is required to be there. The bad are brought in. They are not left as they were found.

What this verse does to a church is simple enough to state and hard to live with. If the servants of the parable are doing their work, the hall will contain people whose lives are visibly a mess, and it will contain them before they are tidy. A congregation with no such people in it has not been more faithful than the parable; it has been more selective. The early church did this so conspicuously — Jew and Gentile, slave and owner, the respectable and the notorious, eating at one table — that the surrounding world could not account for it and wrote about it in bafflement. That was not a lapse in standards. It was the servants doing what they were told.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the king came in to look at the guests, he saw there a man who had no wedding garment. And he said to him, "Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment?" And he was speechless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parable turns without warning, and the turn is the reason it is told. The king came in to look at the guests. He walks the room. Everything up to this point has been about getting people through the door; now the host inspects, and one man is found who does not belong at a table he is sitting at.

Note where the man is standing when the trouble begins. He is inside. He got past the servants, walked the length of the hall, took a place and sat down among the guests, and nothing in the story suggests anybody challenged him. Whatever is wrong here was not detectable at the door. It is detected by the king.

And note what he is called: Friend — hetairos, the courteous, distancing word. Matthew uses it exactly three times, and this is the middle one. It was said to the labourer grumbling at the pay table (20:13), it is said here to a man about to be thrown out, and it will be said in a garden by torchlight to Judas (26:50). Every occurrence is addressed to someone in the wrong, and every occurrence is polite. It is courtesy with the temperature taken out of it — the address of a man who has not raised his voice and has stopped pretending (see on 20:13).

The question put to him is not an accusation but an enquiry, and the man cannot meet it. How did you get in here without a wedding garment? — and he was speechless. The verb Matthew uses is ephimothe, the word for being muzzled. He is not defiant and not apologetic. He has nothing, because there is nothing to have; if he had been poor he could have said so, and if he had been overlooked he could have said that. His silence is the admission.

On the garment itself, be honest about what is known. It is often said that the host provided robes at the door, and if that was the custom the man's silence explains itself completely — he was offered clothing and declined it. The evidence for the custom is thinner than the confidence with which it is usually asserted. But the parable's own logic points the same way whether or not the custom existed: a man dragged in off a road junction at an hour's notice could not possibly be blamed for being badly dressed unless something had been made available to him. He is speechless precisely because he has no grievance. Nothing was withheld from him.

Which is why the standard reading of the garment has held since the Reformers, and why Calvin saw in it the righteousness of Christ put on by faith. The images line up: he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness (Isa 61:10); and at the end, the bride granted fine linen to wear, and the granting is the point (Rev 19:8). Nobody in that hall wove his own clothes. The man was not thrown out for failing to produce something; he was thrown out for declining something. (What that means for the anxious reader — how anyone knows whether he has it — is taken up in the next entry.)

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to the attendants, "Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." For many are called, but few are chosen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The outer darkness — exclusion from joy and light — is the consequence of appearing at the feast without the wedding garment. The garment in its original cultural context was almost certainly provided by the host for those who needed one; to arrive without it was not poverty but refusal. Calvin reads the wedding garment as the righteousness of Christ imputed to the believer: the King provides the clothing required for the feast, and to lack it is to have declined what was freely offered, not to have failed to manufacture what was required. The man's speechlessness is the silence of someone with no defense, because there is none — you cannot explain why you refused the host's own gift. The binding and the outer darkness are the consequence not of dramatic wickedness but of the single refusal of the King's provision. The final verse distills the parable's entire theology: "many are called" (the general gospel offer goes out genuinely and widely to all), "but few are chosen" (effectual calling belongs to the elect whom God draws to the feast). This is not fatalism but the Reformed doctrine of grace: the outward call goes to all without distinction; the inward call secures the response of those God has chosen. That distinction is what makes both evangelism and assurance possible at once: preach to everyone without exception, because the outward call is genuine; and rest, because God secures his own.

The doctrine is stated; the question it raises in an ordinary reader is not. It runs like this: if only the chosen are saved, and I cannot see the list, what peace can I possibly have? What if I want to come and am not one of them? That fear has kept people from Christ for centuries, which is a bitter irony, since the doctrine was given to settle fear and not to create it.

Notice first that nobody in Scripture is ever told to establish that he is elect before coming. Not once, anywhere. In this very parable the instruction to the servants is to go to the main roads and invite as many as they find — no screening, no list, no enquiry into anyone's eternal status. They were not given the names. They were given the invitation.

Notice next that election is not designed to be looked at from the front. Paul writes about it to churches — to people already inside — as an explanation of how they got there and a guarantee that they will be kept. It is the floor under the house, not the door of it. A man standing outside trying to read the foundations before he will step through the doorway has mistaken what the doctrine is for.

And here is where it settles. You will never find your name by staring into the hidden counsel of God, and you are not asked to. Calvin's counsel is still the best on offer: Christ is the mirror in which we contemplate our election — look at him, come to him, and you are looking at the evidence. The promise attached to the coming has no small print: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (Jn 6:37). Nobody in two thousand years has tested that sentence and discovered an exception.

So the instruction is embarrassingly simple: if you want to come, come. And take the wanting itself as the encouragement it is, because you did not manufacture it. No one drags himself toward God unaided — which is the same doctrine seen from the other side, and from that side it is pure comfort. The desire to be at the feast is the surest sign that the One who does the choosing has already been at work.

One guard keeps this from going soft. The man without the garment was not turned out for lacking a ticket he had no way of obtaining. The garment, as Calvin saw, was supplied by the host; that is why the man is speechless. He had no defence because he had not been excluded from something withheld — he had declined something offered. Nobody at that table earned his clothes, and nobody outside it was refused a set.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words. And they sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, "Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully, and you do not care about anyone's opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They plotted how to entangle him in his words. The verb pagideuo comes from the noun for a trap — the snare a fowler sets for a bird, hidden, baited and sprung by the creature's own movement. Matthew is telling us the intention before he reports the conversation, so that we cannot mistake what follows for a discussion.

Then look at who is standing there together, because the alliance is extraordinary. Pharisees were the party of strict Torah observance, who regarded Roman occupation as a defilement of the land and the tribute as a standing humiliation. Herodians were clients of the Herod family, whose entire position — lands, offices, income — depended on Rome's continued goodwill. On the question they are about to ask, these two groups held opposite views with some passion. They agreed on nothing except that this man had to be finished, and that was enough to put them in the same delegation. Hostility to Christ has always been an efficient organiser of people who cannot otherwise be in a room together.

And notice that the Pharisees do not come themselves. They sent their disciples — the students, the younger men, sent to do the work while the seniors kept their distance from whatever happened. It is a small detail and a familiar one.

Now the flattery, which is a small masterpiece: Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully, and you do not care about anyone's opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances. Every clause of that is accurate. He is true; he does teach the way of God truthfully; he is not swayed by appearances. They have described him perfectly, and they do not believe a word of it.

Which is exactly how flattery works, and why Scripture treats it as a form of assault rather than a lapse of taste — a flattering mouth works ruin (Prov 26:28). The purpose here is not to please him. It is to build a box out of his own reputation and shut him in it: we have said in public that you fear nobody, so now you must prove it by answering recklessly. Praise a man for his courage loudly enough and he may do something stupid to keep the compliment.

The technique is still in daily use and worth being able to recognise, because it usually arrives disguised as respect. You are the only one round here who says what he really thinks. You are not like the others, you are not afraid of this. I knew you would understand — you have always been more open-minded than they are. Each of those is a door being held open in a particular direction, and the compliment is the hinge. The test is simple enough: notice whether the praise is describing you or steering you, and whether it arrived just before a request.

verseByVerse.quote: "Tell us, then, what you think. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The question is not academic, and men had died over it within living memory. The tax in view is the kensos, the Roman poll tax — one denarius a year levied on every head in the province, introduced when Judea came under direct Roman administration in AD 6. It was not the amount that stung. It was that a census had counted God's people like Caesar's cattle, and that paying it was a yearly admission of who owned the land. When it came in, Judas the Galilean raised a revolt against it and was destroyed with all his followers — Gamaliel would remind the Sanhedrin of the episode a few years later, and the men listening to this question knew the names (Acts 5:37).

So the trap is real and it is well built. Say yes, and the crowds who had shouted Hosanna four days earlier hear their Son of David endorsing the tribute — and the Pharisees are standing there to make sure they hear it. Say no, and it is sedition, on a charge Rome prosecuted without much interest in nuance — and the Herodians are standing there to make sure Pilate hears that. The delegation had been assembled so that either answer had its own witnesses ready.

And they take care to put it as a question of conscience. Is it lawful? — is it permitted, does the Torah allow it. Framed that way it looks like a scruple rather than a snare, and it makes refusal to answer look like evasion of a religious duty. They are not asking him what is wise. They are asking him to rule.

The shape of it is worth recognising because it has never gone out of use. Almost every generation produces a question designed so that a Christian must offend one group or the other, and the questioner's interest is not in the answer but in the offence. Tell us what you think is very often the most hostile sentence in the room. What Jesus does with it in the next four verses is not a dodge and not a compromise: he refuses the alternatives he was offered and answers a larger question than the one he was asked, which is a thing worth learning from a man who was being watched by people taking notes for a prosecution.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, aware of their malice, said, "Why put me to the test, you hypocrites? Show me the coin for the tax." And they brought him a denarius.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus, aware of their malice. Matthew does not let the scene proceed as though it were a seminar. The word is ponerian, active wickedness, and the courteous preamble about his integrity does not survive contact with it: he calls them hypocrites to their faces before answering a word. It is worth noticing that the flattery did not work even slightly. They told him he was not swayed by appearances, and then discovered that he was not swayed by appearances.

Then the request that wins the argument before it starts: show me the coin for the tax. He does not have one. He asks them.

And they produce it. That single fact is the whole exchange, and it happens in the temple precincts. These are men presenting themselves as troubled in conscience about whether God's people may lawfully pay Caesar's tax, and when a coin is called for, somebody in the group has one in his purse, on the temple mount, and hands it over without a flicker.

It is worth knowing what was on it. The denarius of Tiberius carried the emperor's head in profile with the inscription Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus, and on the reverse the title Pontifex Maximus, high priest. So the object handed to Jesus in the temple of the living God, by men who had just declared themselves scrupulous, was a piece of metal announcing that another man was the son of a god and the chief priest of the world. They had been carrying it around all morning. Whatever their objection to Rome amounted to, it had not reached their pockets.

That is the quiet accusation, and it lands somewhere nearer home than we would like. It is remarkably easy to hold a principled objection to a thing while living comfortably inside it, and to be genuinely unaware of the gap. These men were not consciously lying about their scruples; they had simply never let the scruple and the purse meet. The test is not what you would say if asked. It is what turns up when somebody says: show me.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" They said, "Caesar's." Then he said to them, "Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The image and inscription establish ownership. Caesar's coin bears Caesar's image — return it to him. But humanity bears God's image (Gen. 1:26–27) — render yourselves to God. The two-kingdoms principle is established: civil government has legitimate authority in its sphere; God's authority is ultimate and total. The genius of the answer is that it neither divinises Caesar nor anarchises the gospel, and it does it by asking one question about a piece of metal.

Which leaves the question every Christian eventually has to answer in practice, and it deserves more than a principle: what do I do when the two claims collide — when Caesar commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands? Jesus does not spell it out here, but his apostles did, and they did it in front of this same council. Ordered by the Sanhedrin to stop preaching in the name of Jesus, Peter answered, "We must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29) — and then took the flogging that came with it. That is the shape of the thing throughout Scripture: the Hebrew midwives quietly refusing Pharaoh's order to kill the boys (Ex 1:17), the three young men who would not bow to the statue and told the king to his face that God could deliver them and would not be bargained with either way (Dan 3:16-18), Daniel opening his window toward Jerusalem and praying as he always had, knowing the law and the lions.

But notice two guards on it, because this door is easily pushed too wide. The first is that the exemption is narrow. Paul wrote "let every person be subject to the governing authorities" and Peter wrote "honour the emperor" — and both of them wrote it under Nero, an emperor who would eventually kill them both. So a government being unjust, corrupt, or hostile to the faith is not by itself the ground of disobedience; those apostles knew all of that and still commanded submission. The line is crossed not when the state is wicked but when it requires you to be. The second guard is the manner. Every one of those examples disobeyed openly and then bore the cost — no rebellion, no plotting, no contempt. They declined, they said plainly why, and they accepted the fire, the lions, the prison. Christian disobedience is not the refusal of the state's authority to punish; it is the refusal to sin, with the punishment accepted.

And under all of it lies what Jesus actually said, which is more radical than the tidy division of spheres it is usually reduced to. Caesar's image is on the coin, so the coin is his; give it back and do not make a religion of resenting it. But the image on you is God's. Caesar may have your taxes, your obedience in his own sphere, your honour and your prayers. He may never have the thing that bears the other image. That is not a small reservation quietly held back from the state; it is everything, and every tyrant who has ever tried to take it has found that Christians would give him the coin all day and would not give him that.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard it, they marveled. And they left him and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard it, they marvelled. And they left him and went away. Two sentences, and between them lies the saddest gap in the chapter.

They marvelled. The word is ethaumasan, and Matthew has been sounding this note for two chapters. The chief priests saw the wonderful things he did in the temple and were indignant (21:15). Jesus quoted the psalm about the rejected stone and said it was marvellous in our eyes (21:42). Now his opponents stand in front of an answer they cannot fault and marvel at it. Three marvels in two chapters, and not one of them ends in worship.

Then: they left him. Not the argument — him. Matthew's phrasing is exact and unsparing. They had come with a question, they received an answer better than any of them could have produced, they were genuinely impressed, and they walked away from the person. Whatever had happened in that exchange, nothing had happened to them.

This is the most respectable way of rejecting Christ and by some distance the most common, and it is the particular danger of people who read books like this one. It is entirely possible to find Jesus intellectually magnificent — to enjoy the way he handles opponents, to admire the answer about Caesar as a piece of reasoning, to recommend the passage to somebody else — and to have moved not an inch. Admiration is a comfortable posture. It costs nothing, it flatters the admirer, and it can be maintained for a lifetime.

The test is embarrassingly simple and can be run on the last thing you read. When you finished the passage, did anything change by Thursday? Not did you agree with it, and not did you find it striking. Did you do anything, stop anything, say anything to anyone, ask forgiveness of anyone? These men had the best answer any of them would ever hear, and they took nothing away but a good story about a clever reply.

And the last four words are a warning about where marvelling goes if it is allowed to settle. They left him and went away — and they will come back. The next time these men are in a room with Jesus they will not be asking questions; they will be looking for witnesses who will testify against him (26:59). Admiration that refuses to become allegiance does not stay neutral for long.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–46 — Resurrection, the Great Commandment, and David's Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three delegations in succession, and then Jesus asks a question of his own. The Sadducees construct a levirate-marriage absurdity with seven brothers to make resurrection look ridiculous, and are told they know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God — the resurrection proved out of the Torah they accepted, from the present tense of one verb at the burning bush. The crowd is astonished. The Pharisees regroup and send a lawyer to ask which commandment is greatest, and receive the Shema and Leviticus 19:18, on which the whole Law and Prophets hang. Then Jesus asks whose son the Christ is, quotes Psalm 110, and nobody is able to answer him a word or dares question him again.
verseByVerse.theology: Two failures are named in one sentence and almost every serious error in the church lands under one of them: you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. The Sadducees had the Torah by heart, which is what makes the first charge devastating — knowing the Scriptures is not the same as having them. And they believed in God while not believing he could do anything, which is a God cut down to the size of arrangements we already understand. The resurrection argument turns on covenant: God binds himself by name to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and says I am, not I was, six hundred years after Abraham died. He does not attach his name to dust. Then the double love command, where the verb is krematai — the Law and Prophets hang on two pegs, so the 613 commandments are not separate obligations but the outworking of two. And Psalm 110 closes the sequence: the Christ is David's son according to the flesh and David's Lord according to his eternal nature, which is Matthew's own first chapter put as a riddle (1:23).
verseByVerse.examples: Like angels in heaven needs its guard: it does not mean we become angels or lose our bodies. The comparison is made in one respect only, and the sentence names it — angels do not marry. On the tender question every widow and every married reader brings here, see the verse-by-verse on vv. 29-30: what ends is the institution, not the love. Notice also the woman in the Sadducees' story, whom nobody in it notices — she has buried seven husbands and appears purely as a question of ownership, and Jesus's answer incidentally gives her back what their question took away. As yourself in v. 39 is a measure, not a recommendation of self-esteem: you never have to be reminded to take an interest in your own toothache, and that automatic attention is the standard. Test it where it bites — when something goes wrong for you the mind supplies context, and when it goes wrong at somebody else's hands the mind supplies character. And v. 33 is a warning laid inside a victory: astonishment is not allegiance, and within three days a crowd in this city would be shouting for Barabbas.

verseByVerse.quote: The same day Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection, and they asked him a question, saying, "Teacher, Moses said, 'If a man dies having no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sadducees accepted only the five books of Moses and denied bodily resurrection, angels, and spirits. Their question is designed to make resurrection look absurd by piling up an extreme hypothetical. The premise is Deuteronomy 25:5-6, the law of levirate marriage — so called from the Latin levir, meaning "husband's brother." The law was straightforward: if a married man died without a son, his surviving brother was obligated to marry the widow. The firstborn son of that union would then carry the dead brother's name and inherit his property, preserving the family line and keeping land within the extended family. The purpose was practical and humane: it protected widows from destitution (a widow with no son had no legal protector or means of support in ancient Israel), maintained the continuity of the household, and kept the family inheritance intact. The institution is illustrated in the book of Ruth, where Boaz acts as a kinsman-redeemer for the widow Naomi and her daughter-in-law Ruth. A man who refused his obligation could be publicly shamed — the woman was to pull off his sandal and spit in his face before the elders (Deut. 25:9-10). The Sadducees construct a hypothetical so extreme it borders on comedy: seven brothers, one woman, seven consecutive levirate marriages, all without a son. Their punch line — "in the resurrection, whose wife will she be?" — is designed to make resurrection seem logically impossible or socially absurd. The assumption underneath is that resurrection life must be identical to earthly life, and it is the assumption rather than the doctrine that Jesus will take apart. Like many sophisticated objections to Christianity, theirs is built on a false premise about the nature of the life to come.

It is worth knowing who these men were, because they appear rarely and they mattered enormously. The Sadducees were the aristocratic, priestly party: the high priest belonged to them, they controlled the temple and its revenues, and they held the practical power in Jerusalem. They accepted the written Torah and rejected the accumulated oral tradition the Pharisees prized. They denied the resurrection, and with it angels and spirits (Acts 23:8). And they had made their working arrangement with Rome, which is how a man keeps a position like that under an occupation.

Notice how well those things fit together, because it is not a coincidence. A party with wealth, office and influence in the present world has the least possible incentive to believe in a world to come. If this life is where the accounts are settled, then men in their position have already won, and a coming judgment can only be a threat. It is worth being honest that theology is very rarely held in a vacuum: they were the men whom the doctrine of the resurrection would cost the most, and they were the men who found the arguments against it persuasive.

Which also explains why they are here at all. The Sadducees are not natural allies of the Pharisees and had no interest in Torah minutiae for their own sake; they had watched Jesus clear the temple courts two days earlier, and the temple was theirs. This is not a theological enquiry. It is the men whose market he overturned, coming back with a clever question.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother. So too the second and third, down to the seventh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven brothers, seven marriages, seven funerals, no children. The story is not a case somebody brought to the Sadducees for a ruling; it is a debating-school construction, and the Sadducees have built it the way you build a scenario designed to make an opponent's position collapse under its own weight. The rabbinic schools loved this kind of exercise, and seven is chosen because it is the number of completeness — pile it high enough and the doctrine looks ridiculous.

The logic underneath it is worth stating plainly, because it is the engine of a great many objections that sound more sophisticated than they are. It runs: if your doctrine is true, then this absurd situation follows; the situation is absurd; therefore your doctrine is false. That is a perfectly good argument, and everything depends on the hidden premise. Here the hidden premise is that resurrection means the resumption of this life exactly as it stands, with the same arrangements, the same contracts, the same property law. Jesus is about to deny the premise rather than the conclusion, which is usually where such arguments actually break.

But before that, notice the woman, because nobody in the story does. She is the only person in this scenario who has suffered anything. She has buried seven husbands. She has been handed on from brother to brother as a legal obligation, has borne no children in a society where a childless widow had no protection and no standing, and has ended up dead after a life of accumulating grief. And she appears in the argument purely as a difficulty — an object whose ownership must be determined. Whose wife will she be? The question is about the men.

There is something worth seeing in that. The Sadducees have taken a law that existed precisely to protect destitute widows — the whole point of levirate marriage was that a woman in her position should not be left with nothing — and used it to mock the one hope that would have been of any comfort to her. And when Jesus answers, his answer will incidentally give her back what their question took away: in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, which means that in the world to come she is not the seventh brother's property or the first brother's widow. She is herself.

It is a small thing in the passage and not the main point, and it is not nothing. People who use other people as counters in an argument usually do not notice they are doing it. These men had a woman's entire life in their hands as an illustration, and the only thing about her that interested them was who she belonged to.

verseByVerse.quote: "After them all, the woman died. In the resurrection, therefore, of the seven, whose wife will she be? For they all had her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they all had her. The verb is eschon, from echo, to have and to hold as one's own — and it is the assumption baked into the whole question. Seven men had a claim; the resurrection will therefore produce a dispute; a doctrine that produces disputes about property cannot be true. The argument is only as good as its picture of the life to come, and the picture is this one with the wrinkles ironed out.

That is the error, and it is not confined to Sadducees. Ask most people, including most Christians, what they expect of heaven and you will get a description of the present world improved: the same house without the mortgage, the same body without the pain, the same work without the Monday, the same relationships without the friction, and the dog. It is a perfectly natural way to imagine it, since it is the only material any of us has. But it is an extension, not a transformation, and the New Testament never describes the age to come that way.

It is also, incidentally, why heaven strikes so many people as faintly boring. If the hope is essentially this life continued indefinitely, then honest reflection will find the prospect wearing rather than thrilling, and the fault is not in the hope but in the picture. Paul's answer to the same confusion is worth having beside this passage: what you sow is not the body that is to be (1 Cor 15:37). He compares it to a seed and the plant that comes up — genuinely continuous, unmistakably the same life, and not remotely predictable from the seed. Nobody holding an acorn would guess an oak.

So the resurrection body is not a ghost and it is not a repeat. It is real, physical and recognisable — the risen Christ ate fish in front of his friends and told Thomas to put a finger in the scars — and it is also transformed past anything that can be extrapolated from here. Both halves must be held. Drop the first and you get a vague spiritual mist that Scripture never promises; drop the second and you get the Sadducees' question, and the Sadducees' question has no answer.

Which is why the failure Jesus is about to name is a failure of imagination produced by unbelief. These men were not short of intelligence. They were short of any category for a God who does genuinely new things, and so the only future they could construct was a copy of the past — at which point, quite reasonably, they found it absurd.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus answered them, "You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are wrong. There is no diplomatic opening. The verb is planasthe — you are deceived, led off the road — and it is said to the aristocratic party who ran the temple, in public, in front of a crowd.

Then the diagnosis, in two halves, and it is worth memorising because almost every serious error in the church lands under one of them. You know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. These men had the Torah by heart; that is precisely what makes the first charge devastating. Knowing the Scriptures is not the same as having them, and a man can carry the text in his memory and still not know what it says. And the second is worse: they believed in God and did not believe he could do anything. A God who cannot raise the dead is a God who has been quietly cut down to the size of the arrangements we already understand. Get the Bible wrong, or get the power of God wrong, and everything downstream goes crooked.

Then the answer itself, and it is a denial of the premise rather than the puzzle: in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage. The two phrases are the man's part and the woman's part in the arrangements of that world, and both are simply absent. The Sadducees' question does not get solved. It stops applying.

Like angels in heaven needs its guard, because it is one of the most misread phrases in the Gospels. It does not say we become angels — we do not; Scripture never once suggests that human beings are promoted into a different order of creature, and the sentimental idea that the dead get wings has no footing here or anywhere else. Nor does it mean we become bodiless. The comparison is made in one respect only, and the sentence names it: angels do not marry. That is the whole of the likeness.

But a tender question rises here that no married or widowed reader can help asking: does this mean I will not be with my husband, my wife, in heaven — that the love of a lifetime simply ends? Hear the answer gently. What ends is the institution — the exclusive covenant of marriage, with its vows "till death us do part," its giving and taking in marriage — for it belonged to this age and to the raising of families, and in the resurrection there is no more death to guard against and no more children to bear. But love itself is not abolished; it is perfected. You will not know your beloved less in that day, but immeasurably more — no longer through the narrow, guarded channel of one exclusive bond, but in the wide, unclouded light of a love with nothing left in it to fear or forgive. Marriage was always a signpost, not the destination: a picture of Christ and his church (Eph 5:32), and when the Bridegroom comes and the marriage of the Lamb is spread (Rev 19:7-9), the picture gives way to the reality it was painting all along. We are not told every detail, and we need not be. It is enough to know that nothing good is lost in that country — it is taken up, deepened, and made everlasting. The wife you love in Christ you will love forever; only better, and with him at the center of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God: 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'? He is not God of the dead, but of the living."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch where he goes for his proof. The Sadducees accepted the authority of the five books of Moses and treated everything after them as secondary, which is largely why they denied the resurrection: the clearest statements of it stand in the Prophets and the Writings — Daniel's sleepers who awake, Isaiah's dead who shall live. Jesus does not appeal to any of them. He goes to Exodus, to the burning bush, and argues on the only ground they acknowledged.

And the argument turns on a verb. I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. God says it to Moses at the bush — and by then Abraham had been dead for something like six hundred years, Isaac and Jacob only slightly less. He does not say he was their God. He says he is. The whole doctrine of the resurrection, proved out of the Torah, hangs on the present tense of a single word, and Jesus expects these men to be able to see it.

He is not God of the dead, but of the living. That is the logic underneath, and it is covenantal rather than merely grammatical. God had bound himself by name to these three men — not to a nation in the abstract, not to an idea, but to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as persons. He calls himself by their names. And a God who ties his own identity to a man and then lets that man end as dust has broken the covenant he made; the relationship would be a memorial rather than a bond. If the LORD is still the God of Abraham on the day of the bush, then Abraham is still there to have a God.

Notice too the four words that are easy to skip: what was said to you by God. Not what was said to Moses. Not what was written long ago. He tells men standing in Jerusalem in about AD 30 that a sentence spoken at a bush in the Sinai desert was addressed to them. That is a striking view of Scripture and he assumes it without argument: the text is not a record of God having spoken but an instance of God speaking, and the tense of a verb in it is still live enough to settle a dispute about the dead.

And then stop and consider what God has done with those three names. He might have identified himself to Moses in any terms he chose — maker of heaven and earth, the One who is, the God who parts seas. What he says at the bush, and what he is content to be called for the rest of the Bible, is the God of three men. One of them lied about his wife twice, one was a passive father who loved the wrong son, and one cheated his brother and wrestled God to a draw and limped afterwards. He took their names into his own and kept them there, and on the strength of that arrangement Jesus tells a hostile court that the grave does not get them.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the crowd heard it, they were astonished at his teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd is astonished, and the word is worth pausing over: ekplessomai, literally to be struck out of oneself, knocked sideways. Matthew uses it of the Sermon on the Mount (7:28), of the synagogue at Nazareth (13:54), of the disciples when he said the rich would struggle to enter the kingdom (19:25), and here. It is not mild interest. These people have been hit by something.

And note who they are. Not the Sadducees, who are now silent, and not the Pharisees, who are about to regroup. This is the ordinary crowd in the temple courts — pilgrims up for the Passover, tradesmen, families, the people who had lined the road on Sunday shouting Hosanna. They have just watched their teachers comprehensively beaten by a Galilean, and they are delighted.

Which is exactly why the verse is placed here, and why it should be read with a certain sadness. Matthew has shown us this crowd's astonishment repeatedly and he has also shown us where it goes. Within three days these same courts will be quiet, and a crowd assembled at the governor's residence in the early morning — worked on all night by the men who have just lost this argument — will be shouting for a murderer to be released instead of him (27:20-23).

So the verse is a warning laid quietly in the middle of a victory. Astonishment is not allegiance. It is possible to enjoy Jesus enormously — to relish the way he handles his critics, to feel the pleasure of watching pomposity dismantled, to leave a service genuinely moved — and to be, in the end, one of the crowd rather than one of the disciples. The difference between the two groups in this Gospel is almost never the intensity of the reaction. It is whether anybody follows him out of the building.

There is a fair test in it for anyone who has been in church a long while. Nothing here is against being moved; God gave us the capacity and the Psalms are full of it. But ask what the last thing was that moved you deeply, and then ask what it changed. If the honest answer is that it was a very good hour and nothing further came of it, that is worth knowing, and it is not a reason to despair — it is a reason to ask him for more than astonishment.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. And one of them, a lawyer, asked him a question to test him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. Read what has just happened from their side. Their theological rivals — the party they had argued with for generations about the resurrection, the party they believed to be wrong on the single point Jesus had just defended — have been publicly demolished, and the man who did it did it by defending the Pharisees' own doctrine out of the Torah.

They might have been delighted. He had just won their argument for them, in front of a crowd, better than any of them had ever managed. Instead they close ranks and send in another questioner. It is one of the clearest pictures in the Gospels of what opposition to Christ actually is: not a set of theological convictions that might be corrected by a better argument, but a settled disposition that survives every argument, including the ones it wins.

The verb for their gathering — synechthesan — is the same word the Greek Old Testament uses in Psalm 2, where the kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed (Ps 2:2). The early church saw the connection immediately: after the first arrests, the believers in Jerusalem prayed that psalm back to God and named the people in it — Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered together against his holy servant Jesus (Acts 4:26-27). Matthew's readers would have heard the echo. The men regrouping in the temple court are standing inside a psalm, playing the part the psalm assigned them, and the psalm's verdict on the enterprise is that the One enthroned in heaven laughs.

Then the questioner: a lawyer — a nomikos, an expert in Torah, brought forward because the question is technical and they want it asked properly. And Matthew tells us his purpose in a single participle: peirazon, testing him. It is the word used of the devil in the wilderness (4:1), of the Pharisees and Sadducees demanding a sign from heaven (16:1), and of the Pharisees on divorce (19:3). Matthew has been quietly keeping a list of the people who came to test Jesus, and it has only ever had one kind of name on it.

Which is worth holding on to when the question itself turns out to be a magnificent one. What follows is the greatest answer about the law ever given, and it was dragged out of him by a man who did not want to know. God has never been prevented from saying something glorious by the poor motives of the person who asked.

verseByVerse.quote: "Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which is the great commandment in the Law? To hear it as they heard it, you need to know that the rabbis had counted. The traditional reckoning made 613 commandments in the Torah — 248 positive, one for each bone they believed to be in the human body, and 365 negative, one for each day of the year. And having counted them, the schools argued for generations about their weight: which were heavy and which light, which could be inferred from which, what a man should do when two obligations collided.

So the question was a real one and not invented for the occasion. But in this mouth it is a trap with three jaws. Name one commandment great and you have implied the others are small, which is a charge they can take to the crowd. Name a commandment associated with one party and you have offended the rest. Refuse to answer and you are not the teacher you have been claiming to be. There is no safe reply available.

And underneath the trap sits a deeper problem, which is the assumption the question carries. It treats the law as an inventory — a list of 613 separate items which might in principle be sorted by importance, so that a careful man could work out where to spend his attention. That is a way of holding God's commands that leaves the man himself entirely intact. He remains the one doing the sorting, and however scrupulous he becomes, he is managing a portfolio.

Watch what Jesus does with it. He does not refuse to rank, and he does not pick a safe item from the middle of the list. He names something that is not one of the 613 items at all in the sense they meant, but the thing every one of them is made of — and in doing so he takes the question away from the man's competence altogether. You cannot manage a portfolio of love with all your heart. There is nothing left over to do the managing with.

It is worth asking, before reading his answer, what our own version of this question is. Almost every Christian has a working list of the things that really matter and the things that are technically commanded, and almost nobody has written it down or would defend it out loud. The list is usually shaped to be keepable. That is the instinct this lawyer brought into the temple, and the answer he got is the reason nobody has ever managed to trim it into shape.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:5 — the Shema, the heart of Jewish daily prayer. The command is total: heart, soul, mind — every faculty of the person wholly directed to God. This is the first commandment because all other obedience flows from this center. Love for God is not an emotion added on top of religious duty; it is the animating principle without which no commandment is really kept at all. Which means the command does two things at once, and always has: it exposes what no one has managed, and it describes the shape of the life Christ gives.

A reader who knows this commandment by heart may stop and count. Matthew has three — heart, soul, mind. Mark has four: "heart, soul, mind and strength" (Mark 12:30), and Luke has the same four in a different order (Luke 10:27). And Deuteronomy 6:5, the verse being quoted, has its own three: heart, soul, and might. So which did Jesus say? The question dissolves once you see what kind of list this is. It is not an inventory dividing a person into parts, as though the mind were one drawer and the strength another; it is a Hebrew way of saying all of you, and the terms deliberately overlap and pile up. Nobody reciting it supposed that leaving out a word left something behind. This is also how the rabbis handled the Shema — not recited flatly but expounded, the words turned over and their reach drawn out. Jesus is doing what any teacher does with a text everyone present knows: giving its sense, not its syllables. And the sense is the one thing all four versions agree on perfectly, which is that the list has no edge you can stand outside of. Whatever you were about to hold back is named in it somewhere.

Which leaves the difficulty that honest people actually feel here, and it should be met rather than stepped over: I do not love God like that. I am not sure I feel much at all. And you cannot command a feeling — nobody can be ordered to be fond of someone.

That objection is half right, and the half that is wrong is the definition. Biblical love is more than feeling, though it is never less: the Psalms are full of thirst and longing, and my soul thirsts for you is not a statement of policy. But love in Scripture is chiefly a settled direction of the whole person — which is precisely why it can be commanded, and why the terms pile up as they do rather than naming one faculty.

So the question do I love God? is not answered by taking your emotional temperature on a given morning. Jesus answers it himself, and the answer is usable: if you love me, you will keep my commandments (Jn 14:15). Obedience is not a substitute for love, offered by people who cannot manage the real thing. It is love's most reliable evidence, and it is available on the days when feeling is not.

Then how does it grow, given that it is commanded and cannot simply be squeezed out by effort? Not by working on the love directly, which is like trying to feel warm by concentrating. Love is a response, and it rises in proportion to what is actually seen: we love because he first loved us (1 Jn 4:19). The way to love God more is therefore not to try harder at loving him but to look longer at what he has done — which is why the church has always put the cross at the centre of its worship rather than an exhortation to be more devoted.

In practice that means spending your time where the affections are genuinely fed rather than where they are merely discussed: Scripture read slowly instead of covered quickly, the Lord's Supper, singing with other people, and the deliberate business of remembering particular mercies rather than mercy in general. And obeying in the meantime, without waiting for the feeling to arrive first. Feelings very often follow the feet.

And see what this commandment is doing where it stands. A lawyer asks which command is greatest, and Jesus hands him the one that nobody in the room has kept for a single hour. That is not an accident; the Sermon on the Mount did the same thing. The law's first and greatest word leaves everybody exposed — and the man saying it is on his way to Jerusalem to keep it perfectly on their behalf. You are commanded to love God with all your heart and soul and mind; you have not; and the one who tells you so did exactly that, all the way to a cross, in your place. Start there, and the loving becomes possible, because it is no longer the price of anything.

verseByVerse.quote: "And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a second is like it. The word is homoia — of the same kind, the same order of thing. He does not say the second is nearly as important, or that it follows from the first as an application. He puts loving your neighbour in the same category as loving God, and then, in the next breath, hangs the entire Old Testament on the pair of them.

On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets. The verb is krematai — hangs, as a door hangs on its hinges or a weight hangs on a nail. It is a physical image and worth keeping physical. Everything Moses wrote and everything the prophets thundered is suspended from two pegs; take those out and the whole structure is on the floor. Which means the 613 items the lawyer wanted ranked are not 613 separate obligations at all. They are the outworking of two, and every one of them is either love of God taking a particular shape or love of neighbour taking a particular shape.

Then as yourself, which needs its guard because the modern ear hears a command to self-esteem in it. It is not one. Jesus is not instructing anybody to love himself first and then extend the surplus; he is naming a measure, and the measure is chosen because it is the one thing nobody has to be persuaded of. You do not have to remember to take an interest in your own toothache. Nobody sets a reminder to think about his own future, or has to work up concern about being cold, or needs encouragement to notice when he has been treated unfairly. That automatic, unarguing, ever-present attention to your own case is the standard: give the same to the person next to you.

Which is a considerably harder command than being nice, and it is worth testing at the point where it bites. When something goes wrong for you, the mind produces context immediately — I was tired, the situation was difficult, anyone would have. When the same thing goes wrong at somebody else's hands, the mind produces character instead: he is careless, she is like that. Loving your neighbour as yourself means extending to him the same generous supply of excuses you manufacture effortlessly for yourself, and it would reshape most families and most churches within a fortnight.

And the two commands cannot be separated, however much religion has tried. John puts it as bluntly as it can be put: if anyone says, I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar (1 Jn 4:20). Not mistaken, not inconsistent — a liar. The love of God is not available as a private arrangement between a man and heaven that leaves the people in his house untouched. It comes down the stairs, or it was never on the roof.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question, saying, "What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?" They said to him, "The son of David."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter turns here. All day he has been answered questions — the wedding feast to the chief priests, the tax to the Pharisees and Herodians, the resurrection to the Sadducees, the great commandment to the lawyer. Four hostile delegations, four answers, and not once has he asked anything of his own. Now, while the Pharisees were gathered together, he puts one question to them, and it is the only question in the chapter that finally matters.

What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?

Notice how close that is to the question at Caesarea Philippi. There, in the north, away from the crowds, he had asked twelve friends: who do you say that I am? (16:15). Here, in the temple, surrounded by the men arranging his death, he asks the same question in the third person and lets them answer it about the Messiah in the abstract. It is the same question either way, and it is the question this Gospel has been walking toward since the genealogy. Everyone in Matthew ends up answering it: Peter, the high priest, Pilate, the centurion at the cross.

Their answer comes back immediately and without discussion: the son of David. And it is right. It is the correct, orthodox, scripturally grounded answer, the one any competent student would give, and it is what the blind men on the Jericho road had shouted at him two days before (20:30). These men are not being caught out in an error. They are being caught out in an answer that is true and has stopped short.

Which is the particular danger this passage exposes, and it is not the danger of unbelief. It is possible to hold a completely correct doctrinal position about Jesus Christ and to have got no further than the position. These Pharisees could have passed an examination on the Messiah's lineage; they had the genealogies, the promise to David, the prophecies about Bethlehem. What they could not do was follow their own answer far enough to notice who was asking. A right answer is not the same as a living faith, and the uncomfortable thing about the confrontation that follows is that Jesus does not correct their answer. He simply asks them to keep reading.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "How is it then that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord, saying, 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus cites Psalm 110:1 — the most-quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament. David, writing by the Spirit, calls the Messiah "my Lord" — a form of address no Jewish father would use of his own descendant. The Psalm describes this Lord enthroned at God's right hand, exercising divine authority over all enemies. The implication is inescapable: the Messiah must be more than David's biological heir. He must share the divine identity. He is unveiling his own pre-existence out of the Psalter, in the temple, to the men who recited it.

Everything in that argument hangs on one assumption, and it is worth naming because it is widely denied: that David wrote the psalm. Jesus does not merely assume it, he says it — "David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord." A good deal of modern scholarship assigns Psalm 110 instead to some later court poet writing about a king, in which case there is no puzzle at all, and Jesus's question is built on sand. Three things are worth weighing. The psalm carries its own heading, "A Psalm of David," which is the oldest testimony we possess about it and is not lightly set aside merely because a later age preferred a different theory. More striking is what happens in the room: these are hostile experts who wanted nothing in the world so much as to catch him in a mistake, and the objection was available to them in a sentence — but David did not write that psalm. Read the next verse. Nobody said it. "No one was able to answer him a word" (v. 46), and their silence is the best evidence we have of what everyone in that courtyard took for granted.

And for a Christian the third consideration settles it. Jesus stakes a public argument about his own identity on David's authorship, and does it "in the Spirit." He was not obliged to argue this way; he could have made the same point from a dozen other texts. A Lord who builds his case on a premise he knows to be false is not a Lord worth trusting on anything else. So the authorship is not a detail on the edge of the passage — it is inside the passage, holding it up. Take it away and you have not tidied the Bible; you have removed the floor from under the question that silenced every enemy he had.

verseByVerse.quote: "If then David calls him his Lord, how is he his son?" And no one was able to answer him a word, nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If then David calls him his Lord, how is he his son? The question has no answer inside the framework these men were using, and that is precisely the point of asking it. A descendant is not his ancestor's lord; the whole structure of an ancient household ran the other way, and the more royal the ancestor the more absurd the reversal. Either David spoke carelessly, or the Messiah is something more than the last and greatest king in a line.

There is exactly one arrangement in which both halves are true at once, and it took the church four centuries of argument to state it carefully: the Christ is David's son according to the flesh and David's Lord according to his eternal nature — one person, truly man and truly God, so that the son of Mary who got tired on the road to Jerusalem is the same person who was at the Father's right hand before David was born. Matthew has been saying it since his first chapter, where the child in the genealogy of David is also the one to be called Immanuel, God with us (1:23). The riddle in the temple is his own Gospel's first two chapters, put as a question.

And no one was able to answer him a word. Not a bad answer, not an evasion, not a counter-question. Matthew says oude logon — not a word. The men who had been running delegations at him since Sunday morning stand in silence, and then a sentence that closes a door: nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions.

That is the end of the controversies. From this verse to the arrest, nobody in Jerusalem asks Jesus anything. What follows is not debate but the woes of chapter 23 and the long discourse of chapters 24 and 25 — Jesus talking, uninterrupted, because there is nothing left to say to him. And the next time these men open their mouths in his presence they will not be asking; they will be seeking witnesses who will testify against him (26:59). When argument has been exhausted, what remains is not agreement. It is the plot.

But do not leave the silence there, because there are two kinds and this chapter has shown us both. The man without the wedding garment was speechless because he had no defence (v. 12). These men are speechless because they will not say what they can see. And there is a third kind, which the psalm Jesus quoted points to: the silence of a man who stops arguing because he has finally understood who he is talking to. Every knee will eventually bow and every mouth will eventually be quiet. The only question this chapter leaves open is which sort of quiet a person ends up in — and the whole reason Jesus stood in that court on that Tuesday, answering delegation after delegation and then asking one question of his own, was to give the men in front of him time to choose the right one.

22.theology: Election and the free offer of the gospel. The parable of the wedding banquet and the phrase “many are called, but few are chosen” bring together two truths that Reformed theology has always insisted must be held together. The general call of the gospel goes out to all people without exception — “Go therefore to the main roads and invite as many as you find.” This is the free and genuine offer of the gospel, and it must be preached without restriction. At the same time, the effectual call of God draws the chosen to the feast. Both are real; both are necessary. The preacher does not know who the elect are; he simply opens the banquet doors as wide as the gospel goes and trusts God with the result.
22.examples:
Then: The religious leaders tried to trap Jesus with politics (tribute coin), doctrine (resurrection), law (greatest commandment). He answered all three with Scripture, clarity, and a question they could not answer. The one they thought to judge was the judge.

Now: The same four questions are still asked of Christians today — political, doctrinal, ethical, and Christological. The answers Jesus gives are still sufficient. Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s; God claims your whole self made in his image. The resurrection is secured by the living God who keeps covenant. Love God with everything; love your neighbour as yourself. And the Christ is both Son of David and Lord of David — the God-man who saves.

23.title: Woe to You, Scribes and Pharisees
23.text: <sup>2</sup>The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat, <sup>3</sup>so do and observe whatever they tell you, but not the works they do. For they preach, but do not practice. <sup>4</sup>They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger. <sup>11</sup>The greatest among you shall be your servant. <sup>12</sup>Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. <sup>13</sup>But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people’s faces. <sup>23</sup>Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. <sup>27</sup>Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people’s bones and all uncleanness. <sup>37</sup>O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! <sup>38</sup>See, your house is left to you desolate. <sup>39</sup>For I tell you, you will not see me again, until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’
23.overview:
Chapter 23 is the fifth and final discourse of Matthew — and the most sorrowful. It begins with a warning to the crowds and disciples about the Pharisees (vv. 1–12), then delivers seven woes against the scribes and Pharisees (vv. 13–36), and closes with a lament over Jerusalem (vv. 37–39) that is one of the most heartbreaking passages in all of Scripture. The woes are not vindictive; they are diagnostic. Jesus names the disease precisely so that it can be seen for what it is: a religion of external performance concealing internal corruption, a leadership that burdens rather than shepherds, a tradition that has become a wall keeping people out of the kingdom.

The lament over Jerusalem (“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem”) reveals the heart behind the woes. Jesus does not pronounce judgment with cold severity; he pronounces it with the grief of a hen who would have gathered her chicks but could not because they would not come. The image is maternal, tender, aching. The holy Judge is also the loving Shepherd who weeps over the city he must judge. Both are true: God is not willing that any should perish, and God judges unrepentant hardness of heart. The cross, which is days away, is where both truths converge.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Seven Woes: The Hypocrisy of Scribes and Pharisees (Part One)
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus turns from silencing his opponents to warning the crowds about them, and this is his last public address in Matthew. He concedes the office before he indicts the men: the scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses' seat, so what they read from it binds Israel even when their lives do not match it.
