Three chapters of the most extraordinary material in the Gospels follow — armies, false messiahs, the abomination, the sun darkened, the Son of Man on the clouds, angels and a trumpet from one end of heaven to the other. And it comes to rest on a servant, in a kitchen, handing out food at the proper time. They asked for a date and were given a job.

End on the sobriety and not on terror, because the chapter does. The threat here is not aimed at the frightened; it is aimed at the comfortable, and specifically at the trusted. A servant who is anxious about his master's return is not the man in this parable — the man in this parable had stopped thinking about it altogether. And the next chapter will press the same point three more times, with a wedding, a fortune and a judgment, before the Gospel turns to the cross where the faithful Servant was himself handed over at an hour he knew exactly.

24.theology: The already and the not yet. Matthew 24 is a masterclass in inaugurated eschatology — the kingdom has arrived in Christ (already) but is not yet consummated (not yet). The destruction of Jerusalem (AD 70) was the “already” — the definitive end of the old covenant age, the vindication of Jesus’ word, the sign that the Son of Man had been enthroned. The final return of the Son of Man is the “not yet” — the consummation of all things, the resurrection of the dead, the new creation. Between these two poles the church lives and works: the age has been inaugurated, the mission is underway, the end is certain but its timing unknown. This is the structure of the Christian life: living in the overlap of the ages, working faithfully until the King returns.
24.examples:
Then: For the first generation of Christians, the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 was a cataclysm that could have shaken their faith. Jesus had prepared them: this was prophesied, this is not the end, the gospel must still go to all nations. The church survived because it had been warned.

Now: Every generation has its false prophets announcing the end based on current events — wars, earthquakes, political upheaval. The command of Jesus is consistent: do not be alarmed, do not be led astray, stay awake, keep working. The Son of Man is coming. But the day and hour are known only to the Father, which means the calling of the church today is exactly what it was yesterday: proclaim the gospel to all nations, and be found faithful when he comes.

25.title: Ready, Faithful, and Merciful
25.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went to meet the bridegroom. <sup>2</sup>Five of them were foolish, and five were wise. <sup>3</sup>For when the foolish took their lamps, they took no oil with them, <sup>4</sup>but the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps. <sup>10</sup>And while they were going to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the marriage feast, and the door was shut. <sup>14</sup>For it will be like a man going on a journey, who called his servants and entrusted to them his property. <sup>21</sup>His master said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.’ <sup>34</sup>Then the King will say to those on his right, ‘Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. <sup>35</sup>For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me.’ <sup>40</sup>And the King will answer them, ‘Truly, I say to you, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.’ <sup>46</sup>And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.
25.overview:
Chapter 25 closes the Olivet Discourse with three parables that together answer the question of how to live between the ascension and the return. The ten virgins teach readiness — oil cannot be borrowed at the last moment; what is needed must be present when the bridegroom comes. The talents teach faithfulness — the servant who buries what he has been given is condemned not for wickedness but for fearful inaction. The sheep and goats teach that love for Christ is expressed in love for the vulnerable — the hungry, the stranger, the naked, the sick, the imprisoned.

Together the three parables describe the whole Christian life in the waiting period: ready (sustained by the Spirit’s inward work), faithful (investing rather than hoarding what has been given), and merciful (serving Christ in the face of the suffering neighbour). The final scene — the separation of sheep and goats, the commendation and the condemnation, the declaration of eternal life and eternal punishment — is Matthew’s most solemn eschatological passage. It is not a salvation-by-works text but a fruits-of-faith text: those who truly love the King will inevitably love those he loves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–30 — The Ten Virgins and the Parable of the Talents
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two parables press the same point from opposite sides. Ten girls go out to escort a bridegroom; five have brought a flask of oil and five have not, and the difference is invisible until a cry at midnight and a door that shuts. Then a man going abroad hands three servants a fortune and leaves; two trade and double it, and the third buries his in the ground because he believes his master is a hard man. The first parable asks what you brought. The second asks what you did.
verseByVerse.theology: Neither failure in these parables is an act of wickedness. The foolish girls lacked something inward that could not be borrowed at midnight or bought in a hurry, and the parable declines to name it beyond telling us four things: it is needed for the long haul, it is untransferable, it cannot be acquired late, and it cannot be seen from outside. The one-talent servant did nothing wrong in any ordinary sense; he stole nothing and lost nothing, and his ruin traces to a doctrine of God stated in his first breath, I knew you to be a hard man. Men do not take risks for someone they believe is waiting to catch them out. Both parables define nominal religion: enough to look ready, and nothing underneath that lasts a delay.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch, in v. 13, cannot mean stay awake, because all ten slept and five were commended. It means be provisioned — a state rather than an activity, built in the un-urgent hours of an ordinary afternoon, which is freeing and considerably more demanding than a fever of expectancy. The talents parable removes the commonest excuse: the acceptable minimum was the bank, requiring no skill and no nerve, and it would have been enough. Note too that no servant in the story tries and fails — that scene is missing, and its absence is the point, because it is the scene most of us are afraid of. The failure judged here is not the failed attempt but the burial. And the cure for the third servant is not to try harder but to know God better: this master hands slaves a fortune unsupervised, is delighted rather than grudging when they succeed, and rewards them not with a bonus but with an invitation to come inside and share his joy.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins who took their lamps and went to meet the bridegroom. Five of them were foolish, and five were wise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The custom behind the scene is worth having, because without it the parable is a puzzle. A Jewish wedding began at the bride's father's house, where the terms were settled and the celebration started; then the bridegroom brought his bride in procession to his own home, and the procession went at night. The girls waiting along the route were not guests killing time. They were the escort, and their job was to be at the door with light when he came, and to walk him in.

The word for their lamps is lampas, which can mean a small clay oil lamp but more often means a torch — a rag bound to a stick and soaked in oil, which burns brightly and burns fast, and has to be re-soaked every quarter of an hour or so to keep going. If that is the picture, the flask is not a spare battery but the whole means of lasting the night, and the difference between the two groups is not a small oversight.

Now count what the ten have in common, because the list is longer than anyone expects. All ten were invited. All ten came out. All ten had lamps. All ten were waiting for the same bridegroom, at the same door, on the same night. All ten grew drowsy and all ten fell asleep. All ten woke at the cry and all ten trimmed their lamps. There is exactly one difference between the two groups in the entire parable, and it is a flask that nobody could see.

Matthew's two adjectives are not new either. Wise and foolish — phronimoi and morai — are the same pair he used at the close of the Sermon on the Mount, of the man who built on rock and the man who built on sand (7:24-27). The parallel is exact in the way that matters: those two houses also looked identical, right up until the weather arrived. The difference in both stories is real, decisive, and completely invisible from the street.

Which is the first thing this chapter is doing, and it does it three times. The division at the end does not run between the church and the world. It runs down the middle of the group that came out to meet him — and it cannot be assessed by anybody standing on the pavement watching, including by the girls themselves, who plainly had no idea until midnight.

verseByVerse.quote: "For when the foolish took their lamps, they took no oil with them, but the wise took flasks of oil with their lamps."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parable does not say what the oil is, and it is worth resisting the urge to be more definite than Jesus was. Interpreters have proposed faith, the Holy Spirit, good works, perseverance, grace itself. Each has something to be said for it, and the fact that good men have landed in different places is a fair sign that the story was not built to be decoded item by item.

But if the parable does not name the oil, it tells us four things about it, and together they narrow the field considerably. It is needed for the long haul rather than the opening moments. It cannot be borrowed from somebody who has it. It cannot be obtained in a hurry at the last minute. And it is invisible from outside — nobody watching the ten girls assemble could have told which five had brought a flask.

Whatever meets that description is an inward reality, held personally, acquired in advance, and undetectable by observers. That is enough to be going on with, and it is quite enough to be searching.

Notice also how undramatic the moment of preparation was. Five girls, at some point during the afternoon, picked up a second container. Nothing about that decision felt spiritual. There was no crisis, no cry, no midnight; the bridegroom was not in sight and the street was in daylight, and taking a flask would have seemed a small, fussy, slightly over-careful thing to do. The whole parable turns on it.

Which gives a question worth putting to yourself in the daylight, since that is the only time it can be answered. What in your Christian life exists only for the occasion, and what exists when there is no occasion? The lamp is the part other people see: the attendance, the answers, the role you fill, the way you pray aloud. The flask is whatever is there on a Tuesday when nobody is watching and nothing is required. Everybody has a lamp. Not everybody has brought a flask, and it is entirely possible to reach the age of sixty in a church without ever having been asked the question.

One thing this is not. It is not an instruction to work up more oil by anxious effort, which is precisely what the foolish girls attempted at midnight and precisely what failed. What to do with the fear this raises is taken up at verses 11-12.

verseByVerse.quote: "As the bridegroom was delayed, all ten became drowsy and slept. But at midnight there was a cry, 'Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two details in these verses are regularly preached backwards, and both are worth getting right.

The first is the sleep. They all became drowsy and slept — all ten, the wise as well as the foolish — and the parable does not breathe a word of criticism about it. Sermons on this text routinely scold congregations for spiritual drowsiness, and the story will not support it. The five who are commended were asleep when he came. Whatever readiness means here, it is compatible with being unconscious at the moment of arrival, which is a very different thing from what most people are told.

The second is the delay. The bridegroom was delayed — chronizontos, and it is worth noticing that the wicked servant in the previous chapter used the same word: my master is delayed (24:48). The fact is identical in both stories. What differs is what was made of it. One man drew a conclusion from the delay and reorganised his life around it. These girls simply got sleepy, which is not a sin but a metabolism. The delay is never the problem in either parable. It is only the thing that reveals what was already the case before it began.

And the delay is built into the design rather than being a fault in it. Jesus puts it in deliberately, in a parable about his own return, told to men who would want it soon. Christians who assumed a short wait and grew disillusioned have not been let down by God; they have misread a story in which the waiting is longer than anyone expected and that is the entire point.

Then at midnight there was a cry. Not at dusk, when everyone was alert and the street was full. At the hour of the least possible readiness, when the flasks could not be refilled and the shops were shut and every one of the ten was asleep. The cry itself is wonderful — Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him — and it is the same language of going out to meet an arriving dignitary that runs through the New Testament's descriptions of that day. But it comes once, it comes without warning, and it does not wait for anybody to get organised.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then all those virgins rose and trimmed their lamps. And the foolish said to the wise, 'Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trimming meant cutting away the charred end of the wick, or re-soaking the rag if these were torches — the ordinary business of getting a light to burn properly. All ten do it. It is in the middle of that ordinary operation that five of them discover something has gone wrong.

And note precisely what they say, because the tense matters: our lamps are going out. Not our lamps will not light. Not we have no lamps. They are going out — present tense, in the process, guttering. Which means they had been burning. The foolish girls were not unlit for the whole vigil; they had a flame for hours, and it looked exactly like everybody else's, and it was still burning at eleven o'clock. The failure was never at the beginning. It came at the end of the supply, which is the only place it could ever have shown.

Then the request, and it is the heart of the parable: give us some of your oil. It is a perfectly reasonable request between friends, and it is refused, and the refusal is not unkindness. If the oil stands for an inward reality personally held, then sharing it is not stingy but impossible — in the same way that a man cannot lend another man his eyesight, or eat a meal on his behalf.

That deserves saying plainly, because a great many people are quietly relying on precisely this arrangement. A mother's faith does not cover her son. A congregation's soundness does not cover the member sitting in it. A wife's prayers, however many years of them, do not cover a husband. Godly parents, a Christian upbringing, a name on a roll, a family with a long history in the church — none of it is transferable, and every one of those is a flask belonging to somebody else. On that night, five girls who had known the other five all their lives discovered that proximity carries nothing across.

None of which makes such prayers useless; God has answered ten thousand of them, and a praying mother is one of the great instruments in his hand. The point is narrower and harder. They are not a substitute. They may be the very means by which somebody comes to have oil of his own — but he will have to have it of his own.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the wise answered, saying, 'Since there will not be enough for us and for you, go rather to the dealers and buy for yourselves.' And while they were going to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the marriage feast, and the door was shut."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go rather to the dealers and buy for yourselves. It sounds like practical advice and it is an impossible errand, and everyone listening knew it. It is midnight in a village. The dealers are asleep, the shops are shuttered, and the procession is already in the street. The advice is not cruel; it is simply the only thing left to say, and the parable lets it stand as a measure of how late it now is.

And while they are away, the thing they have waited all night for happens without them. That is the sting of the timing: not that they were absent from the vigil, but that they were absent for the one minute that mattered, and they were absent because they were off trying to fix the problem. The last-minute scramble is not merely too late. It is the very thing that keeps them from the door.

Then four words. And the door was shut.

They are among the quietest and most frightening words in the New Testament, and the quietness is the point — no thunder, no announcement, no scene. In that world the household door was barred once the wedding party was inside, because everyone had come and the night was over and there was no further reason to keep it open. The shutting was not an act of hostility. It was the ordinary end of an evening, and it was final.

Consider who shut it. Not a servant, not an official, not fate. The bridegroom is inside and answers from inside, and the door is his door; it was he they had come to escort, and he who had been waited for, and he who closes it. That is the hardest fact in the parable and there is no way round it.

But weigh what he is doing by telling the story at all. He is describing, in advance and in detail, exactly what it will look like when that door closes — the cry, the scramble, the shops, the four words. A man who intended to catch people out would not publish the method. The warning is itself the mercy, and it is issued while the door is standing wide and the sun is up and there is all the time in the world to find a flask.

verseByVerse.quote: "Afterward the other virgins came also, saying, 'Lord, lord, open to us.' But he answered, 'Truly, I say to you, I do not know you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Lord, lord" — the same double address of Matthew 7:21–23, where those who prophesied in Jesus' name are told "I never knew you." The connection is deliberate. Knowledge here is the intimate, covenant knowledge of personal relationship — not information about Christ but genuine union with him through faith. "I do not know you" is the definitive eschatological verdict on nominal religion: all the external trappings of Christianity (attending the wedding, carrying a lamp, calling him Lord) without the inward reality of new birth and living faith. There are no more terrible words in Scripture.

And now a word must be said to the reader those words have frightened, because this chapter will produce that reader by the hundred. Three parables in a row, and in every one of them somebody who looked like an insider is shut outside: five girls who were invited, a servant who was trusted, a crowd who called him Lord. A tender conscience closes the chapter and asks the obvious question — is that me? Am I one of the five?

Then look hard at the ones who are actually condemned here, and notice what none of them is doing. The foolish virgins are not anxious; they are untroubled right up to the midnight cry, and it never crosses their minds that anything is missing. The one-talent servant is not worried about pleasing his master; he is resentful, and calls him a hard man to his face. The goats are not lying awake wondering whether they have neglected anyone; they are genuinely astonished to hear that they did. Not one of the lost in this entire chapter is troubled about their standing. The very fear you are feeling is the one thing that none of them had. This book has already said the same thing in another place, about another terror — that the man who dreads having committed the unforgivable sin has given the surest evidence that he has not (see on 12:31-32). It is worth hearing twice.

Where, then, does assurance come from? Not from what the foolish girls tried. They went off at midnight to buy oil in a hurry, and that frantic scramble to get right at the last moment is precisely the thing that failed. Assurance is not manufactured by inspecting your own lamp in a panic — that examination will always find too little, because it is looking in the wrong place. It comes from the Bridegroom: from coming to him now, tonight, while the door stands wide, and from the fact that he has never yet turned away one person who came. "Whoever comes to me I will never cast out" is the promise, and it has no small print about how much oil you brought.

So let the warning do its own work and no more. It is real, and it is meant to be felt; Jesus did not tell it to soothe anybody. But its purpose is to send you to him this evening, not to convince you that you are already outside. A warning that drives you to the door is doing exactly what it was given to do. A warning that persuades you the door is shut has been misread. It is still open. That is the entire reason he described what it looks like when it closes.

verseByVerse.quote: "Watch therefore, for you do not know the day or the hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The moral Jesus draws from his own parable contains an oddity that almost nobody notices, and noticing it changes what the word means for the rest of a Christian life.

Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour. Therefore — because of the story just told. But in the story just told, every single one of the ten was asleep when he came, and five of them were commended anyway. If watching meant staying awake, the parable would have condemned all ten, and Jesus has just gone out of his way to tell us that the sleep was not the problem.

So watchfulness here cannot mean vigilance in the moment. It means being provisioned. The five wise girls were unconscious at the hour of the cry and were entirely ready, because everything that made them ready had been done in the afternoon. Their readiness was a state rather than an activity, and it went on being true while they slept.

That is enormously freeing and rather more demanding than the alternative. Freeing, because no Christian is required to sustain a fever of expectancy, scanning the horizon, working himself into urgency; that is not what is being asked, and anybody who has tried it knows it cannot be kept up and produces exhaustion and guilt in about equal measure. Demanding, because it relocates the whole business to the un-urgent hours. If readiness is a state, it is built in daylight, on ordinary days, by people who are not feeling anything much.

Which is roughly what the previous chapter said with a different picture — a servant handing out food at the proper time (24:45-46), not a watchman on a wall. In both parables the person commended is doing something unremarkable when the moment comes. Watchfulness in this Gospel is the alert faithfulness of a sentry who knows his post and does not leave it, and who is therefore found at it whenever the inspection happens to fall.

And count how often he has now said the reason. No one knows that day or hour (24:36); you do not know on what day your Lord is coming (24:42); the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect (24:44); and now you know neither the day nor the hour. Four times in the space of one discourse, which is more often than he repeats almost anything else in it. Every man who has ever published a date has had to get past that sentence four times to do it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For it will be like a man going on a journey, who called his servants and entrusted to them his property. To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his ability. Then he went away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is an irony in the English here worth clearing away before anything else. Our word talent, meaning a natural aptitude, comes from this parable — the metaphor was so widely preached that the money-word turned into an ability-word. Which means most readers arrive at the text with the parable's own afterlife in their heads, and hear a story about using your gifts. It is a story about money, and the money is staggering.

A talent was about six thousand denarii, and a denarius was a day's wage. So one talent is in the region of twenty years of a labouring man's income; five talents is a century of wages. This is not a master handing out pocket money to see how the servants get on. He is putting a fortune into the hands of slaves and leaving the country, and the sheer scale is part of the meaning: what has been entrusted to the servants of Christ between his going and his coming is not small.

Then to each according to his ability, and the phrase carries two comforts and one demand. The first comfort is that nobody in this parable is handed more than he can carry; the master assessed each man before he allocated anything, and the two-talent servant was not set up to fail. The second is that nobody is handed nothing. There is no fourth servant standing empty-handed in this story, and there is no Christian anywhere who has been given no capital to trade with. The demand is that the calibration cuts both ways: being given less is not a reason to expect less to be asked.

And notice how the two parables in this chapter differ, because together they make one point that neither makes alone. The ten virgins turn on what you brought — an inward provision nobody could see. The talents turn on what you did — an outward return everybody could count. Between them they close both escape routes: a man cannot say his private faith is sound while nothing whatever comes of it, and he cannot say his record is impressive while there is no flask.

Then four words that set up everything: then he went away. No supervision, no correspondence, no timetable. The whole test happens in the master's absence, which is the only condition under which what a servant is really like can be discovered.

verseByVerse.quote: "He who had received the five talents went at once and traded with them, and he made five talents more. So also he who had the two talents made two talents more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who had received the five talents went at once and traded with them. The first two words are the whole character of the man. Not after due consideration, not once he had taken advice, not when the market looked favourable. At once — before there was time for the size of the sum to frighten him.

The verb is a merchant's word: he worked with them, put them to work, traded. Which necessarily means he put his master's money at risk, and it is worth sitting with the fact that this is the behaviour being commended. There is no way to double a fortune in the ancient world without the possibility of losing it. Whatever faithfulness means in this parable, it does not mean safety, and the master who gets his money back with interest is a master who was quite prepared to get less back.

Both men double what they were given. The five becomes ten, the two becomes four. Different sums, identical proportion — and in three verses' time, word for word, an identical commendation. The measurement is proportional throughout, which is the mercy in the arrangement: the two-talent man is never once compared to the five-talent man, and the comparison a Christian is most tempted to make is simply not one the master ever performs.

But do not soften what proportional measurement asks. Both men doubled. Neither added a modest percentage and called it a day. The standard is not that the two-talent servant may return a little because he began with a little; it is that he is expected to do with two exactly what the other did with five, which is everything he could. A small allocation is not a light one.

And there is a quiet freedom here for anyone who has spent years measuring his usefulness against somebody more gifted. The five-talent man's ten is not the standard by which the two-talent man will be judged, and never was. Whatever was put into your hands was put there deliberately, by someone who had already weighed what you could carry — and doubling it is a thing you can actually do.

verseByVerse.quote: "But he who had received the one talent went and dug in the ground and hid his master's money."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A detail of ancient law makes this verse sharper than it looks. Burying money was the recognised way of keeping a deposit safe, and it carried a legal advantage: rabbinic ruling held that a man entrusted with money who buried it in the ground was free of liability if it was stolen, whereas one who merely wrapped it in a cloth and hid it was held responsible. So the third servant did not choose the lazy option. He chose the option with the best legal protection available to him. He covered himself.

And that is why he is so uncomfortable to read about. Go through the list of what he did not do. He did not steal the talent. He did not gamble it away. He did not spend it on himself, or lose it through carelessness, or lend it to a friend who defaulted. He did not even lie about it — he still has it, all of it, and can produce it on demand. At any moment during his master's absence he could have given a complete and honest account of his conduct and come out of it perfectly well.

What he did was preserve. And preservation was not the assignment. The money was given to be used; a talent in a hole earns nothing, achieves nothing and advances nothing, and the master returns to find his capital exactly where he left it, having done precisely as much good in the world as if it had never been given.

Which is the indictment this parable exists to make, and it is aimed at a kind of failure that no church discipline has ever caught. It is not a sin of commission. Nothing here would show up in a confession, and the man himself does not think he has done anything wrong — as his defence in a few verses will make abundantly clear. He has simply removed himself from the enterprise, quietly, in a way that looks like prudence, and he is about to discover what his master calls it.

His motive is stated in his own words at verse 25, and it is neither greed nor sloth in the ordinary sense but fear — a fear that traces back to what he believed about the man he was working for. That is taken up at verses 25-26.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now after a long time the master of those servants came and settled accounts with them. And he who had received the five talents came forward, bringing five talents more, saying, 'Master, you delivered to me five talents; here, I have made five talents more.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now after a long time — and the phrase is doing the same work as the delayed bridegroom in the parable before it. Whatever else the servants had to contend with, the chief difficulty was duration. Long enough for the initial excitement of the trust to wear off; long enough for the master to become an idea rather than a presence; long enough for a buried talent to stop feeling like a decision and start feeling like a fact.

Then settled accounts with them — synairei logon, and it is not the first time in this Gospel. It is the identical phrase used of the king who wished to settle accounts with his servants in the parable of the unforgiving debtor (18:23-24). Both reckonings are comprehensive, both are initiated by the master and not requested by anybody, and both bring into the open what had been quietly true for years.

Now listen to how the faithful servant opens his mouth, because it is the whole difference between him and the man who comes third. Master, you delivered to me five talents. He begins with what he was given. Not with what he achieved, not with how hard it had been, not with the state of the market or the length of the wait. His first clause is about the gift, and the results follow as a plain fact in the second.

Set that against the third servant's opening line, four verses on: Master, I knew you to be a hard man. He begins with his opinion of the master. The two accounts diverge in their first breath, long before either man mentions a talent, and the divergence is not about performance. One servant starts with what he received; the other starts with what he thought of the giver — and everything that follows in both lives was downstream of that.

There is no anxiety in the faithful man's report and no special pleading. He does not inflate the figure, and he does not apologise for it either, which is its own kind of honesty. For a servant who has traded faithfully, the reckoning is not an ordeal to be survived. It is the day he has been working toward, and he comes forward first.

verseByVerse.quote: "His master said to him, 'Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.' And he also who had the two talents came forward, saying, 'Master, you delivered to me two talents; here, I have made two talents more.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three things are said to this man, and each is worth taking on its own.

Well done, good and faithful servant. Two words describe him, and neither is about results. Good is character; faithful is reliability. The commendation is not successful or impressive or fruitful beyond expectation, though he was all three. What is praised is the sort of man he turned out to be while nobody was checking.

You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Read that first clause again with the arithmetic in mind. Five talents is a century of a labourer's wages, and the master calls it a little. From where he stands, a fortune that took a lifetime to double was a small thing, a trial run, an entrance examination. Which recalibrates every anxiety a Christian has ever had about the size of what he was trusted with. Whatever you are carrying, and however heavy it has been, the master's own assessment of it is that it was the little one.

And the reward for work well done is more work, on a scale the servant could not previously have carried. Nothing in Scripture suggests that what waits at the end is a long rest from usefulness. The faithful are not retired. They are promoted.

Then the third thing, and it is not like the others: enter into the joy of your master. He is not handed a bonus. He is not given an estate of his own. He is invited inside — into the master's own gladness, the celebration that was already going on before he arrived and did not depend on him. That is a staggering way to end a business transaction. The servant does not receive a share of the profits; he receives a share of the owner's happiness, and the happiness was never about the money.

Then Matthew does something that costs him scroll and space and is entirely deliberate: he writes the whole commendation out a second time, word for word, for the man who brought two. Not a shorter version. Not a lesser one. The identical sentence. Whatever envy a Christian has felt toward the more gifted, and whatever false modesty he has hidden behind, both are answered by a piece of repetition an editor would have cut.

verseByVerse.quote: "His master said to him, 'Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your master.' He also who had received the one talent came forward, saying, 'Master, I knew you to be a hard man, harvesting where you did not sow, and gathering where you scattered no seed,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The commendation stands complete a second time, and then the third servant begins to speak — and what comes out of his mouth first is not an account of his conduct but a doctrine of God.

Master, I knew you to be a hard man, harvesting where you did not sow, and gathering where you scattered no seed. He has had years to prepare this, and it is a theological statement. Before he mentions the talent, before he explains the hole in the ground, he tells his master what he thinks of him. That is the order of the failure, and the parable is insisting on it: what he did with the money was a consequence, and this was the cause.

The charge itself is a charge of exploitation — you take what you have not worked for, you profit off other men's labour, you demand a return on investments you never made. It is the portrait of an owner who is impossible to satisfy and dangerous to disappoint, and a man who believes he is working for such a person will make exactly the calculation this servant made: there is nothing to gain by trying and everything to lose by failing, so the rational move is to protect yourself.

And the accusation is refuted by the thing he is holding while he makes it. He says the master reaps where he did not sow — and he is standing there with a talent in his hands that the master sowed into them. Twenty years of wages, handed over freely, with no supervision and no conditions, to a slave who owned nothing. Whatever else may be said about this master, he did not scatter no seed; the evidence is in the servant's own fist as he speaks.

Which is worth turning into a question, because bad thinking about God is not usually held as a formal belief. It sits underneath, unexamined, and shows up in behaviour long before it shows up in words. So: what do you assume, in the part of your mind that never gets audited, about the God you are serving? Is he pleased with you at the moment, or slightly disappointed? Would he be more interested in you if you were doing better? Nobody says these things aloud. Men simply act on them, and the acting looks like caution, and the caution looks like humility, and underneath it is a picture of a hard man who was never there.

verseByVerse.quote: "'so I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground. Here, you have what is yours.' But his master answered him, 'You wicked and slothful servant! You knew that I harvest where I have not sown and gather where I scattered no seed?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant's defense — "I was afraid" — is accepted as the real explanation and immediately condemned. The master's response is withering: if you believed I was as demanding as you claim, that was all the more reason to act, not to hide. The servant's logic collapses under examination: his theology of God's harshness should have produced urgency, not paralysis. "Wicked and slothful" — wickedness here is not dramatic immorality but the moral failure of willful inaction. Sloth in service of God is not a minor fault but a rejection of the master's trust. Fear of failure, when it paralyses, becomes the very failure it was afraid of.

Of the three failures in this chapter, this is the one most readers will recognise in themselves. The foolish girls are careless; the goats are indifferent; but the third servant is neither, and that is what makes him uncomfortable company. He is frightened, and frightened people are usually sincere.

Notice what he was afraid of. Not of being punished for wrongdoing — he had done nothing wrong. He was afraid of getting it wrong: of losing what he had been handed, of standing in front of his master with less than he started with. So he chose the option with no downside, and it turned out to be the only option in the parable with a guaranteed one.

The modern translations of that sentence are easy to supply. I am not gifted enough to be much use. If I try and it fails publicly, that will be worse than never having tried. Someone else already does this better than I would. I will start when I am more mature, less busy, further on, more certain. Every one of those is the third servant's speech in contemporary clothes, and every one of them sounds like modesty.

The master's reply is brutal and, oddly, a relief: you could at least have put it in the bank. The standard was never brilliance. It was any return at all — the most cautious, least impressive, minimum-effort option would have been accepted. That takes enormous pressure off anyone who has been waiting to be capable of something significant. It also removes the excuse entirely, because the minimum really was available.

And notice who does not appear in this parable. There is no servant who traded and lost. Nobody comes forward and says, I invested and it went badly. That scene is missing, and its absence is worth sitting with, because it is the scene most of us are afraid of. The failure being judged here is not the failed attempt. It is the burial.

Then the root, which the entry above has already named: he had the wrong God. He thought the master hard, and men do not take risks for someone they believe is waiting to catch them out. So the cure is not to try harder but to know God better — and the parable itself supplies the correction. Look at how this master actually behaves. He hands over staggering sums to servants and leaves the country without supervision. He is delighted rather than grudging when they succeed. And his reward is not a bonus but an invitation: enter into the joy of your master — he wants them at the party. That is not a hard man, and the God the third servant was frightened of never existed.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Then you ought to have invested my money with the bankers, and at my coming I should have received what was my own with interest. So take the talent from him and give it to him who has the ten talents.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The master's alternative is almost insultingly modest. Deposit banking was an ordinary feature of that world — the money-changers sat behind tables, trapezai, which is where the Greek word for banker comes from — and a deposit earning interest required no skill, no judgment, no nerve and no work whatever. Hand it over, take the receipt, walk away.

Notice what this does to the servant's defence. He said he was afraid of losing the money. The bank was the one option in the world that removed that risk entirely, and he did not take it either. So the fear he offered as an explanation does not actually explain his conduct; if fear of loss had been the real driver, the bankers were sitting there the whole time. Something else was going on, and the master's you ought to have exposes it in a single clause.

And the standard turns out to be far lower than anyone imagines when they first read this parable. Not brilliance. Not a doubling. Not the five-talent man's flair. The minimum acceptable return was the least impressive, least courageous, most administrative option available — and it would have been accepted. That takes an enormous weight off anyone who has been waiting until he is capable of something significant before he begins. It also removes the excuse entirely, because the minimum really was within reach.

Then the redistribution, which offends most modern readers on first hearing: take the talent from him and give it to him who has the ten. It is not a reward for being rich. The master is doing what any sensible owner does with a resource that is producing nothing — moving it to where it will be used. The talent was never the servant's property. It was capital on loan, and capital that is not working gets reassigned.

Which contains a sober principle about opportunity. What God entrusts is not held on indefinite terms regardless of use. A gift left buried long enough is not merely wasted; it is eventually taken up by somebody else, and the work gets done — the master's estate does not suffer for one servant's caution. The loss in this parable is not the master's. It is entirely the servant's.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For to everyone who has, more will be given, and he will have an abundance. But from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. And cast the worthless servant into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
To everyone who has, more will be given. Read as economics it is monstrous, and it has occasionally been quoted that way, as though Jesus were endorsing the accumulation of wealth. He is stating a law about capacity, and it is one every person has already observed. A language used is a language kept and a language neglected is gone in a decade. A muscle worked grows and a limb in plaster wastes in six weeks. A friendship maintained deepens and one left alone quietly dissolves without anyone deciding to end it. Use enlarges, disuse shrinks, and this is true of every good thing God gives, including grace.

So the sentence is not about the rich getting richer. It is about the difference between a gift that has been exercised and a gift that has been buried, and the fact that the gap between them widens by itself, every year, without anyone intending it.

Then the word the master uses for the third servant: worthless — achreios, useless, of no service. Not thief. Not traitor. Not enemy. The judgment falls on a man whose distinguishing characteristic is that nothing whatever happened because of him. He did no harm and no good; the estate was exactly as it would have been had he never been born into it. That is the whole charge, and it is heavier than it sounds.

Which is the second of the chapter's three warnings, and the three are carefully different. The first parable condemns a woman who lacked something invisible. The second condemns a man who did nothing with something valuable. And the third, shortly, will condemn people who did not notice somebody in front of them. Not one of the three is condemned for an act of wickedness. All three are condemned for an absence, and between them they cover most of the ways a respectable person is actually lost.

The consignment to outer darkness is the same formula that closed the previous chapter (24:51), and it is Matthew's settled language for exclusion. What is new here is the ground of it. The man is not thrown out for what he did to the master. He is thrown out for what he declined to do for him, having been handed a fortune and an absence long enough to use it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–46 — The Judgment of the Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Olivet Discourse closes with the Son of Man enthroned in his own glory, all the nations gathered, and the flock parted as a shepherd separates sheep from goats at evening. Both groups are judged by the same six items — food, drink, welcome, clothing, a visit in sickness, a visit in prison — and both are astonished, the sheep because they cannot remember doing any of it and the goats because they never noticed the chance. The King's ground in each case is the same: as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me. Note that this is no longer a parable; it is a description.
verseByVerse.theology: Who are the least of these my brothers? The narrower reading observes that in Matthew my brothers nearly always means Jesus' disciples, and that the least echoes the little ones and sent messengers of ch. 10, so the nations are judged by their response to the King through his despised people. The broader reading takes it of any suffering person. The first is probably the passage's own point; the principle underneath it is true wherever need is found. Either way the doorway is guarded before a single deed is named: the sheep inherit — nobody earns an inheritance — a kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world, that is, before any of these people existed and before there was anything to reward. The works are produced as evidence, never as the purchase price. Note also the asymmetry at v. 41: the blessing is by my Father and the curse is attributed to nobody, and the fire was prepared for the devil and his angels, not for human beings. And at v. 46 one adjective governs both destinies, which is why the punishment cannot quietly expire unless the life does too.
verseByVerse.examples: Everything on the King's list is a service to somebody who cannot repay it and mostly cannot even report it — which is precisely why it is the list. Prison is the sharpest case: Roman prisons did not feed their inmates, so a man without visitors went hungry, and carrying food through that door announced publicly that you were associated with a criminal. The modern equivalents are the illness where the cards stop after three weeks, the man whose trouble is his own fault, and the visit to someone with dementia who will not remember by teatime that you came. Note what the goats' defence actually admits: we would have, had we recognised you. Their service was available to importance and not to need, and they state it themselves in front of the assembled nations. So the test is whether the trouble you take over a person varies with what that person can do for you. And the sheep could not produce a list of their own good deeds — which is worth weighing by anyone who could.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne. Before him will be gathered all the nations, and he will separate people one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Something changes at this verse and it is easy to read past. The two preceding passages began the kingdom of heaven will be like and it will be like a man going on a journey. This one does not. It begins when the Son of Man comes in his glory, and it never stops being a description. There is a comparison inside it — sheep and goats — but the frame is not a parable at all. He has stopped illustrating and started announcing.

And notice whose glory it is. Two chapters earlier the Son of Man was coming in the glory of his Father (16:27); here it is his glory, and his throne, and the angels are his attendants. This is the Son of Man of Daniel 7, who came to the Ancient of Days and was given dominion — and who is now seated, with every nation of every century assembled in front of him, doing what only God does in the Old Testament, which is judge the earth.

Then the image, and it is more ordinary than it looks. Sheep and goats grazed together in the same mixed flock all day, which is exactly how a Palestinian shepherd worked. They were separated in the evening, because goats needed shelter from the cold night and sheep did not. So the separation was a routine, daily, entirely unremarkable operation, performed at speed by a man who could tell one animal from another at a glance without breaking stride.

That is the concrete comfort buried in a terrifying scene. The sorting of the human race looks, from where we stand, like an impossible task — billions of people, mixed motives, hidden hearts, hypocrites indistinguishable from saints. This chapter has already twice insisted that the difference cannot be seen from outside. To the shepherd it is the work of an evening. He does not investigate; he recognises.

And all the nations — panta ta ethne — settles the scope beyond argument. Not Israel, not the church, not the religious. Every people group and every individual within them, including everyone who never heard of this scene and everyone who was confident it would not happen. Nobody is outside the summons, and the shepherd is the man who was crucified.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he will place the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A small piece of local colour makes the picture sharper. The sheep of that country were predominantly white and the goats predominantly black or dark brown, so once the flocks were parted the two groups were visibly, unmistakably distinct from a distance — two blocks of colour where a moment before there had been one mingled crowd.

Right and left are not arbitrary. In that world the right hand was the place of honour and favour, and this Gospel has already used it at its highest pitch: sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet, the psalm Jesus quoted against the Pharisees three chapters ago (22:44; Ps 110:1). To be placed at the King's right is to be given the position of the honoured.

But the important thing is what the separation does and does not do. It does not create the difference. Nothing happens in this scene to make one animal a sheep and another a goat; the shepherd sorts what is already the case, and the sorting is a revelation rather than a verdict reached on the evidence of the day.

Which is the third time this chapter has said the same thing in three different pictures. Five girls out of ten had a flask, and nobody could tell which. Three servants received the same trust from the same master, and only the reckoning showed what each had done with it. Now one flock grazes together until evening. In every case the division runs through the middle of a group that looked uniform, and in every case it becomes visible only at the end.

That is precisely what Jesus said earlier about the wheat and the weeds — leave them growing together until the harvest, because pulling at them now uproots both (13:29-30). The present church is a mixed flock, and it is meant to be, and no amount of vigilance will sort it. Two things follow, and they are both freeing. You are not the shepherd, and the responsibility for identifying goats has never once been given to you. And the only animal in the flock whose position you have any business examining is the one you are standing in.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the King will say to those on his right, 'Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before a single deed is mentioned, the question of how anybody gets to the right hand has already been settled twice over in one sentence — and it is worth slowing down, because this is the passage most often produced as proof that heaven is earned.

The first word is inherit. Nobody has ever earned an inheritance. It is the one form of getting that depends entirely on whose family you belong to, and a man who worked twice as hard as his brother does not thereby inherit twice as much. The verb settles the matter before the list of works begins.

The second is prepared for you from the foundation of the world. The kingdom being handed over was ready before the universe was made — which is to say, before the first sheep gave the first cup of water, before any of these people existed, and before there was anything whatever to reward. The works in this passage are named in the courtroom as evidence. They are nowhere named as the purchase price, and the timing makes it impossible that they could be.

Then the list starts, and the striking thing about it is how ordinary it is. Hungry, and you gave me food. Thirsty, and you gave me a drink. A stranger, and you took me in. Not one item on the list requires money, training, gifting, a platform, an organisation, or any particular ability. A child could do most of it. The kingdom's evidence turns out to be bread, water and an opened door.

Note the third one especially, because it is the one modern readers skate over. I was a stranger and you welcomed me — xenos, the outsider, the person with no claim on you and no connection to you, who does not belong and whom nobody would blame you for ignoring. Hospitality to people who already matter to us is a pleasure, not a virtue. This is the other kind, and it costs an evening and a certain amount of social awkwardness, and it is on the list the King reads out at the end of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I was naked and you clothed me, I was sick and you visited me, I was in prison and you came to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list continues: clothing the naked, visiting the sick, coming to those imprisoned. These works represent costly, inconvenient, personally engaged care — not institutional programs from a safe distance but the presence of one person with another in their suffering. "You visited me" (epeskepsasthe) carries the force of the shepherd searching for the sheep, the God who sees and comes. The prison visit is perhaps the most striking: it requires entering a place of shame and social stigma. The extent of Christian mercy is meant to match the extent of human need, and these verses define that need comprehensively — physical, social, relational, communal.

Every word of this passage is aimed at the people doing the visiting. But there is somebody else standing in the scene, and the chapter never turns to speak to them — so it is worth doing here.

If you are the one who is ill, or hungry, or out of work, or alone in a hospital bay, or inside a prison of some kind — a literal one, or the sort made of illness or shame or debt or a house nobody calls at — then read what the King actually says about you. He does not say, I saw what they did for you. He says they did it to me.

That claim runs in both directions, and both matter. Where you were visited, Christ counts it as a visit paid to himself. And where you were not — the phone that did not ring, the church that meant to come and did not, the friends who found your trouble awkward and drifted — he counts that as a neglect of himself, and he says so in front of the assembled nations. He is not a spectator of your situation. He has stepped into it and put his own name on it.

Two things follow for anyone in that position. Your circumstances are not invisible to heaven, however invisible they feel from the ward or the flat or the cell; the King has made his identification with people in exactly your position the criterion by which he sorts the human race, which is not the behaviour of someone who has overlooked you. And the kindness you have received was never charity handed down to you from above. It was Christ being served in you — which quietly reverses the whole transaction, and may matter a great deal to someone who has always hated being helped.

He also knows the ground he is standing on. He was hungry for forty days in a wilderness, thirsty on a cross, a stranger with nowhere to lay his head, stripped bare in front of a crowd at his execution, and led away under armed guard. There is not one category on this list that he has not personally occupied. He is not describing a class of people he has heard about.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the righteous will answer him, saying, 'Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink? And when did we see you a stranger and welcome you, or naked and clothe you?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most remarkable thing in this scene is not the King's verdict. It is that the people being commended do not recognise the evidence.

Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you? This is not modesty and it is not a polite deflection of praise. They are asking a real question, because they genuinely do not have the memory. They are being shown a record they cannot recall compiling, and their reaction is bewilderment.

Which tells us something exact about how those acts were done. Nothing was filed. There was no ledger, no mental note, no quiet satisfaction stored away for later — because a man who is keeping account can always produce the account, and these people cannot produce anything. The deeds went out of their minds within the week, the way it does when you help somebody for the ordinary reason that they needed help and you were there.

So there is a test in this, and it is uncomfortable in an unusual direction. Could you produce a list? Most people, asked what they have done for the poor or the sick or the stranger, can retrieve two or three examples fairly quickly — and the retrieval is the problem, not the deeds. The ones commended here could not have answered that question. What they had done had never been converted into evidence about themselves.

One guard, because this can be twisted into a reason to stop planning any good at all, on the grounds that self-consciousness spoils it. It does not follow. A man may deliberately set aside a Saturday to visit a prison, plan it in his diary, and arrange the transport; the deliberateness is not the trouble. The trouble is keeping the receipt. Do it on purpose, and then let it go — and if in forty years you find you cannot remember much of it, you are in the company of the people standing at the King's right hand and asking him what he is talking about.

One more thing about their question, which becomes visible only when the chapter is read whole. Listen to how they address him: Lord, when did we see you hungry? Now listen to the five shut outside the wedding: Lord, lord, open to us (v. 11). And in a few verses, the goats: Lord, when did we see you hungry? — the same word, in the same chapter, from all three groups. Everybody in Matthew 25 calls him Lord. Nobody in this chapter is condemned for failing to, and nobody is saved for managing it, which is exactly what he had said at the close of the Sermon: not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven (7:21). The title is the one thing the whole chapter holds in common.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when did we see you sick or in prison and visit you?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last two on the list are the costliest, and it is worth being specific about why, because they are the two most easily left to somebody else.

Visiting the sick is unpleasant in ways nobody admits. There is a risk of catching whatever it is. There is nothing to achieve — you cannot fix anything, and you will leave having accomplished nothing measurable. You will not know what to say, and much of what you do say will be wrong. And illness is dull; the third visit is harder than the first, and the twentieth is when almost everybody stops.

The prison visit is harder still, and in the ancient world it carried a weight that has been lost. Roman prisons did not feed their inmates properly. A prisoner ate what his family and friends carried in to him, which meant that a man with no visitors did not merely feel forgotten — he went hungry, and could die of it. You came to me was not a courtesy in that world. It was a supply line. And to be seen carrying food through that door was to announce publicly that you were associated with a criminal, which many were not willing to do.

The modern equivalents are not hard to find and are usually going unattended right now. The long illness, where the cards stop after the third week and the casseroles after the second month, and the person is still ill in the second year. The man whose troubles are his own fault, where visiting looks like approval. The relative in a secure ward. And most purely of all, the visit to someone with advanced dementia — who will not recognise you, cannot thank you, will not remember by teatime that you came, and cannot tell anybody you were kind. There is no possible return on that visit of any kind whatever.

Which is exactly why it appears on this list. Everything the King names here is a service rendered to somebody who cannot repay it and mostly cannot even report it. That is the whole class of action he has chosen to identify himself with, and it is the class of action the world has no way of noticing.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the King will answer them, 'Truly, I say to you, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most remarkable claim in the passage: the King identifies himself with the suffering recipients of mercy. "My brothers" — in Matthew, this term refers primarily to Jesus' disciples (12:48–50; 28:10), suggesting the primary referent is the persecuted missionary community. But the Christological claim is broader: Jesus is present in human suffering in a way that makes care for the least a direct encounter with him. This does not collapse the distinction between Christ and humanity; it shows that his lordship reaches us through his identification with the vulnerable. To ignore them is to ignore him; to serve them is to serve him.

It is worth being clear about the debate here, because much hangs on it. Who are "the least of these my brothers"? Two readings compete. The narrower one, favoured by many careful interpreters, notes that in Matthew "my brothers" nearly always means Jesus' disciples (12:49-50; 28:10), and that "the least" echoes the little ones and the sent messengers of chapter 10, where receiving a disciple with a cup of cold water is receiving Christ (10:40-42). On this reading the nations are judged by how they treated Christ's people — especially his persecuted missionaries — which is really a judgment on how they received the gospel those people carried. The broader reading takes "the least" as any suffering human being, so that Christ is met in every hungry, sick, or imprisoned person on earth. The wisest course honours both. The passage's first point is almost certainly the narrower one: a watching world will be sorted by its response to the King through his often-despised people. But the principle underneath it — that the King so identifies with the lowly that what is done to them is done to him — is gloriously true wherever human need is found, and Scripture everywhere commands mercy to all (Gal 6:10; Luke 10:25-37). So the text is not a licence to reduce the gospel to social work, nor an excuse to spiritualise away the plain call to feed and clothe and visit. And guard the doorway: even here the sheep "inherit" a kingdom "prepared from the foundation of the world" (v. 34) — their mercy is the fruit and proof of grace already given, never the price that buys heaven. They are surprised by their own good works precisely because those works flowed from a renewed heart, not a calculating one.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he will say to those on his left, 'Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you gave me no food, I was thirsty and you gave me no drink,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set the two sentences side by side, because the asymmetry between them is deliberate and it is the most merciful thing in the passage.

To the right: Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. To the left: Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

Two differences. The blessing is attributed — blessed by my Father; the curse is attributed to nobody. And the kingdom was prepared for you, while the fire was prepared for someone else entirely. Hell, on the King's own account, was not built with human beings in mind. It was made for the devil and his angels, and the people going there are going somewhere that was never designed for them, having attached themselves to its original occupant. Heaven is a home prepared for guests. Hell is not, and even in the sentence of condemnation Jesus takes the trouble to say so.

Then the charge sheet, and it is the same list as before with every verb negated. What is striking is what is not on it. Nobody is accused of beating a prisoner, or turning a hungry man away from the door, or mocking the sick. There is no cruelty in the indictment at all. The whole case against them is a series of things that did not happen.

That deserves a guard, because it can crush the wrong reader. Anyone who has ever failed somebody in trouble — and everybody has, and most of us can name them — will read this and hear a sentence passed on himself. But what is being described here is not an instance. It is a life: a settled pattern with no exceptions in it, running to the end, in a person who produces at the judgment not one occasion when he did otherwise. And the sheep are not presented as people who never failed anybody either. They are simply people in whom something was true, and it showed, and they did not know it was showing.

verseByVerse.quote: "'I was a stranger and you did not welcome me, naked and you did not clothe me, sick and in prison and you did not visit me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the fourth time the list has been recited in ten verses — spoken to the sheep, queried by the sheep, spoken to the goats, and about to be queried by the goats. Six items, four times over. Nobody talks like that by accident. It is repetition used as a hammer, and by the end of the passage a hearer could recite the six in order, which is presumably the intention.

And what is being condemned, said as plainly as possible, is indifference. Not malice. The goats did not hate the stranger; they had no particular feelings about him at all. They did not refuse the sick man; they simply never went. Every charge in this list is an absence rather than an act, and the King treats those absences as the moral equivalent of a verdict.

Which is worth understanding rather than merely deploring, because nobody walks past need by deciding to. The mechanisms are entirely respectable. There is busyness, which is real and not an excuse anyone invents. There is distance, so that the need is known about rather than seen, and known-about need has never moved anybody. There is the reasonable assumption that somebody else is handling it, that there are agencies and professionals and a pastoral team. There is fatigue, because the need is endless and a person cannot weep at every item on the news. And there is the small, quiet postponement — not now, not this week — which is the wicked servant's sentence from the previous chapter in a gentler key.

Not one of those is wickedness. Together they are how a life ends up with nothing on the list, and how a person arrives at the judgment genuinely puzzled about what he is supposed to have done wrong.

So the practical question this verse puts is not whether you are a cruel person. Almost nobody reading it is. The question is whether anything at all has been costing you lately — an evening, a Saturday, a sum of money you noticed spending, a friendship with somebody who cannot do a thing for you in return. If the honest answer is nothing, that is worth knowing now, while the list can still be added to.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they also will answer, saying, 'Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to you?' Then he will answer them, saying, 'Truly, I say to you, as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The goats ask the same question the sheep asked, and it looks at first like the same bewilderment. It is not, and the difference is buried in what their question actually claims.

Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to you? The implication is unmistakable, and they mean it sincerely: we would have. Had we recognised you, we would have acted. We are not the sort of people who leave the Lord of glory standing in the road.

And that is a confession, though they do not hear themselves making it. They are saying that their service was available — but it was available to importance. Show them a King and they would have moved; show them a hungry nobody and they had other things on. Which is precisely the accusation, stated by the defendants in their own defence. The sheep never asked who the person was. The goats would have needed to know.

Then the King's reply strips the last cover away: as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to me. Note that my brothers does not appear in this second version; it is simply the least of these. Whatever weight that carries for the debated question of who the brothers are (see on v. 40), the point being pressed here is the identification itself, and it is total. There is no gap between the two. Doing nothing for the one was doing nothing for him, and no further step of reasoning is offered or needed.

So the test the passage leaves is a simple and searching one, and it can be run on any ordinary week. Does the amount of trouble you take over a person vary with what that person can do for you? Everybody's does to some extent, and the goats' mistake was not that theirs did but that theirs did entirely. The King has arranged the final examination so that the people who cannot repay you are the ones he is standing behind, and he has told us in advance, which means the arrangement is not a trap. It is an invitation with the answers printed.

verseByVerse.quote: "And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parallelism is exact and sobering: the same adjective ("eternal") governs both punishment and life, ruling out any interpretation that makes the punishment temporary or the life exhaustible. Both are equally permanent, equally real, equally the consequence of relationship — or its absence — with the Son of Man. Calvin writes that the hope of eternal life is the Christian's anchor in every trial, and the reality of eternal punishment is the ultimate ground of urgency in mission. The Olivet Discourse ends here: the King has spoken, the judgment is certain, the separation is coming, and the call of chapters 24–25 is to live now in light of that final day.

The argument in that first sentence deserves to be named, because it is answering something. Two alternatives to everlasting punishment are held today by people who love the Bible. Universalism says that all will be saved in the end, the fire being purifying rather than final. Annihilationism, or conditional immortality, says the lost are not tormented for ever but are finally destroyed — they cease to exist. That second view is not a fringe position; John Stott held it tentatively and with evident sorrow, and others of real godliness have followed him. It should be argued with, not sneered at.

But it must be argued with, and this verse is where the argument lands, because Jesus puts both destinies in one sentence under one adjective: eternal punishment, eternal life. The word need not by itself mean unending — it can carry the sense of "belonging to the age to come" — and that is precisely why the force here is not the bare word but the balance. Whatever weight you give it on the right-hand side, you must give it on the left, for it is the same word in the same breath about the same day. If the punishment quietly runs out, so does the life. The sentence ties the two together with one knot, and there is no way to loosen it at one end only.

Which leaves the question underneath, the one that is really being asked when people press these alternatives: how can a God of love do this? Two things are worth holding. The first is who is speaking. More is said about judgment by Jesus than by anyone else in Scripture — the outer darkness, the closed door, the fire prepared for the devil are all his images, not some later hardening of a gentler message. And this is the same voice that broke over Jerusalem two chapters ago, how often would I have gathered your children, and that within days would be nailed to a cross precisely so that people would not have to hear the words in verse 41. The doctrine did not reach us from hard men. It came from the tenderest voice in the Bible, and it cost him everything to open a way out of it.

The second is how a Christian should carry it. Not with relish, ever — "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD" (Ezek 33:11), and any believer who finds this doctrine comfortable has not understood it. Nor with speculation: Scripture pictures the same reality as fire and as darkness, which cannot both be photographs, and the pictures are given to tell us that the loss is total, not to furnish a map. What we are told is enough, and Calvin's point above is the right response to it — this is the ground of urgency in mission. If it is true, no one who believes it can be casual about the person sitting next to them.

25.theology: Faith and works in the final judgment. The parable of the sheep and goats is sometimes misread as teaching salvation by charity. It teaches the opposite: those who are blessed by the Father (elect from the foundation of the world, v. 34) demonstrate their status through the fruit of mercy. Works do not earn salvation; they reveal it. James and Paul are not in contradiction: Paul says we are justified by faith alone (Rom 3:28); James says a faith without works is dead (Jas 2:26). Matthew 25 stands with James: the living faith that justifies is the faith that produces mercy. The absence of mercy is evidence not of an imperfect Christian but of a heart that has never truly encountered the merciful King.
25.examples:
Then: The early church was remarkable for its care of the poor, the sick, the orphan, and the widow — in a culture that largely left the vulnerable to die. Pagans observed and were astonished. The church was not performing charity as a strategy; it was loving Christ in the face of the neighbour. The Roman emperor Julian complained: “The godless Galileans feed not only their own poor but ours also.”

Now: The parable of the talents is a rebuke of every Christian who sits on their gifts out of fear — fear of failure, fear of criticism, fear of the cost. Every person reading these words has been entrusted with something by the master: a relationship, a skill, a platform, a message, an opportunity. The question at the end will not be “how much did you have?” but “what did you do with what you were given?” Faithfulness, not magnitude, is the measure.

26.title: The Last Supper and Gethsemane
26.text: <sup>26</sup>Now as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to the disciples, and said, “Take, eat; this is my body.” <sup>27</sup>And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, saying, “Drink of it, all of you, <sup>28</sup>for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. <sup>29</sup>I tell you I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom.” <sup>39</sup>And going a little farther he fell on his face and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” <sup>53</sup>Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels? <sup>54</sup>But how then should the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must be so? <sup>63</sup>But Jesus remained silent. And the high priest said to him, “I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God.” <sup>64</sup>Jesus said to him, “You have said so. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.”
26.overview:
Chapter 26 is the most theologically dense chapter in Matthew.
