In a single evening Jesus institutes the Lord’s Supper, reveals his betrayer, predicts Peter’s denial, agonises in Gethsemane, is arrested by a crowd with swords, and is condemned by the Sanhedrin. Every scene is simultaneously the action of history and the fulfilment of Scripture: Judas’ betrayal for thirty pieces of silver (Zech 11:12–13), the scattering of the disciples (Zech 13:7), the suffering servant (Isa 53), the enthroned Son of Man (Dan 7:13).

Gethsemane is the chapter’s theological centre. Jesus does not walk to the cross with stoic detachment; he falls on his face and prays that the cup might pass. His agony is real — the weight of the wrath of God against sin, the drinking of the cup of Jeremiah 25 and Isaiah 51, the bearing of the curse. And then: “not as I will, but as you will.” This is the most perfect prayer ever prayed — complete honesty about human desire, complete submission to divine will. The cross is not the defeat of the Son; it is the triumph of obedience.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–46 — The Plot, the Anointing, the Last Supper, and Gethsemane
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus finishes the last of his five discourses and immediately names the day of his own execution. The council meets to arrange it and rules out Passover; a woman in a leper's house breaks a year's wages over his head and is scolded for waste; Judas goes out and lets the priests set a price. In a borrowed upper room Jesus keeps the Passover with the twelve, names his betrayer, and gives them bread and a cup as his body and his blood of the covenant. Then the Hallel, the walk to Gethsemane, the prediction that all of them will fall away, and three hours on the ground in an olive grove asking for the cup to pass.
verseByVerse.theology: The section's engine is the difference between what appears to be happening and what is happening. The council schedules the arrest for after the feast and he dies during it; Judas names no price and lets them value the Son of God at the compensation rate for a gored slave (Ex 21:32; Zech 11:12-13); the disciples see waste where Jesus sees a burial anointing. At the table the new covenant is inaugurated in the words of Sinai with one word changed — my blood of the covenant (Ex 24:8) — and Jeremiah's promise of forgiveness is attached to a cup. Gethsemane then shows that the atonement was not endured from behind any protective screen: Matthew's verb for his distress is the strongest available in the Greek of the period, and the cup is the Old Testament cup of wrath (Isa 51:17; Ps 75:8). He asked three times for it to pass, was refused, and got up and went to meet the betrayer.
verseByVerse.examples: Three things in this section are unusually usable. The woman's jar had to be broken to be poured, so the extravagance was decided before a drop touched him — and the test she leaves is whether anything in your Christian life has lately been indefensible on grounds of usefulness. You always have the poor with you is quoted to excuse doing nothing, and it is a quotation of Deuteronomy 15:11, where the permanence of poverty is the stated reason for permanent open-handedness; he quotes the middle of the verse and lets the table supply the end. And Gethsemane is the passage for anyone in real mental anguish: he said out loud how bad it was, asked friends to stay near him, asked three times for it to be lifted, and fell on his face — and what heaven sent was not the removal of the cup but strength to drink it. That is very often the shape of the answer, and it is not a lesser one.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had finished all these sayings, he said to his disciples, "You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew has used this formula four times already, at the close of each great block of teaching (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1). Here he uses it for the fifth and last time, and he adds one word: when Jesus had finished all these sayings. All of them. The teaching is over. From this sentence to the end of the book he does almost nothing but suffer.

And the first thing he does with the silence is name the date of his own execution. You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified. Nobody speaks like that. Men who expect to be killed may say so in general terms; they do not hand their friends a timetable with the method on it. He has told them three times already that this was coming (16:21; 17:22-23; 20:18-19), each time in more detail, and now he gives them the day.

Note which day. Not merely Friday, but Passover — the feast that commemorated a night when the blood of a lamb on a doorpost turned away a judgment that would otherwise have fallen on the household inside. Israel had kept that meal every year for something like fourteen centuries, and every year it pointed at something. He arranges to die during it.

Then the verb: will be delivered up — paradidotai, handed over. It is passive, and the passive hides a great deal. Judas hands him over to the priests; the priests hand him over to Pilate; Pilate hands him over to be crucified. But Paul reaches behind all three: he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom 8:32). The chain of betrayals runs all the way back, and at the top of it the Father is handing over the Son, and the Son is walking toward the date he has just announced.

Which sets the terms for everything that follows, and it is worth fixing in mind now, because the next fifty verses will show him bound, struck, spat on, and led about by men who appear to be running the operation. Not one of them surprises him. He named the week.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the palace of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas, and plotted together in order to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two meetings are held in these opening verses, and Matthew sets them side by side deliberately. In the first, a man speaks openly to his friends about his own death. In the second, a group of powerful men meet behind a closed door to arrange it.

Caiaphas is worth knowing. He held the high priesthood from about AD 18 to 36 — an extraordinary run, when his predecessors had lasted a year or two apiece and were removed by the Roman governor at will. He was also the son-in-law of Annas, the previous holder, and between them that family kept the office in its own hands for decades. A man does not survive eighteen years in a post held at Rome's pleasure without being an exceptional political operator. That is who is chairing this meeting: not a fanatic, but a manager, protecting an arrangement that worked.

And the arrangement is what is really being defended. John records Caiaphas making the case in plain words a few weeks earlier — if we let him go on, the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation, and it is better that one man die for the people (Jn 11:48-50). Read as politics that is not even unreasonable. It is the calculation any careful administrator makes: one life against a national catastrophe. He is not cackling. He is managing risk.

Which is the thing worth pausing over. The men who killed Jesus were not monsters and did not think of themselves as opposing God. They were the responsible party, the ones who held things together, doing what responsible people do when something destabilising appears — containing it. Every one of them could have given a reasoned account of his conduct, and several would have described it as a painful duty.

David had already described this scene: the kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed (Ps 2:2). The psalm's next line is what the conspirators never suspect. He who sits in the heavens laughs. Not because their power is imaginary — they will use it, and it will hurt — but because the meeting they think they are convening to end this man's work is the meeting at which his work begins.

verseByVerse.quote: But they said, "Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar among the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One sentence of minutes from that meeting survives, and it is the most quietly devastating verse in the chapter. Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar among the people.

The concern is crowd control. Jerusalem at Passover was not the city of ordinary weeks; pilgrims poured in from across the empire, and the population may have swelled several times over. Josephus, counting lambs, arrives at figures for the festival crowds that are almost certainly inflated but tell you how the thing felt: the city was packed, tense, and full of men who had come to celebrate a national deliverance from a foreign power while a foreign power watched from the fortress. A popular teacher arrested in front of that congregation could have set the whole place alight, and the Roman garrison was reinforced at festivals for exactly that reason. So: wait until the pilgrims go home.

They did not wait. Within about seventy-two hours Jesus is dead, and he dies at Passover, on the one occasion in the calendar the council had specifically ruled out. The single scheduling decision these men made is the single thing they did not get.

And consider what had to happen for their plan to fail in exactly that way. They needed someone inside the group, willing, who knew where he went at night — and while they were still saying not during the feast, Judas was on his way to them. Nobody arranged that in the room. The council set a date and a man they had never met unset it, for money, of his own free will, for his own reasons.

Which is how providence appears to work almost everywhere in Scripture: not by suspending anybody's freedom but by employing it. Caiaphas made a calculation and meant it; Judas made a choice and meant it; and the outcome was that the Lamb of God was killed during the feast of the lamb, at the hour appointed before the world was made. No one in that room was overruled. They were simply used, and the used never notice.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came up to him with an alabaster flask of very expensive ointment, and she poured it on his head as he reclined at table.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Notice first whose house this is. Simon the leper — and the name has stuck to the man, which means everyone knew what he had been. A leper's house was a place no respectable person entered and no respectable person ate in. Either Simon had been healed, presumably by the man now reclining at his table, or the house still carried the name of its ruined owner. Either way, the last meal of hospitality Jesus receives before his death is taken in a house that religious Jerusalem would have crossed the road to avoid.

Then the flask. Alabaster was the standard container for costly perfume, sealed at the neck; nard was imported from the mountains of northern India, carried overland for months, and John prices this one at three hundred denarii — very nearly a labouring man's wages for a year. Whatever the woman's circumstances, this was not a gift she could repeat. It may well have been everything she had, or a family inheritance, or the security a woman without a husband kept for a disaster.

And to use it she had to break the neck of the flask. That is the detail to hold. A sealed alabaster jar cannot be opened by halves; there is no pouring out a measured portion and keeping the rest for later. She broke it, which means that before a drop touched him she had already decided that none of it was coming back. The extravagance was not in the gesture. It was in the decision that preceded the gesture, taken while the jar was still whole in her hands.

Then she poured it on his head. Anointing the head is not what you do to a guest — that is a courtesy of oil, a small thing. Pouring a flask over the head is what Samuel did to David and what was done to Israel's kings and priests at their installation. In a leper's house, at a private supper, an unnamed woman performs a coronation.

She had understood something the men around that table had not, though he had told them three times. The one in front of her was going to die, he was the anointed King, and the moment for arithmetic had passed. It is a striking fact about this Gospel that the person who reads the situation correctly, when the twelve cannot, is a woman whose name Matthew does not even record.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the disciples saw it, they were indignant, saying, "Why this waste? For this ointment could have been sold for a large sum and given to the poor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The objection is unanswerable, which is what makes it dangerous. Three hundred denarii would have fed a great many hungry people in a city with a great many hungry people in it. Nobody at that table was wrong about the arithmetic, and if the question were put in a church meeting today it would carry the room.

The word they use is worth having: eis ti hē apoleia hautē — why this destruction, this ruin, this loss. It is the language of an asset written off. They are looking at an act of worship and seeing a balance sheet with a hole in it, and they are genuinely indignant, and their indignation has a moral shape to it. That is precisely the trouble. Bad motives are easy to identify; this is a good motive standing in the wrong place, which is much harder to see and impossible to argue with.

John tells us that at least one of them had a private reason — Judas kept the money bag and helped himself (Jn 12:6) — but there is no sign the rest were dissembling. They meant it. Which is worse, in a way: the eleven who loved him could look at the most beautiful act recorded in the Gospels and see waste.

So it is worth asking what kind of religion cannot recognise worship when it is standing in front of it. It is the religion that has learned to justify everything by usefulness — where the question asked of any expenditure of time or money or attention is what does it achieve, and where a thing done simply because Christ is worth it has no category to sit in. Such a faith is often very active and very defensible and it can run a long time without anyone noticing what has gone out of it.

The test is not hard to apply. Has anything in your Christian life recently been indefensible on the grounds of usefulness — money given that bought nothing, a morning spent on something with no outcome, a cost incurred purely because he was worth the cost? If everything you do for God can be justified in a report, something has quietly happened. There were twelve men in that room who could have written the report, and one woman who broke a jar, and only one of them was commended.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, aware of this, said to them, "Why do you trouble the woman? For she has done a beautiful thing to me. For you always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He defends her, and he defends her against his own men. That is worth registering before anything else. Eleven of them are ranged on one side of the room with an argument that sounds like conscience, one woman is on the other with an empty jar, and he takes her side.

She has done a beautiful thing to me. The word is kalon, which in Greek means noble and fine as much as lovely — not merely a pleasing gesture but an act of moral excellence. He is not being gallant about a well-meant mistake. He is saying she got it right and they got it wrong.

Then the sentence that has done more damage than almost any other in this Gospel: you always have the poor with you. It has been quoted for centuries to explain why nothing much can be done about poverty — as though Jesus were shrugging, as though the permanence of the problem excused the effort. That reading is not merely wrong; it is the precise reverse of the sentence he is quoting.

Because he is quoting. Deuteronomy 15 is the law of the sabbatical year, and its argument runs like this: there will be no poor among you if you keep the commandment, and then, realistically, there will never cease to be poor in the land — and therefore, you shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor (Deut 15:4, 11). The permanence of poverty is stated in Scripture as the reason for permanent generosity, not as an excuse for resignation. Every Jew at that table knew the verse and knew how it ended. He quotes the middle of it and lets them supply the rest.

So what he actually says is: you will have the poor to serve for the rest of your lives and the obligation never lapses — and you will not always have me. There is a window here, three days wide, that will not come again. This woman has understood that and you have not.

Which is a lesson about timing rather than about priorities in the abstract. There are things that can be done at any point and things that can only be done now, and the second kind are usually the ones that look least urgent. The visit to a dying man can be made this week or not at all. The word of thanks to someone old can be said now or said at a funeral to people who cannot hear it. Care for the poor is a lifelong duty precisely because the poor will still be there. Some things will not be.

verseByVerse.quote: "In pouring this ointment on my body she has done it to prepare me for burial. Truly, I say to you, wherever this gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He tells them what she has done, and it is not what she thought she was doing. In pouring this ointment on my body she has done it to prepare me for burial. Whether the woman understood that is not said and probably not; she came to honour him, and he receives it as embalming. Corpses in that country were anointed with spices before being wrapped, and he is telling a room full of men who will not accept that he is going to die that his body has now been prepared for the grave.

There is a bitter footnote to that. When the women came to the tomb on the Sunday morning with their spices, intending to do this properly, they were too late — he was not there. The only anointing his body ever received for burial was this one, given days early by a woman who was being told off for it at the time.

Then the promise, and it is the largest one he ever attaches to a private act: wherever this gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her. He is standing in a leper's house in a village outside Jerusalem, two days from execution, with a movement of eleven frightened men and one traitor, and he says: this will be told everywhere on earth.

It has been. The sentence is self-fulfilling every time the passage is read, and it is being fulfilled now, in this room, on this page, in a language she never heard of, two thousand years after she broke the jar. There is no other promise in the Gospels that a reader can verify in the act of reading it.

And notice what he does not do. He does not give her name. Matthew never tells us who she was; John identifies her as Mary of Bethany, but in this Gospel the most universally commended human act is performed by a woman with no name in the text — in memory of her, and we do not know who she is. That is its own kind of comfort for anybody whose best work has gone unrecorded and unattributed. He remembers what she did. He was not depending on Matthew to keep the record.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the twelve, who was called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said, "What will you give me if I deliver him over to you?" And they paid him thirty pieces of silver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew's placing is deliberate and merciless. A woman has just poured out a year's wages on him and been called beautiful for it; the very next sentence has a man walking out to find a price for him. Extravagance and calculation, side by side, and the calculation is being done by one of the twelve.

Look at how he opens the negotiation: What will you give me if I deliver him over to you? He does not name a figure. He asks them to. A man selling something valuable states his price; a man who has decided to sell and does not much care what he gets asks what is on offer. Judas let the buyers set the value, and they did.

Thirty pieces of silver. It is not a random sum, and every Jew present would have known where it came from. In the law of Exodus, if an ox gores a slave to death, the owner pays the slave's master thirty shekels of silver (Ex 21:32). That is the compensation rate for a dead slave — not the price of a person but the damages payable for one. Zechariah then uses the same figure with heavy irony: the LORD's shepherd asks his wages, is weighed out thirty pieces of silver, and is told by God to throw the lordly price into the temple treasury (Zech 11:12-13). Judas will do exactly that in the next chapter.

So the amount is a message, whether or not the priests intended it. They valued the Son of God at the insurance payout for a gored slave. And he accepted the figure without negotiating.

What is unnerving about Judas is not that he was a monster but that nobody could see it. He had been on the road for three years. He had heard every sermon in this book from the front, watched the blind receive sight and the dead get up, been sent out to preach and given authority over unclean spirits with the others (10:1-4), and held the common purse because the group trusted him with money. When Jesus said at the table that one of them would betray him, not one of the eleven turned and looked at Judas. They all asked whether it was themselves. Three years at close quarters and he had not given himself away to a single one of them.

verseByVerse.quote: And from that moment he sought an opportunity to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From that moment he sought an opportunity. The word is eukairian — a good moment, the right time. It is the language of a man waiting for a gap in a diary.

That is the sentence to sit with, because it rules out the reading that would make Judas easier to live with. This was not a flash of rage, or a moment of madness, or a man swept away by an impulse he could not control and regretted by morning. He made a decision, and then he went back to work. He ate with them. He walked with them. He kept the money bag and presumably kept it honestly enough that nobody noticed anything. He sat through the supper and dipped his hand in the same dish. And underneath all of it, day after day, he was watching for a convenient evening.

Sin that has become patient is a different order of thing from sin that erupts. The eruption at least announces itself and can be repented of the same night. This is a settled purpose, carried quietly, in ordinary company, requiring the man to be pleasant at breakfast — and every day he sustained it made the next day easier, because a decision that has been lived with for a week has stopped feeling like a decision at all. It has become a fact about him.

And that is how most serious wrong actually gets done. Not in the moment of temptation, where everybody expects the danger to be, but in the long quiet stretch afterwards, when the thing has been decided and is merely awaiting a convenient hour. The affair that has not happened yet but has been agreed to in the mind. The resignation letter written and saved. The lie that will be told when the question finally comes. Judas had weeks in which nothing had happened yet and everything had already happened.

What makes the picture unbearable is that during those weeks he was being loved. He was given the morsel at the table, addressed as friend in the garden, and asked a direct question that would have let him stop. He was still inside the circle, still being reached for. He was simply waiting for a good moment.

verseByVerse.quote: Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying, "Where will you have us prepare for you to eat the Passover?" He said, "Go into the city to a certain man and say to him, 'The Teacher says, My time is at hand. I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus' foreknowledge — sending disciples to an unspecified man in the city — again demonstrates his sovereign command of events. "My time is at hand" (kairos) is the appointed moment in salvation history, not a tragic accident. He is not surprised by what approaches; he has been moving toward it since Galilee. The Passover preparation is itself loaded with significance: they are about to eat the meal that commemorates Egypt's slavery and the redemption by blood — and Jesus will transform it into the memorial of the ultimate redemption. Every detail of the Last Supper is dense with the typological richness of the exodus.

A well-known difficulty stands over this verse, and a reader who has John open will meet it at once. Matthew, Mark and Luke all present this meal plainly as the Passover — the disciples ask where to prepare it, and they prepare it. But John seems to put the whole thing a day earlier: on the morning of the crucifixion the leaders will not enter Pilate's headquarters "so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover" (John 18:28), and John calls that day "the day of Preparation of the Passover" (John 19:14) — as though the meal were still ahead and Jesus died at the hour the lambs were being killed. Which is it?

Two answers carry real weight, and neither requires anyone to have got it wrong. The first is that Preparation (paraskeuē) is simply the ordinary Greek word for Friday — it is still the word for Friday in Greek today — so "the day of Preparation of the Passover" most naturally means the Friday of Passover week, not the day before the meal. On the same reading, "eat the Passover" in John 18:28 refers to the festival meals that ran through the whole seven-day feast (the chagigah offerings), not to the lamb eaten the previous night; a man defiled that morning would have been barred from those, which is exactly what worried them. The second answer is that the day itself was reckoned differently by different Jews — there is evidence that Galileans and Judeans, and Pharisees and Sadducees, did not begin the day at the same hour — so Passover was legitimately kept on two consecutive evenings, and a city swollen with pilgrims accommodated both. Jesus, a Galilean, keeps it with his disciples on the earlier evening; the Judean leadership keeps it on the later one.

What should be resisted is the tidy modern suggestion that John simply moved the date to make a theological point. He is the most precise of the four about hours and feasts, and the suggestion asks us to believe he preferred a symbol to the truth. Besides, the symbol was never his to invent. Whichever reckoning is right, both accounts land in the same place: the Lamb was killed at Passover. It was John's own Gospel that opened with "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29), and Paul says it without a trace of hesitation — "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Cor 5:7). The meal in the upper room and the death outside the wall are the same feast seen from its two ends: the supper he gave them, and the sacrifice he became.

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples did as Jesus had directed them, and they prepared the Passover. When it was evening, he reclined at table with the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two ordinary sentences, and it is worth slowing down over how ordinary they are. Somebody had to buy the lamb and take it to the temple to be killed. Somebody carried the carcass back, and someone else swept the room for leaven, and set out the bitter herbs and the unleavened bread and the wine, and arranged the cushions. It was a domestic evening's work, of the kind done in tens of thousands of houses in that city that week, and the men doing it had no idea they were preparing the most consequential meal in human history.

When it was evening, he reclined at table with the twelve. Reclining is the posture of a free man at a feast — Jews ate the Passover lying on the left side, propped on an elbow, precisely because slaves ate standing and this was the meal of a liberated people. He takes that posture on the last night of his life, hours before he is bound.

And notice: with the twelve. All twelve. Judas is at the table with his fee already agreed. Jesus reclines at a feast of freedom beside the man arranging his arrest.

The new covenant is going to be inaugurated in this room, and the room is a borrowed one, up a flight of stairs, in a house belonging to a man Matthew does not name. Not the temple, where the sacrifices were; not a court, where covenants were witnessed; not before the council, who would have been the obvious parties to such a thing. Thirteen men round a table, one of whom is a traitor, in someone else's dining room.

That is worth remembering by anybody who has felt that his own church is too plain a place for anything eternal to be happening in. The bread on the table in the upper room was the same bread everybody else in Jerusalem was eating that night. God has a settled habit of doing the largest things in the least impressive rooms, with ordinary objects, in front of people who are not concentrating.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were eating, he said, "Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me." And they were very sorrowful and began to say to him one after another, "Is it I, Lord?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He waits until they are eating. As they were eating, he said, Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me. Not before the meal, when it would have ended it; not after, when they were leaving. In the middle, with food in front of them and the man in question within arm's reach.

The setting is the whole weight of it. Sharing a meal in that culture was not a casual arrangement; to eat at a man's table was to be in covenant with him, under his protection, committed to his interests. David had felt the same wound and written it down: even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Ps 41:9). Betrayal from a stranger is a misfortune. Betrayal from a man with your bread in his mouth is something else.

Then the disciples' response, and the Greek is sharper than the English. Is it I, Lord? — meti ego, kyrie. Greek marks the expected answer, and meti expects the answer no. They are saying: it isn't me, is it, Lord? Which is exactly how a man asks a question he badly wants a particular answer to.

And notice what they did not do. Eleven men, told there is a traitor at the table, and not one of them turns and looks at anybody else. There is no accusation, no glance down the table, no comparing of notes. Each asks about himself, one after another. It would have been the most natural thing in the world to start theorising about which of the others it was, and nobody does.

That instinct is worth borrowing, because it is rarer than it looks. The ordinary response to hearing that something is badly wrong in a group is to work out who is responsible, and it can be done with real solemnity and mistaken for discernment. These men had lived with each other for three years and knew each other's weaknesses; any one of them could have made a case against two or three of the others. Told that one of them was capable of the worst thing imaginable, every single one of them thought first of himself — and eleven of them were wrong about it, and were right to ask.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "He who has dipped his hand in the dish with me will betray me. The Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who has dipped his hand in the dish with me. At the Passover meal a common bowl of sauce stood on the table and everyone dipped into it, so the answer identifies nobody in particular — all twelve had dipped. It is not a name. It is a restatement of the horror: the man who will do this is a man whose hand has been in the same bowl as mine tonight.

Then two sentences set side by side that no theologian has ever fully prised apart. The Son of Man goes as it is written of him — the cross is not a breakdown of the plan but the plan, written centuries earlier in Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22 and Zechariah, and Jesus has just been quoting those chapters as his own script. But woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed. The necessity is real and the guilt is real, and neither is allowed to soften the other. This Gospel has already made the reader hold exactly this pair once before, in the same construction — it is necessary that temptations come, and woe to the man by whom they come (18:7, and see there).

What must not be done with it is the thing both sides of the argument reach for. Judas cannot be excused on the ground that prophecy required somebody: the woe is pronounced on him, by name, by the man he is selling. And God cannot be charged with the crime: nothing in the text has anyone forcing Judas's hand, and Judas himself will shortly say I have sinned and mean it. Scripture holds the two and does not explain the join.

Then the last clause, which is among the most terrible in the Bible: it would have been better for that man if he had not been born. There is no way to read that as anything but a statement about a fate worse than never existing. Jesus said it, quietly, at a supper table, about a friend sitting a few feet away.

And notice who is speaking. Not a preacher working up a congregation. The man about to die for the sins of the world, on the last night of his life, saying of one particular soul that non-existence would have been the kinder outcome. Whatever weight a reader gives to the doctrine of judgment, it will not do to say it comes from hard men who did not love sinners.

verseByVerse.quote: Judas, who would betray him, answered, "Is it I, Rabbi?" He said to him, "You have said so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every other man at that table has just said Lord. Judas says Rabbi.

It is not an insult. Rabbi is a respectful word — teacher, my master in the sense a student means it. That is exactly what makes it revealing. Judas has a category for Jesus and it is a perfectly honourable one; he simply has not the category the others have. He calls him what you call a man whose instruction you value. He will use the same word in the garden, an hour or two later, as the signal for the arrest: Greetings, Rabbi.

Which is a warning worth taking seriously, because the ground Judas stood on is more populated than the ground anybody expects. A very high regard for Jesus — his teaching unmatched, his ethics unequalled, his insight into human nature unrivalled — is not the same thing as calling him Lord, and it can be held for years by a man in constant attendance. Judas is the proof that it can be held to the end, at the table, in the inner circle, by somebody sent out to preach.

Then Jesus answers him: You have said so. Two words, quiet, and they mean yes. He does not denounce him to the room, does not name him to the others, does not have him removed. He simply lets Judas know that he knows.

That is the last door held open. Judas is now aware that he is not getting away with anything, that the man he is selling has seen the whole transaction, and that nothing has yet been said in front of the others. He could have stood up at that moment and been the second great restoration story of the New Testament, and John records that he went out — and it was night.

Which leaves the most sobering fact in the chapter, and it is not that Judas fell. It is that he was seen, addressed, offered the morsel, given a direct answer to a direct question, and called friend in the garden, and none of it reached him. He had three years of the closest possible exposure to Christ, and it left him unchanged — not because Christ was distant, but because a man can sit that close and keep the door shut.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to the disciples, and said, "Take, eat; this is my body." And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, saying, "Drink of it, all of you,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The institution of the Lord's Supper transforms the Passover's backward-looking memorial into a forward-looking and present-tense proclamation. "This is my body" — the debate over the precise meaning divided the Reformation and continues to divide the church. Standing behind the whole debate was the view the Reformers were answering: the Roman Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation, defined at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and reaffirmed at Trent. On this view, at the priest's words of consecration the whole substance of the bread becomes the substance of Christ's body, and the wine his blood, while only the outward "accidents" — the look, taste, and feel of bread and wine — remain; the consecrated host is therefore Christ himself, to be adored, and the Mass re-presents his one sacrifice at the altar. Against this backdrop three Protestant positions emerged. Luther held that Christ's body and blood are physically present in, with, and under the bread and wine (sometimes called consubstantiation) — the elements are truly his body and blood regardless of the faith of the recipient. Zwingli held the opposite: the Supper is a memorial only, the elements purely symbolic, signifying Christ's sacrifice without conveying his presence. Calvin — and following him the Westminster Confession — charted the position that Reformed theology has made its own: Christ is truly and spiritually present in the Supper, not by any physical transformation of the elements, but by the Holy Spirit making the broken bread and poured cup effectual means of genuine communion with the risen Christ, who is received by faith. Against Zwingli, Calvin insisted the Supper is not merely a reminder of an absent Lord but a genuine feeding on the living Christ. Against Luther, he insisted the feeding is spiritual and received by faith, not physical and automatic. The Westminster Confession (29.7) puts it precisely: worthy receivers "do then also inwardly by faith, really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally, but spiritually, receive and feed upon Christ crucified." "All of you" — the cup is not restricted to the clergy but given to all the disciples. This democratization of the covenant meal is itself a theological statement about the priesthood of all believers.

Where Protestants press back on Rome is not the reality of Christ's self-giving but two things Scripture guards. First, "this is my body" was spoken by Jesus while his body sat whole and living at the table — the same manner of speech as "I am the door," "I am the vine," and "the Rock was Christ" (1 Cor 10:4); the bread signifies and conveys, it does not become. Second, and weightier, the Mass understood as a re-presented sacrifice sits uneasily with Hebrews, which insists Christ "offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins" (Heb 10:12-14) — once, finished, unrepeatable. Yet it is worth saying honestly what unites rather than only what divides: Rome, Luther, and Calvin all confess that Christ truly gives himself to his people at this table, against any notion of a bare and empty symbol. The Reformed answer keeps both truths — a real feeding on the living Christ, and a finished cross received by faith, not re-offered by a priest.

verseByVerse.quote: "for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. I tell you I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every phrase in this sentence is quarried out of the Old Testament, and a Jew at that table would have heard all of it at once.

My blood of the covenant. At Sinai, Moses took the blood of oxen, threw half against the altar and half over the people, and said behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you (Ex 24:8). Those words are said once in the Law of Moses and nowhere else in it, and they were said at the founding moment of the nation. Jesus takes the sentence, puts my in front of it, and hands round a cup.

And Jeremiah had promised there would be another one: a new covenant, not like the covenant made when God took them by the hand to bring them out of Egypt, which they broke — this one written on hearts, with the promise attached, I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more (Jer 31:31-34). Jesus does not say he is renewing the old arrangement. He says the blood is his and the covenant is new.

Poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. The many are Isaiah's: the servant who bore the sin of many and makes many to be accounted righteous (Isa 53:11-12). And the purpose clause is the plainest statement of what the cross achieves that Jesus ever gives — not an example, not a demonstration, not a tragedy that God later turned to good account, but blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins.

Then he stops, and takes a vow. I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom. He is fasting from wine until the wedding feast, and he says so at the end of the last meal he will eat. It is worth following what happens to that vow: within a day he is offered wine mixed with gall on the way to the cross, and he tastes it and will not drink it (27:34). He keeps his fast through the crucifixion.

And do not hurry past the two words in the middle of the promise: with you. He is sitting with eleven men who will all abandon him within hours and one who has already sold him, and he is making an appointment to drink wine with them at his Father's table. He knew exactly what they were about to do. The invitation was issued anyway, and it was issued before the failure, not after it.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. Then Jesus said to them, "You will all fall away because of me this night, for it is written, 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had sung a hymn. It was almost certainly the second half of the Hallel, Psalms 115 to 118, sung at the close of every Passover — and it is worth knowing what the words were, because he sang them on his way out to be arrested.

He sang the snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me (Ps 116:3). He sang precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints (116:15). He sang all nations surrounded me; in the name of the LORD I cut them off (118:10). He sang the stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (118:22) — the verse he had quoted against the chief priests in the temple two days before, now sung in his own voice about himself. And he sang the last line: Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures for ever (118:29).

He went to Gethsemane singing about the goodness of God, having just described his own death, with the man who sold him newly gone from the room.

Then, on the road: you will all fall away because of me this night. All of them. Not one exception is offered, and it is said to their faces on the walk out. The word skandalisthesesthe means to be tripped, made to stumble — he is not predicting treachery like Judas's but collapse, the sudden giving way of men whose legs will not hold them.

And he grounds it in Zechariah: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered (Zech 13:7). Note who does the striking in that verse. It is not the soldiers, and not the council. I will strike — God is speaking, and the sword is his. The scattering of these men is not an accident that befalls the operation; it is written into the same prophecy as the smiting of their Master, and it is God's doing. Which means that when they run, hours from now, they will be running inside a sentence Jesus has already quoted to them, and he will know exactly where they have gone.

verseByVerse.quote: "But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee." Peter answered him, "Though they all fall away because of you, I will never fall away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read verse 32 slowly, because of where it sits. He has just told eleven men that every one of them will desert him tonight. The next thing out of his mouth is not a reproach or a condition. It is an arrangement: but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.

He is making a plan to meet them afterwards. Before the desertion has happened, he has named the place they will regroup. There is no if you repent and no those of you who come back — just a shepherd telling scattered sheep, in advance, where the flock will re-form. And Galilee is where he found most of them in the first place: he will take them back to the beginning and start again.

That is worth holding against every instinct we have about how forgiveness works. We assume restoration is arranged after the failure, in response to sufficient contrition. Here the reunion is booked before the betrayal, by the one who is going to be betrayed, and the men it is booked for are at that moment insisting it will not be needed.

Which brings us to Peter, who hears the prophecy of collapse and the promise of restoration in the same breath — and answers only the first, to contradict it. Though they all fall away because of you, I will never fall away.

Notice what is in that sentence besides courage, because there is a good deal. There is a comparison: though they all — Peter's confidence is stated at the expense of the other ten, in front of the other ten. And there is a flat contradiction of something Jesus has just said. He is not merely overestimating himself; he is correcting his Lord's assessment of him, which is a strange thing to do about your own heart in the presence of the one who made it.

He meant every word. That is what makes it useful. Peter was not boasting emptily — within the hour he will draw a sword against an armed detachment, which is more than the other ten manage. His courage was real. It simply was not as deep as his estimate of it, and there was no way for him to discover the difference except the way he discovered it.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Truly, I say to you, this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times." Peter said to him, "Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you!" And all the disciples said the same.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The specificity of Jesus' prediction — three times, before the rooster crows, this very night — is a mark of his divine foreknowledge. Peter intensifies his commitment: not just "I will not fall away" but "even if I must die." And all the disciples agree. This corporate overconfidence sets up the corporate failure of verse 56 — "all the disciples left him and fled." The distance between the upper room's declarations and Gethsemane's abandonment is a matter of hours. Spiritual confidence resting on self-knowledge rather than on the grace of God is always exposed in the end as presumption.

The entry above praises the precision of the prediction, and it is worth noticing that Mark is more precise still — and differently. Where Matthew has "before the rooster crows," Mark has "before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times" (Mark 14:30), and Mark alone then records the second crowing when it happens (Mark 14:72). Luke and John agree with Matthew. This is a small thing, and it has an unusually satisfying answer.

Begin with the fact that cockcrow was a clock. The Romans named a watch of the night after it — gallicinium, cockcrow, running roughly from midnight to three — and Mark uses that very term a few verses later (13:35). So "before the rooster crows" was an ordinary way of saying before this night is out, which is precisely how Matthew reports the rest of the sentence: this very night. Three of the four give the saying in that everyday form, as any of us would.

And then consider which Gospel keeps the extra detail. From the earliest days the church held that Mark wrote down the preaching of Peter — and it is Mark, alone of the four, that counts the crowings. That is the one man in Jerusalem who had reason never to forget how many times that bird called out before dawn. It is also worth noting the direction of this: usually Matthew is the shorter account and Mark the fuller (cf. 9:18), and here that holds again. The others tell you what Jesus said; Peter's Gospel tells you what Peter heard, twice, and could not stop hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus came with them to a place called Gethsemane, and he said to his disciples, "Sit here, while I go over there and pray." And taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and troubled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gethsemane means oil press. It was an olive grove on the slope of the Mount of Olives with a press in it — a great stone wheel, or a beam weighted with stones, that crushed the fruit until the oil ran. Jesus chose to spend the last free hours of his life in a place named after the machine that squeezes something until it yields.

He takes three men further in: Peter, James and John. These are the same three who were taken up the mountain and saw his face shine like the sun (17:1). They are the only human beings who have seen him in glory, and they are now the only ones who will see him in this condition. He is showing the same three the two ends of who he is.

Then Matthew's verbs, which he does not use lightly: he began to be sorrowful and troubled. The second word, ademonein, is the strongest term for distress in the Greek of that period — a word for anguish bordering on horror, the state of a man in the grip of something he can hardly bear. Mark reaches for a similar word. This is not a description of solemnity. It is a description of a man coming apart.

And it begins here — he began. Whatever was in front of him had been in front of him for years; he had spoken of it calmly a few days earlier and named the date without a tremor. In this garden it arrives, and the composure that has held through the whole Gospel gives way.

Which is the thing the church has always found hardest to look at directly and must not look away from. There is a version of Christianity in which the Son of God walked to the cross serene, knowing the outcome, insulated by his divinity from the worst of it. Matthew will not allow it. He tells us the man in the garden was sorrowful, and horrified, and asked his friends to stay near him, and went down on his face. Whatever he was about to bear, he was not protected from feeling the whole weight of it in advance — and he went anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to them, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death; remain here, and watch with me." And going a little farther he fell on his face and prayed, saying, "My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Sorrowful even to death" — the grief is so intense it threatens life itself. The cup is the Old Testament cup of divine wrath (Isa. 51:17; Ps. 75:8) — not merely physical suffering but the experience of bearing the full weight of God's righteous judgment against sin. The prayer is both fully human ("let this cup pass") and fully surrendered ("not as I will, but as you will"). This is the Son's prayer from within the covenant of redemption — not rebellion but the genuine expression of a real human will that is yet perfectly submitted to the Father. The prayer shows that the cross was no easier for knowing it was necessary. Necessity does not reduce suffering; it only gives it a purpose.

Set the theology down for a moment and watch what he actually does here, because this is the passage in Scripture for anyone who has been in real mental anguish — the kind that frightens you, that arrives at three in the morning, that makes the next day look unsurvivable. Christians in that condition are often quietly ashamed of it. They should read this paragraph slowly.

He said out loud how bad it was. My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. There is no stoicism here, no managing of appearances, no assurance to his friends that he was fine. He named the extremity of it in plain words to the people nearest him.

He wanted company in it. Remain here, and watch with me — he asked three men to stay close, not to fix anything or say anything, simply to be awake nearby. He was disappointed three times and went back and asked again. Wanting people near you in the worst hour is not weakness, and it does not stop being right when they let you down.

He asked for it to be taken away. Not once but three times, in the same words. Submission did not mean declining to ask; the nevertheless came after the asking and not instead of it. Anyone who has been told that a truly surrendered Christian would stop pleading for relief should notice who is on his face in this garden, asking again.

And he fell on his face — the posture of collapse, not of composure. Luke, a doctor, adds that his sweat became like great drops of blood, and that an angel came and strengthened him (Lk 22:43-44). Notice what heaven sent. Not removal of the cup, which he had asked for; strength to drink it. That is very often the shape of the answer, and it is not a lesser one — it is what was given to the only perfectly faithful man who ever prayed.

So if you are in that country: say how bad it is, to God and to somebody; ask for it to be lifted, and ask again tomorrow; let people sit near you even though they will sleep; and do not read the absence of rescue as the absence of God. The Son of God went through this before you, and he was not delivered from it. He was strengthened in it, and came out the other side, and went on to do the thing he had been dreading.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to the disciples and found them sleeping. And he said to Peter, "So, could you not watch with me one hour? Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Could you not watch with me one hour? The question is put to Peter, by name, and Peter is the one who said an hour ago that he would die first. It is not sarcasm. It is grief.

Then the diagnosis, and it is remarkably gentle: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. He does not say they were faithless, or that they did not care. He says the wanting was genuine and the equipment was not up to it. Luke, a doctor, adds the observation that they were sleeping for sorrow (Lk 22:45) — they had been told that night that one of them was a traitor, that all of them would run, and that their Master was about to be killed, and grief of that order does not keep a man awake; it flattens him. Their failure was, in part, exhaustion from caring.

He is more generous about them than they would have been about themselves, and considerably more generous than most Christians are about their own equivalent failures. There is no suggestion here that a sincere man should be able to override his body by determination. The flesh is weak; that is stated as a fact about human beings, not a charge against these three in particular.

But he does not leave them there, and the prescription is precise: watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The word for temptation is peirasmos, and it is the same word these men had been taught to use every day in the prayer he gave them: lead us not into temptation (6:13). He is telling them, in the last hour before the test, to pray the prayer he had already put in their mouths — and they sleep through it, and within hours every one of them enters exactly the trial he had told them to ask to be spared.

Which is a lesson about when prayer has to happen. The disciples did not fail in the courtyard; they failed in the garden, an hour earlier, while nothing was happening. Peter's denial was decided before the servant girl opened her mouth. By then there was no time to acquire what he needed, and the hour in which he could have acquired it had been spent lying on the ground asleep, in the company of the only man who was using it properly.

verseByVerse.quote: Again, for the second time, he went away and prayed, "My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done." And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second prayer is not a repetition. Something has moved, and the change is in one clause.

The first time: if it be possible, let this cup pass from me. The second time: if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done. The request has been answered in the only way it could be, and he has heard the answer. He is no longer asking whether the cup can go. He is agreeing to drink it.

And listen to the words he uses to agree — your will be done, genetheto to thelema sou. That is not a phrase he improvised in the dark. It is a line from the prayer he taught these men on a hillside in Galilee, which they had been saying ever since and are asleep instead of saying now: your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven (6:10). On the worst night of his life, the Son of God prays his own prayer, and he prays it in the hardest possible circumstances — as a man asking for something and being told no.

Which quietly settles what that petition means for everyone who has ever recited it without thinking. Your will be done is not a formula for tidying up the end of a prayer. It is what Jesus said in a garden with his face on the ground, having asked three times for another outcome and not received it. Anyone who says those words in that condition is in company.

Then, flatly: again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. Matthew does not moralise about it. He simply records that the loneliest man who ever lived went back for company a second time and found the three asleep again, and went away and prayed a third time by himself.

It is worth noticing what he does not do. He does not wake them and demand support, and he does not abandon the prayer because his friends have let him down. He goes back to the Father. When human company fails in the hour you most need it — and it does fail, and often for reasons as ordinary as tiredness — this is the pattern: not resentment, and not despair, but a third time on the ground alone.

verseByVerse.quote: So, leaving them again, he went away and prayed for the third time, saying the same words again. Then he came to the disciples and said to them, "Sleep and rest later on. See, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three times. Matthew says it plainly: he went away and prayed for the third time, saying the same words again. The same words. He had nothing new to say and he said the old thing again, which is what people actually do in real distress, and it is worth noting that this is not the vain repetition he warned against in the Sermon (6:7). Repeating a prayer because there is nothing else left in you is not heathen babbling. He did it.

And then it is over. Something has been settled in that third prayer, because the man who gets up from the ground is not the man who went down on it. From this point to his death he does not waver once — not before the council, not under the whip, not on the cross. Every trace of the anguish that filled this garden is spent here, in the dark, in front of nobody. The composure the world will see for the next eighteen hours was purchased on this ground.

Which is worth saying to anyone who assumes that the strong Christians they know were issued with steadier nerves. What is done in public was done first in private, and usually on the floor. Nobody saw this. Three men who might have seen it were unconscious a stone's throw away, and the only reason we know it happened at all is that he told them about it afterwards.

Then he wakes them: the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. He has been speaking of the hour for three years, always as something not yet arrived. It has arrived. And he announces it in the passive again — is betrayed, handed over — the same verb that has been running under this whole chapter.

Note the last phrase: into the hands of sinners. That is what is about to take place, stated without euphemism. The sinless one is being handed over to the custody of sinful men, who will do what sinful men do, and he says so a minute before it starts, and he stands up to meet it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three words, and they reverse the direction of the whole night: Rise, let us be going.

Every instinct expects the opposite. A man who knows an armed party is coming for him, who has spent three hours in agony over it, who has a hillside of olive trees behind him and the Judean wilderness beyond that, and who has friends with him — that man says let us go and means away. The Greek verb is the ordinary one for setting off, and it can mean either. What settles it is the next clause: see, my betrayer is at hand. He is not moving away from the torches. He is walking toward them.

Nothing compelled that. He has just told the disciples that twelve legions of angels were available for the asking, and he is about to say it again out loud. He could have left the garden ten minutes earlier and the arresting party would have found an empty grove. Judas knew the place; that is all Judas had. There was no cordon, no watch on the roads, no warrant out in the city. The only thing keeping Jesus in Gethsemane was that he had decided to be there.

So the arrest that follows is not something that happens to him. It is something he goes out to meet, and Matthew has arranged the sentence so that a reader cannot miss it: the betrayer is approaching, and the betrayed stands up and starts walking in his direction.

And notice the pronoun in the middle of it. Not I am going but let us be going. He takes the three with him — the same three who could not stay awake, who are about to run, one of whom will curse his name in a courtyard before morning. They have failed him for the last three hours and he does not go on without them.

What was decided face-down in the dark is executed on his feet in the open. The prayer ended your will be done; the action begins let us be going. Between those two sentences there is nothing at all — no interval, no second thoughts, no gathering of resolve. He got up and went.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 47–75 — The Arrest, the Trial before the High Priest, and Peter's Denial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judas arrives with an armed crowd and identifies Jesus with a kiss; a disciple draws a sword and is told to sheathe it; every one of the eleven runs. Jesus is taken to the high priest's house, where a court that cannot assemble two agreeing witnesses finally convicts him out of his own mouth when Caiaphas puts him on oath. He is condemned, spat at and blindfolded and struck. Outside in the same courtyard, warming himself at the fire, Peter is asked three times whether he knows him, and says no three times, and hears a rooster.
verseByVerse.theology: Two men are on trial in this section and Matthew cuts between them deliberately. Inside, under oath, with his life at stake, Jesus tells the truth about who he is; outside, with nothing at stake but embarrassment, Peter lies about knowing him. The confession that condemns Jesus is word for word Peter's own confession at Caesarea Philippi (16:16), which is why the pairing is so pointed. And the answer Jesus gives is the most exalted claim ever made in a courtroom: Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13 combined, so that the prisoner tells the court the seating will be reversed at the next hearing, beginning from now on. Caiaphas understood him exactly, which disposes of the notion that the claim to deity was a later invention of the church: the one man in the room with every professional reason to find a smaller meaning heard it instantly and called it blasphemy.
verseByVerse.examples: The phrase to carry away is following at a distance (v. 58). Peter has more courage than the ten who ran — he is the only one who follows at all — and it is the distance, not the flight, that undoes him: far enough in to be recognised, far enough back to want not to be. The ten were never asked, because they were not there. Note too where the ground is actually slippery. Peter had prepared, sincerely, to die; he had not prepared for a servant girl by a fire, and the accuser with no authority to arrest anybody is the one who brings him down. Most denials of Christ happen exactly there — in the staff room, at the family table, where a laugh is available and the cost of being counted in suddenly seems out of proportion to the occasion. And the escalation is the signature of a lie under pressure: evasion, then an oath, then a self-curse, each answer defending the one before it rather than defending anything worth defending.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the elders of the people. Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, "The one I will kiss is the man; seize him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was still speaking — the timing is exact, and Matthew wants it noticed. The words are barely out of his mouth before the thing he has just described walks into the garden.

And Matthew names Judas the way he has named him all chapter: one of the twelve. He has already told us that (v. 14) and he tells us again. It is not information; it is the wound. The man leading an armed detachment against Jesus is a member of the group that ate with him three hours ago.

Look at the size of what they have brought. A great crowd with swords and clubs — temple police with the clubs, and behind them, John tells us, a detachment of Roman soldiers with the swords. They have come by night, in force, with lanterns and weapons, to arrest one unarmed teacher and eleven fishermen. It is an absurd deployment and it is a confession: they expected resistance, or they were afraid of him, or both. Nothing about that party looks like men who are in control of the situation.

Then the sign. The one I will kiss is the man. A kiss on the cheek or hand was the ordinary greeting of a disciple to his teacher — the mark of respect and affection, the thing Judas had presumably done a hundred times on ordinary mornings. He selects it as the identifying signal.

He did not have to. In a garden lit by torches, with eleven men present, a pointed finger would have done, or a name spoken aloud, or simply standing next to him. There were a dozen ways to identify a man to soldiers, and Judas chose the one that required him to put his face against his Master's face. That is the particular horror of this verse, and it is not accidental: sin habitually takes the forms of love and uses them backwards, because those are the forms that get close enough to do damage. Nobody betrays you from a distance.

And weigh the detail Matthew adds about the arrangements: the betrayer had given them a sign. Judas had thought this through in advance. Somewhere on the walk out from the city, with the torches behind him, he worked out the logistics and briefed the officers on what to watch for. The kiss was not a sudden piece of theatre. It was planned, discussed, and agreed.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came up to Jesus at once and said, "Greetings, Rabbi!" And he kissed him. Jesus said to him, "Friend, do what you came to do." Then they came up and laid hands on Jesus and seized him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he kissed him. The Greek is stronger than the English lets on. The verb is kataphileo, an intensified form — to kiss warmly, fervently, repeatedly. It is the word used of the father falling on the neck of the prodigal, and of the woman who would not stop kissing Jesus' feet. Judas did not give a perfunctory signal and step back. He kissed him warmly.

And then Jesus speaks to him, and the word he chooses is the last mercy Judas ever receives: Friend, do what you came to do.

Friend here is hetairos, and Matthew has used it twice before — to the labourer grumbling about his wages (20:13) and to the man at the wedding without a garment (22:12). It is not the warm word for a bosom friend; it is the word you use to someone with whom you have a bond that the other party is currently abusing. It carries reproach. But it is still an address, still a relationship named out loud, and it is a great deal more than the man had any right to.

Consider what is not said. No curse. No traitor. No appeal to the crowd to see what this man is doing. No withdrawal of the face that is being kissed. He submits to the kiss, and calls the man friend, and tells him to get on with it.

Then: they came up and laid hands on Jesus and seized him. Matthew has used the phrase laid hands on repeatedly in this Gospel, and every previous time the hands were his — laid on a leper, on a fever, on children, on the dead girl's hand. Hands that had only ever been laid on people to heal them are now taken hold of and bound. The direction of touch has reversed, and it will not reverse again until Sunday.

One more thing about do what you came to do. It is not permission and it is not resignation; the Greek is compressed and reads almost as an instruction — get on with it. He is running his own arrest. The party has come with swords and lanterns expecting to take a man who does not want to be taken, and the man they have come for tells the signal-giver to complete the signal.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand and drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. Then Jesus said to him, "Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John tells us who drew the sword, and nobody is surprised: it was Peter. The man who had sworn he would die first, and who could not stay awake, wakes up fighting.

And it is worth being fair to him. He is one of two armed men facing a detachment of soldiers and temple police in the dark, and he draws anyway. That is not cowardice; it is the bravest act of the night by anyone except Jesus. He simply had the wrong weapon, at the wrong moment, for the wrong kingdom — and he very nearly killed a man over it. The servant's name was Malchus, and the ear was struck off, and Luke records that Jesus touched it and healed him (Lk 22:51). It is the last recorded healing before the resurrection, and it is done for one of the men who has come to arrest him, and it repairs damage done by his own disciple.

Put your sword back into its place. Not throw it away — back in its sheath, where it belongs. And then the principle: all who take the sword will perish by the sword.

What that sentence forbids needs stating carefully, because it has been stretched in both directions. It is not a blanket condemnation of every use of force by anybody; Jesus does not tell the soldier to leave the army here or anywhere else, and Paul will say plainly that the civil authority does not bear the sword in vain. What is forbidden is precisely what Peter was attempting — advancing or defending the cause of Christ by violence. Peter had the best motive available to a human being: he was defending the Son of God from unjust arrest. And he was told to put it away.

If that motive does not license the sword, none ever will. Which is the standing judgment on every crusade, every burning, every armed defence of the faith the church has undertaken in nineteen centuries: it was tried first in a garden, by an apostle, on behalf of Christ himself, in his presence — and he stopped it, and healed the casualty, and went with them quietly.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels? But how then should the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must be so?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is standing with his hands being tied, and he tells them what he could do instead.

More than twelve legions of angels. A Roman legion at full strength was around six thousand men, so twelve legions is something over seventy thousand — and he says more than. The number is not chosen at random either: twelve, one for each disciple in the garden, or one for each tribe of Israel. And measure it against what one angel has been known to do in Scripture: a single angel of the LORD went out in a night and struck down a hundred and eighty-five thousand men in the Assyrian camp (2 Kgs 19:35). Against that arithmetic, the detachment holding him is a rounding error.

And they are available at once, for the asking. He does not say his Father could be persuaded, or that a case could be made. One request, immediately answered. The rescue was one sentence away for the whole of that night, and it stayed one sentence away through the trial, the flogging and the six hours on the cross.

So the question the passage forces is the right one to ask about every part of the passion: what is holding him? Not the ropes — Matthew has just told us what the ropes are worth. His answer is a single clause: how then should the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must be so?

That is the only constraint operating anywhere in this chapter. Not the soldiers, not Caiaphas, not Rome, not Judas. The Son of God is held in place by the Father's stated purpose and by nothing else whatsoever — which means every image of Jesus as a good man overwhelmed by forces too strong for him is exactly wrong. He was never overwhelmed. He was committed.

And the commitment has a name attached. He is not submitting to an abstract necessity; he is keeping faith with what was written about him, because if he called for the legions the Scriptures would fail and no one would be saved. Between seventy thousand angels and the salvation of the people who were arresting him, he chose, and he chose while they were putting the ropes on.

verseByVerse.quote: At that hour Jesus said to the crowds, "Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I sat in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But all this has taken place that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled." Then all the disciples left him and fled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word he uses is lestes — have you come out as against a robber? It does not mean a pickpocket. A lestes was a brigand, an armed insurgent, the kind of man who took to the hills and raided; the Romans crucified them. It is precisely the word Matthew will use of the two men crucified on either side of him (27:38). They have turned out in force as though arresting a guerrilla, and in three days they will hang him between two of the real thing.

Then the rebuke, and it is quietly devastating: day after day I sat in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. He had been in their own building, in daylight, every day that week, seated in the posture of a teacher, entirely available. If the charge were genuine and the case were sound, they could have arrested him at any point in front of witnesses. They came at night with clubs instead, and the manner of the arrest is a confession about the strength of the case.

That is a mark worth remembering. Truth does not need darkness, and a process that avoids daylight is telling you something about itself before a word of evidence is heard. These men knew their case could not survive an audience.

But all this has taken place that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. He says it and then, Matthew tells us, the last sentence of the paragraph happens: then all the disciples left him and fled.

All of them. The number is stated because it matters — not most, not the weaker ones. The three from the mountain, the man who drew the sword, the whole company. They had said in unison two hours earlier that they would die with him, and they ran, and Mark adds the detail of a young man who ran so hard he left his clothes behind (Mk 14:51-52).

And that fulfils what he quoted on the road: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered. Their desertion is a failure and it is also a prophecy, and both are true at once. Which means that at the moment he was most alone, and most abandoned by the men he had trained, the thing that was happening was not the collapse of his mission. It was a line of Zechariah, coming true on schedule, exactly as he had told them it would.

verseByVerse.quote: Then those who had seized Jesus led him to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders had gathered. And Peter was following him at a distance, as far as the courtyard of the high priest, and going inside he sat with the guards to see the outcome.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two men are followed in this verse and Matthew tracks them both, because the rest of the chapter is going to cut between them: Jesus taken inside to the high priest, Peter stopping in the courtyard outside. Inside, a man tells the truth and it kills him. Outside, a man tells lies to stay alive. Matthew puts the two scenes in the same building, at the same hour, separated by a doorway.

But first the phrase that has probably described more Christians than any other in this Gospel: Peter was following him at a distance.

Give him his due. Ten men are gone; he is here. He has followed an armed party through Jerusalem at night and walked into the residence of the man who is trying to kill his Master, which took more courage than anyone else could find. He has not abandoned Jesus. He is simply not standing next to him.

And it is the distance, not the flight, that undoes him. The ten who ran were in no danger of denying anything by a charcoal fire, because they were not there to be asked. Peter has put himself in exactly the position where he will be questioned and has left himself exactly the amount of commitment that cannot answer the question. Far enough in to be recognised, far enough back to want not to be.

That middle distance is a real place and a great many believers live there — close enough to be counted a Christian by anybody who looked properly, not close enough to be conspicuous; in the courtyard rather than the hall. It is the most uncomfortable position available and it feels like a compromise between two risks, and this chapter is about to show what it actually is.

Then the last clause, which is oddly bleak: he sat with the guards to see the outcome. He has taken a seat among the men who arrested Jesus, to watch how it turns out. He is not there to help; there is nothing he can do. He has become a spectator of his own Lord's trial, warming himself at the enemy's fire, and the next four verses are what happens to a man in that seat.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking false testimony against Jesus that they might put him to death, but they found none, though many false witnesses came forward. At last two came forward
verseByVerse.commentary:
