The council begins with its conclusion (death) and works backward to find a charge — the definition of a show trial. "The whole council" — the Sanhedrin, the highest Jewish judicial body — is assembled for a predetermined verdict. The procession of false witnesses who cannot agree is both legally fatal (two witnesses must agree, Deut. 19:15) and ironically revealing: Jesus is so innocent that even those trying to condemn him cannot find consistent false testimony. The very impossibility of assembling a charge is Matthew's quiet argument for his sinlessness: a court of his enemies, working without scruple, could not make anything stick.

Look at what the sentence actually admits: they were seeking false testimony. Matthew does not say they were seeking evidence and finding only lies. He says the object of the search was false testimony, and that the highest court in Israel could not obtain it. They had motive, authority, time, and no scruples, and the supply of usable perjury against Jesus of Nazareth ran out.

And they needed two who agreed, because their own law required it — only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established (Deut 19:15). Witnesses came forward in numbers and their stories would not line up, which is what happens when men are inventing independently. The one procedural rule they still honoured that night was the one that nearly stopped the trial.

It is worth knowing how far outside their own rules these men had stepped. Later Jewish law, collected in the Sanhedrin tractate of the Mishnah, preserves the safeguards that were meant to govern a capital trial, and this proceeding breaks them one after another. Capital cases were to be heard in daylight; this one is held at night. A death sentence could not be handed down on the same day as the hearing — a night had to pass first, deliberately, so that mercy had time to work; here the verdict is reached before dawn. The court was to sit in its own chamber within the temple precincts; this one convenes in the high priest's private house. And capital cases were not to be tried on the eve of a Sabbath or a festival; this is the eve of Passover. Every protection the law had built for an accused man is quietly set aside for this one accused man. They were not merely mistaken about who he was. They were in a hurry, and their hurry is on the record.

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "This man said, 'I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to rebuild it in three days.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here at last is the charge that sticks, and it is a half-truth, which is always the most serviceable kind.

He had said something like it. John records the words, spoken in the temple courts near the start of his ministry: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up — and John adds, in case anyone should miss it, but he was speaking about the temple of his body (Jn 2:19-21). Two things have been altered in the retelling, and both matter. Destroy this temple was an imperative addressed to them — you destroy it — and it has become I am able to destroy, a boast about what he intends. And the reference to his body has been quietly dropped, so that a saying about resurrection becomes a threat of arson.

Nobody had to invent anything. They simply repeated what he said with the frame removed, and every word they reported was traceable to his mouth. That is how the most effective false witness has always worked, in courts and in churches and in families: not fabrication, which can be disproved, but accurate quotation with the context stripped off. It is far harder to answer, because the accused finds himself denying something he did in fact say.

And the charge was well chosen. The temple was the centre of the nation's identity, its economy and its worship; a man threatening it was threatening everything at once, and the accusation would carry political weight with Rome as well as religious weight with the council.

What none of them can see is that the distorted version is truer than the accurate one. The temple was about to be destroyed — not by him, and not in three days, but within forty years, and he had wept over the city and said so plainly two days earlier. And the true temple, the one he actually meant, was standing in front of them bound, and would be pulled down on Friday and raised on Sunday, after which the building they were defending would have nothing left to do. They condemned him for a prophecy they thought was a boast, and it came true on both counts.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest stood up and said, "Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?" But Jesus remained silent. And the high priest said to him, "I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus remained silent. The high priest has stood up — the gesture of a man losing control of his own courtroom — and demanded an answer, and gets nothing.

The silence is not sullenness and it is not tactics. Isaiah had described it seven hundred years earlier: he was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth (Isa 53:7). The Servant does not defend himself. Jesus has spent the week answering every question the authorities could devise, in public, with answers that silenced them; he could have dismantled this testimony in a sentence. He declines.

Then Caiaphas changes the ground entirely. I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God. This is the formal oath of adjuration — the legal instrument by which a Jewish court placed a witness under obligation before God to answer. Having failed to convict him on evidence, the high priest puts the accused on oath and asks him to convict himself.

And notice the words he uses, because they have been in this Gospel before, in exactly this form. The Christ, the Son of the living God is what Peter said at Caesarea Philippi, and Jesus told him no man had taught him it — his Father in heaven had (16:16-17). The most exalted confession in Matthew and the formal charge in Matthew are word for word the same sentence. One man said it and was called blessed; the other says it and is looking for a capital conviction.

Which is the strangest thing about this trial. The question Caiaphas asks is the right question — the only question that matters, the one the whole Gospel has been driving toward — and he asks it under oath, in the name of the living God, and he is entirely correct that everything depends on the answer. He gets the answer. It is the truth. And he tears his clothes.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "You have said so. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven." Then the high priest tore his robes and said, "He has uttered blasphemy. What further witnesses do we need? You have now heard his blasphemy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has been silent through the whole proceeding. Put on oath by the living God, he speaks, and what he says is the most extravagant claim ever made by a human being in a courtroom.

You have said so is a formal affirmative, not an evasion — Judas got the same answer at the table and understood it perfectly well. But Jesus does not stop at yes. He adds a sentence nobody asked for, and it is built out of the two highest texts in the Hebrew Bible. Seated at the right hand of Power is Psalm 110:1, the psalm he had used against these same men in the temple three days before. Coming on the clouds of heaven is Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man comes to the Ancient of Days and receives a kingdom that shall not pass away.

Put together, they say this: you are trying me tonight, and you will stand in front of me. The prisoner tells the court that the next hearing will have the seating reversed. And the phrase from now on makes it worse — not at some remote future date, but beginning here, in this room, from this moment. The enthronement starts with the condemnation.

Caiaphas understood him exactly. That should be said plainly, because it disposes of the suggestion that Jesus never claimed to be divine and that his followers invented it later. The one man in the room with every professional reason to find a lesser meaning heard the claim, recognised it instantly, and called it blasphemy — which it would be, from anyone else.

Then he tears his robes, and there is an irony in the gesture that a Jewish reader would catch at once. Tearing the clothes was the prescribed response to hearing blasphemy. But the law had a standing exception for one man: the priest who is chief among his brothers… shall not let the hair of his head hang loose nor tear his clothes (Lev 21:10). The high priest, uniquely in Israel, was forbidden to do this. In the act of condemning the Son of God for blasphemy, Caiaphas breaks the law of his own office, in his own house, in front of the council — and the garments of the old priesthood are torn by the last man who should have touched them, at the exact moment the true High Priest is condemned to die.

verseByVerse.quote: "What is your judgment?" They answered, "He deserves death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is your judgment? He does not ask for deliberation. He asks for a verdict, immediately, having just told them what conclusion to reach — you have now heard his blasphemy — and having supplied the only evidence himself.

They answer in one voice: He deserves death. The Greek is two words, enochos thanatou, liable to death. There is no recorded dissent, no adjournment, no request to hear the accused's defence, no counting of votes. The most consequential judicial decision in human history is taken in the middle of the night by acclamation, in under a minute, in a private house.

And this is the destination the Gospel has been travelling toward since chapter 21. The leaders questioned his authority, and he told them about a vineyard whose tenants killed the owner's son; they knew he was speaking about them and wanted to arrest him then (21:45-46). He pronounced seven woes over them and wept over their city. Now the tenants have the son, and they say what the parable said they would say.

It is worth being exact about who these men were, because it is the whole point. This was not a mob and it was not Rome. This was the supreme court of the people of God — the most learned, most religious, most scripturally literate body on earth, men who had given their lives to the study of the Law and the Prophets, assembled to determine whether the man in front of them was the Messiah those Scriptures promised. They had every advantage. They reached a unanimous verdict, and it was the worst verdict ever returned.

Which is a warning aimed squarely at the religious, and there is nobody else it could be aimed at. It is possible to know the Scriptures thoroughly, to hold the highest office, to be scrupulous about the details, and to be so certain of your own reading that when the truth walks into your courtroom you condemn it for blasphemy — and go home believing you have defended God.

And there is an irony in their verdict that they could not have seen. He deserves death — enochos thanatou — is a legal finding about liability, and it was the one thing they said all night that was true of nobody in the room but themselves. The only man present who did not deserve death was the one they were sentencing, and the sentence they passed on him is the sentence he was on his way to bear for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they spit in his face and struck him. And some slapped him, saying, "Prophesy to us, you Christ! Who is it that struck you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verdict is delivered and the court dissolves into a beating. These are not soldiers yet; that comes later, under Rome. This is the council and its attendants, and what follows a religious trial in the small hours is men spitting in a bound man's face.

Spitting was the ultimate expression of contempt in that culture, and the Law itself treats it so: when Miriam was struck with leprosy the LORD said to Moses, if her father had but spit in her face, should she not be shamed seven days? (Num 12:14). It is the gesture reserved for someone placed outside the community altogether.

Then they play a game with him. Prophesy to us, you Christ! Who is it that struck you? Mark tells us they covered his face first (Mk 14:65), which is what makes it a game — blindfold the prophet, hit him, and ask him to name the hand. It is mockery of a specific kind: they are not merely hurting him, they are ridiculing the one claim he made under oath.

And Isaiah had written the scene down: I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting (Isa 50:6). Every element is there — the blows, the face, the spitting. They are mocking him for claiming to be the one the prophets spoke of, while acting out a paragraph of the prophets.

But take their question seriously for a moment, because it has an answer. Who is it that struck you? He knew. He had just told the court he would be seated at the right hand of Power and would come on the clouds of heaven; the men taking turns at a blindfolded prisoner were asking the coming Judge to identify them, and he could have named every one of them, and their fathers.

He said nothing. And within weeks Peter would stand up in Jerusalem and preach to a crowd that certainly contained some of them, and offer them forgiveness in the name of the man they had blindfolded — which is the only reason any of us should be glad he did not answer the question.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. And a servant girl came up to him and said, "You also were with Jesus the Galilean." But he denied it before them all, saying, "I do not know what you mean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew cuts from the hall to the courtyard, and the contrast is the whole architecture of the chapter. Inside, under oath, before the supreme court, with his life at stake, Jesus confesses who he is. Outside, at a fire, with nothing at stake but embarrassment, Peter denies that he knows him.

Look at who does the asking. Not a magistrate, not a soldier, not an officer of the court. A paidiske — a servant girl, probably young, the lowest-ranking person in that courtyard, with no authority to arrest anybody or charge anybody. She is not conducting an interrogation. She has recognised a face and said so out loud.

And Peter, who three hours earlier drew a sword against an armed detachment, cannot handle it. That is the thing to notice about the whole scene: he did not fail where he expected to fail. He had prepared himself, sincerely, for death — even if I must die with you — and he was probably capable of it. He had not prepared for a girl by a fire on a cold night, and nobody does.

His answer is not a considered repudiation. I do not know what you mean is the reflex of a man buying three seconds: not quite a lie about Jesus, not quite an answer, just enough fog to make the conversation move on. It is the smallest possible step in the wrong direction, and it is the one that makes the next two possible.

Which is how it usually goes. Very few denials of Christ happen under interrogation. They happen in the pub, in the staff room, at the family table, in the moment when the subject comes up and a laugh is available and the cost of being counted in suddenly seems out of proportion to the occasion. Nobody plans it. The mouth is faster than the conviction, and it is over before the will is consulted — and it is worth knowing in advance that this, and not the courtroom, is where the ground is slippery.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he went out to the entrance, another servant girl saw him, and she said to the bystanders, "This man was with Jesus of Nazareth." And again he denied it with an oath: "I do not know the man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He moves. When he went out to the entrance — away from the fire, toward the gate, which is what a man does when he is thinking about leaving and has not quite decided. He does not go. He stays in the gateway, which is the worst place in the courtyard: still inside, already looking out.

A second girl recognises him, and this time she does not speak to him. She says it to the bystanders — this man was with Jesus of Nazareth — so the denial has to be made in front of a small audience rather than to one person. The pressure has risen a step, and so does the denial.

Now it comes with an oath. That is the change, and it is a large one. The first denial was a mumble about not knowing what she meant; this one calls God to witness. And it is more definite in the other direction too: not I do not know what you mean but I do not know the man. He has stopped fogging the question and started answering it, falsely.

There is a bitter detail here that Peter himself would have felt afterwards. It was this same Lord who had told them, in the Sermon, not to swear at all — let what you say be simply Yes or No, because anything more comes from evil (5:34-37). Peter is breaking that instruction in the act of denying the one who gave it, and using God's name to make the denial more convincing.

And note the phrase he chooses, because it will be quoted back at him in a way he cannot have anticipated. I do not know the man — ouk oida ton anthropon. Weeks later, on a beach, the risen Christ will ask him three times whether he loves him, once for each denial, and Peter will say each time, Lord, you know. The man who claimed not to know will end up resting everything on being known.

Escalation is the signature of a lie under pressure. A single untruth is almost never stable; it has to be defended, and each defence costs more than the last, and the man telling it is not choosing freely by the third round. Peter is not a worse man at the gateway than he was at the fire. He is a man further down a slope he stepped onto with one small evasion twenty minutes earlier.

verseByVerse.quote: After a little while the bystanders came up and said to Peter, "Certainly you too are one of them, for your accent betrays you." Then he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, "I do not know the man." And immediately the rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This time it is not one accuser but a group, and the evidence against him is his own mouth. Your accent betrays you. Galileans were known in Jerusalem for their pronunciation — they were said to slur the guttural letters that Judeans sounded distinctly, enough that a Galilean could be identified by a sentence. Peter has been in the courtyard for hours, and the more he has talked the more obvious he has become. Every denial made the next one likelier by keeping him in conversation.

And so the third denial, which goes as far as language allows. He began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear. The first is anathematizein — to call down destruction, to say in effect may God damn me if I am lying. He is asking God to destroy him if he knows Jesus, and he knows Jesus, and Jesus is fifty yards away being spat at.

Three stages in perhaps an hour: evasion, then an oath, then a self-curse. Nothing in Peter's character changed in that hour. What changed is that each answer had to cover the one before it, and by the third he was defending not Jesus but his own previous two sentences.

And immediately the rooster crowed.

Matthew does not comment. He puts the crow directly against the curse with nothing in between, and the effect is of a door closing somewhere in the building. It is an ordinary bird doing an ordinary thing at the ordinary hour, in a city full of them, and it is the most precisely timed sound in the New Testament.

And consider what the crow actually is. Peter had been told this would happen, in those words, by the man he has just cursed himself for knowing. The sound is not merely an alarm; it is evidence that his Lord had been exactly right about him, at the very moment he most needed to know that his Lord understood him and had not been surprised. It is a hard mercy and it is unmistakably a mercy: God arranged, in advance, for Peter to be stopped before he could go a step further, by a sound he could not possibly mistake.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter remembered the saying of Jesus, "Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times." And he went out and wept bitterly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Peter remembered" — this is the turning point. Memory of Christ's word, confronting his own failure, produces not despair but grief. The bitter weeping is genuine repentance — not Judas's remorse that leads to destruction but Peter's sorrow that leads to restoration (2 Cor. 7:10). He goes out — away from the courtyard, away from the scene of failure — and weeps. The chapter that began with the woman's extravagant love ends with the apostle's extravagant tears. Both are beautiful in different ways: her love anticipated his burial; his tears begin his restoration. Bitter weeping before God is one of the most hopeful sounds in Scripture. It means the heart is not dead but awake to its own failure, and hearts that are awake can be healed.

Which raises the question this chapter is built to raise, because Matthew has deliberately braided the two men together: Judas betrays and Peter denies, both on the same night, both wretched about it afterwards — and one is restored and one is destroyed. Anyone who has failed badly reads that and wants to know which of the two he is.

Start by refusing the answer that suggests itself first, which is that Peter's sin was smaller. It was not obviously smaller. Peter denied with oaths and curses, three times, having been warned by name a few hours earlier; and he did it publicly while his Lord was on trial for his life. If the difference were the size of the sin, the verdict could have gone either way.

The difference is the direction the sorrow travels. Both men felt terrible; Matthew says Judas was seized with remorse and Peter wept bitterly. But remorse is what a man feels about consequences and about himself — Judas went to the priests, tried to undo the transaction, and when that failed he went out alone. He never went to Jesus. Peter's grief drove him in exactly the opposite direction: back to the only person who could do anything about it, and within weeks he is eating breakfast on a beach with him. Paul's line for the distinction is exact — godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation, and worldly grief produces death (2 Cor 7:10). One kind of sorrow ends in a rope; the other ends in a charcoal fire and a threefold restoration.

So the practical test is not how badly you feel. It is which way you are facing while you feel it. Are you running from him, or toward him? Do you find, underneath the shame, that you still want him — or only that you want the mess undone? A man may be genuinely disgusted with himself and still have no desire whatever for Christ, and that is Judas. A man may be in pieces and still be crawling in the right direction, and that is Peter.

And if you are not sure, notice what the fact of the question suggests. Judas asked nothing; he simply left. The very anxiety about which of the two you are is a movement toward the one who can answer it — so take it to him, tonight, and stop conducting the trial yourself. He restored a man who cursed his name in a courtyard, and he did it without a single reproach on the beach. There is no reason to believe he has changed his practice.

26.theology: The cup of wrath and substitutionary atonement. The cup that Jesus prays might pass in Gethsemane and then drinks on the cross is the Old Testament cup of divine wrath — the concentrated judgment of God against human sin. That he drinks it “for many” (26:28) and “for the forgiveness of sins” is Matthew’s clearest statement of penal substitutionary atonement: Christ in the place of sinners, bearing the penalty that was theirs, so that the forgiveness that is his might become theirs. This is the heart of the gospel — not merely that God loves us (though he does) or that Jesus shows us how to live (though he does) but that the holy God, in the person of his Son, absorbed the full penalty for human sin so that justice and mercy could be simultaneously satisfied at the cross.
26.examples:
Then: The disciples slept in Gethsemane while Jesus prayed. They could not watch one hour. Their failure is not recorded to condemn them but to reveal the bankruptcy of human resolve — and to show that the cross was accomplished not by the strength of the disciples but by the obedience of the Son, alone, in the dark, sustained only by the Father.

Now: Every celebration of the Lord’s Supper is a proclamation of Gethsemane and the cross. The bread and cup carry the weight of that night — the betrayal, the agony, the submission, the arrest, the trial. To eat and drink worthily (1 Cor 11:27–29) is to remember not merely a past event but the present ground of our standing before God: his blood, poured out for many, for the forgiveness of sins. That includes every sin we brought to the table today.

27.title: The Crucifixion of the King
27.text: <sup>29</sup>and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on his head and put a reed in his right hand. And kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” <sup>35</sup>And when they had crucified him, they divided his garments among them by casting lots. <sup>37</sup>And over his head they put the charge against him, which read, “This is Jesus, the King of the Jews.” <sup>45</sup>Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land until the ninth hour. <sup>46</sup>And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?” that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” <sup>50</sup>And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and yielded up his spirit. <sup>51</sup>And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. And the earth shook, and the rocks were split. <sup>54</sup>When the centurion and those who were with him, keeping watch over Jesus, saw the earthquake and what took place, they were afraid, and said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” <sup>60</sup>and laid it in his own new tomb, which he had cut in the rock. And he rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb and went away.
27.overview:
Chapter 27 is the centre of the universe. Everything in the Old Testament moves toward it; everything in the New Testament moves from it. The crucifixion of Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews, is the event by which God reconciles a broken world to himself. Matthew narrates it with restraint — he does not linger on the physical agony of crucifixion — but saturates every scene with Old Testament allusion: Psalm 22 (the cry of dereliction, the dividing of garments, the mocking); Zechariah 11 (thirty pieces of silver); Isaiah 53 (numbered with transgressors, interceding for sinners).

The theological climax comes in three simultaneous signs at the moment of death: the tearing of the temple veil, the earthquake and split rocks, and the opening of tombs. The veil torn from top to bottom is God’s own act: the barrier between the holy and the profane is removed. The way into the presence of God is now open to all who come through the crucified King. The centurion’s confession — “Truly this man was the Son of God!” — is the Gentile answer to the question Jesus asked in chapter 16: spoken at the foot of the cross, by a soldier, at the moment of death.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–44 — The Trial before Pilate and the Crucifixion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The council reconvenes at dawn to give the night's verdict a legal form, then takes Jesus to Pilate, because they may condemn but may not execute. Judas returns the silver, is told to see to it himself, and hangs himself; the money buys a burial field for foreigners. Before Pilate the charge is quietly rewritten from blasphemy to kingship. Pilate tries the Passover custom, is warned by his wife, finds no fault, washes his hands, and condemns him anyway. Barabbas goes free. Jesus is scourged, mocked by the cohort, crowned with thorns, and led out to Golgotha, where he is crucified between two brigands and jeered at by passers-by, priests and the dying.
verseByVerse.theology: Substitution is not imposed on this section by later theology; it is the shape of the narrative. One cross and two candidates: a guilty insurrectionist walks free for exactly one reason, which is that the innocent man took his place, and Matthew records both in a single verse (v. 26). The mockery carries the same doctrine inside out. He saved others; he cannot save himself is true in every word and false in every intention: not a failure of power, but a necessity built into substitution, since a substitute who steps out from under the weight has stopped being one. He could have saved himself or saved them. There was never an afternoon in which he did both.
verseByVerse.examples: Pilate is the study in this section, and he is a modern figure. Nobody in the chapter sees more clearly: he is amazed at the prisoner, warned by his wife, told by his own judgement that the charge is driven by envy, and states twice that he finds no fault. And nobody does less with what he sees. He never once considers simply doing what a judge is for; he looks instead for a procedure that will produce justice at no personal cost — the crowd, the custom, the basin — and when no such route exists he chooses the cost he can bear and lets the innocent man pay the other. Admiration is not allegiance. Pilate was impressed by Jesus at nine in the morning and signed his death warrant before noon.

verseByVerse.quote: When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death. And they bound him and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate the governor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When morning came. They reconvene at first light, and the reason is procedural. Everything done in Caiaphas's house during the night was irregular by their own rules, so a second session is held in daylight to give the verdict a form that will stand. It changes nothing; the decision was taken hours ago. This is paperwork.

Then a detail that explains the whole rest of the chapter: they take him to Pilate. Under Roman administration the Sanhedrin retained wide powers but had lost the right of capital punishment — it is not lawful for us to put anyone to death, as they tell Pilate in John's account (Jn 18:31). They can condemn; they cannot execute. Which means that to kill him they must persuade a Gentile governor, and to persuade a Gentile governor the charge must change. Blasphemy is nothing to Rome. Kingship is everything to Rome. Watch how the accusation is quietly reworded between this verse and verse 11.

And notice the verb once more: they delivered him over — paradidomi, for perhaps the tenth time since chapter 26. Judas delivered him to the priests; the priests deliver him to Pilate; Pilate will deliver him to be crucified. Every party in the story is handing him on to somebody else, and each hand-off is a small act of evasion — nobody wants to be the one holding him at the end.

Under all of it Paul puts the sentence that reaches behind every human hand in the chain: he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom 8:32) — and the verb Paul uses is the same one. The passing of the parcel that looks like a series of men avoiding responsibility is, at another level, the Father handing over the Son, on purpose, for us.

One more word: they bound him. He had spent three years loosing people — a bent-over woman loosed from her infirmity, a dead man loosed from his grave clothes, sinners loosed from their debts. The last thing done to him before the Gentiles take him is that his hands are tied.

verseByVerse.quote: Then when Judas, his betrayer, saw that Jesus was condemned, he changed his mind and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and the elders, saying, "I have sinned by betraying innocent blood." They said, "What is that to us? See to it yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The trigger is precise: when Judas saw that Jesus was condemned. Something he had not expected has happened, and the most likely reading is the plainest one — he had not thought it would go this far. Perhaps he assumed the council would humiliate Jesus and release him, or that Jesus would finally act and force the confrontation everyone had been waiting for. The verdict lands and the thing becomes real.

Matthew's verb is metamelomai — he was sorry, he regretted it. It is not the word this Gospel uses for repentance, which is metanoia, a change of mind that turns and goes the other way. Judas felt the full weight of what he had done. What he did not do was turn round.

And his confession is theologically flawless. I have sinned by betraying innocent blood. He names the act, calls it sin, uses the first person, and declares the victim innocent — which is more than Caiaphas said, more than Pilate managed, and more than the crowd would allow. If words could save a man, these words would have done it.

He said them to the wrong people. That is the tragedy of the verse. Fifty yards away was the only man in Jerusalem who could have done anything with that sentence, and Judas took it to a committee of priests, who gave him the answer committees give: What is that to us? See to it yourself. They had used him, paid him, and were finished with him, and they tell him his conscience is his own business.

Watch that phrase, because Matthew is about to use it again. In twenty verses Pilate will wash his hands in front of the crowd and say see to it yourselves — the same formula, handed on from the priests to the governor and back to the people. Everybody in this chapter is trying to put the blood somewhere else. Judas tries to give the money back; the priests will not take it into the treasury; Pilate calls for a basin; the crowd shouts that they will have it on their own heads. Not one of them can get rid of it, because there is only one place that blood can actually go, and none of them will take it there.

verseByVerse.quote: And throwing down the pieces of silver into the temple, he departed, and he went and hanged himself. But the chief priests, taking the pieces of silver, said, "It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, since it is blood money."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas throws the silver into the temple — perhaps toward the sanctuary — as a futile act of rejection. Then he hangs himself. His death is recorded without embellishment; Matthew's theological point is already made. The priests' scrupulous concern about the legal status of blood money is devastating irony: they will not defile the treasury with money used to purchase innocent blood, yet they have just condemned innocent blood to death. Their legal fastidiousness is hypocrisy at its most refined — straining out the gnat of treasury regulations while swallowing the camel of judicial murder. It is as clear a case of religion without conscience as the Gospels contain: the rulebook consulted over the accounting of the money, and never once over the murder it paid for.

"He went and hanged himself" is four words, and they collide with the only other account we have. Luke, reporting Peter's words in Acts, says of Judas that "falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out" (Acts 1:18) — and adds that Judas acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, where Matthew says the priests bought it. Two deaths and two buyers, say the critics. In fact both pairs settle without strain.

Take the death first. The two statements are not rivals; they are the beginning and the end of one event. A man hangs himself, and the body stays where it hangs. Then something gives — the rope, the branch, or the hand of whoever finally cut him down — and the body falls. The traditional site is a cliff above the valley of Hinnom, which makes the fall a long one; and a corpse that has hung for a day or more in that climate does exactly what Luke describes when it strikes rock. Matthew tells you what Judas did to himself. Luke tells you what was found, and why the place got the name it did. Neither has to be corrected for the other to be true.

The field is simpler still. The money was legally Judas's — that is precisely the priests' problem, which is why they will not put it in the treasury and why they must spend it on his behalf rather than their own. A purchase made with a dead man's money, in a matter he set in motion, is naturally credited to him; we still speak that way about estates. Acts is not picturing Judas out inspecting land. It is saying what his thirty pieces of silver finally bought.

And notice what the two accounts share, which is more striking than what divides them: a field in Jerusalem that everybody could point at, with a name in the local dialect that everybody knew — Akeldama, Field of Blood. Invented stories do not usually come with an address.

verseByVerse.quote: So they took counsel and bought with them the potter's field as a burial place for strangers. Therefore that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will not put the money in the treasury and they cannot give it back, so they spend it — and the committee's solution is a burial ground for foreigners. Jerusalem at festival time was full of pilgrims from across the empire, and some of them died there; a plot for strangers was a genuine civic need, and buying one was a respectable use of awkward funds. They have found a way to be charitable with the price of a man's life.

A potter's field was worked-out ground — clay quarried until the soil was useless, littered with the broken pots that failed on the wheel. Nothing would grow there. It was cheap because it was finished.

So the thirty pieces buy a piece of exhausted earth full of smashed pottery, to bury foreigners with no family to claim them. And within a few years the message the priests were protecting the treasury from would be carried by Jewish believers to exactly those foreigners — to Cyrene and Rome and Ethiopia and Asia — and the men buried in that field as nobodies were the very sort of people the Son of God had just died for.

Then Matthew's aside: therefore that field has been called the Field of Blood to this day. He is writing decades after the event, in a city where the place still had the name, and where anybody reading his account could walk out and look at it. Luke gives the Aramaic — Akeldama (Acts 1:19). The priests bought a plot to keep their books clean, and instead they erected a permanent public monument to what they had done, with a name attached that no one could scrub off.

They were careful men, and it is worth noticing what carefulness achieved here. They protected the treasury and named a graveyard after their own crime.

And the reasoning that got them there is one Matthew has shown us before. Twelve chapters earlier Jesus had exposed the trick by which a man could declare his money dedicated to God and thereby avoid supporting his own parents — so for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God (15:5-6). The mechanism is identical here. The silver is treated as the thing that has been defiled, and the men who paid it out are treated as untouched. Money can be unclean; the hand that spends it apparently cannot. It is possible to build an entire moral system that asks scrupulous questions about objects and no questions at all about the man holding them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then was fulfilled what had been spoken by the prophet Jeremiah, saying, "And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him on whom a price had been set by some of the sons of Israel, and they gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord directed me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An honest reader with a reference Bible will stop here, and should. Matthew says this was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah, and then quotes something that reads much more like Zechariah — the thirty pieces of silver, weighed out as the price of a shepherd and thrown to the potter in the house of the LORD (Zech 11:12-13). Turn to Jeremiah for those words and you will not find them. What is going on?

Four explanations are offered and three of them are serious. A copyist's slip is possible but weakly supported. More likely is that Matthew is doing something Jewish writers did regularly: citing a composite of prophetic texts under the name of the more prominent prophet. And there is a genuine Jeremiah strand in the material — Jeremiah is the prophet of the potter (he is sent to watch a potter work in ch. 18, then buys an earthen flask and smashes it at the Potsherd Gate in ch. 19), and Jeremiah is the prophet who buys a field with weighed-out silver as a sign (ch. 32). The potter, the field, and the weighed silver all come from Jeremiah; the thirty pieces and the throwing into the house of the LORD come from Zechariah. Matthew has fused them and named the collection after the major prophet — and there is evidence that in some Jewish orderings Jeremiah stood first among the prophetic books, which would make his name a natural label for the whole scroll.

Now notice what Jeremiah 19 actually says, because it is more than a source for a word. Jeremiah is told to take the elders and priests out to the valley of Hinnom by the Potsherd Gate, smash a jar in front of them, and announce that because they have filled this place with the blood of innocents, it will be called no longer Topheth but the Valley of Slaughter, and they will bury in it until there is no room (Jer 19:1-6, 11).

A field of broken pottery. Priests and elders standing in it. Innocent blood. A burial ground. A new name for the place. Six centuries later the same officials, in the same valley, buy the same kind of ground with blood money, and the city gives it a new name — and Matthew, who knew his Jeremiah, saw the shape of it and told us where to look.

Which is the point worth taking from a technical footnote. The men handling that silver thought they were tidying up an administrative problem. They were walking, step by step, through a prophecy about themselves, and the name of the field is still on the map.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor asked him, "Are you the King of the Jews?" Jesus said, "You have said so." And when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, he gave no answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charge has changed. Before Caiaphas the question was are you the Christ, the Son of God; before Pilate it is are you the King of the Jews? Blasphemy would not interest a Roman governor for a moment. Sedition would end a career if it were ignored. The same man is being accused of a different crime in a different building an hour later, and everyone involved knows why.

Pilate's question has an emphatic pronoun in it — you are the King of the Jews? — and the emphasis is almost certainly contempt. He is looking at a man who has been up all night, beaten, bound, deserted by his followers and handed over by his own nation's leadership. Rome had seen pretenders before; they generally arrived with an army. This one has arrived with rope marks on his wrists.

You have said so. It is the same form of words he gave Judas at the table and Caiaphas in the night — an affirmative, but one that hands the sentence back to the speaker. Yes, and you have no idea what you have just said. Pilate means a rival to Caesar in a troublesome province. The answer is yes to something immeasurably larger, and Pilate will shortly write it on a board and nail it over his head without believing a word of it.

Then the accusations come, and he stops answering. Isaiah had said so: he was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth (Isa 53:7). It is worth remembering what he was capable of in argument. This is the man who had silenced the Pharisees on tribute, the Sadducees on resurrection, and the lawyers on David's son, all in one afternoon, so completely that no one dared to ask him any more questions (22:46).

He could have taken this court apart. There was no case; the witnesses had already contradicted each other once. He says nothing, and the silence is not helplessness — it is the loudest thing in the room. A man who could clear himself and will not has decided something in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pilate said to him, "Do you not hear how many things they testify against you?" But he gave him no answer, not even to a single charge, so that the governor was greatly amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate cannot understand it. Do you not hear how many things they testify against you? — and the astonishment in the question is genuine. He is offering the prisoner an opening. Say something. Give me one thing I can work with.

Then Matthew's verb: the governor was greatly amazed, thaumazein, the word this Gospel has used of crowds watching a paralytic walk and a storm go quiet. The man who represents the power of Rome in Judea is the one left staring.

And it is worth asking what exactly astonished him, because Pilate had presided over a great many trials. He had seen men beg, bribe, bluster, weep, and inform on their friends. What he had presumably never seen was a defendant with nothing to say — not sullen, not broken, not defiant, simply not interested in the one thing every other prisoner had wanted, which was to get out.

That is the beginning of a pattern in this chapter, and it is the saddest thing about Pilate. He is amazed at the prisoner. He is warned by his wife. He states twice that he can find no fault. He knows the charge is driven by envy. He tries three separate manoeuvres to get the man released. Nobody in the story sees more clearly than Pilate, and nobody does less with what he sees.

Which is worth naming plainly, because it is a modern position as much as an ancient one. A great many people are impressed by Jesus. They find him remarkable, unlike anyone else, impossible to dismiss; they will say so warmly and mean it. Pilate was impressed. He was amazed at him at nine in the morning and signed his death warrant before noon, and the amazement made no difference to the outcome whatever, because admiration is not the same thing as allegiance and never once has been.

One more detail in the Greek is worth having, because it sharpens the silence. Matthew does not merely say Jesus gave no answer; he writes that he did not answer him to a single charge — not one word, to not one accusation. It is emphatic and it is total. Isaiah had described exactly this: like a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth (Isa 53:7). What Pilate took for an inexplicable failure of self-preservation was a prophecy being kept in front of him, by a man who had decided in a garden the night before that he was not going to be talked out of this.

verseByVerse.quote: Now at the feast the governor was accustomed to release for the crowd any one prisoner whom they wanted. And they had then a notorious prisoner called Barabbas.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The custom is not otherwise attested outside the Gospels, though the practice of a goodwill release at a festival is entirely plausible for a Roman administrator managing a restive province at its most crowded and most nationalistic moment. Pilate keeps a card to play at Passover.

And the man in the cell is described by Matthew as notorious, episemos, literally marked or distinguished — he had a reputation. Mark and Luke fill it in: he was in prison with the rebels who had committed murder in the insurrection (Mk 15:7). So Barabbas is not a burglar. He is a nationalist fighter who has killed for the cause of getting Rome out of Israel, and he is precisely the kind of messiah a great many people in that city were hoping for.

Then his name, which is a sermon by itself. Bar-Abba means son of the father. And there is a genuine textual question worth knowing about, because a number of manuscripts, and some early versions, give his full name as Jesus Barabbas — and Origen in the third century knew the reading and disliked it, thinking it improper that a criminal should share the Lord's name. That kind of squeamishness is exactly how a name gets quietly dropped from a text, which is why many scholars think the longer reading is original.

If it is, then the question Pilate is about to put to the crowd is almost unbearable: which Jesus do you want — Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ? Two men with the same name, one the son of a human father and one the Son of the eternal Father, and a crowd is asked to choose.

Whatever the manuscripts finally say, the substance is not in doubt, and it is the clearest picture of substitution in the New Testament. There is one cross and two candidates. Barabbas is guilty and everyone knows it — he has no defence and expects none. He is released, and he is released for exactly one reason: the other man took his place. Every person who has ever been forgiven is standing where Barabbas stood that morning, listening through a cell door to a crowd deciding, and walking out into the sunshine while somebody else is led away to the cross that had his own name on it.

verseByVerse.quote: So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, "Whom do you want me to release for you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?" For he knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate is not stupid and he is not confused. Matthew tells us flatly what he had worked out: he knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up.

Phthonos is a precise word and it is the right diagnosis. Not fear of blasphemy, not zeal for the law, not concern for public order — envy, the resentment of a man's standing that curdles into a wish to see it destroyed. The crowds had gone after him. The temple courts had emptied of their audience and filled with his. Whatever the theological charges said, the council's motive was that this Galilean had taken something that belonged to them, and Pilate — a professional reader of provincial politics — saw it in about five minutes.

So the offer is shrewd. Give the crowd the choice, and let the crowd's affection for Jesus override the leaders' spite. It has the enormous advantage of costing Pilate nothing: he does not have to acquit anybody or defy anybody; he merely opens a door and lets public opinion carry the prisoner out.

And that is the whole of Pilate's method. He never once considers simply doing what a judge is for. He has an innocent man, he knows the accusation is malicious, and he has absolute authority in the province — and instead of releasing him he goes looking for a procedure that will release him without anybody being able to blame Pilate for it. He will try the crowd, then the custom, then a basin of water. All three are ways of arriving at justice without paying for it.

There is no such route, and this chapter exists partly to say so. Doing right when it is unpopular has a price, and the price is the whole point; anything that removes it has also removed the rightness. Pilate wanted a way to be just at no personal cost, and when he could not find one he chose the cost he could bear and let the innocent man pay the other.

And a word about the envy Pilate spotted, since it is the one sin in this chapter that most readers will have committed this month. Envy never arrives announcing itself. Not one of those priests woke up thinking he wanted the Galilean dead because the crowds preferred him; each of them had a reason, and the reasons were theological, and they would have been genuinely offended to hear the charge. That is how it works. Envy borrows the language of principle, because it cannot survive being named. The test is simple and unpleasant: when a person doing your kind of work is praised, do the objections you raise to his methods occur to you before or after the praise?

verseByVerse.quote: Besides, while he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent word to him, "Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered much because of him today in a dream."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the middle of the trial, a note arrives. Somebody has to carry it through the praetorium and put it into the governor's hand while he is sitting on the judgment seat, which means his wife thought this urgent enough to interrupt a capital case in public.

Her message is short and it contains the only unambiguous verdict anyone gives in the chapter: have nothing to do with that righteous man. Not innocent of this particular charge — righteous, dikaios. The council would not say it. Pilate never quite says it. Judas said it and threw the money at the priests. A Gentile woman who has never met him says it from her own bedroom on the strength of a dream.

And Matthew, of all the evangelists, is the one who would notice. Open his Gospel at the beginning: an angel warns Joseph in a dream to take the child (1:20); the magi are warned in a dream not to go back to Herod (2:12); Joseph is warned in a dream to flee to Egypt, and again to come home (2:13, 19). Matthew's account of the birth is full of God protecting his Son by warning people in their sleep — including foreigners.

Now, at the end of the same Gospel, one last dream, one last warning, one last foreigner. The bookend is exact and the outcome is opposite. Every warning at the beginning was heeded and the child lived. This one is set aside, and the man dies.

It is worth sitting with what that arrangement says about God. He is under no obligation to warn Pilate. The trial is a formality, the outcome is fixed, the prophecies require the death — and heaven still sends word into the governor's house, at the last possible hour, through the one person who might reach him. God will not have it said that no one told him. Even in the hour of the greatest crime ever committed, the mercy is still working, still knocking, still going to the trouble of a dream at dawn for a man who will wash his hands and do it anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus. The governor again said to them, "Which of the two do you want me to release for you?" And they said, "Barabbas."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd. Matthew is careful here and the care matters. The crowd does not arrive with a demand; it is worked. The verb is the one for winning somebody over by argument and pressure, and it takes time and effort and people moving through a gathering having quiet conversations.

So consider who is actually standing in that courtyard at daybreak. It is not the nation of Israel, and it is not the Passover pilgrim crowd — most of Jerusalem is asleep or preparing for the feast, and the great majority of Jews alive that morning were scattered across the empire and had never heard of the case. This is a body of people assembled at short notice, at dawn, outside the governor's residence, by men with a specific outcome in mind. Rented crowds have been a standard instrument of politics in every century since.

That has to be said plainly, because this scene has been pressed into service for centuries as a charge against a whole people, and Christians have used it to do great harm. There is no doctrine of collective guilt available here. The man on trial is a Jew; his mother is a Jew; every apostle is a Jew; the women at the cross are Jews; Joseph who buries him is a Jew; the author of this Gospel is a Jew; and within weeks three thousand Jews in this same city will believe and be baptised. A managed crowd at a dawn hearing is not a people, and anyone who has read this chapter as a warrant for contempt has read it exactly backwards.

What the scene does teach is something about crowds generally, and it is not comfortable for any of us. These were not monsters. Five days earlier a crowd in this city had spread cloaks on the road for him and shouted Hosanna; some of the same people may well have been in both. What changed was not the evidence but the direction of the pressure and the identity of the men doing the talking.

Which is why a Christian should be permanently suspicious of the safety of numbers. The instinct to go with the room is the strongest social force there is, and it does not feel like cowardice while it is happening — it feels like consensus, and it feels like being sensible, and it can move a hundred ordinary people from Hosanna to Crucify inside a week.

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate said to them, "Then what shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?" They all said, "Let him be crucified!" And he said, "Why? What evil has he done?" But they shouted all the more, "Let him be crucified!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then what shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ? Pilate asks it as a procedural question by a man who has run out of manoeuvres, and it is the question the whole Gospel has been driving toward. He is not asking what is true about Jesus. He is asking what he is going to do about him, which is the harder question and the only one that ever gets anybody anywhere.

Notice that the one option not available to him is the one most people assume they have. He cannot leave the prisoner in the cell and think about it. There is a man in front of him who must be either released or executed before the feast begins, and doing nothing is a decision with a body attached. Pilate would have given a great deal for a third door, and there was not one.

Then his last flicker of conscience: Why? What evil has he done? It is the right question, asked by the right official, in the right forum, and it is the only genuinely judicial sentence spoken in the entire proceeding. Nobody answers it. Matthew does not record a single charge in reply — they shouted all the more. That is the answer, and it is the answer a crowd gives when it has no answer: not a better argument but a louder one.

The escalation is worth watching because it is the ordinary physics of a mob. First a verdict — let him be crucified. Then a question they cannot meet. Then the same verdict at greater volume. No new evidence has entered the courtyard and nobody's mind has changed; the noise is doing the work that reasons cannot. Anyone who has watched a public argument in our own day, where volume and repetition settle what evidence never will, has seen this precise mechanism at work in a milder form.

And Pilate's question is still open. It cannot be handed back to a crowd, and it cannot be deferred indefinitely, and there is no neutral answer to it — because the choice is not between accepting him and leaving him alone. It is between accepting him and sending him away, and Pilate found out that morning that sending him away is also something you have done.

verseByVerse.quote: So when Pilate saw that he was gaining nothing, but rather that a riot was beginning, he took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, "I am innocent of this man's blood; see to it yourselves." And all the people answered, "His blood be on us and on our children!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The basin is theatre, and it is borrowed theatre. Washing the hands to disclaim responsibility for blood is a Jewish rite, not a Roman one: when a body was found in open country and the killer unknown, the elders of the nearest town washed their hands over a heifer and said our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it shed (Deut 21:6-7). Pilate, who cares nothing for the law of Moses, performs a ceremony from it in front of a Jewish crowd, because it is the gesture they will understand.

And it settles nothing. The rite in Deuteronomy is for men who genuinely did not do it and genuinely do not know who did. Pilate knows exactly who is doing this, because he is: he holds the authority, he has heard the case, he has stated twice that he finds no fault, and in the next verse he signs the order. A judge cannot become a bystander by getting his hands wet. I am innocent of this man's blood is the only demonstrably false statement anybody makes in the trial.

Then the crowd's answer, and it must be handled with great care, because these words have been quoted over centuries to justify appalling cruelty against Jewish people — pogroms, expulsions, ghettos, and worse. That use of this verse is not a regrettable excess. It is a flat contradiction of the New Testament, and it should be said so plainly that no reader is left in any doubt.

Consider what the sentence actually is. It is a shout from a managed crowd in a courtyard at dawn (see on vv. 20-21), not a legal instrument, and no crowd on earth has the authority to bind its children, still less the unborn generations of a whole people. Scripture rules the principle out in terms: the son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father (Ezek 18:20). And the New Testament nowhere charges the Jewish people with the death of Christ. It charges the human race, and it charges the reader. Peter tells a Jerusalem crowd they crucified him and then baptises three thousand of them the same day. Paul, a Jew, writes that the rulers of this age crucified the Lord of glory, and that his heart's desire and prayer for his own people is their salvation.

And now the thing that turns the verse inside out, which is why a Christian should be the last person on earth to use it as a weapon. They said his blood be on us — and his blood coming down on a person is the best thing that can happen to anyone alive. Seven weeks later Peter stood up in that city and preached to people who had been in that crowd, and three thousand of them went down into the water; and the blood they had called down on their own heads landed on them exactly as they had asked, and it did not condemn them, it washed them. Nobody, shouting in a courtyard, ever asked for something better than they knew. The curse they pronounced on themselves is, word for word, the prayer of every Christian who has ever come to the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, delivered him to be crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two clauses, and Matthew will not linger on either. He released for them Barabbas — the guilty man walks. Having scourged Jesus, delivered him to be crucified — the innocent man is flogged and handed over. Substitution is not a doctrine imposed on this verse by later theologians; it is the shape of the sentence.

The flogging was not a beating. The Roman flagellum was a short whip of several leather thongs weighted with pieces of bone or metal, laid on a man stripped and tied to a post. Roman scourging had no fixed limit of strokes as Jewish law did. Eusebius, describing martyrdoms he had seen, says the victims' veins and inward organs were laid bare; the historians record that men sometimes died under it before ever reaching a cross. It was administered before crucifixion precisely to shorten the ordeal by weakening the condemned.

Matthew gives it a participle. Not a sentence, not a paragraph — a subordinate clause on the way to something else. The restraint of all four Gospels here is remarkable and it is deliberate. They are not writing to harrow the reader's feelings, and there is a kind of devotion that dwells on the physical horror until the emotion produced becomes the point. The evangelists refuse it. What they want understood is not chiefly how much it hurt but what it accomplished.

Which is where Isaiah has been waiting for seven hundred years: he was wounded for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his stripes we are healed (Isa 53:5). The word is stripes — the marks left by a lash. Isaiah saw the flagellum before Rome had invented it, and he saw whose it was, and he wrote the pronoun: our.

So keep the two clauses of this verse side by side, because they belong together and the gospel lives in the gap between them. A convicted murderer went home to his own street that afternoon a free man, and never had to explain why, and did nothing whatever to earn it. Down the corridor, the man who had taken his place was being tied to a post. That is not an illustration of the atonement. On that Friday it was the plain municipal record of what happened, and it is the reason the word gospel means news rather than advice.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the governor's headquarters, and they gathered the whole battalion before him. And they stripped him and put a scarlet robe on him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They take him inside, and Matthew notes the numbers: they gathered the whole battalion — the cohort, on paper up to six hundred men, though the detachment on duty would have been smaller. Whatever the exact figure, the point stands. Word has gone round the barracks that there is something worth watching in the courtyard, and the off-duty soldiers come out to see.

This is the part of the Passion that is easiest to skip and hardest to explain. It serves no judicial purpose whatever. The verdict is given, the execution detail is forming, and nothing that happens in this courtyard advances the case by a minute. It is done because they felt like it, and because it was funny, and because he could not stop them.

They strip him — the second stripping of the day, and not the last. And then the scarlet robe, which was almost certainly a soldier's own cloak, the faded red military cape that every man in that yard was wearing. Somebody took his off and put it round the prisoner's shoulders, and the joke was that it looked near enough to imperial purple to pass.

That is worth pausing over, because of what it says about the appetite being fed. Boredom in an occupying garrison, a prisoner who will be dead by evening, an afternoon to fill, and a man available who cannot retaliate — and out of those ordinary ingredients comes a piece of cruelty that is entirely gratuitous. Nobody in that courtyard was a monster. They were soldiers with an hour free.

And the deepest irony of the Passion is running underneath the whole scene. Every single element of the mockery is true. The robe is a real coronation robe, on a real King. In a few hours a sign will be nailed over his head naming his title, in three languages, by order of the governor. They are dressing him for a throne while thinking they are dressing him for a laugh, and the only person in the courtyard who knows what is actually being enacted is the man in the cloak.

verseByVerse.quote: and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on his head and put a reed in his right hand. And kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" And they spit on him and took the reed and struck him on the head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crown was not a costume piece. Thorn scrub grows everywhere in that country and the spines on some of it are two or three inches long; somebody went out, cut a handful, twisted it into a circle, and pressed it down. It was the last item needed to complete the outfit.

And of all the things a soldier could have grabbed for a joke, this one reaches back to the third chapter of the Bible. When the ground was cursed for man's sake the sentence was thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you (Gen 3:18). Thorns are the visible signature of a world under judgment — the thing that grows where nothing was planted, in every garden anyone has ever tried to keep. The curse of the ground was gathered into a circle and pushed onto the head of the man who came to carry the curse away, by soldiers who thought they were being witty.

Then the reed in his right hand — a mock sceptre, the hand of authority given a piece of grass. And the kneeling, which is the most extraordinary detail in the scene, because genuflection before a king was a real act with a real form, and they performed it correctly in order to make it ridiculous. Hail, King of the Jews is a parody of Ave, Caesar.

They were rehearsing. One day every knee in heaven and on earth and under the earth will bend at this name, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Phil 2:10-11). The first knees ever bent to the crowned Christ belonged to a Roman execution detail in a barracks yard, and they did it as a joke, and they were not wrong about the posture — only about the reason.

And then the spitting, and the reed taken back out of his hand and used to strike him on the head, which drove the thorns further in. It is worth being clear who is receiving this. The man being spat at by a bored garrison is the one who holds their hearts beating in his hand; a word from him and the courtyard would have been empty and silent. He had told Peter in the garden a few hours earlier that he could ask his Father for twelve legions of angels. The Roman cohort in that yard was one legion's worth of men at the very most, and it was playing games with the one person present who could have ended it, and who had already decided not to.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the robe and put his own clothes on him and led him away to crucify him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The game finishes the way such things do — abruptly, because the shift has started. They take the cloak back. Somebody folds it and returns it to its owner, and the man who was Caesar for ten minutes is put back into his own clothes.

The detail is practical: a condemned man was normally walked to execution in his own clothing so the crowd could see who was being crucified, and the garments came off again at the site. So he is dressed twice and stripped three times in a single morning — once for the scourging, once for the joke, and once at Golgotha. Whatever else the day did to him, it kept taking his clothes.

And then four words that carry the whole distance: led him away to crucify him. Matthew has been building to this since the sixteenth chapter, when Jesus first told them plainly that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things and be killed. He has said it three times. Every time, the disciples argued or misunderstood or fell asleep.

What should be held onto here is that not one step of this walk is being forced on him. He chose it in the garden, out loud, twice, with his face on the ground — not as I will, but as you will. He could have stayed in Galilee. He could have accepted the crowd's crown after the loaves. He could have answered Pilate and walked out. At every junction there was a door standing open and he did not take it.

So the little procession that leaves the praetorium is not a man being swept along by events larger than himself. It is the most deliberate walk in the history of the world, taken by the only person on the road who knew exactly where it ended and exactly why he was going — and the reason he kept walking was that the people he was doing it for could not have walked it themselves.

And keep an eye on the clothes he is wearing out of that gate, because they have four verses left. They were taken from him for the flogging and given back; put on for the walk so the crowd could see who was being executed; and at the top of the hill they will come off for the last time and be divided among the execution party, who will throw dice for the best piece. He walks to Golgotha dressed in the last thing he owns.

verseByVerse.quote: As they went out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name. They compelled this man to carry his cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cyrene was a city in North Africa, in what is now Libya, with a large and long-established Jewish population. Simon has come the best part of a thousand miles for Passover — the pilgrimage of a lifetime for a devout man from the diaspora, saved for and planned. He is walking into the city on the morning of the feast when a soldier picks him out of the crowd.

The word for what happened to him is angareuo, a technical term for the right of requisition: a Roman soldier could compel any provincial to carry his kit for a distance, and the resentment it caused was universal. Matthew's readers knew the word well, and they had met it before in this Gospel — in the Sermon on the Mount, from the mouth of the man now being led up the road: if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two (5:41).

So the sentence Jesus preached about being conscripted is now applied to a stranger, in order to carry the cross Jesus can no longer carry himself. That he could not carry it is itself a piece of evidence about what the scourging had done to him; Roman practice was for the condemned to carry the crossbeam, and they only substituted a bystander when the prisoner was failing and they wanted him alive at the site.

Simon appears in three Gospels and Mark adds a detail he expects his readers to recognise: he is the father of Alexander and Rufus (Mk 15:21), naming two men as though the church already knew them. And when Paul sends greetings to Rome he includes Rufus, chosen in the Lord, also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well (Rom 16:13). It cannot be proved that this is the same family. It is a very natural reading, and if it is right, then the woman who mothered the apostle Paul was married to the man who carried the cross.

Which is worth holding onto, because Simon did not volunteer for any of this. He was seized. Whatever he had planned for that morning was ruined by a soldier's hand on his shoulder, and he walked up the hill under a piece of timber that was not his, for a condemned man he had never met, in front of a crowd, at the worst possible moment. It was, by any ordinary reckoning, a disaster of a day. It is also the only reason anybody has ever heard of him, and it appears to have put his sons in the church and his family in the Scriptures.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to a place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull), they offered him wine to drink, mixed with gall, but when he tasted it, he would not drink it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Golgotha is Aramaic for skull, and Matthew translates it for readers who would not know. The name most likely came from the shape of the outcrop rather than from bones lying about — Jewish burial customs make the second unlikely. It was outside the wall and beside a road, because the entire point of crucifixion was that people should see it on their way past. The writer of Hebrews makes something of that location: he suffered outside the gate, where the bodies of the sin offerings were burned (Heb 13:11-12).

Then the drink. Wine mixed with gall — Mark says myrrh — was a rough narcotic, and Jewish tradition records that the women of Jerusalem provided it to men going to execution as an act of mercy, on the strength of the proverb about giving strong drink to one who is perishing (Prov 31:6). It was the one kindness available on that road, and it was offered by women.

When he tasted it, he would not drink it. Both halves matter. He tasted it, so he knew what it was and what it would do — the refusal is informed. And he refused it, which is the more remarkable given that he had every reason to take it and no one would have thought less of him for it.

The reason is in the garden. Twice that night he had prayed about a cup, and twice he had said that if it could not pass, he would drink it. He was not going to numb the cup he had agreed to drink. And there is a further note, easy to miss: at the table a few hours earlier he had told them he would not drink of the fruit of the vine again until he drank it new with them in his Father's kingdom (26:29). He keeps that too. The next wine offered him is declined.

So the whole of it was borne awake. Everything that follows — six hours on the wood, the mockery, the darkness, the cry — was undergone by a man in full possession of his senses, because he had turned down the only anaesthetic on offer. There is a kind of love that will not take the edge off the thing it has agreed to carry, and this is the only recorded instance of it in the history of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had crucified him, they divided his garments among them by casting lots. Then they sat down and kept watch over him there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had crucified him. Matthew does not describe it. Neither does Mark, Luke, or John. Four writers who were there or knew those who were give the central event of human history a subordinate clause, because their first readers needed no explanation whatever — and a modern reader needs it badly, since almost nothing about the word survives in ordinary speech.

Crucifixion was reserved for slaves, rebels, and the worst class of criminals; Roman law exempted citizens from it. The condemned was stripped naked, part of the humiliation, and fastened to the wood — nailed through the wrists, since the hands alone will not carry a body's weight, with the arms extended and slightly raised, and a nail driven through the feet onto a small block.

The design was engineered for duration. Hanging from outstretched arms makes exhaling possible and inhaling nearly impossible; to take a breath the victim had to push upward against the nail through his feet, lift the body a few inches, fill the lungs, and sag back down. Every breath was bought at that price, and the cycle could go on for hours or days. Death came by asphyxiation, exhaustion, or blood loss. When the Romans wanted to end it quickly — as they would that evening, before the Sabbath (Jn 19:31-32) — they broke the legs, so that the man could no longer push up, and it was over in minutes.

And it was public by design: a naked body at eye level beside a road, for as long as it took. Cicero called it the most cruel and horrifying of punishments and said the very word should be kept far from the ears of Roman citizens. That the apostles went out and preached a crucified Messiah was therefore not merely a theological difficulty but a social obscenity — which is exactly what Paul meant by calling it a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Greeks (1 Cor 1:23). Nobody invents a founder who died this way.

Then, while that is happening above them, the detail sit down and gamble for his clothes. A crucified man's garments were the perquisite of the execution party, and they divide them and throw dice for the last piece. It is written a thousand years earlier, in the psalm he will quote from the cross in a few hours: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots (Ps 22:18). Four soldiers playing a game to pass a slow afternoon are, without the faintest idea of it, performing a line of Scripture.

Then they sat down and kept watch over him there. It is the flattest sentence in the chapter and one of the most terrible. This was a shift. They had done it before and would do it again next week; there was nothing to do now but wait for the man to die, so they sat in the shade with the dice and their lunch. The most significant six hours in the history of the universe were, to the men closest to it, a slow day at work. Some of the greatest things God has ever done have looked, to everyone standing nearby, like nothing much happening.
